articles.title: Capitalizing on Controversy: Humor, Scandal Entrepreneurship, and the Rise of the Far Right
articles.authors: Dick Zijp; giselinde kuipers
articles.abstract: Right-wing public figures, from comedians to politicians, increasingly use humor strategically to provoke scandal. While scandals are typically understood to damage the reputations of norm transgressors, the rise of successful right-wing scandal makers challenges this assumption. In this article, we introduce the concept of ‘scandal entrepreneur’ to theorize the rise of celebrity figures who deliberately create or amplify scandals for personal or political gain. Integrating insights from political scandal research, sociological work on cultural and moral entrepreneurship, and critical humor studies, we develop an innovative approach to scandal that combines dramaturgical and conjunctural analysis. Drawing on a quantitative mapping of Dutch humor scandals between 1990 and 2024 and an in-depth qualitative analysis of two cases, we trace both the steep rise in humor scandals in the early twenty-first century and the increasing professionalization of scandal entrepreneurship, which has turned scandal-making into a profitable business model. Based on our analysis of the Nekschot cartoon scandal (2008) and the VI-Akwasi scandal (2020), we demonstrate that, within the current cultural conjuncture, right-wing actors are best positioned to capitalize on scandals and successfully dramatize social and cultural divides through humor. Our approach offers valuable analytical tools for humor and scandal scholarship and the field of right-wing studies, providing a critical lens through which to examine wider cultural changes.

articles_hidden.title: What research culture is for: a six-dimensional framework co-created to cultivate researcher wellbeing
articles_hidden.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Karel Svadlenka; Yukiko Watanabe; Sano Satoshi; Ayako Y. Murayama; Akane Tezuka; Ataru Igarashi; Norihiro Sadato; Kazuhiro Hayashi
articles_hidden.abstract: Research culture, the soil in which scientific inquiry grows, shapes the quality and sustainability of research, yet remains invisible to science, technology and innovation indicators. Three converging crises signal deteriorating conditions for research: the reproducibility crisis, the productivity paradox, and a global crisis of researcher wellbeing. Reform initiatives have transformed how outputs are assessed, but no validated, internationally comparable framework captures the cultural conditions of research practice. This article reports a six-dimensional research culture framework. The framework was co-created through structured stakeholder dialogue on a principle of equal voice: a workshop of researchers, administrators, funders and policymakers, then an open symposium of approximately 300 participants. It was iteratively refined through domestic and international expert consultation, with a transparent audit trail of what entered at each stage and why. Subjective experience sits at the core, surrounded by social, epistemic, methodological, temporal and evaluative dimensions. Each is operationalised as three items on a common 0–10 scale, in Japanese and English within an instrument pairing internationally standardised wellbeing measures with the Interdependent Happiness Scale, and visualised as a radar chart for team-level dialogue, not institutional ranking. A crosswalk locates the contribution: reform effort concentrates on the evaluative dimension, while the instruments that do measure address only two of the six, the social and the evaluative, treating the other four as symptoms or facets of other constructs, if at all. A nationwide survey planned for fiscal year 2026 provides the first psychometric test, under a design fixed in advance: the six-dimension structure will be compared with rivals in a held-out half of the sample. Grounded in human flourishing theory and aligned with ISO 25554:2024, the framework treats research culture not as a variable to be audited but as a capability to be cultivated.

articles_hidden.title: How has the disciplinary composition and preregistration practice of psychology evolved on the OSF (2020–2025)? A meta-science analysis of the diffusion of preregistration.
articles_hidden.authors: Albie Duffy
articles_hidden.abstract: Preregistration has become one of psychology's most prominent methodological reforms, but its uptake has been characterised at field level, leaving open where within psychology the practice has spread and whether the registrations themselves have changed. This study analysed 47,524 psychology preregistrations carrying a subdiscipline label on the Open Science Framework, created between 2020 and 2025 and retrieved via the public OSF API. Cochran-Armitage trend tests examined change in each subdiscipline's share of the labelled corpus, and a nested regression examined a six-item, text-derived indicator of methodological thoroughness net of document length, registration template, and year. The labelled corpus grew 2.37-fold. All eight subdisciplines predicted a priori to rise showed significant positive trends after false discovery rate correction, and no other subdiscipline did; Clinical Psychology expanded from 9.7% to 18.5% of the labelled field. Social and Cognitive Psychology declined in share while continuing to grow in absolute number. Subdiscipline was associated with registration template (bias-corrected V = .125) and explained incremental variance in the thoroughness indicator after adjustment (ΔR² = .014), with all six rising subdisciplines that survived pooling scoring below the Social Psychology reference. Once disciplinary composition was held constant, no independent temporal trend in thoroughness remained. The composition of psychological preregistration therefore changed substantially across six years while the textual detail of individual registrations did not, indicating that the diffusion of a practice and the development of its content are separable dimensions.

articles.title: From Concept to Classroom: Teachers Implementing Mindfulness-based Interventions
articles.authors: Mary L. Phan; Tyler L Renshaw; Melanie M. Domenech Rodríguez; Maggie Chan; Erik J. Reinbergs; Christopher Liang; Stephanie M. Hernandez; Natascha Meyer-Pérez; Amanda Paur; Ginny Watts
articles.abstract:
Objectives: This study evaluated a collaboratively developed, teacher-implemented mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) targeting teacher stress and coping and students’ prosocial behavior. The study also examined implementation fidelity, social validity, and sustainment.

Methods: Six elementary school teachers in grades 1–3 participated in a single-case multiple-baseline design across participants. Teachers implemented a four-week MBI consisting of daily teacher self-practice and twice-daily classroom mindfulness exercises. Daily measures assessed teacher stress and coping and classroom academic engagement, respectful behavior, and disruptive behavior. Outcomes were evaluated through visual analysis, descriptive statistics, and Non-overlap of All Pairs (NAP) and Improvement Rate Difference (IRD). Fidelity, social validity, and follow-up outcomes through two months post-intervention were also assessed.

Results: Functional relations were not consistently demonstrated across teachers. However, several teachers showed reduced stress and improved coping, while several classrooms showed increased academic engagement and respectful behavior and reduced disruptive behavior. Across outcomes, NAP ranged from .36 to 1.00 and IRD from .28 to 1.00. Teachers reported high social validity, and fidelity was high (self-report: M = 98.33%; observed: M = 93.33%).

Conclusions: Findings support the feasibility and acceptability of brief, teacher-implemented MBIs. Although functional relations were inconsistent, individual patterns suggest potential benefits for teacher coping and classroom behavior. Flexible, context-responsive implementation may support sustained use in schools.

articles.title: The Nature of Phonological Impairments in Dyslexia and Stuttering: Evidence from Phonemic, Semantic, and Design Fluency Tasks
articles.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; James H Smith-Spark; Richard Kirkden
articles.abstract:
Objective: Given that dyslexia and stuttering are defined by phonological processing challenges, we investigated whether these challenges stem from poor, or inefficient access to, phonological representation. This study aimed to dissociate these cognitive mechanisms underlying verbal fluency in adults who stutter (AWS) and dyslexic adults. 
Method: An online, unsupervised sample of 62 AWS, 62 dyslexic adults and 62 neurotypical adults completed a modified, typed version of semantic and phonemic fluency with a mouse-drawn version of design fluency as a nonverbal control. We analyzed switching (shifting between subcategories; proxy for retrieval efficiency) and cluster size (words per subcategory, proxy for representational integrity). 
Results: Controlling for nonverbal IQ and language measures, hierarchical regression showed that dyslexia and stuttering significantly predicted reduced overall phonemic output, whereas semantic and design fluency remained unaffected. Both groups showed reduced switching, though more pronounced in the dyslexia group. Conversely, only stuttering predicted reduced cluster size.
Conclusion: These findings suggest in dyslexia, the access to phonological representations is affected, while it is the representations themselves in stuttering. Given the heterogeneity of these neurodivergent profiles, these challenges are not universal. However, for individuals presenting these specific cognitive signatures, interventions could be tailored toward either retrieval strategies or representational strengthening.

articles.title: COMPREHENSION VALIDATION OF THE REVISED EAWS DANGER SCALE DESCRIPTORS: LESSONS FROM A LARGE-SCALE EUROPEAN END USER SURVEY ON AVALANCHE RISK PERCEPTION
articles.authors: Philip Alexander Ebert; Frank Techel; Matthias Walcher; Benjamin Reuter; Igor Chiambretti; Lorenzo Bertranda; Montse Bacardit Pennaroya; Jaka Ortar; Mark Diggins; Karsten Müller
articles.abstract: The descriptors of the European avalanche danger scale, in use since 1993, are being revised. In June 2025 EAWS forecasters agreed on a new provisional wording and, in doing so, provided its content validation. Because the descriptors are first of all a public communication tool, we ran a comprehension validation: a survey testing whether end users read the wording as forecasters intend. It ran online from 3 February to 8 April 2026 in six languages and retained 17,335 responses after cleaning, of which 15,749 were completed. All wording comparisons were randomised between subjects. We evaluated each proposal against three conditions: correctness (do users recover the order forecasters intend?), simplicity (how easy is the task?), and increase (does the wording convey how much the danger increases from level to level?). For avalanche occurrence the main finding is reassuring: all four wording variants were ranked accurately (83–92% correct), and most differences that reach significance in the pooled data do not survive within individual languages. Only the variant that drops the distribution wording is clearly weaker. On the increase condition the variants do separate. Respondents placed the four statements on a continuous danger scale; wording level 2 as “in some places” rather than “in a few places” moves it closer to level 3 and shrinks the perceived difference between moderate to considerable from 36% to 31% of the distance between levels 1 and 4 (Cohen’s d = 0.39, p < 0.001). For size and impact the wording effect is large: adding size class words (small, medium, large, very large) to the impact wording raised accuracy from 61% to 95% and self-reported ease from 4.7 to 6.1 (Cohen’s d = 1.04). Most of that failure comes from using “bury and kill” at both levels 1 and 2, which makes them hard to tell apart. We also report how users read seven phrases that forecasters already use. For avalanche occurrence, the largest differences are between languages rather than between wordings.

articles.title: Questionable prospective effects between maternal health literacy, psychological empowerment, and health-promoting behaviors among pregnant women: A reanalysis of Chen et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Chen et al. examined temporal relations among maternal health literacy, psychological empowerment, and health-promoting behaviors and interpreted their findings as evidence of reciprocal longitudinal influences. However, significant cross-lagged coefficients do not necessarily demonstrate true prospective effects, as such estimates may arise from methodological and statistical artifacts. Using simulated data constructed to match the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Chen et al., we assessed the stability of the reported findings across several analytically plausible models. The results differed markedly depending on the specification employed. Some models suggested positive longitudinal effects, whereas others indicated negative or non-significant associations. After combining all estimates using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. These findings indicate that the conclusions drawn by Chen et al. should be interpreted with caution and that the reported cross-lagged associations may not reflect genuine prospective influence. In accordance with multiverse analytic principles, researchers should routinely evaluate multiple reasonable model specifications and synthesize evidence across models before drawing substantive conclusions.

articles.title: Pinholes, apertures, monocular stereopsis, and the perils of classroom theorizing:  A response to McIntosh (2025).
articles.authors: Dhanraj Vishwanath
articles.abstract: Monocular stereopsis is a compelling perceptual effect wherein viewing a picture of a 3-dimensional scene with one eye through an aperture generates a perceptual impression of depth similar to binocular stereopsis. Here I provide a critique of a recently published report in the journal i-Perception (McIntosh, 2025) along with some relevant empirical data.  In the report, McIntosh claims to adjudicate on explanations of the monocular-stereopsis effect—and the phenomenology of stereopsis more broadly construed--on the basis of a 15-minute informal test during a classroom lecture break. The author suggests the monocular-aperture effect is best explained by a short 100-year-old description of the phenomenon. I argue that McIntosh’s report demonstrates a lack of understanding of the modern empirical facts and theoretical concepts relevant to the phenomenon, and neglects the demands of conducting an interpretable perceptual test.

articles.title: Brief Summarization Improves Effectiveness of Fact-Checks, whereas a Mental-Imagery-Based Mnemonic Does Not
articles.authors: Lucy Butler; Constantina I. Gile; Toby Prike; Ralph Hertwig; Briony Swire-Thompson; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: Fact-checks reliably reduce belief in misinformation, but their effects diminish over time, partially due to forgetting—this is known as belief regression. Across two experiments, we tested whether memory-enhancing techniques could improve the long-term efficacy of fact-checks. In Experiment 1 (N = 555; one-week delay) we examined a mental-imagery-based mnemonic linking false and true claims to a ‘liar’ and ‘truthteller’, respectively, alongside conditions varying the extent to which active encoding of the fact-check was encouraged. The mnemonic did not improve fact-check memory or reduce belief regression. In contrast, briefly summarizing fact-checks improved memory and sustained belief change relative to a control condition. Experiment 2 (N = 269) replicated the enhanced effectiveness of fact-checks in the summarization condition over a longer delay period (two weeks); however, belief regression did not significantly differ from control. These findings suggest that low-barrier interventions implemented at the time of encoding can improve the effectiveness of fact-checks but may not slow the rate of belief regression. To provide theoretical and practical insight into the drivers of belief regression, future research may benefit from examining the impact of retrieval-based interventions.

articles.title: Instrumentalising gender conspiracy theories: how narratives about gender ideology may both reflect and fuel general institutional distrust
articles.authors: Peter Teličák; Jakub Šrol; Eva Ballova Mikuskova; Magdalena Adamus
articles.abstract: In two cross-sectional and one longitudinal study conducted in Slovakia and Czechia (total N = 2339, 50,7% women; aged between 18 and 89 years), we tested whether gender ideology narratives are linked with conspiratorial thinking - operationalised as either specific conspiracy beliefs or conspiracy mentality - and pinpointed their most pronounced correlates as political ideologies and institutional distrust. The cross-sectional results show that support for gender ideology narratives is associated with conspiratorial thinking and, albeit unrelated to sociodemographic variables, shows systematic associations with institutional distrust and political stances as expressed by either collective narcissism or conservative political orientation. The preregistered Study 3 fine-tunes the findings by revealing some bidirectional temporal patterns at the within-participants level only with institutional distrust. The results point to a mutually reinforcing nexus between the gender ideology narratives and distrust thereby fostering the understanding of the narratives as embedded within a wider context of power challenging conspiracy theories. Finally, the paper offers insights into how–by exploiting and instilling the sense of distrust–gender ideology narratives can be instrumentalised to tilt political preferences towards anti-establishment, non-mainstream parties that present themselves as beacons of traditional values.

articles.title: Dissociating motion adaptation and action expectation effects when viewing another's gaze
articles.authors: Christian Renet; Ronja Löfström; Arvid Guterstam
articles.abstract: Recent publications have reported that brief exposure to static images depicting an agent actively gazing at an object produces a motion adaptation effect congruent with the direction of the gaze, suggesting that encoding of an implied motion in that direction occurs. Three accounts can explain this finding: either the agent’s attentive gaze (attention-motion hypothesis) or an expectation that the agent will perform an action toward the target of gaze (action-expectation hypothesis) is encoded as implied motion, or both. We directly contrasted these hypotheses by replicating the original experiment with one key change: the static image was replaced with one in which the directions of attentive gaze and action expectation were dissociated. A significant motion adaption effect in the agent-to-object direction was detected, which disappeared when the agent was blindfolded. This finding supports the attention-motion hypothesis and rules out action-expectations as an (exclusive) explanation of the previously reported effect.

articles.title: The Utilities of Beauty and Money are Largely Additive
articles.authors: Youjing Luo; Anna Bruns; Laurence T. Maloney; Olivia S. Cheung; Denis G. Pelli
articles.abstract: Beauty is typically excluded from quantitative models of economic value. We use BDM-auction and 2AFC tasks to find instead that the feeling of beauty increases willingness to pay, and its utility combines with that of money in a largely additive way. The contribution of beauty to utility is nearly independent of money’s contribution, with only a small interaction effect. These results show that incorporating beauty as a component of utility can greatly enhance prediction of choice and valuation.

articles.title: Fine-grained variation in caregivers’ /s/ predicts their infants’ /s/ category
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Within the debate on the mechanisms underlying infant perceptual acquisition, one hypothesis proposes that infants’ perception is directly affected by the acoustic implementation of sound categories in the speech they hear. In consonance with this view, the present study shows that individual variation in fine-grained, subphonemic aspects of the acoustic realization of /s/ in caregivers’ speech predicts infants’ discrimination of this sound from the highly similar /S/, suggesting that learning based on acoustic cue distributions may indeed drive natural phonological acquisition.

articles.title: Generics and stereotypes: A cognitive account
articles.authors: Jérémie Lafraire; Adoracion Guzman Garcia
articles.abstract: Generic statements about social categories (e.g., “Women are nurturing”, “Boys don’t cry”) are a pervasive vehicle for expressing stereotypes. Although descriptively framed, they often generate normative expectations about how members of social groups should think, feel, or behave. Drawing on philosophy of language, developmental psychology, and social cognition, this chapter argues that such normativity does not arise from linguistic meaning alone, but from the interaction between generic language and two cognitive mechanisms: psychological essentialism and the inherence heuristic. By highlighting category-level regularities, generics can encourage socially produced patterns to be interpreted as reflecting deep, stable, and inherent properties of groups, thereby making stereotypes appear natural and normatively appropriate. At the same time, these effects are neither inevitable nor uniform: different linguistic framings and explanatory contexts can substantially alter how social generalizations are interpreted. We conclude by reviewing linguistic and explanatory strategies that can constrain essentialist interpretations and help negotiate or counteract stereotypical norms.

articles.title: Toward a Sequencing Framework for Teaching and Using Self- Enactable Behavior Change Techniques: A Conceptual Review and Proposed Approach
articles.authors: Alexandre Mazéas; Nikos Ntoumanis
articles.abstract:
Objective: Self-enactable behavior change techniques (BCTs) may help individuals initiate and sustain health behavior change. However, existing taxonomies provide limited guidance on how such techniques should be selected, taught, combined, and sequenced over time. This perspective aimed to review previous approaches and to develop a conceptual framework for organizing and sequencing self-enactable BCTs for intervention design and participant learning.
Methods: A critical conceptual review was conducted to identify published approaches to BCT grouping, temporal organization, prerequisites, and stage-specific sequencing. Literature identified through four databases was synthesized alongside the compendium of self-enactable BCTs to inform a five-step framework-development process. 
Results: The review showed that existing taxonomies and sequencing approaches provide useful classifications but limited guidance for progressive teaching and self-enactment. To address this gap, we proposed a framework comprising 108 self-enactable BCTs organized into nine clusters and 27 groups. We mapped prerequisite relations, classified techniques by their predominant prospective or reactive function, and sequenced their groups across the Model of Action Phases. 
Conclusion: Our framework provides a theory-informed structure for teaching and applying self-enactable BCTs. It is intended to guide intervention design and generate testable hypotheses about technique sequencing that need to be empirically explored in future studies.

articles.title: Affect, Social Support and Gratitude among Ukrainian University Students in the Acute Phase of War, November 2022
articles.authors: Volodymyr Evheniiovych Momot
articles.abstract:
Research on the psychological impact of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has been dominated by distress instruments and by data collected retrospectively or through online snowball recruitment. Comparatively little is known about the resource side of the acute phase: what remained intact, and in what form.

This study reports data collected in a single session on 15 November 2022, three weeks after the first sustained Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, from second- and fourth-year students at a private university in Dnipro (aged approximately 17-18 and 19-20). Four instruments were administered consecutively in a 20-minute window following a deliberately non-reassuring reflective framing: SoZU-14 (N = 146), PANAS (N = 103), GQ-6 (N = 117) and a 15-item proactive-position scale (N = 114).

The affective profile did not correspond to acute distress. Negative affect was indistinguishable from the published normative mean (18.0 vs. 17.4, d = +0.10, p = .43), whereas positive affect was reduced (30.7 vs 33.3, d = -0.36, p = .001). Within negative affect the elevated items were those of chronic friction, while acute-threat and self-blame items sat at the floor (scared 1.40, ashamed 1.37); within positive affect, engagement was preserved (interested 3.47, active 3.44) while peak states were suppressed (proud 2.83, excited 2.47).

The relational instruments showed a parallel asymmetry along an unexpected line. SoZU-14 items did not separate close from distant ties; they separated the presence of supportive relationships (4.39) from turning to them for help (3.83; dz = 1.00, 82% of respondents). The three items shared with the F-SozU K-3, near-identical in a German representative sample (4.29, 4.30, 4.21; range 0.09), spread across 0.63 here, with the presence item above the German mean and both mobilisation items below it, while the three-item total matched the German norm (12.27 vs 12.33). Support was normal in volume and atypical in structure. Gratitude fell below undergraduate norms (d = -0.52 to -0.62) and attached to life in general (6.27) rather than to a wide range of people (4.80; dz = 0.90). The three comparisons form a gradient ordered by how much outward investment each construct presupposes. No cohort difference appeared on any instrument.

The dissociation was graded by resource state: the presence-mobilisation gap fell to near the German value in the highest quintile of support and followed an inverted-U, peaking not among the most deprived but among those with substantial close ties and limited overall resource (quadratic R2 = .205 vs .055 linear, p < .0001; replicated on gratitude).

We interpret this configuration as resource conservation rather than depletion: the stock of affective and relational resources is intact while its expenditure is restricted. Conservation of Resources theory accounts for rationing of a preserved stock; Socioemotional Selectivity Theory for which states and network layers were retained.

articles.title: LLMs reveal how ideology and time shape intuitive vs. deliberative rhetoric across 31 European parliaments
articles.authors: Julian Kauk; Edda Humprecht; Stefan R. Schweinberger; Tobias Rothmund
articles.abstract: Democratic deliberation depends on how political actors balance intuitive, affective appeals with analytically structured argumentation. Yet how ideology and time shape this rhetorical balance across diverse national contexts at large scale remains poorly understood. Informed by dual-process theories, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to analyze 3.3 million speeches from 31 European parliaments (2004–2023), quantifying two fundamental rhetorical styles: intuitive rhetoric, characterized by affective and heuristic expression, and deliberative rhetoric, characterized by analytical and evidence-oriented language. Across parliaments, ideological position is systematically associated with rhetorical style through curvilinear relationships. Intuitive rhetoric increases toward both ideological extremes, whereas deliberative rhetoric peaks near the political center and declines toward the fringes, forming a robust ideological horseshoe across institutional contexts. Temporal dynamics further document a shift toward greater reliance on intuitive rhetoric, accompanied by a modest decline in deliberative rhetoric, while the curvilinear ideological structuring of rhetorical styles persists throughout. These trends are consistent with a gradual adaptation to attention-driven communication environments, which structurally favor intuitive and affective expression over analytical depth. Together, our findings map the ideological and temporal contours of deliberative erosion in European democracies, with implications for institutional design and the resilience of democratic discourse.

articles.title: Conversing with a disagreeing LLM improves people’s inaccurate predictions
articles.authors: Emir Efendic; Philippe van de Calseyde
articles.abstract: Accurately predicting the outcome of future events improves decisions in domains ranging from health to finance, yet prediction errors are common. One reliable way to improve accuracy is to engage with disagreeing views through dialogue, which can reveal weak assumptions and facilitate belief revision. However, people often avoid disagreeing exchanges because they are socially and emotionally costly or inconvenient to seek out. Here, we examine whether a disagreeing large language model (LLM) can provide the benefits of disagreement while sidestepping these interpersonal barriers. Across two experiments (total N = 807 adults making 4,564 predictions; Experiment 2 was incentivized and preregistered), participants: i) predicted the likelihood of various events, ii) discussed each prediction with an LLM by articulating their reasoning, and iii) submitted final predictions. Crucially, we manipulated the LLM’s stance during these discussions: it responded either supportively (agreeing) or critically (disagreeing) to participants’ reasoning. The results showed that, when initial predictions were erroneous, conversing with a disagreeing LLM produced more accurate final predictions than conversing with a supportive one. This advantage was primarily driven by directionally correct revisions, with participants shifting their final predictions more often toward the realized outcome. However, interacting with an LLM was not uniformly beneficial as it decreased accuracy when initial predictions were already accurate. These findings underscore the value of designing LLMs that challenge rather than affirm users’ views and opinions, while highlighting the importance of tailoring their responses to the expected accuracy of initial predictions.

articles.title: Not All Eye Occlusions Are Equal: Expressive and Mechanical Eye Occlusion Differentially Shape Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracked Visual Attention
articles.authors: Daniel Granja; Nicolas Burra
articles.abstract: Emotion recognition from facial expressions is commonly assumed to depend on the visibility of diagnostic features, particularly the eyes. Accordingly, eye occlusion is often treated as a unitary manipulation, under the assumption that comparable informational loss yields equivalent perceptual consequences. The present study challenges this assumption by testing whether expressive (closed eyes) and mechanical (sunglasses) forms of eye occlusion differentially affect emotion recognition and visual attention. In a preregistered within-subjects experiment combining multidimensional emotion ratings with eye-tracking, participants judged emotional and neutral faces presented with open eyes, closed eyes, or sunglasses. The results revealed a critical dissociation: closed eyes reduced emotion recognition more strongly than sunglasses, yet elicited longer fixation durations on the eye region. Notably, fearful faces with closed eyes were associated with increased pleasure ratings, indicating a reinterpretation of the expression rather than simple signal loss. This fixation pattern rules out attentional withdrawal as an explanation for reduced recognition, as participants attended more, rather than less, to closed eyes. Together, these findings demonstrate that eye occlusion alters emotion recognition through interacting perceptual and interpretive processes. Distinguishing between expressive and mechanical eye occlusion provides a refined framework for understanding how reduced eye visibility shapes social perception.

articles.title: Validating LLMs as Coders of Cultural Constructs: a Large-Scale Test of Minimally Counterintuitiveness using Pokémon
articles.authors: Masaki Suyama; Yo Nakawake
articles.abstract: Minimally counterintuitiveness (MCI) theory predicts that concepts violating a small number of intuitive ontological expectations (1--2 violations) are transmitted more successfully than either fully intuitive concepts or maximally counterintuitive (3+ violations) ones. Testing this inverted-U prediction at scale has been limited by the cost of human content coding. We evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as valid, scalable coders of MCI violations, and use a validated pipeline to re-test the inverted-U prediction on a substantially larger sample than prior work. In Study 1, zero-shot coding by two LLMs (Claude and Gemini) against a human-coded baseline showed only moderate agreement driven by systematic over-attribution of violations. In Study 2, a leave-one-out few-shot calibration procedure -- coding each item zero-shot while supplying the other human-coded items as in-context examples -- raised agreement to nearly double specificity while preserving sensitivity. In Study 3, we applied the calibrated pipeline to Generation 2+ Pok\'{e}mon and merged the result with an independent popularity ranking to test the inverted-U prediction. The predicted curvature became significant, with the fitted parabola's vertex at MCI score 2.04, overlapping theory's predicted optimum. Together these studies show that a modest human-coded seed set can calibrate an LLM coder well enough to test a classic cultural-transmission theory at a scale far beyond what human coding alone permits.

articles.title: Visual hemifield dominance during interocular conflict and why it matters
articles.authors: Chris Paffen; David Alais; Andre Sahakian
articles.abstract: Due to the eyes being separated about six centimeters horizontally, the visual system is often confronted with non-overlapping visual input, especially in the visual periphery. Apart from supporting stereovision, non-overlapping – conflicting – visual input can potentially hinder perception of distant, fixated objects of interest. Here we review, on first sight conflicting, studies on interocular conflict in the visual periphery that reported either nasal or temporal visual field preferences during interocular competition. While these studies interpreted hemifield preferences mainly in terms of neuro-anatomical aspects of the visual system, we here argue that they have a functional goal: to suppress information that hinders perception of distant fixated objects of interest. Optimizing hemifield preferences towards this goal leads to a temporal visual field preference at around fixation, a nasal visual field preference in the near periphery, and a temporal visual advantage in the far periphery. Our functional account of hemifield preference during interocular competition thereby reconciles inconsistencies in the literature by analyzing at what eccentricities the interocular conflict in the studies was evoked. Finally, our proposal once more shows that interocular conflict in general, as well as binocular rivalry specifically, are not merely a laboratory curiosity.

articles.title: Affective benefits of daily life activity and experiential diversity are associated with catecholamine systems across the adult life span
articles.authors: Jennifer Lee Crawford; Johanna Matulonis; Mariah Lewis; Hsiang-Yu Chen; Jacob M. Hooker; Heidi I. L. Jacobs; Aaron S Heller; Anne S. Berry
articles.abstract: Engaging in varied behaviors promotes well-being in both humans and non-human animals. The current study tested whether the diversity of daily life activities and experiences are associated with affect and cognition across adulthood. Additional analyses explored the role of the catecholamine systems in sustaining the benefits of daily life diversity. Participants (N=184) ages 18-87 completed three weeks of daily life sampling that included repeated measurements of activities, affect, and geolocation. In a subset of these participants, we used MRI (N=72) and PET (N=35) to measure catecholamine systems. Both activity and experiential diversity were independently associated with affect, but not cognition. Interestingly, the coupling between affect and activity diversity was related to the dopaminergic system, whereas the coupling between affect and experiential diversity was associated with the noradrenergic system. These findings suggest that catecholamine systems play complementary roles in supporting the affective benefits of activity and experiential diversity across adulthood.

articles.title: Knowledge in the Post-Truth Era: The Relations of Established Personality Traits, Exclusionary Authoritarian Worldviews, and Planetary Health Knowledge
articles.authors: Franziska Rees; Oliver Wilhelm
articles.abstract:
Fact knowledge accumulates throughout life and its acquisition is determined by fluid 
intelligence, personality traits, domain-specific interests, and education. Research on 
misinformation and cultural cognition suggests that worldviews influence how individuals 
select and evaluate information, but their contribution to individual differences in factual 
knowledge remains unclear. We investigate whether ideological worldviews explain 
individual differences in Planetary Health Knowledge (PHK), beyond formal education and 
broad personality traits. A sample of 878 U.S. adults completed a 14-item PHK test, reported 
educational attainment, and answered a 76-item personality inventory and various measures 
of ideological worldviews, including right-wing-authoritarianism, conspiracy beliefs, and 
climate change skepticism. The strongest worldview correlates of PHK were combined into a 
factor for Exclusionary Authoritarian Ideology (EAI). In latent regression models, education, 
personality, and EAI jointly explained up to 44% of the variance in PHK. EAI was the 
strongest predictor for PHK, incrementally explaining up to 27%. Openness to experience was 
positively associated with PHK, whereas dark personality showed a weak-to-moderate 
negative association. These findings suggest that a general ideological factor captures a 
substantial share of factual knowledge about contemporary global issues. Unlike other 
knowledge areas, PHK is determined by ideological worldviews—which should be 
considered in political controversies and educational interventions.

articles.title: The structure and correlates of beliefs about mental state intensity dynamics
articles.authors: Landry S Bulls; Mark Allen Thornton
articles.abstract: The intensity of mental states varies over time. Within a given instance of a cognitive or emotional state, the strength of that state’s hold on the mind ebbs and flows. Although different instances of the same state will exhibit different temporal dynamics, certain states are associated with certain dynamics. For example, surprise tends to arise sharply, whereas tiredness generally accumulates gradually over time. This paper investigates the structure and correlates of people’s beliefs about these mental state dynamics. We measure these beliefs using a freeform drawing task in an online sample (Sample 1; N = 457), and preregistered replication sample (Sample 2; N = 1435). We observe that people attribute consistent, differentiable intensity dynamics to a wide range of mental states. These beliefs are optimally characterized by a replicable 3-dimensional structure. We go on to examine the correlates of these beliefs about intra-state dynamics (Study 2). We find that they are associated with variability in mental state similarity judgements, transition probability ratings, and natural language use. Together these findings show that people hold robust, structured beliefs about mental state dynamics, and that these beliefs are reflected in other facets of mental state understanding.

articles.title: Self-attributed success gates higher-order updating after stroke: a three-layer comparator model
articles.authors: SHU MORIOKA
articles.abstract: Stroke rehabilitation cannot be fully explained by impairment severity alone and presents three dissociations: patients who can move a paretic limb but do not use it (learned nonuse); patients with mild motor paresis who nevertheless walk slowly; and patients with unilateral spatial neglect whose recovery plateaus despite preserved compensatory capacity. We hypothesize that these dissociations reflect a shared problem in cross-layer updating. We model the self as three hierarchically coupled comparators operating over distinct temporal scales: a sensorimotor comparator (the meter), which integrates predicted and actual sensory feedback within a millisecond-scale window and provides evidence for the feeling of agency; an intention–outcome comparator (the judge), which integrates action–outcome evidence over seconds and supports judgment of agency; and a narrative-self comparator (the author), which represents a months-to-years biographical horizon. Precision-weighted prediction error provides a common currency across layers, with social input operating at each layer, from joint action to social support. The model proposes that error-based adaptation occurs within layers, whereas recovery-supporting cross-layer revision is gated by self-attribution and personal meaning. Accordingly, revision of the generative models that support recovery requires success to be attributed to the self at the intention–outcome level and integrated as meaningful at the narrative level. This update rule frames learned nonuse as hypothesized under-crediting of self-generated success, slow walking despite mild paresis as hypothesized precision misallocation, and the neglect plateau as a hypothesis-generating extension involving narrative-level updating. We derive layer-specific rehabilitation principles, including perceptual learning, agency-amplifying technology, and narrative goal-setting mapped onto the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), and state falsifiable predictions. The model complements the philosophical framework of narrative embodiment by specifying computational processes that link embodied and narrative selves and may become dissociated after stroke.

articles.title: My Personality—Wrapped: Protocol for a Measurement-Burst Design Study to Investigate the Development and Dynamics of Individual Differences Across Time
articles.authors: Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Michael Dominik Krämer; Nicholas Poh-Jie Tan; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: People and their environments continuously shape one another across time. Understanding these person-environment transactions is essential for describing, predicting, and explaining the dynamics and development of individual differences. Yet, progress on this has been constrained by two common limitations: study designs driven by practical rather than theoretical considerations and neglecting how person-environment processes unfold across multiple timescales. To address these limitations, we present the rationale and design of the My Personality—Wrapped (MPW) Study, a 1-year-long measurement-burst study designed to investigate how individual differences in personality, well-being, attitudes, social and interpersonal behaviors, and health develop across multiple timescales and fluctuate alongside environmental influences. Participants complete baseline (T0) and post-study (T6) assessment batteries, five bimonthly surveys (T1–T5), and 15 pseudorandomly scheduled 1-week bursts comprising mobile sensing, experience sampling, daily, and weekly surveys. This intensive, multi-method study provides comprehensive cross-timescale data on psychological constructs and contextual experiences over 1 year. The MPW Study is designed to advance the field’s understanding of temporal dynamics underlying individual differences by disentangling within-person processes from between-person differences, facilitating theory development and testing of multi-timescale person-environment transactions, and informing future theory-driven research on the dynamics of personality and well-being, social and health processes, and life disruptions.

articles.title: Sleep and Routine Difficulties Related to Emergent Indicators of Autism in the First Year
articles.authors: Italia N. Camillone; Erin M. Andres; Cynthia Loncar; Casey A. Cragin; Barry M. Lester; Melissa A Clark; Stephen J. Sheinkopf
articles.abstract: Establishing healthy daily routines, including sleep, is a common area of challenge for children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD), but the development of these issues in infancy is not well understood. This longitudinal general-population birth cohort study examined 1150 infants (569 females; 782 White, non-Hispanic). Infants were categorized into three groups based on presence or absence of sleep difficulties at 9 and 12 months of age: Persistent Problems, Inconsistent Problems, or No Problems, based on maternal report on the Survey of Well-being of Young Children-Baby Pediatric Symptom Checklist (SWYC-BPSC). Parent report on the First Year Inventory-Lite (FYI-Lite, version 3.1b) measured emerging indicators of autism at 12 months and was compared across the three sleep difficulty groups. Controlling for infant sex, maternal education, and racial and ethnic minority status, infants with persistent sleep difficulties at 9 and 12 months had significantly higher scores on the FYI-Lite than infants with no sleep difficulties (p’s < .001). Persistent difficulties with sleep in infants were related to more autism-related social communication and sensory regulatory difficulties at 12 months of age. These findings suggest that difficulties regulating and establishing daily routines, including sleep, may emerge prior to formal autism diagnosis. These findings point to the potential value of combining autism screening tools with general pediatric surveillance to capture parental concerns related to problems that often co-occur with autism.

articles.title: ‘For Your Brain’: Neural connectivity tracks perceived personalization success of the TikTok algorithm
articles.authors: Anthony G Vaccaro; Elizabeth Escalante; Kaitlyn Burnell; Mitchell J Prinstein; Eva H. Telzer
articles.abstract: Personalized recommender algorithms are among the most influential design features of modern digital platforms. Yet, most neuroscience research on social media relies on controlled stimuli sets, or associating behaviors with general neuroimaging tasks; these methods cannot capture the dynamic process of how the brain responds to feeds that learn user preferences over time. To address this gap, we used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to develop a highly naturalistic paradigm where 72 young adults scrolled on the For You page of a brand new TikTok account for 35 minutes while neural connectivity was measured.Participants reported that content was signifi cantly more personally relevant at the end than at the beginning of scrolling, and durations of felt boredom significantly decreased. Despite all participants encountering unique content and scrolling at their own pace, neural connectivity of prefrontal and temporal regions tracked the emergence of perceived personalization, and these trajectories varied by problematic social media use. These findings suggest that the dynamic neural changes as personalization occur can give insights into problematic social media use tendencies, and highlight the feasibility and value of highly ecologically valid paradigms in understanding digital media use.

articles.title: How Task Demands Shape Reading Behavior: Evidence from Sentence Processing Experiments
articles.authors: Jan Chromý; Markéta Ceháková; Radim Lacina; Jakub Dotlacil
articles.abstract:
Post-reading tasks are a common component of sentence-processing experiments, but their influence on online reading behavior is not fully understood. In the present study, we investigated how different post-sentential tasks affect processing in the word-by-word moving-window self-paced reading paradigm. Three experiments used identical Czech stimuli set but differed in the task administered after each sentence: yes/no comprehension questions, open-ended recall questions, or naturalness judgments. The materials included six item types: garden-path sentences, plausible vs. implausible sentences, grammatical vs. ungrammatical sentences, sentences containing gender interference, sentences comprising generic masculine ambiguity, and sentences with differences in information structure. Across all experiments, we analyzed reaction times in theoretically relevant sentence regions as well as responses in the post-reading task.

The results showed clear effects of task type on overall reading behavior. Participants expecting recall questions read more slowly than participants answering yes/no questions, whereas participants making naturalness judgments read fastest. Despite these differences in overall reading speed, several well-established processing effects proved remarkably stable across tasks. Garden-path, plausibility, and grammaticality manipulations produced similar processing costs in critical and spillover regions regardless of the anticipated post-reading task. In contrast, the strongest task-related differences emerged in sentence-final wrap-up regions. For several item types, naturalness judgments produced patterns that differed substantially from those observed in comprehension-based tasks, including reversals of difficulty effects.

These findings suggest that readers adapt their reading strategy to the demands of the expected task. At the same time, established online processing effects appear relatively robust across different post-reading tasks. More generally, the results indicate that post-reading tasks are an important part of the experimental context and can influence reading behavior in systematic ways.

articles.title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-being on Instagram
articles.authors: Gregory John Depow; Christopher Oveis; Emily Zohar; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: Most of the global population spends significant time browsing social media making it critical to understand how to improve experiences online to support well-being. Here, we test whether a brief intervention training individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. In an ecological momentary intervention, we trained half our sample (N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative posts. Using experience sampling (Nobs. = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online—boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing, and compassion for negative emotions—while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons, and personal distress. When participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media.

articles.title: Organization-level Inclusion Signals: Positive Effects for Both LGBT and non-LGBT Employees
articles.authors: Alexandra Figueroa; Sarah Lian Jensen; Jesse Graham
articles.abstract: This work examines organizational-level inclusion signals and their subsequent effects on employees. Answering the call for more research on concealable stigmatized identities, we consider the effect of such organization-level inclusion signals for sexual and gender minorities (lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender employees) while also considering the effect on non-target employees. In a time-lagged observational study (N = 1,165 ), archival data (N = 229), and a randomized experiment (N = 380), we show that organizational-level inclusion efforts lead to more positive perception of the organization’s psychological climate for sexual and gender minorities, closing the psychological safety gap between non-LGBT and LGBT employees.. Notably, these intentional inclusion efforts also benefit non-LGBT employees, which contradicts recent theoretical assertions that intentional inclusion can harm majority groups, or that organizational inclusion is a zero-sum game.These signals shaped positive behavioral intentions for all employees, leading to non-LGBT employees engaging in more individual ally work, and LGBT employees feeling more free to share their identities. Unexpectedly, inclusion signals even made non-LGBT employees less likely to conceal intimidating parts of their identity (e.g. religion, parental status) as well. In sum, we show that such signaling improves psychological safety for all employees, reducing or eliminating the deficit between target and non-target employees while also encouraging value-aligned positive behaviors.

articles.title: Not Everyone Slows Down After a Mistake: Individual Differences in Post-Error Slowing
articles.authors: Sven Lesche; Carla Michel; Kathrin Sadus; Wiebke Bernhardine Hemming; Dirk Hagemann
articles.abstract:
Does everybody slow down after an error? Across 34 behavioral datasets comprising more than 4,000 participants, we found that some participants reliably do not. While most participants exhibited post-error slowing, a subset reliably showed post-error speeding, often accompanied by reduced accuracy. Bayesian model comparisons consistently favored specifications that allowed for post-error speeding, providing clear evidence for individual differences in the direction of post-error behavior even among participants exposed to the same experimental conditions. 

Additionally, heterogeneity extended beyond response times to post-error accuracy adjustments. Whereas some participants exhibited patterns consistent with adaptive control, characterized by more accurate responding following errors, others showed maladaptive adjustments marked by reduced accuracy. Together, these results suggest that current group-level theories of post-error behavior are incomplete and must be expanded to account not only for posterror speeding, but also for individual differences in the direction of post-error accuracy changes. Rather than reflecting a single underlying mechanism, our findings are more consistent with multiple cognitive, motivational, and affective processes that are jointly engaged following errors. We propose that these processes are present across individuals but vary in their relative contribution, leading to systematic differences in observed behavior, including whether individuals show post-error slowing or speeding.

articles.title: Transdiagnostic factors differentially shape choices and reaction times in social evaluative learning
articles.authors: Aamir Sohail; Aleksandra Magda; Muna Said; Laura Phillips; Yifei Lu; Georgina Reynolds; Alice Comer-Fenn; Jessie Russell; Huafeng Lu; Tally Sims
articles.abstract:
Background
Learning from feedback provided by others is important for navigating complex social environments. Aberrant processing of such social feedback is implicated in the psychopathology of several mental health disorders including social anxiety and depression. Recent psychiatric research increasingly adopts transdiagnostic approaches that examine mechanisms and constructs cutting across traditional diagnostic categories. 

Methods
Here, we applied reinforcement learning models together with transdiagnostic measures of psychopathology to formally assess social evaluation learning. Human participants (n = 193) completed the Social Evaluation Learning Task, learning whether computer personas ‘liked,’ ‘disliked,’ or were ‘neutral’ toward them. Participants also completed six questionnaires assessing socially relevant psychiatric traits. 

Results
Computational modeling revealed that a model with separate learning parameters for positive and negative feedback best accounted for the learning behavior. Exploratory factor analysis identified three transdiagnostic factors. A factor reflecting social avoidance predicted enhanced learning from negative feedback and a reduced positive learning bias. Socially avoidant individuals with heightened negative learning rates additionally showed faster reaction times specifically in positive social contexts. A second factor linking with emotional insensitivity for others predicted a lower choice accuracy in both positively and negatively valanced conditions and was associated with faster reaction times overall. No significant associations emerged for a third factor reflecting depressive and mood-related symptoms. 

Conclusions
These results demonstrate how transdiagnostic trait dimensions shape social learning mechanisms through specific behavioral and computational processes.

articles.title: How attentional states shape interpersonal physiological synchrony: current evidence and a mechanistic model
articles.authors: Sarah Boukarras; Giorgia Mason; Federico Rossano; Tiago Bortolini; Vanessa Era; Salvatore Maria Aglioti
articles.abstract: Interpersonal physiological synchrony (IPS), the temporal alignment of autonomic signals across individuals, has been documented across a wide range of contexts, both during reciprocal social interactions—here referred to as reciprocal IPS (R-IPS)—and when individuals process a common dynamic stimulus, termed stimulus-based IPS (S-IPS). Moment-to-moment fluctuations in autonomic activity reflect not only emotional processes but also cognitive functions, including attentional states. Consistent with this view, studies on S-IPS have shown that physiological synchrony is systematically shaped by attention and engagement. By contrast, although attentional constructs are frequently invoked to explain R-IPS findings, the empirical evidence supporting this relationship and the mechanisms linking attention to synchrony remain unclear. In this article, we first review studies that have assessed or manipulated attention and related constructs such as engagement and social monitoring in both S-IPS and R-IPS contexts. We find that direct evidence for the role of attentional states in reciprocal interactions remains surprisingly sparse, despite their widespread use as explanatory constructs. To address this gap, we propose a mechanistic framework grounded in the intimate relationship between cognition, attention, and autonomic activity, and in the distinction between externally and internally directed attention. Specifically, we argue that IPS is driven by attentional alignment: when individuals attend to common or reciprocally coupled streams of information, their autonomic activity becomes shaped by shared dynamics and consequently synchronized. Conversely, shifts toward internally generated contents disengage autonomic activity from the interaction and increase the influence of idiosyncratic internal dynamics, thereby attenuating synchrony. By integrating findings from psychophysiology, cognitive neuroscience, and social interaction research, the proposed framework provides a biologically plausible account of interpersonal physiological synchrony and generates a series of experimentally testable predictions.

articles.title: Elected by the face? Facial impressions of honesty and competence made under suboptimal conditions predict voting intentions
articles.authors: Antonio Olivera-LaRosa; Guido Corradi; Sergio Barbosa; Sissy Delgado-Pacheco; William Jimenez-Leal; Gonzalo Luna-Cortes; Javier Villacampa; Jaume Rosselló
articles.abstract: Rapid judgments based on political candidates' facial features often predict electoral outcomes. Building on this, we explored how facial impressions of honesty and competence—formed under suboptimal processing conditions—predict voting intentions for actual political candidates. In this study, 484 participants (Colombians: 199; Peruvians: 285; male: 30.2%) were exposed to candidate faces from Colombia and Peru under time constraints (33 ms or 100 ms). Participants rated these faces on honesty and competence and subsequently indicated their likelihood of voting for each candidate. Our findings demonstrate that these rapid facial impressions consistently predict voting intentions regardless of candidate familiarity, evaluative dimension, or exposure duration. Specifically, both honesty and competence impressions were formed with as little as 33 ms of exposure and significantly predicted voting preferences. By utilizing real candidate photographs, this study confirms that rapid facial impressions align with electoral preferences in naturalistic settings. These results demonstrate that electoral choices are anchored in early, heuristic-driven processing.

articles.title: From Research Assistant to Surrogate Supervisor: A Qualitative Study Exploring PGR Students’ Diverse Uses of Generative AI
articles.authors: Gaurav Saxena; Aisling Tierney; Hannah Grist; Ros O’Leary; Amy Palmer
articles.abstract: Research on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has expanded exponentially in recent years. However, research examining postgraduate research (PGR) students remains limited. In response to this gap, the present study explores how PGR students negotiate the opportunities and challenges associated with integrating GenAI into their research, with particular attention to how supervisory practices and institutional guidance shape their use of these technologies. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 15 PGR students across three faculties at a UK Russell Group institution. Using reflexive thematic analysis, four themes were generated: (a) Negotiating Acceptable Use of GenAI examines the diverse ways in which PGR students use, or choose not to use, GenAI to support their research; (b) Agency, Authenticity, and Resistance explores how the growing integration of GenAI affects PGR students’ sense of agency and perceptions of authenticity in their research; (c) (Resisting) GenAI as Surrogate Supervisor examines PGR students’ perspectives on using, or being expected to use, GenAI to support their research in place of their supervisors; and (d) Navigating GenAI Use with the University captures students’ views on how institutions can support them in understanding the productive, responsible, and acceptable use of GenAI. Drawing on these findings, the study proposes recommendations for institutions to support PGR students in using GenAI responsibly and effectively.

articles.title: Practice elements of effective digital media interventions for youth: A distillation and matching approach
articles.authors: I. Chaplinska; Peter Nikken; Jertberg Robert M; Hilde Brons; Smixioti Efthymia; H.M. Koning Ina; Yvette Edelaar; Carlo Schuengel
articles.abstract: Digital media interventions for youth pursue diverse goals, including media literacy, online safety, cyberbullying prevention, critical information evaluation, and digital participation. They may nonetheless share practice elements – discrete, operationally defined units of action – that recur across interventions effective for particular targets, groups, and contexts. This study applied the Distillation and Matching Model to 91 nominally effective digital media intervention records drawn from a scoping-review database. Intervention content was coded first with predefined elements from youth psychosocial interventions and then inductively to capture digital-media-specific practice elements. Interventions were classified as risk-oriented, opportunity-oriented, or mixed, and element profiles were compared across target-population and implementation characteristics using intraclass correlation coefficients. Seventeen predefined and 15 digital-media-specific elements exceeded the preregistered frequency threshold. Among predefined elements, Psychoeducation (child), Insight Building, Accessibility Promotion, Support Networking, and Talent / Skill Building were most frequent. Among digital-media-specific elements, Content creation and Critical media analysis predominated, followed by Source evaluation, Digital media education, Search training, Cyber safety training, and Regulating digital media use. Participant age group differentiated profiles most strongly: middle childhood and adolescence, the groups with enough records for stable comparison, were organised around content creation and critical media analysis, whereas early childhood (accessibility and support) and young adults (heterogeneous profiles) could be characterised only descriptively. Opportunity-oriented interventions centred on content creation and mixed interventions on critical media analysis, whereas risk-oriented interventions showed more dispersed profiles. These configurations were not fixed but varied with the developmental stage of the audience and with the duration and orientation of the intervention, while delivery mode differentiated profiles least. The study contributes a taxonomy of digital-media-specific practice elements and a transferable vocabulary for designing and comparing interventions, while underscoring that the population and implementation characteristics needed to match elements to contexts remain too often unreported.

articles.title: Broadening the Recipe to Strengthen Democracy
articles.authors: Gijs Schumacher; Jakob Kasper; Mariken Anna Catharina Geertruida van der Velden; Max Zaslove; Matthijs Rooduijn; Bert N. Bakker
articles.abstract: Deep concerns about the ability of democracies to cope with polarization, political violence, and anti-democratic attitudes have motivated social scientists to develop interventions that strengthen democracy. The emerging evidence base has impact on policy globally but is predominantly based on American findings. To strengthen democracies, we need a broader evidence base. To this end, we conducted an intervention tournament (14 interventions, 23,146 participants) in a very different democracy – the Netherlands. Some successful interventions in the US replicate, with others failing to replicate. We identify a newly constructed narrative-based intervention as the most successful in strengthening democracy. By developing a theoretical framework to compare interventions and innovations in our research design we lay the groundwork for a global intervention tournament.

articles.title: Affective Reactivity and Approach-Avoidance Behavior in Daily Life: Insights from Vignettes and Ambulatory Assessment Data
articles.authors: Joana Christine Thiel; Daniel Powell; Andreas B. Neubauer
articles.abstract: The present study examined whether individual differences in affective stress reactivity are associated with stressor avoidance (intentions) in everyday life. We distinguished perceived affective reactivity, defined as participants’ self-estimated tendency to respond affectively to stressors, and experienced affective reactivity, operationalized as the within-person association between momentary stressor occurrence and negative affect. The multimethod preregistered study included 200 healthy participants. At baseline, we applied the novel Perceived Affective Reactivity Scale (PARS) alongside a vignette study capturing stressor avoidance intention in five everyday life scenarios varying in stressor intensity and benefit. In the following two-week ambulatory assessment, we assessed experienced affective reactivity using six momentary assessments per day and stressor avoidance behavior in the evening. Perceived affective reactivity was not associated with avoidance intention assessed with either method. In contrast, experienced affective reactivity was positively associated with both the frequency of stressor avoidance during the same assessment period and avoidance intentions in vignette scenarios involving low-intensity stressors with high potential benefits. Beyond these primary associations, we found (a) a moderate positive association between perceived and experienced reactivity, and (b) everyday avoidance behavior was linked to vignette-derived avoidance intentions only for low-intensity, high-benefit stressors. These findings suggest that (a) – while distinct –experienced and perceived affective reactivity share an underlying core and (b) daily stressors may oftentimes reflect situations of lower stressor intensity and high potential benefits.

articles.title: Sampling Fast and Slow Changes Inferences About Well-Being Dynamics
articles.authors: Michael Aristodemou; Manuel Voelkle; Charles C Driver
articles.abstract: Subjective well-being unfolds over time, but inferences about its dynamics may depend on how often it is measured. We examined whether the same well-being processes yield different conclusions when observed annually versus bimonthly. Using two large German population-based panels, the annual SOEP study and the bimonthly GESIS panel, we fit continuous-time structural equation models to 10 cognitive and affective well-being domains. We used propensity-score matching to reduce observed demographic differences between panels. Our results showed that annual and bimonthly data were not fully exchangeable. Independently fitted models best captured the full predictive distribution. However, pooled models often predicted expected well-being levels as well as, or better than, independent models. Descriptive comparisons showed that baseline levels of subjective well-being were relatively similar across designs, whereas dynamic features differed. Deviations from baseline persisted four to eight times longer in annual than bimonthly data; long-run within-subject correlations were stronger in the bimonthly data for most domain pairs; and long-run within-subject variances were consistently larger in the annual data. Within-sample thinning analyses showed that sparser sampling did not necessarily alter recovered dynamics within the temporal ranges examined. These findings suggest that subjective well-being is a multi-timescale system where different observation schedules reveal different aspects of persistence, fluctuation, covariation, and heterogeneity. Temporal design should therefore be treated as a central determinant of substantive inferences.

articles.title: What parents want their children to become: Character strengths as a framework for understanding parental socialization goals
articles.authors: Lisa Wagner; Nina Vaupotič; Johannes Bodo Heekerens; Fabian Gander
articles.abstract:
Objective: Which personality traits do people consider worth fostering? Parents’ aspirations for their children provide a developmental perspective on this question. We examined whether the Values in Action (VIA) classification of character strengths captures these aspirations.
Method: In an online survey, German- and English-speaking parents and expecting parents (N = 1,410; Mage = 31.2 years; 94.3% women) either described the qualities they hoped their children would develop or rated the desirability of the 24 VIA character strengths and ten comparison traits (e.g., intelligence) for their children. Participants also rated their own character strengths.
Results: All 24 character strengths were regarded as desirable, although to varying degrees. Across ratings and open-ended responses, parents consistently prioritized love, honesty, kindness, and social intelligence. Character strengths were generally valued more highly than comparison traits, particularly academic achievement and attractiveness. Parents also placed greater value on strengths they themselves scored higher on. Desirability was also associated with perceived contribution to well-being and, depending on the method, normative levels and societal valuation.
Conclusions: Character strengths capture many of the personality traits parents most want their children to develop, highlighting parental socialization goals as a valuable perspective on desirable personality.

articles.title: Man vs Machine: Electrodermal and Behavioural Responses to Human and AI‑Generated Faces
articles.authors: Giulia Panozzo
articles.abstract:
As technology advances and AI-generated faces increasingly resemble real human faces, it remains unclear whether human autonomic responses differ when viewing human and synthetic faces before explicit judgement. This study investigated whether electrodermal activity (EDA) can reveal pre-conscious physiological differences during the visual presentation of human versus AI-generated faces. Twenty-three adults (25–65 years) viewed static faces from three categories—human, hyper-realistic AI, and less realistic AI-generated faces—while continuous EDA was recorded during an initial passive viewing phase. Participants then completed an active categorisation task in which they classified each face as "human" or "AI", followed by a questionnaire assessing prior exposure to AI-generated content.
Human faces elicited significantly higher skin conductance level (SCL) than both AI-generated categories during passive viewing, indicating stronger autonomic engagement with human faces than synthetic faces prior to explicit categorisation. In the active task, participants correctly classified 89% of human faces and 99% of less realistic AI faces, but only 78% of hyper-realistic AI faces, misclassifying 22% of them as human (60/276 trials across participants). These findings suggest that autonomic sensitivity to human social stimuli persists even when highly realistic AI faces are behaviourally difficult to distinguish from human faces, indicating that pre-conscious physiological responses do not straightforwardly translate into explicit behavioural discrimination. Self-reported familiarity with AI-generated content predicted behavioural performance but was unrelated to autonomic differentiation, further supporting a dissociation between physiological and explicit measures.
Overall, the findings suggest that autonomic responses, explicit behavioural judgements, and prior experience capture complementary aspects of Human–AI face perception. Together, they indicate that increasing visual realism alone is insufficient to eliminate autonomic differentiation. These findings provide a basis for understanding how increasingly realistic AI-generated media are processed and, ultimately, for examining their broader societal implications, with relevance for the ethical development and deployment of synthetic media.

Keywords: electrodermal activity, human-AI perception, Uncanny Valley, autonomic nervous system, artificial intelligence

articles.title: Self-Perceptions on Social Media vs. Offline Contrast With Those Perceived in Generalized  but not Close Others
articles.authors: Cameron James Bunker
articles.abstract:
Self-perception varies across contexts. Do perceptions of others across contexts vary in the same 
way? Here, a multi-study mapping of context-framed person perception addressed this question. 
Participants (N = 1748) reported perceptions of the Big Five personality traits specifying two 
contexts that dominate daily life (offline and social media) regarding three targets: self, the 
typical person (Studies 1-3, 5), and peers (Studies 4 and 5). The perceptions were examined both 
within-person via profile agreements and normatively via mean levels. Profile agreement 
analyses suggested that the similarity between offline and social media contexts was strong in 
self-perceptions (and perceptions of peers) but moderate in perceptions of the typical person. 
Mean level analyses further suggested generally lower trait levels on social media vs. offline in 
self-perceptions (and perceptions of peers). However, perceptions of the typical person showed 
the opposite or attenuated effects in terms of 3/5 traits (openness, extraversion, and neuroticism). 
Perceptions of all three targets showed lower levels of agreeableness on social media than 
offline. Conscientiousness was the only trait to show inconclusive patterns across the studies. 
Together, the findings suggest that self-perceptions on social media vs. offline contexts contrast 
with those perceived in generalized (but not close) others.

articles.title: Cognitive Heterogeneity, Health Dynamics, and Subjective Well-Being Across Adulthood: Evidence from the German SOEP Longitudinal Panel
articles.authors: Kerstin Erdal; Johanna Finnemann
articles.abstract:
Background
Self-rated health is an important correlate of life satisfaction, but the strength of this association varies across individuals. The present study examined whether cognitive clusters derived from performance-based measures of verbal knowledge and response-time characteristics moderate the within-person association between changes in self-rated health and life satisfaction.
Methods
Performance-based cognitive measures from the German Socio-Economic Panel Innovation Sample (SOEP-IS) were used to derive cognitive profiles based on verbal knowledge, processing speed, and processing-speed variability. Cognitive profiles assessed in 2014 were linked prospectively to longitudinal observations from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP-CORE) collected between 2014 and 2023. Random-effects within-between linear mixed-effects models examined the association between within-person changes in self-rated health and life satisfaction and tested whether this association was moderated by cognitive profile. Additional between-person analyses examined associations between cognitive profiles and self-rated health, life satisfaction, and affect.
Results
Cognitive clusters were associated with between-person differences in self-rated health and subjective well-being. In the primary longitudinal model, within-person improvements in self-rated health were associated with small increases in life satisfaction, although this association was attenuated in the survey-weighted sensitivity analysis. Cognitive clusters did not explain individual differences in how changes in self-rated health translated into changes in life satisfaction over time, a finding that was consistent across sensitivity analyses.
Conclusions
Findings suggest that the cognitive performance measures examined here are associated with between-person differences in self-rated health and subjective well-being but do not systematically account for individual differences in how life satisfaction responds to changes in self-rated health over time.

articles.title: Errors in social network knowledge predict how ties evolve in the future
articles.authors: Alice Xia; Yi Yang Teoh; Apoorva Bhandari; Oriel FeldmanHall
articles.abstract: A striking feature of people’s social knowledge is that it is riddled with errors. These errors—e.g., making mistakes about who are actually friends in a social network—has typically been attributed to cognitive limitations or heuristics that prioritize knowledge of general social patterns over details about specific ties. Here, we demonstrate that such errors instead reflect an adaptive link prediction process that anticipates how the network will evolve far into the future.
