By longitudinally following a large, real-world social network (N=196) and tracking the formation and dissolution of social ties over the course of a year, we show that judgments that are wrong in the moment accurately forecast which relationships will emerge or dissolve up to six months later. On average, participants’ errors predicted tie formation nearly 3x, and tie loss more than 1.2x above chance levels. Beyond the use of simple heuristics like triadic closure and homophily, computational modeling reveals that successful link prediction relies on mental representations of the social network that integrates information about both direct and indirect, long-range ties between individuals. Having a social network representation that is future-oriented yields distinct social advantages: those who are better able to predict changes in the network become more centrally positioned over time, contingent on their initial position.

articles.title: Learning with Human Peers and AI Chatbots: Evidence from Two Experimental Studies
articles.authors: Yiliang Jiang; Talia Waltzer; Michelle L Rivers; Gail D. Heyman
articles.abstract: Discussion with peers is a well-established strategy for promoting learning. Because AI chatbots like ChatGPT can respond continuously to students’ questions and explanations, they may serve some of the functions traditionally provided by human discussion partners in learning contexts. Across two pre-registered randomized experiments, we compared learning with human peers and AI chatbots and experimentally manipulated how students interacted with ChatGPT. In Study 1, students learned an unfamiliar physics concept and then discussed the material either with human peers (n = 47) or with ChatGPT (n = 44). Learning outcomes were generally similar across conditions even though many students in the ChatGPT condition just used the chatbot as an answer-generating machine. Study 2 examined whether guidance designed to promote more active engagement with ChatGPT would influence learning with a new set of materials. Participants were assigned to a human-peer condition (n = 43), an AI condition without instruction (n = 43), or an AI condition with instruction (n = 44). The instructional intervention led to more sophisticated prompting and discussion strategies but did not improve learning. Taken together, the findings suggest that learning with ChatGPT can produce outcomes comparable to learning through peer discussion and that even a brief intervention can increase students’ use of recommended interaction strategies. The results also highlight an important distinction between changing how students use AI and changing what they learn from it.

articles.title: Effects of Autism Spectrum Disorder on Discourse: A systematic review
articles.authors: Charalambos Themistocleous; Maria Andreou; Eleni Peristeri
articles.abstract: Language deficits in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are manifested in discourse, yet a systematic characterization of these deficits is lacking. To determine deficits in discourse macro-structure and micro-structure in individuals with ASD, we conducted a systematic review of recent studies in Covidence following PRISMA guidelines. This review showed language deficits on both narrative microstructure and macrostructure. The evidence indicates that individuals with ASD produce narratives that are shorter, lexically less diverse, and syntactically less complex than those of neurotypical peers. Morphosyntax is preserved particularly in individuals without comorbid language impairments, though morphosyntactic deficits can emerge under high discourse demands. At the macrostructural level, individuals with ASD include fewer complete story grammar elements, show weaker causal/temporal linking, use sparser mental-state vocabulary, and display greater referential ambiguity. The reviewed evidence suggests that narrative difficulties are primarily associated with deficits in discourse planning and socio-cognitive processing, with structural linguistic forms though being relatively more preserved.

articles.title: Can People Detect an AI Mediator? A Pilot Turing-Test Study of AI-Assisted Conflict Resolution
articles.authors: Paweł Kleka; Anna Szwal
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in social and interpersonal contexts, yet little is known about whether people can identify an AI interlocutor in naturalistic, emotionally salient interactions. We report a pilot experiment in which 20 participants (10 dyads) engaged in a 60-minute text-based mediation of a simulated interpersonal conflict on Discord. Dyads were randomly assigned to a human mediator (control, n = 5 dyads) or to ChatGPT-4 acting as mediator (experimental, n = 5 dyads); the study was single-blind (participants were unaware that AI mediation was possible). After the session, each participant attempted to determine whether their mediator was human or AI. Identification accuracy did not differ from chance ($\chi^2$(1) = 0.20, *p* = .655), and Bayesian analyses indicated a general tendency to attribute mediation to a human agent rather than reliable detection of AI. Self-reported mediation effectiveness did not differ statistically between conditions in a two-sided test. However, equivalence testing did not support practical equivalence, and the observed effect pattern consistently favoured the AI mediator. Taken together, the results provide no evidence for human-mediator superiority and suggest a non-significant numerical trend favouring AI-mediated sessions (Hedges's *g* = −0.77, 90% CI [−1.50, −0.03]). Given the pilot nature and small sample size, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and require replication in larger, preregistered studies.

articles.title: Young people’s political curiosity: Question-asking before and after the 2024 U.S. presidential election
articles.authors: Isobel Azani Heck; Ellen Kneeskern; Nicole Hanna Park; Bryanna Boone; Candelas Distefano
articles.abstract: Children’s questions provide a window into both their existing knowledge and what they want to understand. Here, we examined young people’s questions about politics and the 2024 U.S. presidential election as a lens into political development and meaning-making during a moment of political change. In a pre-registered study, we surveyed politically and socioeconomically diverse U.S. parents of 4- to 17-year-old children (N = 338) in the weeks before and after election day. Pre-election, parents reported up to three questions their children had asked about (i) politics broadly and (ii) the election specifically; post-election, parents reported up to three questions since election day. For each question, parents reported the child’s age and their own response. Parents reported N = 2,373 questions, with questions common among even the youngest children. By linking features of questions and responses to child age, timepoint (pre- vs. post-election), and children’s political contexts, we examined developmental and election-based changes in children’s political curiosities, and how children’s political contexts shaped these trajectories. Our results reveal that children’s political curiosities are meaningfully varied and dynamic, and that features of children’s questions often predicted whether parents shared political opinions, more so than did aspects of parents’ own political views. Notably, parents reported that both they and their children initiate political conversations, but that children were most likely to do so, particularly near the election. Together, this work underscores the content of early-life political discussions as an underutilized yet powerful lens into political socialization as it unfolds in everyday family life.

articles.title: Undergraduate students' interest in classroom: what does it look like, and where does it come from?
articles.authors: Yanyan He; Hanning Wang; Bingyu Yang; Yinqi Chen; Chengxuan Zheng; Amrita Kaur
articles.abstract: Student interest in the classroom is at the heart of student engagement and academic performance in higher education. Instructional techniques, interventions, teaching contents, pedagogy, and classroom dynamics can successfully trigger and sustain classroom interest. This ethics-approved study utilized qualitative exploratory design to explore how undergraduate students in a Sino-US university campus in China experience the state of interest and factors that contribute to the development of students' interest in the classroom. Twenty students across several colleges from the university were recruited to participate in the study. Data were collected using a semi-structured, face-to-face in-depth interview and experience sampling method (ESM). Deductive thematic analysis provided two primary themes and six subthemes indicating students' state of interest and factors that contribute to the development of interest. Students' experiences of interest include cognitive, affective, and action behaviors, while factors that determine students' interest include subject and content, instructor and pedagogical, and personal factors. Implications are discussed for instructors and undergraduate pedagogy.

articles.title: The Neural Processing of Speech Temporal Modulations During Early Phonological Development
articles.authors: Monica Susheela Hegde; Laurianne Cabrera
articles.abstract:
Purpose:
Infants gradually attune to the consonants of their native language throughout the first year of life. This study investigated the role of auditory temporal processing in this early perceptual attunement.
Method:
We used electrophysiological measures to investigate the processing of temporal modulations, the amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) in speech. Cortical auditory evoked potentials (CAEPs) were measured for native (voiced /b/ and unvoiced unaspirated /p/) and nonnative (unvoiced aspirated English /p/) consonants in French-learning 6-month-old and 10-month-old infants. We also included a group of young adult listeners to serve as a reference group for qualitative comparisons with infants, as there were no prior studies on the effects of temporal degradation on adults' CAEPs. The three consonants were presented under three conditions where AM and FM were differentially degraded or preserved: (a) original FM and AM preserved (no stimulus degradation), (b) fast AM (degrading FM and preserving the original AM), and (c) slow AM only (degrading FM and faster AM fluctuations).
Results:
Temporal degradation affected CAEPs differently across infant age groups, suggesting ongoing development of auditory processing mechanisms for FM and AM cues. Six-month-olds exhibited heightened sensitivity to the reduction of fast AM cues, whereas 10-month-olds were more sensitive to FM degradation.
Conclusions:
Age significantly shapes cortical auditory responses to speech temporal cues. Six-month-olds' neural responses were primarily influenced by fast AM reduction (> 8 Hz), whereas 10-month-olds' responses were more susceptible to FM degradation. Adults did not show either pattern, indicating that the perceptual weighting of temporal modulations in speech continues to develop beyond infancy.

articles.title: Informing patients about their surgery’s environmental impact: an effective pathway to sustainable healthcare?
articles.authors: Monique Chambon; Stijn Bluiminck; Carys Batcup; Jonas Dalege; Sanne de Wit; Nicole D. Bouvy; Philip R. de Reuver; Frenk van Harreveld
articles.abstract: The healthcare sector contributes significantly to climate change. Reducing the number of patients receiving resource-intensive procedures such as surgery can lower carbon emissions, particularly when two treatments with comparable clinical outcomes are available. Nevertheless, the impact of incorporating environmental considerations into patients’ decision-making processes remains underexplored. We examine how including information about the environmental impact of treatment options in a gallstone decision aid affects patients’ real-life choice between surgery and the more sustainable alternative of conservative treatment. Moreover, we examine whether factors such as severity of symptoms moderate the relation between sustainability information and patients’ treatment choice. An exploratory vignette study informed the hypotheses that will be tested among actual patients with gallstones making actual treatment decisions. The results of this ecologically valid study have implications for both clinical practice and healthcare policy by offering insight into the effectiveness of pathways to include patients in the transition towards sustainable healthcare.

articles.title: From Extended Minds to Coupling Flexibility: Cognitive Eco-Sourcing and Generative AI in Education
articles.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo
articles.abstract: Debates about generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education often oppose enhancement to diminishment. This framing obscures important differences in how learners recruit AI and how cognitive labour is distributed between agents and technological resources. We introduce cognitive eco-sourcing as a framework for analysing these relations. It distinguishes four non-parallel and potentially overlapping forms of cognitive coupling: offloading, which reorganises cognitive demands; uploading, through which constructed niches come to supply stable cognitive functions across agents and time; delegation, in which an external resource executes an operation while the agent remains substantively within its production loop; and outsourcing, in which external execution occurs without effective supervision or authorship. These forms are analysed through four dimensions: integration, execution, supervision, and authorship. Education makes these distinctions developmentally significant because activities are intended not merely to produce outcomes but to cultivate capacities. We claim that no form of cognitive eco-sourcing is intrinsically beneficial or harmful. Its educational value depends on the function involved, the target capacity, the learner’s competence, the organisation of the coupling, and its trajectory over time. We conclude that educational environments should cultivate coupling flexibility: learners’ ability to understand, evaluate, select, and reorganise relations with technologies in accordance with changing epistemic and educational aims.

articles.title: 文明的周期 基于道家整体观思想认知人类文明的发展规律
articles.authors: Jicheng Chen
articles.abstract: 为什么东方没有产生“科学”？为什么科学无法解释“意识体验”？本文认为：李约瑟难题与意识难问题共享同一根源。科学是人类认知规律的活动，但它并不等价于物质观和还原论。由于所应对的主要矛盾不同，东方与西方形成以整体观和还原论为主导的认知范式，由此产生了形式迥异但功能等效的社会应用，塑造了东西方截然不同的社会文明形态。一方面，两种范式表观对立：还原论范式呈现出“显性”（阳）特征，整体观范式则呈现出“隐性”（阴）特征，这种特征差异使我们容易将还原论视为人类唯一的认知方式，导致李约瑟之问。另一方面，两种认知范式实则功能互补关系。单一认知范式都具有所自所擅长范围和局限性，还原论擅长处理简单系统，然而，它也导致了以意识难问题为代表一系列科学瓶颈问题，在产生了阴-阳失衡的社会现象，而整体观认知范式可以通过实证的方式弥补其局限性。以上线索暗示，人类的认知和文明的发展或许不是线性进步的，它同样也遵循“从对立到统一”的普遍运行规律（太极三原理），以上推论自然地指向一种可能—我们或许正处在新轴心时代这一极为特殊的历史阶段。

articles.title: Default Mode Network Distinguishes Self from Other During Counterfactual Language Comprehension: Evidence from Multivariate EEG Decoding and LLMs
articles.authors: Cheng Jia; Xiaodong Xu
articles.abstract: Person perspective fundamentally shapes how individuals mentally simulate counterfactual scenarios, yet the neural mechanisms underlying this distinction remain poorly understood. Traditional EEG studies rely on anatomical electrode groupings that may obscure functionally coherent network dynamics. This study investigated whether functionally defined brain networks—particularly the default mode network (DMN)—provide superior sensitivity for capturing person-perspective effects during counterfactual comprehension. We analyzed EEG data from native Mandarin Chinese speakers processing first-person versus third-person counterfactual and causal sentences. Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) with spectral power features (theta, alpha, beta bands), we compared classification performance between traditional 10–20 anatomical groupings and Yeo-7 functional network parcellation. Results revealed that Yeo-7 functional parcellation significantly outperformed anatomical groupings across all classifiers, demonstrating lower inter-model variability and more stable cross-subject generalization. Crucially, within the Yeo-7 framework, the DMN exhibited the strongest discriminative power, with theta-band DMN features emerging as top predictors of person-perspective. Time-resolved representational similarity analysis (RSA) revealed that DMN activity dynamically aligned with Chinese-BERT semantic representations during first-person counterfactual processing, with alignment emerging even before stimulus-onset. This alignment was absent for third-person and causal sentences, and whole-cortex RSA showed no significant clusters, confirming spatial specificity to the DMN. These findings demonstrate that person perspective is neurally implemented through predictive semantic simulation mediated by the DMN, which constructs rich, contextually sensitive situation models during self-referential counterfactual comprehension. Our results provide quantitative evidence that functional network parcellation substantially enhances EEG sensitivity to subtle semantic distinctions, establishing network-based approaches as essential for investigating high-level language processing.

articles.title: Competition between memory and goals shapes the neural dynamics of attention, working memory, and recognition
articles.authors: Igor Utochkin; Edward K. Vogel
articles.abstract: Many everyday decisions require selecting between competing options on the basis of episodic memory while pursuing a behavioral goal. Although the neural basis of recognition memory has been extensively studied using single-item old/new judgments, little is known about how memory and current goals jointly control attention and working memory when multiple objects compete. In two experiments, we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while participants performed a two-alternative forced-choice between a previously studied (old) and a new object presented simultaneously in opposite visual hemifields. By instructing participants to report the location of either the old or the new object, we dissociated memory history from goal relevance. We identified a sustained lateralized ERP component, which we term retrieval-related contralateral delay activity (r-CDA), that tracked the evolving allocation of attention and working memory during memory-guided decisions. The r-CDA initially favored the familiar object regardless of task goals, revealing an early familiarity-driven priority state. Only later did its amplitude diverge according to whether the familiar or novel object was task-relevant, indicating subsequent goal-dependent modulation. Classical recognition-related components showed complementary dynamics: the FN400 remained insensitive to goal relevance, whereas the later LPC reflected target-dependent recognition processing. Representational similarity analysis further demonstrated that distributed neural activity was organized first by memory history and only later by behavioral goals. Together, these findings reveal that attention and working memory deploy following a dynamic competition between memory and goals, and introduce the r-CDA as a neural marker of internally generated priority during memory-guided decisions.

articles.title: Shared Identity and Felt Understanding in the Context of Sexual Minority Stress:  Who Gets Me, and Why?
articles.authors: Emma Laurel McGorray; Khava Gillespie; Elsie Newburg; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract: Although sexual minority stress often predicts lower well-being, LGBQ+ people may be protected against these effects if they receive support that helps them feel understood. What processes are linked to greater felt understanding? Across four studies, we tested the hypothesis that LGBQ+ people feel more understood by LGBQ+ (vs. heterosexual) support providers and tested two possible explanations for this relationship: (1) LGBQ+ support providers offer higher-quality support (the support quality explanation) and (2) people’s beliefs about shared identity are linked to how they evaluate support (the interpretive filter explanation). Using varied methodologies—participants reflecting on their close relationships and evaluating both genuine and experimentally manipulated support messages—we found limited evidence for the former explanation but more robust evidence for the latter. These findings underscore the power of sharing an identity with a support provider when experiencing minority stress, while also suggesting that mere beliefs about shared identity may be a major source of that power.

articles.title: A ‘Basin of Attraction’ Theory of Speech Initiation and Stuttering
articles.authors: Frank H H Guenther; Soo-Eun Chang; Jonathan Cannon
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Purpose. Recent work in motor neuroscience suggests that well-learned actions are implemented as stable, stereotyped trajectories in neural state space. The purpose of this article is to propose a theory of stuttering that formalizes this idea for speech production and identifies a specific neural impairment underlying speech dysfluency.
Method. We advance a conceptual and computational framework in which the motor program for a familiar word corresponds to a stable neural trajectory with an associated basin of attraction. We integrate findings from primate motor control, human speech neuroscience, and basal ganglia physiology to specify the role of cortico–basal ganglia–thalamo–cortical (BGTC) circuits in initiating these trajectories.
Results. We propose that fluent speech depends on the ability of the BGTC circuit to initialize the distributed speech motor network within the basin of attraction of the upcoming word’s motor program. Stuttering arises when this initialization process is unreliable or poorly coordinated, preventing the motor program from being executed until the neural state is corrected or the effective basin of attraction is broadened through compensatory mechanisms.
Conclusions. This basin-of-attraction framework provides a unifying account of diverse behavioral and neural findings in stuttering, aligns stuttering theory with contemporary dynamical systems approaches to motor control, and generates testable predictions for future neurophysiological and neuroimaging studies.

articles.title: Measurement Invariance and Sociodemographic Differences at the Lowest Level of the Psychopathology Hierarchy: An Analysis of the German HiTOP-SR
articles.authors: Benno T. T. Trummer; Leon Patrick Wendt; Ulrich Schroeders; Johannes Zimmermann
articles.abstract: Comparisons of mental health problems between sociodemographic groups are interpretable only if measures function equivalently across groups, yet measurement invariance has rarely been tested at the lowest level of the psychopathology hierarchy. Using the validation sample of the German Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology Self-Report (HiTOP-SR; N = 1,049 general-population adults), we tested measurement invariance across sex, age, and socioeconomic status (SES) for all 87 facets in ordinal multigroup confirmatory factor analyses and, where scalar invariance held, estimated standardized latent mean differences. Of the 261 cases (87 facets × 3 grouping variables), 74.3% reached scalar invariance, 14.6% showed non-invariance (usually small to medium in magnitude) and 11.1% were not estimable owing to low base rates. On invariant facets, women scored higher on internalizing and lower on externalizing facets, symptom levels declined with age, and higher SES was associated with lower symptom levels, with facet-level heterogeneity revealing where these differences were most pronounced. The results identify which facets permit meaningful sociodemographic comparisons and inform future revisions of the instrument.

articles.title: Loneliness and Resting Parasympathetic Activity Interact to Influence Approach Motivations
articles.authors: Anita Restrepo; Mary Mousa; Alexander C. Henoch; Emily M. Silver; Gregory Norman; Kelly E. Faig; Karen E Smith
articles.abstract: Loneliness, or perceived social isolation, increases motivation to approach and reaffiliate while simultaneously enhancing sensitivity to potential threats, allowing individuals to avoid further social threats. Some individuals successfully leverage these competing motivations to reduce feelings of loneliness. However, others further withdraw, perpetuating a harmful cycle of loneliness. What drives this variability in responses to loneliness is still not well understood. Prior research found that resting parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) activity, linked to increased regulatory capacity and more flexible adaptation, moderates responses to loneliness. Individuals with higher resting PNS activity and higher levels of loneliness demonstrate enhanced approach of both positive and negative information. Here, we aimed to replicate and expand on this research, examining whether this effect is more pronounced for social information. 107 participants (ages 18 to 56 years) completed an approach-avoidance task in which they made decisions about whether to approach or avoid positive and negative social or non-social images. For individuals with higher resting PNS activity, loneliness was associated with reduced approach of negative information, but no differences in approach of positive information. These effects were comparable for social and non-social stimuli. Our findings suggest lonely individuals with higher resting PNS activity may be better able to flexibly leverage shifts in approach and avoidance motivations in a context-dependent manner, contributing to the field’s understanding of how loneliness shapes motivated behaviors as a function of environmental context, particularly the social nature of incoming valenced information.

articles.title: Simulating the Unreal: Neural Mechanisms of Counterfactual Comprehension
articles.authors: Cheng Jia; Xiaodong Xu
articles.abstract: Counterfactual reasoning—the ability to construct scenarios that contradict known facts—is central to complex human cognition. However, little is known about how such reasoning unfolds in languages like Mandarin Chinese, which lack explicit morphological markers for counterfactuality. In this study, we used a discourse-based manipulation with tightly controlled syntactic and lexical features to examine the neural mechanisms of Mandarin counterfactual comprehension via functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Activation and graph-theoretical analyses revealed that counterfactuals, compared to hypothetical and causal statements, elicited heightened activity and enhanced network efficiency in sensorimotor regions (PreCG, PoCG), alongside increased engagement of the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG). Inter-subject representational similarity analysis (IS-RSA) further demonstrated that these effects were modulated by individual differences in working memory and Theory of Mind, with WM supporting dual representation and ToM facilitating higher-level inferencing. Together, these findings provide converging evidence for the Mental Simulation Hypothesis: counterfactual comprehension recruits embodied sensorimotor processes to simulate unreal events, particularly in the absence of overt grammatical cues. By integrating individual-difference measures with network-level analyses, this study advances our understanding of the neural architecture of counterfactual thinking and raises questions about how grammatical marking may shape counterfactual processing across languages.

articles.title: That’s Just Like Your Opinion, Man: Effort Legibility in The Big Lebowski
articles.authors: Emily Zohar; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: The cult classic The Big Lebowski helped normalize a slacker lifestyle, inviting viewers to “take it easy”. Here, we use the film to examine a puzzle in the psychology of effort: why observers so often get it wrong. The contrast between Jeffrey “The Dude” Lebowski and Mr. Lebowski reveals a gap between actual and perceived effort. The Dude appears lazy–unemployed, broke, dishevelled, and often smoking a joint–yet repeatedly exerts effort toward intrinsically valued goals, including replacing his “valued rug”. Mr. Lebowski, by contrast, is celebrated as an “Achiever” and insists that he's a very busy man, despite frequently delegating his efforts to others. This misalignment matters because effort is largely private. Observers infer it from visible cues such as strain, struggle, and reward, but these cues can mislead. We argue that people are praised and punished based on effort legibility–how effortful they appear–rather than how much effort they exert. The film reveals what observers routinely miss: the Achiever may be coasting while the slacker is working, and whether we notice depends on which cues we’re seeing. Or, as the Dude puts it, “Yeah, well, that’s just, like, your opinion, man”.

articles.title: Debunking decreases mistaken causal inferences: A direct replication of Irving et al. (2022)
articles.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Keyi Zhang; James Edward Bartlett
articles.abstract: We conducted a direct replication of Irving et al. (2022) examining whether a debunking statement reduces mistaken causal inferences from correlational evidence. We randomly allocated participants to read a news article containing either a correction statement (n = 65) or a no-correction control (n = 64). Participants in the correction group made fewer causal inferences (delta = 0.65, 95% HDI [0.30, 1.00]) and more correlational inferences (delta = 0.72, 95% HDI [0.36, 1.07]) compared to the no correction group. In exploratory analyses, we also supported the robustness of their findings to alternative modelling choices. Our findings represent a successful direct replication of Irving et al.

articles.title: The Sound of Meaning: Prosody Distinguishes Affirmation from Negation in Early Speech Input
articles.authors: Sakine Cabuk-Balli; Volker Dellwo; Aylin C. Küntay; Paul Widmer; Sabine Stoll
articles.abstract: A central feature of human language acquisition is the ability to extract meaning from the linguistic input children encounter. Prosody, a fundamental component of spoken communication, conveys broad communicative intent, but it remains unclear whether it also provides reliable cues to support the learning of more fine-grained semantic distinctions. This study investigates whether prosody can in principle serve as a meaningful signal for distinguishing negative from affirmative declarative utterances in the speech that surrounds children. By analyzing child-directed and child-surrounding speech, we assess whether the prosodic patterns available in learner's input are sufficiently systematic to support the acquisition of these semantic contrasts. We tested (i) whether machines and humans can differentiate between affirmative and negative utterances, and (ii) whether humans are able to categorize specific negative functions (prohibition, rejection, non-existence, and inability) based on their acoustic features. Our dataset comprises affirmative and negative declarative utterances drawn from longitudinal child language acquisition corpora in five typologically diverse languages: Chintang, English, Indonesian, Kurdish, and Turkish.  First, using Support Vector Machines, we evaluate the extent to which prosodic cues (pitch and duration) contribute to the classification of affirmative and negative utterances. The results reveal high accuracy in distinguishing between affirmative and negative utterances across all five languages.  Second, in two behavioral experiments with 300 native and non-speakers of three languages (English, Kurdish, and Turkish), we examined whether there is a difference between the two speaker groups in classifying utterances based on intonational contours. Experiment 1 revealed that native speakers successfully distinguished affirmative from negative utterances based on pitch and amplitude, an ability not shared by non-speakers. Experiment 2 demonstrated that prohibition is identified with the greatest accuracy by both speaker groups. The characteristic elevated pitch of prohibitive utterances appears to function as a universal prosodic marker that facilitates their recognition irrespective of linguistic background. We conclude that prosodic cues in child-surrounding speech form a dynamic and functionally rich acoustic framework that serves as universal signals. These cues facilitate children’s ability to discern meaning and to identify essential negative functions, thereby supporting foundational processes in early semantic interpretation.

articles.title: Cross-Linguistic Variation in Wrap-Up Effects Reflects Adaptive Sensitivity to Information Structure
articles.authors: Inbal Kimchi; Amit Avigdor; Leon Hager; Paul van den Broek; Sascha Schroeder; Victor Kuperman; Noam Siegelman
articles.abstract: The wrap-up effect, i.e., the inflation of reading times on sentence- or clause-final words relative to preceding words, is a robust finding in reading research, typically interpreted to reflect integrative processing of meaning. However, recent cross-linguistic evidence has cast doubt on its generalizability across languages, raising questions about the mechanisms that underlie it. Here, we test an information-theoretic account of the wrap-up effect, according to which the effect reflects readers’ adaptive behavior to where semantic information resides in their written language. We start by showing in a large-scale text reading database (N=1,234 from 20 languages) that there is, in fact, systematic cross-linguistic variation in wrap-up effects. Then, we use sentence-embeddings to quantify languages’ trajectories of semantic informativeness in sentence endings, showing that they closely align with the observed cross-linguistic variability in wrap-up effects. Specifically, languages with increasing informativeness in sentence endings also show canonical wrap-up effects, whereas languages with declining informativeness patterns have no or reversed effects. Lastly, we show that these correlations are driven by readers’ general expectations regarding the structure of their written language. This is revealed by models showing that global (i.e., language-specific mean) informativeness trajectories rather than local (i.e., sentence-level) changes predict the magnitude of the wrap-up effect in a given sentence. Together, these findings provide a novel interpretation of the mechanisms underlying the wrap-up effect, positioning it as a consequence of learning computations that readers use to assimilate their writing system’s structure, thus offering a principled explanation for its cross-linguistic variability.

articles.title: The impact of problematic social media use on loneliness, procrastination and self-esteem: a cross-sectional study in Greece
articles.authors: Zoe Katsiroumpa; Polyxeni Mangoulia; Evmorfia Koukia; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE To explore the impact of problematic social media use on loneliness, procrastination and self-esteem. Additionally, we examined sex and generation differences. METHOD We carried out a cross-sectional study involving a convenience sample of 1033 individuals, all of whom had at least one social media account. To assess problematic social media use, we employed the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Additionally, we evaluated loneliness, procrastination, and self-esteem using the UCLA 3-Item Loneliness Scale, the Irrational Procrastination Scale, and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, respectively. To control for confounding variables such as sex, age, educational level, socioeconomic status, daily social media usage, and the number of social media accounts, we conducted multivariable linear regression analysis. RESULTS Our findings revealed a positive association between problematic social media use and both loneliness and procrastination, while a negative association was observed with self-esteem. Stratification analysis indicated a stronger link between problematic social media use and procrastination among females and Generation Z. Furthermore, the association between problematic social media use and loneliness was more pronounced in Generation X and Millennials, while the association with self-esteem was stronger in Generation Z. CONCLUSIONS Our findings support the association between problematic social media use and issues such as loneliness, procrastination, and self-esteem, with notable differences based on sex and generation. As social media usage continues to rise, healthcare professionals should remain vigilant in identifying high-risk groups susceptible to problems stemming from problematic social media use

articles.title: Symptom Recognition, Help-seeking behaviour, and Joint Decision-making among Parents of Children with Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder
articles.authors: Quirina Engels; Lilian Lechner; Yil Severijns
articles.abstract:
Objective: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) is a relatively new diagnosis for the eating disorder in which children avoid food due to lack of interest, sensory characteristics, or fear of aversive consequences of food. Early recognition and treatment of ARFID is crucial, as delays in diagnosis can lead to serious medical consequences and increased psychosocial burden for both the child and the parents. In the Netherlands a qualitative study was conducted with the research question "Which factors influence parental help-seeking behaviour when suspecting ARFID in their child, and what differences exist between fathers and mothers?".
Methods: Ten semi-structured interviews were conducted with parents of children with ARFID (aged 4-12 years). Nine parental couples and one single parent (N=19) were interviewed. The data were analysed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA).
Results: Parents recognized various symptoms of ARFID in their child, with growth problems and selective eating behaviour being most common. Parents help-seeking behaviour was stimulated by urgent medical consequences and concerns about psychosocial limitations in their child. However, it was hindered by a lack of reference framework with a first child and a wait-and-see attitude of healthcare providers, who viewed the eating problems as a neophobic phase. Differences that emerged between parents were that mothers more often took the initiative to seek help and experienced more guilt about eating behaviour, while fathers more often applied coercion during mealtimes.
Conclusion: The diagnostic trajectory of ARFID was stressful for parents, experiencing frustration, powerlessness, guilt, and lack of support from both healthcare providers and their environment. Recommended is peer support, training of healthcare providers in recognition of ARFID, and a family-centred approach with attention to emotional support.

articles.title: Online Discourse is Falsely Polarized by Self-Selection
articles.authors: Will Schulz; Claire Elizabeth Robertson; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Ashwini Ashokkumar; Lisa Oswald; JungHwan Yang; Simon Munzert; Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Andrew Markus Guess
articles.abstract: We present comprehensive evidence quantifying the magnitude and scope of false polarization (i.e. the impression that opinions on political issues are more polarized than they actually are) on social media, driven by users' selective posting behavior. Using more than a decade of social media behavior connected to individual ideological attitudes in 1.7 million posts, a series of controlled experiments, and a large global survey covering 40 countries (total N = 49,222), we find that (1) strong ideologues post their opinions significantly more often than moderate individuals, and (2) extreme attitudes are posted more often than moderate attitudes. This general pattern replicates robustly across 40 countries, spanning diverse political cultures. Indeed, across studies we find extreme opinions are overrepresented on social media by at least 6% and up to 22% compared to their true prevalence in our samples. Furthermore, the opinions that users post are more hostile and toxic than the beliefs they keep to themselves.  These results were not explained by political interest or consistent left-right differences, suggesting that political extremity has an independent effect on social media behavior. Thus, most of the observed polarization of online discourse in recent years may be attributable to the systematic over-representation of pre-existing extreme political views, rather than the causal effects of platforms.

articles.title: BLM-Hum1800: A Human-Validated Benchmark for Linguistic Competence in English and French
articles.authors: Marion Bouffier; Giuseppe Samo; Chunyang Jiang; Vivi Nastase; Paola Merlo; Valentina Borghesani
articles.abstract:
Evaluating the fine-grained linguistic competence of Large Language Models (LLMs) requires diagnostic
benchmarks anchored by controlled syntactic paradigms and human behavioral baselines. Here, we
present a bilingual dataset comprising 1,800 human-validated linguistic problem instances across English
and French. Based on the Blackbird Language Matrices (BLM) framework, the dataset targets three core
grammatical phenomena (i.e., Subject-Verb Agreement, Change-of-State and Object Drop verb
alternations) across three levels of lexical variability (Types I, II, and III). In BLM-Hum1800, we provide
item-level behavioral data from 1,349 human participants, capturing selection accuracy, reaction times,
and click counts, alongside baseline evaluations from two modern LLMs tested across two distinct
reasoning configurations. BLM-Hum1800 serves as a standardized resource for evaluating syntactic rule
extraction and pattern generalization in artificial intelligence models, as well as for comparative
psycholinguistic and cognitive modeling in humans. All problem instances, raw and aggregated behavioral
data, anonymized participant demographics, and evaluation scripts are publicly available in an
open-access repository.

articles.title: A Bayesian Model of Sequential Collaboration: Understanding Dependent Numerical Judgments Through Expertise and Social Influence
articles.authors: Maren Mayer
articles.abstract: The wisdom-of-crowds phenomenon demonstrates that aggregating judgments across multiple individuals can produce remarkably accurate estimates. However, research has shown that dependent judgments in sequential collaboration, where contributors revise or maintain previous judgments, can equal or outperform traditional aggregation methods based on independent judgments. Recently, a computational model of sequential collaboration has been proposed, but its assumptions and predictions could only be tested qualitatively. To address this limitation, a Bayesian model of sequential collaboration was developed that relies on the same cognitive processes and allows model parameters to be estimated directly from observed judgments and decisions. Simulation studies demonstrated accurate parameter recovery across a wide range of sample sizes and item sets. Applying the model to four empirical datasets showed that estimated parameters aligned with empirical findings for sequential collaboration. Model comparisons further revealed that accounting for response biases substantially improved model fit in homogeneous estimation tasks, whereas other model variations received no support. These findings extend the theoretical framework of sequential collaboration by enabling quantitative testing of cognitive mechanisms underlying dependent judgments. More broadly, the model integrates ideas from wisdom-of-crowds research, cultural consensus theory, anchoring, and group decision making, providing a foundation for future research on collective judgment and social influence.

articles.title: Future Anxiety Affects Youth’s Democratic Support and Engagement
articles.authors: Olaf Borghi; Katharina Lawall; Kaat Smets; Manos Tsakiris
articles.abstract: Many of today’s young people are anxious about the future. Yet the consequences of their anxiety on democratic support and engagement remain underexplored. In this preregistered survey experiment we tested the causal effects of future anxiety on youth’s democratic attitudes. We exposed young people (N = 1,895; ages 16–26) to social media posts about the cost of living which were manipulated to induce future anxiety, reduce it through hope, or serve as a control. Increasing their future anxiety (vs. hope) resulted in a small but precisely estimated decrease in democratic support (−2.5 percentage points; 95% CI [−4.3, −0.8]), but without any effects on a behavioural candidate-choice task or on self-reported willingness to participate in politics. Conversely, hope (vs. control and anxiety) increased young people’s likelihood to seek information on how to get democratically involved (+6.9 percentage points; 95% CI [1.7, 12.0]). These findings provide experimental evidence that future-oriented feelings shape youth’s democratic support amidst multiple crises.

articles.title: Low-Level Visual and Auditory Features Predict Preferences of Commercials
articles.authors: Valentina Parada; Inbal Gur Arie; Levy Dino
articles.abstract: Video content has become a dominant form of digital marketing, increasing the need to understand which features make videos more appealing and effective. Prior studies showed that low-level visual features in static images affect saliency and consumer preferences, while low-level auditory features influence preferences for music clips. However, it remains unclear how these features and their interaction shape preferences for dynamic stimuli such as video commercials. In this study, 165 participants watched 100 video commercials and rated how much they liked each commercial and their willingness to pay (WTP) for the advertised product. We extracted low-level visual and auditory features from the commercials (e.g., colorfulness, scene frequency, loudness, zero-crossing rate) and used them as inputs to linear and non-linear prediction models. Both visual and auditory low-level features significantly predicted liking and WTP, with the combined model performing best. Importantly, these low-level features also predicted the aggregate engagement metrics at the population level as measured on YouTube, demonstrating the generalizability of our findings and their external validity. These findings show that low-level sensory information influences consumer preferences and ad effectiveness and demonstrate how computational tools can be used to evaluate video effectiveness.

articles.title: Vibe shift or partisanship: Unequal changes between and within American political groups’ perception of misinformation and its solutions after the 2024 US Election
articles.authors: Tobia Spampatti; Laura K. Globig; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract: Citizens across the globe are torn between addressing misinformation versus guaranteeing individual freedom of expression. Democratic elections provide a chance for not only selecting among competing policies, but also for shifting societal norms about societal issues. The 2024 US Presidential election was heralded as a “vibe shift” with public support swinging away from content moderation and towards freedom of speech. However, the shift in societal norms may have been illusory and Americans may have remained highly polarized along partisan lines. In this preregistered study with data collected before and after the 2024 Presidential Elections (N = 1,377 representative US sample), we tested how electoral results, interpreted according to partisan identity, changed attitudes towards misinformation and censorship, perceived prevalence of misinformation, and support for approaches to curtail misinformation (i.e., digital content moderation) over protecting freedom of expression. Post-election, Americans worried more about misinformation, misinformation spreaders, and censorship. Supporting a partisanship hypothesis, Americans identifying as Democrats worried more about misinformation and spreaders of misinformation than Republicans post-election. Exploratory analyses suggest that, post-election, Democrats supported content moderation strategies even more after the election of Donald Trump while lean Republicans became more likely to choose to protect free speech, whereas strong Republicans were relatively more likely to prefer preventing misinformation from spreading. These results suggest that people’s perception of misinformation and censorship changed after the election, and these perceptions were determined by partisanship rather than reflecting a broader societal shift in social norms.

articles.title: When Democracy Is Worth the Effort: Seeing the Other Side as Willing Strengthens Pro-Democratic Motivation
articles.authors: Olaf Borghi; Manos Tsakiris; Mariana Von Mohr
articles.abstract: Democracy takes effort, and these efforts do not always benefit one’s own political side. Across two preregistered studies (total N = 916), we used computational modeling of effortful behavior to measure US partisans’ motivation to strengthen democratic engagement in rural (traditionally Republican-leaning), urban (traditionally Democratic-leaning), or all US areas. Study 1 showed that participants were generally willing to make pro-democratic efforts, but less so when efforts benefited out-group areas, particularly among more affectively polarized participants. We hypothesized that this asymmetry is sustained by misperceptions about out-partisans’ willingness to engage in cross-partisan pro-democratic efforts. Study 2 showed that most participants (87%) underestimated out-party effort willingness. Importantly, correcting this misperception increased motivation to support out-group areas without significantly reducing in-group motivation. These findings suggest that cross-partisan pro-democratic motivation is common but partly obscured by misperceptions about out-partisans’ willingness, and that making this willingness visible might help sustain the collective effort democracy depends on.

articles.title: Virtual Empathy Scale (VES): Development and Psychometric Validation Among Indian Young Adults
articles.authors: Aishu S Gowda; Akash Nethravathi Raju; Dhiksha J
articles.abstract:
This research was targeted at constructing and testing the virtual empathy scale (VES) that is intended to assess the empathy that is realized in the online communication between young college-going adults. It is based on multidimensional empathy models and is composed of three: empathic expression, cognitive empathy, and affective empathy. There was a generation of a pool of 49 items, and it underwent the face and content validity examination by experts reducing the pool to 41 items. Then we performed EFA on a sample of 421 college going students. This gave a 32-item scale, and good factor loading. We subsequently applied CFA to another sample of 331 students, and this supported the three-factor model, with reasonable fit statistics (CFI= .90, TLI=.899, RMSEA=.061). To conduct the reliability analysis, it was demonstrated that the results had high internal consistency (α > 0.87, ω > 0.87) in all three factors. The scale demonstrated convergent validity as demonstrated in high factor loading and composite reliability, however, the average variance extracted was a little below the optimal thresholds. And lastly, discriminant validity with some factor correlation approaching upper limits was determined with the use of HTMT. This scale has demonstrated high psychometric characteristics and is a potentially useful instrument to measure empathy in digital communication and can be used in a variety of psychological studies, online learning, and digital wellbeing intervention.
Keywords: virtual empathy, digital communication, psychometric validation, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, young adults.

articles.title: Language preference of adults with lived experience of ADHD: a cross-country study
articles.authors: Joske Rijmen; Oana Denisa Mateut; Erica Fongaro; Madeleine Groom; Diane Purper-Ouakil; Jan R. Wiersema; Blandine French
articles.abstract:
Terminology used to describe neurodevelopmental conditions is increasingly contested, reflecting tensions between medical and neurodiversity-informed frameworks. While a growing body of research has examined terminology preferences within autism, comparable empirical work focusing specifically on Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) remains notably limited. We examined ADHD-related language preferences among adults with lived experience across three languages and four countries. 
An online cross-sectional survey was completed by 2,340 adults with lived experience of ADHD: 359 English-speaking (United Kingdom), 1,749 French-speaking (France), and 232 Dutch-speaking (Belgium and the Netherlands). Linear mixed-effects models were used to test the effects of term, spoken language, and their interaction, with participant as a random intercept. 
Preferences varied by spoken language. English- and Dutch-speaking participants favoured neurodiversity-aligned terms (e.g., “neurodivergent person”, “brain difference”, “traits”), whereas French-speaking participants more strongly endorsed medicalised descriptors (e.g., “person with ADHD”, “disorder”, “symptoms”). However, explicitly deficit-oriented terms (e.g., “abnormal”, “deficits”) were broadly opposed across spoken languages. 
There is no cross-language consensus on ADHD terminology and even within one language preferences vary substantially. These findings caution against the use of universal, prescriptive guidance and underscore the need for culturally and linguistically sensitive language in research, clinical, and policy contexts.

articles.title: How does familiarity impact the computational processes that support face recognition?
articles.authors: Fournier Raphaël; Paul Downing; Richard Ramsey
articles.abstract: Recognising a familiar face is a fundamental social cognitive ability, yet the computational mechanisms that underlie this capacity remain poorly understood. Prior research has established that familiarity affects face recognition performance, but has relied primarily on manifest measures — accuracy and response time — that cannot distinguish between qualitatively different sources of performance change. Here, we used evidence accumulation modelling across a series of experiments to ask not merely whether familiarity affects face recognition, but how — specifically, which latent computational processes are modulated. Experiments 1 and 2 examined visual familiarity (briefly learned faces versus novel faces) and Experiments 3, 4 and 5 examined person knowledge (famous versus novel faces). Fitting linear ballistic accumulator models to recognition data revealed a consistent computational signature across experiments: novel faces produced substantially higher drift rates than familiar faces, accompanied by a smaller but reliable increase in response caution. The dominance of the drift rate effect localises familiarity’s primary influence to the quality of evidence accumulation — how cleanly the perceptual system extracts decision-relevant information — rather than to response bias. We interpret thes findings as reflecting a novelty pop-out effect combined with unstable memory traces for familiar faces. These findings demonstrate that computational modelling reveals dissociable mechanisms underlying face recognition that are invisible to manifest measures alone, and provide a foundation for understanding how familiarity shapes the decision processes that support social perception.

articles.title: FEEDBACK Faces: An Image Data Base With Communicative Facial Expressions of Appreciation and Criticism
articles.authors: Ronja Ochs; Elisabeth Prestele; Christine Altstötter-Gleich; Ulrike Basten
articles.abstract: Facial expressions of appreciation and criticism play an important role for positive and negative reinforcement in social communication. Existing databases of face stimuli for experimental research, however, mainly cover basic emotions and lack specific expressions of positive and negative reinforcement. The aim of the current study was to develop an image database of communicative facial expressions of appreciation and criticism (FEEDBACK Faces) that can be used for experimental research on social reinforcement. In a first step, to generate new photo stimuli, we took pictures of appreciative, critical, and neutral facial expressions from 30 models using three different instruction techniques (imagination of predefined scenarios, recall of personal experiences, and imitation of prototypical expressions). In a second step, we conducted a validation study in which 33 participants rated the extent to which they recognized appreciation vs. criticism in the photographed expressions. Based on the ratings, we selected two separate sets of stimuli for the final database: (A) The set FEEDBACK-AC contains unambiguous expressions with correct identification rates of 88.21% for appreciation, 97.30% for criticism, and 92.76% for neutral expressions (54 images of 18 models, 9 female, 9 male). (B) The set FEEDBACK-AC-Ambiguous contains particularly ambiguous expressions that allow for interpretation as either appreciation or criticism and are intended for research on interpretation biases (16 images of 16 models, 8 female, 8 male). The stimuli can be used for a wide range of applications in behavior research and are freely available for scientific purposes (find link to database website in project repository https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20284150).

articles.title: The Paradox of Modern Love:  Why Romantic Signals Decline in Developed Societies
articles.authors: Edgar Dubourg; Julien Lie-Panis; Valentin Thouzeau; Coralie Chevallier; Marta Kowal; Piotr Sorokowski; Nicolas Baumard
articles.abstract: Converging evidence shows that the cultural importance of romantic love has increased dramatically with societal development; it now serves as a primary criterion for choosing partners, a foundation for family formation, and a pervasive theme in cultural production. Yet here we show that this rise does not continue indefinitely: romantic love peaks and then declines at the highest levels of development. This rise-and-fall pattern emerges both cross-nationally (9,474 participants across 45 countries) and diachronically (automatic annotations of 13,409 U.S. movies, 1971–2020). This poses a puzzle: if romantic love sustains long-term pair-bonds, and if safer, more affluent environments make such bonds more viable, why would love decline where it should thrive? We resolve this paradox by proposing that what declines is not love itself, but the need to signal it. Using a formal model and cross-national analyses (N=7,333 and 84,382), we show that when long-term commitment becomes common, overt romantic signaling becomes unnecessary and even counterproductive: the most committed individuals benefit from not signaling, because doing so would reveal that they expected the relationship to need reassurance. In affluent societies, love becomes quieter not because bonds are weaker, but because they are more secure.

articles.title: A cross-linguistic, multi-construct survey for assessing children's beliefs about learning experiences and environments
articles.authors: Lijin Zhang; Amy Lightbody; Robert Zane Sparks; Mika Braginsky; Nichola Jenkins; Daniel Ansari; Maria Camila Perfetti; Julián P. Mariño; Luise Hornoff; Manuel Bohn
articles.abstract: Children's beliefs about their learning experiences and environments play a central role in shaping academic engagement, motivation, and developmental trajectories. Constructs such as academic perception, belonging, and growth mindset are widely studied in developmental and educational research, yet most measures have been developed and validated within limited cultural and linguistic contexts. This raises concerns about whether these instruments capture the same constructs across diverse settings. The present study introduces a cross-linguistic, multi-construct survey for children aged 5-12 years across multiple international sites. The instrument is designed to assess learning-related attitudes across five key constructs: academic perception, belonging, growth mindset, peer relationships, and teacher-student relationships. Using data from three sites in Canada, Colombia, and Germany, we evaluated the reliability and validity of these survey tools. The scales demonstrated good reliability, structural validity, and discriminant validity. The measurement structure was largely invariant across sites, with only a small number of parameters showing noninvariance that did not substantially affect factor score estimation. We further examined relationships among constructs and how these associations vary with age. These findings support the use of the survey instrument to capture developmental and contextual variation in children's attitudes toward learning.

articles.title: “Suicide is cringe!”: Content analysis of 46,071 mental health videos from adolescents’ TikTok feeds
articles.authors: Rebecca Godard; Amber van der Wal; Ine Beyens
articles.abstract: This manuscript presents a content analysis of 46,071 mental health videos viewed by adolescents over a span of five years. The most frequently-discussed topics included mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g., autism, ADHD, depression), mental health symptoms and experiences (e.g., anxiety and depressive symptoms, trauma), positive aspects of mental health (e.g., recovery, coping, healing), and mentla health treatment (e.g., therapy, inpatient treatment, medication). Videos were primarily personal stories and often contained humorous elements and supportive messages. Yet areas of concern, such as videos that encourage harmful behaviour (e.g., suicide, self-harm, disordered eating) and false of misleading claims of expertise from video creators, also emerged.  Findings highlight the need for a nuanced approach to studying mental health content and its impacts on adolescents, with the aim of empowering youth to harness the potential benefits of this content while minimizing its potential harms.

articles.title: Reconciling principles of cortical organisation: A historical review of areas and gradients
articles.authors: Casey Paquola; Simon Eickhoff; Matthias Kirschner; Jonathan Smallwood; Boris C. Bernhardt
articles.abstract: A debate is raging in human neuroscience over the foundational principles of cortical organisation, chiefly whether the cortex is best characterised by discrete areas or continuous gradients. Though fuelled by recent insights from in vivo neuroimaging, the debate is in fact centuries old. Classic works in neuroanatomy and neurophysiology hold insights that can still shape our theories today. Tracing the origins of these schools of thought also sheds light on where prevailing models simplify cortical organisation for purposes of utility. In this scoping historical review, traversing across methods as varied as vivisection, skull morphology, neuropathological lesions, histology and modern neuroimaging, we trace a persistent tension between modular and integrative accounts of cortical organisation. Yet several principles consistently emerge, even among competing schools, (i) hard boundaries are the exception rather than the rule, (ii) parcellations and gradients can be thought of as complementary descriptions operating at different spatial scales, and (iii) a more realistic cortical map would be multi-dimensional. We close by reflecting on how a multi-scale, multi-dimensional conceptualisation of the cortex offers a flexible framework for investigating how dynamic cortical function maps onto relatively stable cortical structure.

articles.title: Perspective Taking Shapes Creative Performance in Human–AI Collaboration
articles.authors: Man Zhang; Yang Peng; Yajie Wang; Huiqing Hu; Shi Chen; Qingbai Zhao
articles.abstract: This study compared human–human and human–AI collaboration in creative performance and perspective-taking behavior and further examined whether the relationship between perspective-taking and creative performance differed between the two forms of collaboration. According to the actor–partner interdependence model, an individual’s creative performance is influenced not only by their own perspective-taking behavior (actor effect) but also by their partner’s perspective-taking behavior (partner effect). The results showed that: (1) In both the Alternative Uses Task (AUT) and Product Improvement Task (PIT), human–AI collaboration produced significantly higher mean idea novelty and more frequent perspective-taking behavior than human–human collaboration. (2) The effects of perspective-taking on creative performance differed between the two forms of collaboration. In human–human collaboration, both actor and partner effects of perspective-taking significantly and positively predicted idea fluency in both tasks; in the PIT, partner perspective-taking also significantly and positively predicted idea flexibility. In human–AI collaboration, in the AUT, AI’s immediate perspective-taking significantly and positively predicted both its own and its human partner’s idea fluency, whereas humans’ immediate perspective-taking significantly and negatively predicted both their own and AI’s idea flexibility. In the PIT, humans’ delayed perspective-taking significantly and positively predicted both their own and their AI partner’s idea fluency and flexibility, whereas AI’s delayed perspective-taking significantly and negatively predicted both its own and its human partner’s idea novelty. These findings indicate that perspective-taking operates differently in human–AI collaboration than in human–human collaboration and that its effects vary by collaborator role for specific tasks and creativity indicators, providing new evidence for understanding the mechanisms of creative interaction in human–AI collaboration.

articles.title: Articulation Through Iteration: The Career Readiness Pathway as a Boundary-Crossing Framework for Student Development and Stakeholder Alignment
articles.authors: Caleb Braxton Bragg
articles.abstract: The Career Readiness Pathway (CR Path; Bragg & Conway, 2026) presents career readiness as achieved through four iterative components: career-specific knowledge, skills, and abilities (CS-KSAs); core competencies; experiential learning opportunities (ELOs); and career mentorship. The framework emerged from a gap in the career readiness, higher education, and workforce development literatures: no existing framework connected students, faculty, employers, and administrators within a shared logic for understanding what college produces and why it matters. This paper extends the original framework in three ways. First, I present iteration, not sequence, as the mechanism through which career readiness develops. The original paper acknowledged that the path was not strictly sequential; this paper makes a stronger claim: iteration is the framework's developmental engine, a distinction whose consequences only became visible through operationalization. Second, I identify the articulation problem, the systematic inability of students in non-professional fields to name what they have learned in language that travels beyond the classroom, and describe the tools built to address it. Third, I follow the iterative logic to its conclusion: some CS-KSAs constitutively require multiple disciplinary perspectives to reach proficiency and cannot complete their development within any single department. For those skills, the CR Path does not break—it extends, pointing toward the pedagogical architecture such skills demand: the Translational Literacy Framework (Bragg, 2026b). Throughout, I argue that the CR Path functions not merely as a pedagogical recommendation but as a coordination framework, a shared language linking what students do in college to everyone who needs to understand it.

articles.title: Mild Punishment and Everyday Rule Compliance: Deterrent and Normative-Signaling Pathways
articles.authors: Qun Yang; 史少佳; 孟雯超; Zhuo Yang; Yang Su; Li baoqian
articles.abstract: Punishment is commonly assumed to promote rule compliance by increasing the costs of violation, but it may also communicate normative information about what people do and ought to do. The present research examined whether mild punishment—whose costs remained below the potential benefits of rule violation—promotes everyday rule compliance through deterrent and normative-signaling processes. Across four laboratory and online studies using increasingly explicit and ecologically relevant paradigms, mild punishment generally increased compliance despite leaving rule violation materially advantageous. Interpersonal impact strengthened this effect in some, but not all, studies. Study 4 further showed that mild punishment promoted compliance through both concern about material loss and changes in empirical and normative expectations, supporting deterrent and normative-signaling pathways. These findings suggest that punishment can regulate behavior not only through material costs but also by communicating normative information, highlighting the importance of considering both what punishment costs and what it communicates.

articles.title: Turning to AI Chatbots to Cope with Loneliness and Social Isolation: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Online Perceptions and Experiences
articles.authors: Ahmed Al-Asmar; Edy Henich; Vincent Paquin
articles.abstract: Loneliness is a public health concern, and people increasingly turn to AI chatbots for social and emotional needs. Empirical research on whether AI chatbots alleviate loneliness remains mixed and is constrained by a lack of naturalistic data that may not capture highly isolated individuals. This study characterized public perceptions and experiences of AI chatbot use in the context of loneliness and social isolation, drawing on naturalistic discussions from Reddit. We retrieved 930 posts and 1,095 comments from AI- and loneliness-focused subreddits. A pipeline combining LLM-assisted screening, sentiment analysis, and perspective classification with CAST topic modelling identified 79 topics organized into five themes: loneliness as a driver, bonding with an AI companion, instrumental and bounded use, dependency, and macro-level debate over the practice. Human raters verified the LLM-assisted outputs, yielding strong agreement. Chatbot use was more often positioned as a reflection of loneliness than its cause. Users held a dual stance, calling the companion “code” while continuing to relate to it as meaningful, engaging with it on terms distinct from human connection. Users credited constant availability, non-judgmental responsiveness, and memory with providing comfort, and blamed the same features for diminishing returns and dependent use. Stigma relocated disclosure into identity-affirming communities for some users while deterring it for others, deepening isolation and discouraging help-seeking. These findings position social chatbot use as a marker of unmet relational need, and carry implications for clinical practice, companion technology design, and retention-focused regulation.

articles.title: Development of noisy-channel parsing: Age-related changes in children’s prior expectations
articles.authors: Yi Ting Huang; Kuan-Jung Huang; Mackensie Blair; Chloe Wright; Sam Van Horne; Giovanna Morini; Amanda Van Horne
articles.abstract: Compared to adults, school-aged children parse sentences more slowly, incorporate discourse and world knowledge less readily, and often misinterpret infrequent and garden-path structures. While prior research focuses on isolating the cause of developmental differences, there remains a fundamental need to characterize how children’s parsing strategies interact with context properties. Adopting an eye-tracking paradigm, the current study investigates the extent to which typically developing 4- to 9-year-olds rely on prior expectations when interpreting sentence meanings in contexts that induces substantial uncertainty about who did what to whom. Across transitive and relative clause structures, children revealed distinct performance in off-line vs. on-line comprehension. While action accuracy improved with age for all sentence types, analysis of correct fixations after disambiguation revealed greater age-related changes for canonical (actives, subject RCs) compared to non-canonical structures (passives, object RCs). Age effects on comprehension of canonical structures persisted even when off-line construction-specific accuracy was accounted for. Our findings are consistent with the development of noisy-channel parsing, whereby children solve uncertainty about signal properties across development through enhanced reliance on prior expectations, which are structured according to frequent representations that generate cross-situational variability over the entirety of their language.

articles.title: The SPOT Grid: Naturalistic Images with Predefined Settings, Patterns, Objects, and Textures
articles.authors: Zall Hirschstein; Mariam Aly; Christopher Baldassano
articles.abstract:
In the natural world, higher-level visual features (e.g., scenes and objects) systematically covary
with specific lower-level constituent features (e.g., textures and patterns). This natural covariation
makes it diﬃcult to isolate aspects of behavior or brain activity that are specific to a single level of
the feature hierarchy. For example, a particular neural or behavioral response may reflect
recognition of a “jungle” scene, or it may reflect sensitivity to the lower-level features — leaf
textures, dense vertical lines, etc.
— that constitute jungle scenes. To address this challenge, we
developed a novel approach for partially decoupling higher- and lower-level features in
naturalistic images. We employed a Stable Diﬀusion image generation framework to create a
naturalistic image set in which setting–object pairings and texture–pattern pairings are factorially
combined, enabling systematic manipulation of higher-level and lower-level image content. To
validate our approach, we used state-of-the-art image processing models to confirm that
higher-level features are represented similarly regardless of their lower-level constituent features
and, conversely, that lower-level features are represented similarly regardless of the higher-level
objects/settings they constitute. We then confirmed that human participants can readily and
rapidly categorize these features in our generated images. We present the image generation
framework and introduce the SPOT (Settings, Patterns, Objects, Textures) Grid, a publicly
available stimulus set accompanied by image-specific metrics (upon request:
forms.gle/X2HpzRYUGigFS1S27). This resource provides new opportunities for investigating
hierarchical visual representations, feature binding, and abstraction across perception, behavior,
and the brain.

articles.title: Policy, Ethics, and Youth Digital Rights
articles.authors: Kelila Kahane; Chaden Noureddine; John Torous
articles.abstract:
The youth mental health crisis is well established, and social media has emerged as
a putative contributor. In the last three years, legislators, courts, schools, communities, and
industry itself have pursued a range of strategies to change how adolescents engage with social
media. Some government approaches focus on banning social media based on age, with
Australia's national ban taking effect in December 2025, and France and the UK to follow in
2027. Some US states have suggested changes to the ways adolescents are shown content on
social media, and others have suggested warning labels akin to cigarette packs, which as of this
writing have not been shown to users. At the same time, there has been some push for industry to
self-regulate and schools and families have introduced their own standards, with at least 39 states
as of this writing banning phones in schools to some degree. In sum, the landscape is fragmented
and changing quickly, but understanding its core features is essential for anyone working with
and advising children and families. In this chapter, we will map the evolving layers of regulation.
We will then examine the legal, practical, and rights-based challenges that complicate policy.
Lastly, we will close with the clinician's role in this shifting space and four priorities for future
youth social media policy.

This is a preprint of a chapter to be published in Teens, Screens, and Social Connection: An Evidence-Based Guide to Key Problems and Solutions, 2nd edition (Springer).

articles.title: Upstream of Ideology: Measuring the Values That Generate Political Positions
articles.authors: Jason W. Payne; Aisha Mir; Nathan Oesch; David Samson
articles.abstract: Existing political psychology instruments tend to measure political orientation by aggregating known political positions. As such, the resulting instruments are contaminated with the very political content they are meant to predict. Alternatively, underlying value commitments could be used but historically these have been measured only piecemeal and without a framework specifying how values produce position-taking. Sowell (2007) proposes such a framework. Sowell makes claims about human nature, knowledge, and social processes from which political orientations may be derived. The present instrument seeks to operationalize these commitments at the value level. In a large adult sample (N = 1,532), confirmatory and exploratory analyses converged on five value dimensions. Correlations with Right-Wing Authoritarianism, Social Dominance Orientation, and Conway's Left-Wing Authoritarianism showed only partial overlap. An instrument that measures values independently of positions permits questions that current tools cannot ask: whether values predict voting and other downstream behaviour more strongly under effortful reasoning, and whether ideological change is value change or merely repackaging of the same commitments.

articles.title: The Tug of War between Taxonomic and Thematic Relations in Young Toddlers
articles.authors: Kim Plunkett; Irina Lepadatu; Janette Chow; Armando Quetzalcóatl Angulo-Chavira
articles.abstract:
Adult semantic memory contains distinct taxonomic and thematic memory systems.
Whether these systems are anatomically separate or should best be characterized as
functionally separable is unclear. We review evidence for the emergence of these
memory systems during infancy and toddlerhood and describe an experiment that
pits taxonomically and thematically related objects against each other in a visual
world task. The results of the experiment indicate that toddlers (and adults) prefer to
fixate both types of foils, as compared to unrelated foils, though thematic foils tend
to attract more fixations during the later stages of an experimental trial. The latency
of initial fixations towards these semantic foils do not differ. Similar results were
obtained for adults using the same set of stimuli, though their interest in the taxo-
nomic foil evaporated halfway through a trial. These results show that toddlers are
not only sensitive to the taxonomic and thematic relations between named objects but
that the processing of these relations are different. One possibility is that taxonomic
relations are processed in a fast and automatic fashion whereas thematic relations are
