Unsupportive emotion socialization strategies were associated with less positive parenting, and supportive emotional socialization strategies were associated with more positive parenting, but only for White adolescents. Dyad race did not moderate longitudinal effects on ratings of positive parenting or adolescents’ mental health, but Black adolescents reported higher positive parenting and lower externalizing symptoms at follow-up, compared to White adolescents, controlling for earlier levels. Findings suggest often-termed “unsupportive” and “supportive” emotion socialization may show expected correlations with psychosocial outcomes more in White vs. Black dyads, implicating these distinctions as racialized concepts relevant to researchers and practitioners.

articles_hidden.title: Musica ex machina: Towards AI-supported research into mechanisms of music-based therapies and interventions
articles_hidden.authors: Daniela Ruiz; Alejandra Perez; King-Chi Yau; Che Ling Michelle Mok; Vincent Zhong; Martina de Witte; Mario Valderrama; Mark Ettenberger; Artur Jaschke
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The expanding literature on music-based therapies and interventions makes it increasingly difficult for clinicians and researchers to identify relevant evidence on treatment mechanisms, moderators, mediators, and outcomes. 

Objective: This study explored whether artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) methods could support the organisation and retrieval of information from this literature.
Methods: An automated PubMed search using the terms “music therapy”, “music intervention”, and “sound therapy” retrieved 4,396 articles. Four approaches were evaluated: (i) expert-defined terminology, (ii) KeyBERT-based keyword extraction with k-means clustering, (iii) Word2Vec-based abstract representations with k-means clustering, and (iv) a BERT-based question-answering (QA) system for retrieving specific answers and source passages.

Results: The expert-defined approach identified a limited set of frequently occurring terms, whereas KeyBERT generated a broader vocabulary and 10 clusters of related abstracts. Word2Vec produced 50 clusters, but the mean silhouette coefficient was 0.20, indicating weak cluster separation. The QA system retrieved potentially relevant passages from source articles. However, its answers and scores changed when the amount of input text or wording of the query was modified.

Conclusions: AI-supported clustering and QA methods may help clinicians and researchers navigate the growing literature on music-based therapies and interventions. However, these findings are preliminary. Further work should focus on improving domain-specific model performance and representativeness. Such systems should support literature retrieval and professional judgment rather than replace clinical expertise.

articles_hidden.title: Artificial Intelligence and Metacognitive Knowledge: LLMs Can Report Decision Weights as Faithfully as Humans in Multi-Attribute Choice
articles_hidden.authors: Trent N. Cash; Daniel Oppenheimer
articles_hidden.abstract: Users have become increasingly reliant on Large Language Models (LLMs) to complete a wide range of reasoning tasks, from managing workplace projects to giving personal advice. However, LLMs function as black boxes, leaving users with minimal insight into how they generate the responses that they do. One way that users can attempt to peek into these black boxes is by asking LLMs to explain their reasoning processes. The nascent literature on LLM faithfulness suggests that LLMs – like humans – often fail to accurately identify the information they use to inform their reasoning, suggesting a lack of metacognitive knowledge. We extend this research to the context of value-based, multi-attribute choice, tasking both LLMs and human participants (n = 436) with completing the Knowledge of Weights paradigm. Participants first completed a series of choice tasks in which they picked between homes that varied on six attributes, then self-reported the decision weight they believed they had placed on each attribute in two different formats. We found that ChatGPT4o, the oldest model tested, self-reported weights that were significantly less reflective of its choice behavior than humans. However, three newer, more-advanced LLMs (ChatGPT5, Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Flash) self-reported weights that were as accurate or more accurate than those provided by humans. These results suggest that LLMs can generate and maintain accurate metacognitive knowledge of their own decision-making processes as well or better than humans, but that this is a relatively new ability. Practical and theoretical implications are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Age as a Central Dimension of Support for Political Violence
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Lyons
articles_hidden.abstract: Using the Polarization Research Lab's large U.S. survey panel (N = 161,000) with replications across the ANES, CES, WVS, and secondary analyses of six additional studies, I show that age is a robust correlate of support for political violence. This finding appears across general population and partisan samples, multiple operationalizations of violence, different political contexts, and adjustments for inattentive or low-quality responding. Political engagement and partisan attachment do not generally account for declines across age, and sometimes predict greater support among younger adults. Antisocial dispositions such as trait aggression and need for chaos are more consistent predictors. Across every dataset containing relevant measures, these characteristics are also more prevalent among younger adults, and in several datasets, they are also considerably more strongly associated with violence among them, suggesting that age may shape how underlying dispositions are translated into political attitudes. Although cross-sectional, the consistency of these findings suggests that age should be treated as an important organizing dimension in research on political violence rather than merely as a demographic control.

articles_hidden.title: Local average treatment effects on latent outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Sanford R Student; Joshua B Gilbert; William Young
articles_hidden.abstract: Instrumental variables (IV) regression models for causal inference have received increased attention in psychology, but to date this work has largely dealt with observed, continuous variables and has not yet dealt with the assumption of heterogeneous treatment effects or a latent outcome. Yet, latent outcomes are ubiquitous in psychology and research designs involving non-binding treatments and encouragement/manipulation designs are widespread. We consider IV with a binary instrument and treatment to estimate the \textit{local average treatment effect} on a latent variable, or the latent local average treatment effect (LLATE). The LLATE, derived under the potential outcomes framework, is the average of heterogeneous treatment effects for the population of individuals whose realized treatment depends on the instrument. We show that heterogeneous treatment effects imply that a single-group SEM with residual normality of the outcome is misspecified, though this misspecification does not directly imply that LLATE estimates from such models must be biased. We propose a multiple-group estimator that accounts for heteroskedasticity implied by heterogeneous treatment effects and/or selection on gains. This model can also go beyond LLATE recovery to test for heterogeneous treatment effects and characterize compliers. We demonstrate that the multiple-group estimator recovers the LLATE with negligible bias, while two single-group estimators yield bias that is persistent, testing for heterogeneous treatment effects is possible but limited to larger samples. We conclude that IV with a latent outcome is a viable means of estimating causal effects in psychological studies and that the four-group approach is the safest way to do so. Two empirical examples illustrate the model's use in an RCT with non-compliance and in a manipulation study.

articles_hidden.title: Psychosocial determinants of cerebrovascular aging: A narrative review and conceptual framework
articles_hidden.authors: Chrystal Spencer; Gabriella M Alvarez; Rebecca G Reed; Minjie Wu; Howard Aizenstein; Peter J. Gianaros
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychosocial factors may shape brain health long before clinical symptoms of age-related cognitive decline appear. This theoretically grounded narrative review selectively synthesizes findings on psychosocial influences on white matter hyperintensities (WMH), which are neuroimaging markers of cerebrovascular aging, in otherwise healthy adults. We selectively synthesized literature on psychosocial factors, including psychological stress, depression, anxiety, trauma, and neuroticism, and their associations with WMH burden in healthy midlife and older adult samples. Evidence links multiple psychosocial factors to WMH burden, though findings are inconsistent across studies. Integrating these findings, we propose a conceptual framework in which chronic psychological stress contributes to WMH development and progression through hypertension-mediated mechanisms. The framework situates this pathway within the broader context of biological aging, cumulative stress exposure, and social determinants of health, including race and socioeconomic status. This framework is offered to guide future research on the psychosocial determinants of cerebrovascular aging and advance understanding of inequalities in brain and vascular health.

articles_hidden.title: Infant event-related positive slow wave (PSW) during a face recognition task longitudinally predicts executive functioning in childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Michaela K. Haig; Yiyu Liu; Elizabeth A. Enright; Andréa Aguiar; Susan L. Schantz; Daniel C. Hyde
articles_hidden.abstract: Although executive functions (EF) have been extensively documented to include multiple distinct but related subcomponents (i.e., working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility) in childhood, whether these distinctions are present from infancy or arise later through development remains unclear. Part of the challenge in understanding the nature of EF stems from the current lack of specificity of the common behavioral measures of infant EF, including looking time and reaching. Here we assess the potential utility of infant brain measures to provide novel insight into early EF by analyzing the longitudinal relationship between infant event-related potentials (ERPs) during a face recognition task and later EF abilities in childhood using a pre-existing dataset. Specifically, we extracted the differential sensitivity to novel compared to familiar faces from four ERP components of interest (N290, P400, Nc, and PSW) measured around 8 months of age and analyzed their relationship to parental reports of EF at 4 years of age. After controlling for language and correcting for multiple comparisons, only infant PSW predicted later childhood EF, most robustly the working memory subscale. Our results validate interpretations of infant PSW as reflecting memory updating and also suggest that working memory may already be a distinct component of EF by the end of the first year of life.

articles_hidden.title: The Cumulative Cost of Adaptation: Individual and Structural Factors Associated with Autistic Burnout Severity
articles_hidden.authors: Capucine Rebours; Jeanne Kruck
articles_hidden.abstract:
Autistic burnout is characterized by chronic exhaustion, cognitive disruption, and loss of functional skills. Despite growing interest, the incremental contribution of psychosocial and structural factors alongside established individual-level predictors has not previously been examined in a multivariate framework.
We conducted an exploratory cross-sectional study with 117 French-speaking autistic adults. An online survey included validated measures of burnout severity (ABSI-Fr), camouflaging (CAT-Q), executive functioning (BRIEF-A), autistic traits (RAADS-R), anxiety (GAD-7), and depression (PHQ-9), alongside an adapted risk factor questionnaire in which participants rated potential contributors to their burnout experience. Exploratory factor analysis identified latent dimensions of perceived risk, and hierarchical linear regression (n = 113) examined their incremental contribution above and beyond individual-level predictors.
Five latent risk dimensions were identified: Expectations-Resources Mismatch, Unaccommodating Neurotypical Systems, Sensory Overload, Task Interruption, and Self-Regulation Difficulties. Individual-level predictors collectively explained 47.7% of variance in burnout severity; structural factors contributed an additional 9.8%, for a total of 57.5% (adjusted R² = .534). Camouflaging and executive functioning independently predicted burnout severity across model specifications. The predictive contribution of autistic trait severity was substantially attenuated once structural predictors were included, consistent with a person-environment fit account. Among structural dimensions, Expectations-Resources Mismatch was the sole robust independent predictor, suggesting that the chronic mismatch between environmental demands and available resources constitutes a meaningful and structurally addressable contributor to burnout severity.
These findings support framing autistic burnout as the cumulative outcome of sustained adaptation to non-accommodating environments rather than a personal deficit, and highlight the importance of incorporating structural variables into quantitative models of burnout risk.

articles_hidden.title: Reassessing longitudinal relations between depression and suicidality among graduate students: A simulation and reanalysis of Liu et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Liu et al. interpreted longitudinal associations among depressive symptoms, suicidality, and perceived social support as evidence of reciprocal temporal influences. However, statistically significant cross-lagged coefficients do not necessarily indicate genuine prospective effects because such coefficients can arise as methodological artifacts. Using simulated data designed to reproduce the sample size and correlation structure reported by Liu et al., we examined whether the reported findings would remain consistent across alternative analytic specifications. Results varied considerably depending on the model employed. Some analyses suggested increases in subsequent outcomes, whereas others indicated decreases. When all estimates were synthesized using meta-analytic techniques, the overall effects were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that the original conclusions may be premature and that the observed cross-lagged associations could reflect statistical artifacts rather than substantive prospective influence. Consistent with multiverse methodology, we recommend the routine evaluation of alternative analytical models and the integration of findings across specifications before drawing substantive conclusions.

articles_hidden.title: The Early Segment of Long-Delay Signals Fails to Show Pavlovian Inhibitory Properties in Human Conditioned Avoidance
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Vega-Silvestre; Jose E. Callejas-Aguilera; Juan M Rosas
articles_hidden.abstract: When encountering a long-delay warning signal, organisms learn to pause their responding during its early moments. While Pavlov termed this "inhibition of delay," it remains debated whether this behavior reflects an active suppressive mechanism or a simple interval timing. We investigated the properties of this early segment using an online, arcade-style human avoidance task. Experiment 1a used a summation test to determine if the early portion of a long-delay signal could suppress avoidance behavior triggered by a separately trained excitatory signal. However, neither the long-delay signal nor a standard differential inhibitor altered responding to the excitatory signal. Experiment 1b used a disinhibition test by adding a brief, novel signal to disrupt potential active suppression. While this novel signal successfully increased responding to a standard differential inhibitor, it had no effect on the long-delay signal. Together, these findings provide no evidence of active suppression, suggesting that the early portion of a long-duration signal does not necessarily operate through standard Pavlovian inhibitory mechanisms in all inhibition of delay procedures.

articles_hidden.title: Mood recovery via positive autobiographical recall: The roles of perceived importance and emotional intensity
articles_hidden.authors: Jiaqi Zhong; Shu Imaizumi
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined how the perceived importance of positive autobiographical memories (PAMs) is associated with emotion regulation following anger and sadness induction. Utilizing a 2 (high vs. low memory importance) × 2 (anger vs. sadness induction) between-participants design, 282 adults underwent a negative mood induction via video, followed by a PAM recall task. Analysis controlling for depressive symptoms showed significant mood recovery from post-induction to post-recall, but the experimental manipulation of memory importance did not significantly affect the magnitude of recovery. Initial structural equation modeling showed that perceived memory importance was positively associated with self-relevance, reliving, imagery, and emotional intensity, but only emotional intensity uniquely predicted mood recovery. The specific indirect effect of perceived importance on mood recovery through emotional intensity was significant, although the overall model showed poor fit. Exploratory analyses focusing on emotional intensity showed a similar indirect pathway in both the anger and sadness conditions, which remained significant after accounting for emotion-regulation strategies. These findings suggest that perceived memory importance may be indirectly associated with short-term mood recovery through emotional intensity during recall, whereas its direct contribution appears limited.

articles_hidden.title: ISIT: A Frame-clustering Implicit Measure of Situated Experience
articles_hidden.authors: Aldo Gangemi; Chiara Lucifora
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction. The Implicit Situation Intensity Test (ISIT) is a method for converting participants’ verbal reports about an experience into a quantitative, per-participant implicit measure of how strongly cognitive, emotional, behavioural, and value-laden frames have been activated by that experience.
Method. ISIT operates by clustering frames extracted from the verbal report’s extended knowledge graph – the structured representation produced by the POLANYI++ neurosymbolic pipeline – into a Frame Ontology and scoring each frame’s salience for each participant on a normalised scale. The implicit measure produced by ISIT is designed to be combined with explicit measures from standardised questionnaires, implicit measures from physiological sensors, and participant profile information, in a single multivariate analysis of situated experience, producing participant-level scores, suitable for psychometric integration.
Results. We illustrate the method through the Lucifora et al. (2025) study on virtual male embodiment in a catcalling scenario (n = 36), in which a 37-indicator Frame Ontology spanning four domains (emotional states, behavioural responses, violence perception, semantic markers), whose
frame clusters entered the study’s multivariate correlation structure alongside the standardised instruments and emotion ratings; safety-related frames showed the differential correlation patterns with anger and sadness versus with fear that simpler instruments do not capture. To place the extraction itself on an auditable footing, every frame the pipeline produced was adjudicated by a tacit-aware judge (DEEPJUDGE) and human-verified: frame-level precision on a warrant criterion was high (0.95–0.96 across two foundation-model backends, with near-zero over-projection), and the two backends produced markedly more similar profiles for the same report than for different ones.
Discussion. ISIT shares with grounded theory and computational grounded theory the inductive commitment that situational structure should emerge from data, but it differs in three operational respects: it operates on structured extended knowledge graphs rather than raw text; it produces participant-level numerical scores rather than corpus-level qualitative themes; and it integrates by design with other measurement channels rather than standing as a free-standing qualitative analysis. ISIT fills the verbal-channel gap in the cognitive-science measurement ecosystem: it is the implicitmeasure complement to autonomic, behavioural, and questionnaire-based instruments, not their replacement. Convergent and divergent validity against standard implicit measures, predictive validity against behavioural outcomes, and multi-modal  integration validation are set out as a defined roadmap.

articles_hidden.title: Similarities in lexical predictive processing in children with and without dyslexia
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren K Salig; Molly Leachman; Rachel L. Eggleston; Chi-Lin Yu; Ioulia Kovelman; Jonathan R. Brennan
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence is mixed regarding whether or not individuals with dyslexia struggle with higher-level spoken language comprehension, including predictive processing. We posit that this uncertainty may be explained by experiments’ task designs—with decontextualized tasks suggesting more extensive differences in dyslexia and more naturalistic tasks suggesting equivalent language comprehension in dyslexia. Children with dyslexia (n=73) and typical readers (n=96) listened to a story during fNIRS neuroimaging. Focusing on predictive processing as a measure of higher-level language comprehension, we used GPT-2 to quantify each word’s predictability within the story’s context, allowing us to identify brain regions engaged in predictive processing. Our findings indicate similar neural responses to word predictability for children with dyslexia and typically developing readers during naturalistic listening. These results highlight the use of contextual lexical prediction during naturalistic language processing as a potential strength in children with dyslexia, while underscoring the continued importance of dyslexia screening and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: ‘It is no longer left solely to expert clinicians to define autism’: An autistic commentary on Frith (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Viney Jones
articles_hidden.abstract:
Uta Frith’s 2026 editorial in Psychological Medicine argues that autism spectrum disorder has lost clinical meaning, that many people diagnosed later in life may belong to other categories, and that the field should recover by giving more weight to careful objective observation. This commentary responds from an autistic perspective and examines three problems with the proposal.
First, the proposal depends on clinical observation. Observational assessment records how a person appears to a trained stranger in a short, unfamiliar, socially demanding appointment. Perceptual control theory holds that behaviour is the control of perception, so an observer records the side effects of control rather than the variable a person controls. Mansell et al. (2019) demonstrated observers identifying the wrong goal while watching a full task at leisure.
Second, the sources do not support the case. O’Nions et al. (2023), cited as evidence of over-recognition, reports substantial underdiagnosis. Zhang et al. (2025) describes its diagnostic-age groups as relative rather than discrete, and lists healthcare access, gender bias, stigma, ethnicity, and camouflaging among the factors it cannot separate.
Third, the proposal changes the evidential standard by speaker. Self-report is treated as treacherous where it supports an autism diagnosis, and as sufficient in the categories offered instead. Fricker (2007) names this testimonial injustice.
The commentary argues for rebuilding the construct with autistic people involved rather than pruning it, and sets out what a narrower definition would cost in a system holding 294,792 open referrals.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in generative search efficiency are not predicted by sub-clinical psychopathological traits
articles_hidden.authors: Freya Losvik; Paul Rauwolf; Neil R Bramley; Samuel David Jones
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to search complex problem spaces efficiently is a hallmark of intelligent behaviour, yet how search varies between people, and whether that variation is systematically associated with sub-clinical psychopathology, remains relatively underexplored. To address this, N = 203 adults completed a generative search task known as 'Zendo', in which the aim is to discover the hidden rules governing visual arrays of cones of varied size and colour by constructing and testing novel arrays. Two-hundred participants also completed the 53-item Brief Symptom Inventory, which measures anxiety, depression, hostility, interpersonal sensitivity, obsessive-compulsive behaviour, paranoid ideation, phobic anxiety, psychoticism, and somatisation. Analyses reveal significant individual differences in generative search behaviour that meaningfully shape learning outcomes. Individuals tailor their search to the structure of the problem space in light of the feedback that they elicit, and those who elicit a balance of positive and negative feedback narrow the problem space most effectively and show a learning advantage at test. Although we report reliable variation in sub-clinical psychopathological traits, converging analyses, including Bayes factor analysis and equivalence tests, provide positive evidence for a true null at the intersection of psychopathological traits and generative search behaviour, which is bounded at most to a small-to-moderate effect for a reliable measure of search efficiency. Overall, people show significant individual differences in their ability to search complex problem spaces efficiently, though this variation is largely orthogonal to sub-clinical psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Self-attributed success gates higher-order updating after stroke: a three-layer comparator model
articles_hidden.authors: SHU MORIOKA
articles_hidden.abstract: Stroke rehabilitation cannot be fully explained by impairment severity alone and presents three dissociations: patients who can move a paretic limb but do not use it (learned nonuse); patients with mild motor paresis who nevertheless walk slowly; and patients with unilateral spatial neglect whose recovery plateaus despite preserved compensatory capacity. We hypothesize that these dissociations reflect a shared problem in cross-layer updating. We model the self as three hierarchically coupled comparators operating over distinct temporal scales: a sensorimotor comparator (the meter), which integrates predicted and actual sensory feedback within a millisecond-scale window and provides evidence for the feeling of agency; an intention–outcome comparator (the judge), which integrates action–outcome evidence over seconds and supports judgment of agency; and a narrative-self comparator (the author), which represents a months-to-years biographical horizon. Precision-weighted prediction error provides a common currency across layers, with social input operating at each layer, from joint action to social support. The model proposes that error-based adaptation occurs within layers, whereas recovery-supporting cross-layer revision is gated by self-attribution and personal meaning. Accordingly, revision of the generative models that support recovery requires success to be attributed to the self at the intention–outcome level and integrated as meaningful at the narrative level. This update rule frames learned nonuse as hypothesized under-crediting of self-generated success, slow walking despite mild paresis as hypothesized precision misallocation, and the neglect plateau as a hypothesis-generating extension involving narrative-level updating. We derive layer-specific rehabilitation principles, including perceptual learning, agency-amplifying technology, and narrative goal-setting mapped onto the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), and state falsifiable predictions. The model complements the philosophical framework of narrative embodiment by specifying computational processes that link embodied and narrative selves and may become dissociated after stroke.

articles_hidden.title: Coupling between statistical learning and interference suppression
articles_hidden.authors: Kata Horvath; Dezso Nemeth; Karolina Janacsek; Andrea Kóbor
articles_hidden.abstract: In an ever-changing environment, synchronizing automatic and controlled behaviors is essential for successful adaptation. Yet, the relationship between these behaviors is often debated, partly because of the diverse approaches used to investigate them. The present study examined how statistical learning of environmental regularities, a process that supports automatic behaviors, and interference suppression, which contributes to controlled responding in the presence of distraction, interact when both operate concurrently. Participants completed a visual four-choice reaction time paradigm that combined a statistical learning task with the Eriksen flanker task. In this novel paradigm, a central target stimulus, surrounded by flanker stimuli, was either predictable or unpredictable based on the statistical regularities induced by the sequence of target stimuli. Statistical learning was indexed by the performance difference between predictable and unpredictable trials, whereas interference suppression was reflected by the flanker congruency effect (i.e., the performance difference between congruent and incongruent trials). Reaction times revealed a significant interaction: the flanker congruency effect was reduced on predictable trials, and the behavioral expression of statistical knowledge was larger in the incongruent than in the congruent condition. Together, these findings provide a proof-of-concept demonstration of a behavioral interaction between statistical learning and interference suppression within the present paradigm. Although this experimental design does not establish the causal direction of the interaction, the observed pattern indicates that learned predictability is associated with a reduced cost of conflicting distractors.

articles_hidden.title: Unresolved craving and the transition to snacking in daily life
articles_hidden.authors: Giuseppe Marrazzo; Trung Dung Tran; Leonardo Pimpini
articles_hidden.abstract: Snacking on calorie-dense foods is often assumed to follow from craving, yet in daily life craving and snacking are only loosely coupled. In a secondary analysis of a preregistered EMA study of 136 young women with healthy-range BMI (3, 6, or 9 prompts/day for 21 days), we examined craving, snack occurrence, perceived control over snacking, and stress around snack episodes and asked whether craving reliably precedes snacking. Because these EMA items are interval-referential, referring to the period since the previous prompt, a within-window craving–snack association conflates co-occurrence with sequence. Matched within-person comparisons showed a sharp rise in craving at snack windows, but craving at t−1 did not differ from matched non-snack windows (+1.3, q = .343) and was lower at t+1 (−5.3, q = .007), providing no evidence of pre-snack build-up and indicating a post-snack decline. Craving and snacking frequently co-occurred within the same reporting window, while unresolved craving was disproportionately followed by snacking at the next prompt. This transition was enriched 1.3–1.4-fold relative to a time-of-day-preserving surrogate distribution (p < .001) and remained reliable in a stricter day-level coupling sensitivity analysis. Low perceived control over snacking was elevated during snack-reporting windows but not before or after them, whereas stress showed only a small focal elevation. Everyday snacking was therefore characterized by a brief craving elevation, while craving without snacking increased the likelihood of snacking at the next prompt. More generally, these findings show why temporal claims from interval-referential EMA should rely on across-interval rather than within-window associations.

articles_hidden.title: Humans adaptively delay planning using cognitive maps
articles_hidden.authors: Paul B. Sharp; Eran Eldar
articles_hidden.abstract: Planning is an expensive computational operation that easily exhausts our cognitive resources. For this reason, it is critical to learn strategies to initiate planning wisely. To understand how humans adaptively initiate planning, we developed a task where humans can learn to delay planning at certain timepoints when all actions are equally likely to reach an instructed goal. Across two pre-registered studies, we show that humans adaptively delay planning, and improve in their ability to do so with experience. To explain this behavior, we formalize a model of the underlying meta-control computations. Our model demonstrates how strategies to delay planning are not learned from experienced outcomes, but rather, from searching a cognitive map of the task to determine at which points it is more valuable to delay control. We thus establish that humans can adaptively delay planning, and learn to do so by means of a cognitive map.

articles_hidden.title: ‘National IQ’ datasets do not provide accurate, unbiased or comparable measures of cognitive ability worldwide
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Sear
articles_hidden.abstract: In 2002, Lynn and Vanhanen produced a dataset which claimed to provide average ‘national IQs’ for nation-states worldwide. Despite extensive critique, this dataset, and subsequent updated versions, have been used in many empirical publications. Here I evaluate the latest version, produced in 2019 by Lynn and Becker, and show that this dataset is not fit for purpose. The primary data sources are inadequate for calculating ‘national IQs’. Most data originates from samples which are wholly unrepresentative of their national populations. Many are convenience samples with small sample sizes, collected over a wide date range (the oldest from the 1940s), often including only children and often including individuals selected because they had particular characteristics (i.e., were deliberately chosen to be unrepresentative). The transformation of cognitive test data from these sources into ‘national IQs’ involved a series of questionable assumptions and arbitrary adjustments. Some of these assumptions were based on Lynn and Becker’s prior beliefs about intelligence, including that regional and racial differences in IQ exist. These methods will result not just in error in the dataset but systematic bias. Even if representative data and appropriate methods were available for constructing ‘national IQs’, it is impossible to generate comparable measures of cognitive ability from culturally diverse populations across the globe. ‘National IQ’ datasets therefore do not provide comparable, accurate and unbiased measures of cognitive ability worldwide, and should not be used to draw inferences about global variation in intelligence.

articles_hidden.title: Developing a Generative AI Agent to Support Science Curiosity: A Theory-Informed Development and Initial Evaluation Study
articles_hidden.authors: Zepeng Liu; Ying Zhang; Haoyan Huang; Kui Xie; Xin Tang
articles_hidden.abstract: Science curiosity is a key motivational driver of learning, yet higher education often provides limited opportunities for students to pursue scientific questions through sustained and individualized support. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) creates new possibilities for designing pedagogical agents that can respond to learners’ emerging questions, provide timely feedback, and maintain inquiry across learning episodes. However, most GenAI agents in education are designed as general learning assistants rather than as theory-informed systems for supporting curiosity. Grounded in the reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition, this study aimed to develop and test a curiosity-oriented GAI agent to foster both science state curiosity and science trait curiosity among university students. The agent was developed through a process integrating theory-based functional analysis, peer consultation, user testing, and successive revision. An initial mixed-methods evaluation was conducted with 137 university students randomly assigned to either a GAI agent-interaction condition or an active self-questioning comparison condition across three science-learning sessions. Quantitative findings indicated that both conditions supported within-session increases in state science curiosity, whereas the agent condition showed greater short-term gains in self-reported trait-level science curiosity. Qualitative findings suggested that students experienced the agent as providing cognitive, affective, and protective support that helped close curiosity loops and accumulate rewarding inquiry experiences. The study contributes design principles for curiosity-oriented GAI agents and provides preliminary evidence regarding their feasibility and motivational potential in higher education.

articles_hidden.title: Attrition in the Twins Early Development Study: predictors, consequences, and corrections
articles_hidden.authors: Giacomo Bignardi; Thalia Catherine Eley; Celestine Laetitia Lockhart; Christopher Rayner; Kate Tilling; Tom McAdams
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Attrition in longitudinal studies often leads to healthier, more educated and less demographically representative samples at follow-up. The extent to which attrition impacts results from twin studies, and the efficacy of methods to correct for attrition, remains unclear. 
Methods
We address these questions using data from the Twins Early Development Study (TEDS). First, we found that baseline variables, including twin sex, zygosity, ethnicity and maternal socioeconomic status, predicted 5–7.5% of the variance in follow-up participation. Next, we examined the impact of attrition by comparing estimated means, variances, correlations, and genetic and environmental influences before and after removing participants who did not participate at follow-up. We evaluated a range of twin measures from the Year 2, 12 and 16 time points, including internalising, externalising, educational and cognitive measures. 
Results
Attrition affected means and variances, but had little material effect on correlations and genetic and environmental variance components. Finally, we evaluated the efficacy of two popular correction methods—inverse probability weighting and multiple imputation—to reduce bias, focusing on adolescent outcomes. Both methods partially reduced bias in mean estimates; however, imputation also introduced bias for some effects. 
Conclusions
Our results suggest that for the variables we examined in TEDS, correlations and genetic and environmental variance components are not strongly impacted by attrition. Imputation and weighting methods can reduce attrition bias when estimating means and variances but may introduce bias into estimates of association.

articles_hidden.title: Predictive Biases in Emotional Perception: Differential Influence of  Mood and Affective Primes in Individuals with and without Mood  Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Alexane Leclerc; Ladislas Nalborczyk; Louise Kauffmann; Yann Leprince; Josselin Houenou; Lucie Berkovitch; Pauline Favre
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction Predictive processing models perception as an interplay between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory inputs. When signals are ambiguous, perception increasingly relies on prior expectations. In emotional contexts, mood and affective primes may act as endogenous and exogenous predictions, biasing emotional perception, particularly in mood disorders, where predictions may become overly strong or unstable.
Methods Eighty-four participants (53 healthy controls, HC; 31 with self-reported mood disorders) completed an online affective priming task on unambiguous and ambiguous (morphs) facial expressions, preceded by masked or unmasked faces. Participants rated target emotions and completed mood questionnaires. Principal Component Analysis extracted latent mood dimensions. Drift Diffusion Modeling (DDM) estimated cognitive processes underlying ambiguous face perception. 
Results In HC and bipolar disorder (BD), happy primes increased positive morph categorization, while in depression (DEP), masked sad primes increased negative categorizations more than in HC and BD. Masked primes accelerated responses to morphs in HC, while BD showed faster responses regardless of priming type, with stronger facilitation than HC and DEP. No reaction time priming effects were observed in DEP. DDM revealed pre-decisional biases induced by primes, while mood only subtly influenced evidence accumulation. 
Conclusions Findings suggest group-specific predictive biases: HC used masked primes to resolve emotional ambiguity, BD showed stronger reliance on external cues regardless of priming type, and DEP showed reduced sensitivity to primes alongside a selective negativity categorization bias. These biases may underlie core clinical features of mood disorders and may point to new targets for interventions aiming to restore adaptive emotional inference.

articles_hidden.title: A Stress Beliefs Intervention Reduces Daily Somatic Symptoms and Negative Affect: Results of a Two-Center Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Susanne Fischer; Daniela Conrad; Dario Bender; Johannes Andreas Christoph Laferton
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative stress beliefs (e.g., “stress is dangerous”) have been associated with poorer stress-related emotional and physical health, including heightened negative affect and somatic symptom burden. However, evidence that interventions targeting stress beliefs can improve both daily affect and somatic symptom burden remains scarce. This two-center randomized controlled trial investigated whether a multi-session, group-based stress beliefs intervention (OPTI-Stress) could improve daily affect and somatic symptom burden. Forty university students were randomised to OPTI-Stress or a control group. The OPTI-Stress group received three weekly group sessions targeting stress beliefs. The control group received no intervention. Stress beliefs were assessed before and after the intervention/waiting period. Daily stress, positive and negative affect, and somatic symptom burden were assessed five times per day across five days before and five days after the intervention/waiting period using ecological momentary assessment. Compared with control, OPTI-Stress resulted in greater reductions in negative stress beliefs (F = 7.26, p = .011), daily negative affect (b = -0.47 [-0.917, -0.023], p = .040), and daily somatic symptom burden (b = -0.30 [-0.583, -0.021], p = .035). A multi-session, group-based stress beliefs intervention may improve daily affect and somatic symptom burden. Larger trials are needed to confirm efficacy and to evaluate whether OPTI-Stress can improve mental and physical health in the long term.

articles_hidden.title: Fifty Shades of Well-Being: Addressing an Overlooked Source of Confusion in the Science of Well-Being.
articles_hidden.authors: Joffrey Fuhrer
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite constant progress, the science of well-being remains marked by confusion, with a proliferation of competing conceptual frameworks, theoretical approaches, and measurement tools undermining both scientific progress and real-world applications in areas such as counseling, therapy, and public policy. This paper identifies an overlooked contributor to this confusion: the adoption of Philosophically Dense Concepts (PDC) into empirical science, facilitated by academic practices that favor theoretical novelty and discourage interdisciplinary collaboration. Using a conceptual genealogy of the hedonic-eudaimonic well-being distinction as a paradigmatic example, I show how such PDC, when translated from philosophy into psychology and social and health sciences, became semantically fuzzy and led to inconsistent theoretical frameworks and measurement tools. The paper concludes with recommendations on how to better deal with PDC in well-being research and the emerging science of flourishing.

articles_hidden.title: Disentangling the Effect of Letter Frequency, Bigram Frequency and Inter-item Similarity in Recognition Memory: A Global Matching Model Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Lyulei Zhang; Adam Osth
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous studies have reported a memory advantage for words with rarer letters; however, the specific sources of this feature frequency effect remain unclear. The current study aimed to disentangle the relative contributions of letter frequency, bigram frequency, and inter-item similarity to recognition memory performance through both empirical experimentation and computational modelling. Across three recognition memory experiments, we manipulated orthographic feature frequency at the level of letters (Experiment 1), bigrams (Experiment 2), and their factorial combination (Experiments 3). While both letter and bigram frequency produced mirror effects, such that words composed of rarer features showed higher hit rates and lower false alarm rates than words composed of more common features, we found bigrams as the primary driver of the observed feature frequency effects. Moreover, the relative roles of feature frequency and inter-item similarity were characterized through formal modelling. Results were fit with global matching models with words’ orthographic representations where the underlying features were either equally weighted or with weights proportional to their frequency in language. Models with differential feature weights outperformed the equal weight models, specifically in capturing target performance. Moreover, models incorporating bigram frequency, rather than letter frequency captured the feature frequency effect on hit rates in Experiment 3. The necessity of differential feature weighting was further validated through fitting with a recognition memory mega-study where differential feature weighting improved the model’s ability to capture variability in hit rates across individual words.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Browser-Based Administration of a Repeated Self-Control Choice Task on Participants’ Own Smartphones: Pragmatic and Controlled Comparisons
articles_hidden.authors: Aya Katayama; Tomohisa Asai; Daisuke Saeki
articles_hidden.abstract: Browser-based experiments administered on participants’ own smartphones offer practical advantages for psychological research, but their comparability with laboratory administration remains task- and context-dependent. This study examined whether a browser-based implementation of a repeated self-control choice task (SCT) administered on participants’ own smartphones yields data comparable to those obtained under laboratory administration. Rather than treating comparability as a single criterion, we evaluated mean levels, changes across blocks, preservation of participants’ relative standing, mean bias, scale differences, and procedural stability. In Experiment 1, we conducted a pragmatic comparison in undergraduate and non-student adult samples, allowing multiple implementation-related factors to vary as they would in realistic web-based research contexts. Self-control choices increased across blocks in all groups. Mean levels were broadly similar between web-based and laboratory administration among undergraduates, whereas adults showed fewer self-control choices in the web condition; however, this difference reflected a pragmatic bundle of differences in recruitment, testing context, device, software, and supervision, rather than an isolated administration-mode effect. Experiment 2 used a within-participant, same-device design in which participants completed the SCT under both web and lab conditions. In the with-loss condition, mean-level web–lab differences were small, but participant-level correspondence was accompanied by substantial uncertainty and possible scale differences. Comparability varied across task conditions, with weaker correspondence in conditions less suited to discriminating individual differences. An auxiliary N-back task showed no clear evidence of general performance disruption under web-based administration. Overall, browser-based SCT administration on participants’ own smartphones was practically feasible, but mean-level similarity alone was insufficient to establish methodological comparability. Evaluations of web-based repeated-choice tasks should distinguish average performance from preservation of individual differences, systematic bias, scale differences, and implementation robustness.

articles_hidden.title: Recognition Matters: Exploring Wellbeing for Students with Dyslexic-Type Challenges
articles_hidden.authors: Jane Mosco; Megan Frances Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: High school students with dyslexia, characterised by reading and spelling struggles, are at greater risk of experiencing poorer wellbeing at school than their peers. Yet there has been limited exploration of wellbeing for students with reading struggles through the lens of recognition theory. We aimed to further understand students’ wellbeing through an exploratory study foregrounding students’ views, alongside those of their educators, to inform school practices. Participants included 22 high school students aged 12-18 years (Years 7-12) from eight regional Australian NSW schools, and 23 of their educators. High school students participated in student focus groups or interviews (Phase 1) and could join student art workshops to elicit insights through images and text (Phase 2). These served as stimuli for subsequent teacher interviews (Phase 3) and intentionally brought students’ views into dialogue with educators', strengthening qualitative data findings. Thematic Analysis generated three overarching factors that potentially influence student wellbeing: 1) Interpersonal interactions and relationships at school; 2) teaching and learning attuned to students’ needs, and 3) relational pedagogy. Further theoretical analysis utilising recognition theory deepened understanding, highlighting how intersubjective and structural recognition can both shape students’ wellbeing. Students and educators highlight significant learning and wellbeing entanglement, describing instances of recognition and misrecognition at school. School psychologists can help improve conditions by reduce instances of misrecognition whilst increasing recognition. Mutual dialogue with students alongside attuned neurodiversity-affirming quality teaching and school practices can simultaneously create the conditions for recognition, enhancing students' learning and wellbeing.

articles_hidden.title: Language Mixing Does Not Disrupt Word Recognition in Singaporean Bilingual Children
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Paquette; Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Language mixing is common in bilingual communities, yet its consequences for children’s real-time language processing may depend on characteristics of individual switches and language experience. Little is known about whether the naturalness of a switch influences word recognition. We examined word recognition in 44 English-Mandarin bilingual 3–6-year-olds in Singapore, where language mixing is prevalent. Using a Looking-While-Listening task, children heard target words in English- or Mandarin-only, or natural or unnatural mixed-language sentences. Target preference was higher for natural mixed-language than English-only trials. Responses to mixed-language speech varied by switch direction, with greater target preference when switching into children’s more dominant language. Age, language exposure, and vocabulary knowledge were not associated with overall target preference. These findings suggest that bilingual children efficiently recognize words in mixed-language speech, while responses to switches are shaped by switch direction and language experience, highlighting the importance of considering community-specific patterns of language use.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond a Single Factor: Evidence of Multidimensionality in the ASQoL and Its Implications for Scoring
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah Viner; Philipp E. Sischka; Anna E. Kornadt
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose
The Autism Specific Quality of Life measure (ASQoL) is widely used to assess aspects of QoL
that are important to autistic people. However, concerns have been raised about its
psychometric validity, with limited examination beyond the initial validation study, particularly
with older age groups. Furthermore, cross-country measurement invariance remains untested.
Thus, the present study investigated the ASQoL's psychometric properties in autistic adults in
mid- to late life in the UK, Germany, and Luxembourg.

Methods
A total of 383 autistic adults aged 40 and over completed the ASQoL, mental health and
loneliness measures. Using dimensionality assessment techniques and an item response theory
bifactor modelling approach, we examined (a) the factor structure of the ASQoL, (b) the
implications of using total scores, (c) cross-country measurement invariance and (d)
associations between the ASQoL and known correlates of QoL.

Results
The ASQoL exhibited multidimensionality and imposing a unidimensional model led to
substantially biased person scores and inflated reliability estimates. A bifactor model with one
general factor and two specific factors (“social” and “barriers”) exhibited a substantially better
fit. The measure demonstrated at least partial invariance across the UK and
Germany/Luxembourg. The general factor and specific factors explained unique variance in
mental health and loneliness outcomes, further supporting the bifactor structure.

Conclusion
Using the ASQoL total score results in psychometrically biased estimates. Researchers should
examine the underlying factor structure of the ASQoL in their data before conducting analyses.
Furthermore, we urge caution comparing mean scores across countries.

Keywords: ASQoL; autism; quality of life; psychometric properties; item response
theory; measurement invariance

articles_hidden.title: Political Perspectives and Religiosity Contribute to Homonegative Attitudes among Sicilian Psychologists
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Julie Vargo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Mental healthcare professionals’ pathologizing views of LGBT+ people can compromise adherence to deontological principles and the very effectiveness of mental health interventions. This study aimed to explore homonegative attitudes of licensed psychologists in Sicily, Italy. The study replicated a survey previously administered in other Italian regions for data collection, to promote systematic comparability and future replication studies. Descriptive and exploratory data analyses were conducted. The sample (n = 727) corresponded to 8% of psychologists registered in the region in 2021. When exploring participants’ assumptions on the origin of homosexuality, a lack of knowledge on the topic of sexual diversity and its normal variations emerged. Moreover, 27% of participants partially or completely agreed that a professional should help a patient/client change their sexual orientation, despite the ban on conversion practices established by the Italian Psychologists Association. Participants describing themselves as religious and right-wing politically affiliated held higher levels of homonegative attitudes, beliefs and opinions. Homonegative attitudes emerging from politically conservative and religious groups should be further explored, to ascertain whether underlying constructs, such as authoritarianism, are determining the observed trends. These findings also evidence the need for more thoughtful training experiences that can help psychologists deconstruct negative stereotypes on sexual identities.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Visual Articulatory Gestures and Orthography in Perceptual Training  of Non-Native Phonemic Contrasts
articles_hidden.authors: Chotiga Pattamadilok; Sophie Restoy; Michael Douglas Tyler; Pauline Welby
articles_hidden.abstract: Experiments on non-native phonemic contrast learning typically use either lexical or perceptual training. However, few studies have compared their efficiency using comparable protocols. In our previous study (Pattamadilok, Welby, & Tyler, 2022), we applied a lexical training protocol to examine the contribution of articulatory and orthographic cues to new word learning. Native speakers of French were trained to associate unknown objects with minimal-pairs of new English pseudowords differing in the initial /f/ versus /θ/ phoneme, a contrast that does not exist in French (e.g., fedge, thedge). The presence of an orthographic cue during training led to an overnight improvement of both retention of new word-object associations and the ability to perceive the /f/-/θ/ contrast. Here, we employed the same material and assessment tasks while employing perceptual, rather than lexical training; that is, the visual cues were presented during a phoneme discrimination training. The benefits of the visual cues differed from those of the initial study. While both articulatory and orthographic cues enhanced phoneme discrimination ability during the training phase, only the articulatory cue yielded an overnight improvement in perceptual ability without generalizing this benefit to the retention of word-object associations. Together, these two datasets demonstrate that, even in well-matched experimental protocols, different training methods can yield distinct learning outcomes. Optimal training protocols must consider the complex interplay between the level of language representations targeted by the training, the differential benefits of input modality, and the short- versus long-term training effects on different processing levels.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive and Clinical Predictors of Camouflaging and Autistic Burnout Severity in Autistic Adults: A Structural Equation Modeling Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Capucine Rebours; Jeanne Kruck
articles_hidden.abstract:
Autistic burnout is a debilitating condition characterized by exhaustion, loss of skills, and reduced tolerance to stimuli, yet its cognitive and clinical predictors remain poorly understood. This study examined whether autistic traits, executive dysfunction, and mental health predict camouflaging, and whether camouflaging mediates their relationship with autistic burnout severity.
A sample of 115 autistic French-speaking adults reporting varying degrees of autistic burnout severity completed validated self-report measures. Structural relationships were tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM).
The model explained 21.3% of variance in camouflaging and 36.9% in burnout severity, with approximate model fit (SRMR = 0.094). Executive functioning difficulties and autistic trait severity significantly predicted camouflaging, while mental health did not meet the pre-specified significance criterion as a direct predictor of camouflaging. Camouflaging emerged as the strongest predictor of burnout severity, followed by a direct effect of mental health. Significant indirect effects on burnout via camouflaging were found for both executive functioning and autistic traits, consistent with a partial mediating role for camouflaging.
These findings provide initial quantitative evidence consistent with camouflaging as a central pathway through which individual cognitive and clinical characteristics relate to burnout severity, and underscore the importance of examining structural and psychosocial contributors.

articles_hidden.title: No convincing evidence for prospective effects between harsh parental discipline, negative automatic thoughts, and depressive symptoms: A reanalysis and comment on Fu et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Fu et al. (2026) recently reported significant associations in a cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) analysis and interpreted these findings as evidence of mutually reinforcing relationships among harsh parental discipline, negative automatic thoughts, and depressive symptoms. Yet it is well established that cross-lagged coefficients can arise from statistical artifacts rather than genuine prospective influences. To evaluate the robustness of these conclusions, we fitted a set of alternative models to data simulated to approximate the characteristics of the dataset analyzed by Fu et al. Depending on the analytic specification, estimated relationships among the study variables were either positive or negative. When these alternative estimates were synthesized meta-analytically, the resulting effects generally did not differ significantly from zero. Consequently, the associations reported by Fu et al. may reflect spurious rather than substantive prospective relationships, rendering strong interpretations premature. Researchers should remain cautious when interpreting correlations, including cross-lagged effects, obtained from observational data. We therefore recommend evaluating findings across multiple analytic specifications and drawing conclusions only after considering the consistency of results across models.

articles_hidden.title: From Symptoms to Structures: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Major Depressive Symptom Networks
articles_hidden.authors: Charles Jack Strathdee; Phuong Linh Dang; isabel Krug; Litza Kiropoulos; Charles Benjamin Malpas
articles_hidden.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading condition examined using network analysis. However, meta-analytic evidence is limited for MDD symptom network studies. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses reporting guidelines, we searched Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL and bibliographies of previous literature for articles that have produced MDD symptom networks. After screening, 104 articles (N = 875,852) were included in this review, consisting of 85 cross-sectional and 19 temporal network analysis studies. A random-effects Meta-analytic Gaussian Network Aggregation (MAGNA) of MDD symptom networks was estimated based on available data. Despite a pronounced variation in MDD measures and sample demographics, findings consistently showed that depressed mood and fatigue emerged as the most central symptoms. Collectively, this systematic review and meta-analysis underscores network analysis as a technique for understanding MDD symptom dynamics and one that has the potential to improve psychological interventions. Ongoing efforts toward intensive longitudinal datasets and improved reporting practices represent two key avenues for MDD network analysis research.

articles_hidden.title: Chunking improves working memory via compression, not direct retrieval from long-term memory
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Manuel Chau Delgado; Joel Shebioba; Anna Pitt; Matias J. Ison; Nicholas E. Myers
articles_hidden.abstract: Working memory (WM) capacity is severely limited. Chunking, the process of grouping related items in WM, circumvents this limit and drastically improves performance. Despite decades of research, the mechanism underlying this benefit remains debated. One account proposes that statistical regularities allow multiple items to be compressed into structured WM representations, whereas another argues that structured associations are stored in long‑term memory (LTM) and reinstated at recall, effectively offloading storage demands. These accounts imply fundamentally different interactions between WM and long-term knowledge, yet in most paradigms, they make indistinguishable behavioural predictions. Here, we dissociate them by introducing small, continuous trial‑to‑trial variations in the hues of learned colour pairs, allowing us to test whether chunking benefits arise from compressed memory for the current hue (WM) or retrieval of long‑run feature means (LTM). Across two delayed colour report experiments, chunking reliably improved recall relative to unchunkable arrays. Participants remained sensitive to trial‑specific feature variations, indicating that responses were not driven by retrieval of feature means from LTM templates. At the same time, responses were systematically biased toward each item’s long‑run mean, especially on chunkable trials. To explain this bias, we fit psychophysical models derived from the competing compression and LTM‑retrieval accounts. The compression-based model, in which compression produces graded biases toward learned means within WM, outperformed the LTM-retrieval and baseline models. In a second experiment, we examined whether these biases arise during encoding/maintenance or at the recall stage. Cues in the maintenance period indicating which item would be probed improved recall accuracy but did not reduce bias toward learned structure, indicating that the bias arose during encoding or early maintenance rather than retrieval. These findings show that chunking enhances WM by integrating learned structure into WM representations through compression, rather than by offloading to LTM.

articles_hidden.title: Sonority-driven stress: codas in Brazilian Portuguese
articles_hidden.authors: Guilherme D. Garcia; Kevin Ryan
articles_hidden.abstract: This study provides experimental evidence for sonority-driven stress in Brazilian Portuguese (BP). We show that speakers systematically prefer final stress when the ultima contains a sonorant coda {N, l, r} rather than the obstruent coda {s}. The effect is specific to the ultima, the position where weight is otherwise most relevant to BP stress. A lexical analysis of monomorphemic words corroborates the experimental pattern: /s/-final words receive final stress less often than sonorant-final words. We further show that this asymmetry cannot be reduced to morphological factors (the plural suffix /-s/ is invisible to stress), nor to a sonority-free account on which final /s/ is a prosodic appendix. These findings bear on a contested question in metrical phonology (whether, and how, segmental sonority conditions stress placement), on which experimental evidence has so far been scarce.

articles_hidden.title: Observers exhibit greater caution and faster evidence accumulation when identifying joint versus individual actions
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad; Patric Bach; Anna Zamm; Natalie Sebanz
articles_hidden.abstract: Coordination requires anticipating and adapting to others' actions in real time. While research has shown that observers predict others’ solo actions, little is known about how predictive processes change when observing joint actions. We tested whether, for joint actions, observers form (1) stronger predictions because they expect others to act more reliably due to social considerations (e.g., commitment), or (2) weaker predictions because they expect coordination to introduce additional sources of error (e.g. due to miscommunication). To this end, we presented participants with image sequences depicting either one or two actors building a block tower. The solo actor added blocks, alternating between her left and right hands, while the joint actors took turns adding blocks with one hand each. Participants made speeded responses to identify the side from which the block came. Of interest was how accurately participants identified the block’s side when it violated the alternating pattern, with errors indicating anticipation for the alternating pattern to continue. Participants were less likely to make anticipatory errors on violation trials for joint actions, indicating weaker action predictions (Study 1). Hierarchical drift-diffusion modelling (Study 2) revealed that this was due to participants accumulating sensory evidence more rapidly and responding more cautiously on joint action trials, relying less on their prior expectations about an action’s identity and more on incoming sensory information. This strategy might serve to enable observers to flexibly update their predictions about unfolding actions in the face of coordination-induced errors.

articles_hidden.title: Food Concepts and Eating Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Jérémie Lafraire
articles_hidden.abstract:
Food enjoyment is often understood as a matter of sensory pleasure or biological need satisfaction. This chapter argues that such a view overlooks how conceptual knowledge and the inferential processes it supports shape both food enjoyment and food aversion. The food domain is epistemically opaque in a broad sense: many of the properties that matter for eating are not directly available to perception, it blurs the distinction between artifacts and natural kinds, and the same item can be categorized through different, and sometimes competing, schemes.
The chapter discusses two cognitive responses to this opacity. Food neophobia is interpreted as a cautious response to non-recognition under asymmetric risk. Psychological essentialism is then analyzed as a way of stabilizing what foods really are by attributing to them hidden natures, origins, and causal histories on which category membership ultimately depends. The chapter shows that essentialist reasoning can generate pleasure, rejection, and even aestheticized forms of disgust. Finally, the chapter extends this framework from essentialized foods to essentialized eating relations, including relations between foods and meal contexts and between foods and eaters, showing how food pleasure and rejection may depend on perceived fits among foods, contexts, and selves.

articles_hidden.title: What Features of Mind-wandering episodes Predict their Recall? A Think-Aloud Study
articles_hidden.authors: Arya Gilles; Arnaud D'Argembeau; David Stawarczyk
articles_hidden.abstract: Mind-wandering (MW) refers to task-unrelated thoughts that are decoupled from the surrounding environment. Although often considered disruptive, MW has been proposed to support functions such as creativity, problem solving, and planning, which presuppose that its content is encoded in memory and later retrieved when relevant. Yet, factors determining whether MW episodes are remembered or forgotten remain poorly understood. To address this gap, participants completed a 10-min Think-Aloud Protocol, during which they continuously verbalized their thoughts, followed by an unexpected free-recall test after a one-day delay. After recall, participants rated the phenomenological characteristics of each MW episode, allowing direct comparisons between recalled and forgotten episodes to identify content-related and temporal predictors of recall. Our results showed that recall probability increased with episode length and for episodes involving other people, rated as more important, goal-related, structured, deliberate, routine, and recurrent in daily life. Recall probability was also higher for episodes with temporal and functional future orientation, whereas episodes with no apparent function were less likely to be recalled. In a combined model including all significant predictors, only episode length, involvement of other people, future temporal orientation, and absence of function uniquely predicted recall. In addition, recall exhibited primacy and recency effects, as well as a tendency to follow the original chronological order of MW episodes. Together, these findings indicate that memory for MW episodes is not random but rather shaped by their phenomenological characteristics and temporal dynamics, suggesting that it follows organizational principles similar to those observed for externally perceived stimuli.

articles_hidden.title: Automated analysis of vocal maturity from daylong audio recordings of children with Angelman, Down, and fragile X syndrome
articles_hidden.authors: Lydia Wiernik; Boshang Yin; Elika Bergelson; Bridgette Kelleher; Amanda Seidl; Lavechin
articles_hidden.abstract: The emergence of canonical babbling is a critical milestone that predicts later spoken language outcomes, often varying in timing and frequency in children with neurodevelopmental diagnoses. However, measuring when and how often children babble canonically has historically required time-intensive manual annotation and specialized expertise. Here, we tested an automated pipeline for measuring vocal maturity from daylong audio recordings. The pipeline identifies child vocalizations using a speaker segmentation algorithm, transcribes them into the International Phonetic Alphabet using BabAR (a multilingual phoneme recognition system), and derives vocal maturity estimates from the resulting transcripts. We compared this pipeline’s performance against manual annotation using 220 daylong recordings from 157 U.S. children 4-60 months across four groups: children with Angelman (n = 39), Down (n = 45), and fragile X (n = 20) syndromes, and children with no known diagnoses or genetic risk factors (n = 53). Automatic vocal maturity estimates, operationalized as canonical proportion (CP, the proportion of canonical vocalizations), correlated strongly with manual estimates per-group and overall (Pearson’s r between 0.90 and 0.98). Automated and manual estimates also converged on the same pattern of CP trajectories: low risk children demonstrated rapid early gains; children with Down and fragile X syndromes showed slower upward trajectories; and those with Angelman syndrome exhibited downward trajectories. Our approach reduces months of manual annotation to overnight processing, making existing large-scale datasets, such as LENA® recordings, reusable and opening vocal development research to larger, more diverse populations.

articles_hidden.title: Social prescribing link workers’ views of training and perceived training needs for supporting people experiencing loneliness: a qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Robert J Booth; Ayabonga Sithole; Joely Wright; Emeline Han; Daisy Fancourt; Daniel Hayes
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Link-worker training varies, although supporting people experiencing loneliness can involve emotionally difficult conversations. This study explored their training, preparedness and further learning needs.
Methods: Fifteen participants with experience of delivering or managing social prescribing took part in semi-structured interviews lasting 35–75 minutes. Reflexive thematic analysis compared their previous experience, training, preparedness and work with different age groups.
Results: Four themes were developed: (1) different starting points and uneven preparation; (2) relational skills and role boundaries; (3) understanding loneliness and tailoring support; and (4) learning through practice and ongoing support. No participant described a dedicated loneliness course. Previous counselling, mental-health, social-work, youth-work or community experience often helped participants feel prepared. They wanted learning on how loneliness varies across the life course, sensitive conversations, mental health, tailored responses, boundaries and escalation. They also valued simulation, supervised practice, peer learning, lived-experience input and knowledge of local services. Training alone could not address unsuitable referrals or gaps in community provision.
Conclusions: All link workers need introductory training covering loneliness, relational skills, boundaries and escalation, alongside learning suited to the people and places they serve. Supervision, reflection and protected learning time should reinforce this. The aim is safe, person-centred practice within a clear non-clinical role, not to turn link workers into therapists.

articles_hidden.title: Improving Brain-Behaviour Causality with Neurofeedback
articles_hidden.authors: Theo Ferreira Marins; Michal Ramot; Aurelio Cortese; Ranganatha Sitaram; Guilherme Wood
articles_hidden.abstract: A robust and reliable causal mapping of human brain function requires ruling out multiple sources of bias and confounding. New standards for causal inference suggest that the causal evidence provided by traditional methods, such as lesion mapping and non-invasive brain stimulation, may have critical gaps. Based on recent evidence, we discuss how brain-behaviour causality has been assessed in humans with well-established tools, and the extent to which emerging techniques, such as neurofeedback, provide additional insights. Finally, we introduce the Causal-Neurofeedback, a unifying framework based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) that dictates experimental and analytical choices designed to address new standards for causality with high granularity. This framework consists of manipulating fine-grained neural signatures and adopting key experimental and analytical control strategies to improve causal robustness. We conclude by discussing the potential of neurofeedback, through this framework, to provide robust causal evidence across diverse experimental contexts.

articles_hidden.title: What to pre-register to severely test theories: Thirteen years of lessons from editing Registered  Reports
articles_hidden.authors: Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: Severe theory testing is greatly facilitated by concisely laying bare before the study is run the essence of the scientific process. (See for example the Study Design Template of Peer Community In Registered Reports.) Testing a theory involves testing a nexus of claims each of which plays an inferential role in deciding whether the evidence counts for or against a substantial theory. Each claim should be explicitly stated in a way that shows what is at stake in testing that claim. The substantial theory is the most general claim that could have evidence count against it - and ideally should be explanatory (having an internal structure that is not free to vary). Psychologists have not been very good at explicitly stating what claim is actually at scientific stake. It should be made clear what theory is being tested by each stated prediction. Predictions should be statistically modelled with a specified test that allows evidence both for or against the prediction.  The study should be shown to have a size that could show the theory wrong. How the test will be used to draw conclusions for or against each theory should be specified. This whole structure should be stated so concisely and systematically there is no verbiage to hide behind - the skeleton of the scientific process laid naked so that its integrity can be easily evaluated. The structure can be debated, then the inferential chain nailed down as data collection commences. Researchers can change their mind later - but in full transparency of what is happening.

articles_hidden.title: The Nature and Origins of Depression in Late Life: Restoring the Focus on Severe Illness
articles_hidden.authors: Malcolm Forbes
articles_hidden.abstract: Late-life depression is used for states ranging from understandable sadness to psychotic or melancholic illness. Divergent prevalence estimates partly reflect the fact that clinical judgement, diagnostic interviews, and symptom questionnaires do not count the same phenomenon.
