This Special Article argues for a conservative clinical boundary that preserves the reality and priority of severe depressive illness and avoids treating every painful response to adversity as disorder. Ordinary low mood may remain responsive to context and serve regulatory or social functions. Disorder requires harm together with evidence that the regulation of mood, motivation, bodily function, or cognition has failed. Severe late-life depression is considered as a multilevel process that changes over time. Historical and modern inpatient and electroconvulsive therapy cohorts show heterogeneous routes into illness, coupled disturbances of movement, belief, nutrition, sleep, and cognition, rapid treatment response in some patients, and substantial recurrence. Clinically, this view gives greater weight to context, the observed mental state, collateral history, bodily compromise, and longitudinal course. Research should recruit patients with severe illness, use repeated low-burden measurements, and explore dynamic models to improve the prediction of meaningful future outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Exogenous Valuing: A Resource-Rational Account of Openness to Enviornmental Influence
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander de Guzman; Sara Aronowitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Our environment can influence what we like. Advertisements may lead you to care about trendy foods, or a friend may push you towards a genre of music. Yet, the adoption of values from the world around us is not typically within the scope of theories of rationality in philosophy and cognitive science. In this paper, we take a first step in understanding how environmental influences on values fit into a picture of rationality. Leveraging work on persistent attentional biases, we argue that exogenous direction of attention can under some conditions drive value change through two connections: in the moment attention leading to the acquisition of longer-term attentional patterns, and longer-term attentional patterns driving the agent’s structuring of tasks. These changes are intimately related to values, and on some accounts constitute value change. Crucially, we argue that openness to environmental influence on values is not an unfortunate flaw that we happen to suffer, but an efficient, resource-rational solution to a constrained optimization problem.

articles_hidden.title: The cogmod R Package: Easy-to-Use Bayesian Cognitive Models for Reaction Times, Choices and Subjective Ratings, with Applications to Computational Neuropsychology
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Makowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive tasks produce structured distributions of reaction times, choices, and subjective ratings, yet these data are often reduced to condition means before analysis. This can obscure differences in variability, distributional shape, and the latent processes that generate behaviour. We introduce `cogmod`, an R package that brings Bayesian cognitive models into the regression workflow used by psychologists. `cogmod` implements descriptive response distributions, evidence accumulation models, and models for bounded ratings as brms custom families, allowing model parameters to be predicted by covariates and random effects using familiar formula syntax. Fitted models remain standard brmsfit objects and therefore support established tools for priors, diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, model comparison, and post-processing. Across worked examples, we show that this framework enables direct comparison of competing decision models, quantifies the reliability of model parameters as individual-level measures, and reveals clinically relevant differences that are invisible in conventional mean-based analyses. By placing models spanning the descriptive-to-generative continuum within a common Bayesian regression framework, `cogmod` lowers the practical barrier to richer analyses of cognitive data and makes the choice of model an empirical question rather than a software constraint. `cogmod` is openly available at .

articles_hidden.title: Editorial Perspective: Connecting Transdiagnostic Mechanisms Targeted in Cognitive Behavioral Therapies with Empirically-Based Symptom Dimensions
articles_hidden.authors: Kasey Stanton; Jack D Burke; Helena Towne; Isabella Whitesides
articles_hidden.abstract: Various avenues of transdiagnostic research hold promise for improving diagnosis and treatment but remain fragmented in some ways. We provide recommendations for integrating dimensional assessment guided by the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) framework into clinical practice by more effectively connecting the HiTOP with social-cognitive vulnerability (SCV) mechanisms targeted in cognitive behavioral and third-wave therapies. Specifically, we present concrete ideas for (a) comprehensively understanding HiTOP symptom dimension-SCV associations, (b) integrating measure development efforts spanning the HiTOP and SCV literatures, and (c) sharpening terminology for improving construct description and clinical communication. We draw on studies from the 2026 Special Issue of JCPP Advances on Transdiagnostic Approaches to Child and Adolescent Mental Health (e.g., Carrington et al., 2026; Lloyd et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026) that provide helpful examples illustrating these points, and we use these study examples to demonstrate how HiTOP-based assessment connects with personalized treatment planning.

articles_hidden.title: Conventional psychometric practices preordain support for unidimensionality of diagnostic criteria sets: DSM-5 substance use disorder as a case example
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph F. Sexton; Abbe Knutsson; Ashley L. Watts
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychometric methods are inseparable from contemporary psychiatric classification efforts but were not developed with psychopathology in mind. Here, we consider how conventional psychometric approaches are ill-equipped to characterize the structure of mental disorders and lead researchers to adopt unidimensional conceptualizations of them. Using the DSM-5 substance use disorder criteria set as a case example, we examine the validity of a unidimensional factor model in a large epidemiologic sample (n = 104,944) across 11 classes of psychoactive drugs. Traditional fit indices, factor loadings, and eigenvalues appeared to justify a unidimensional model, but evidence for unidimensionality faltered when using updated model fit indices, model-based fit benchmarks, and manipulating the extent of skew by restricting analyses to symptomatic individuals. Exploratory factor analyses further underscored evidence of multidimensionality in substance use disorder. We situate our findings in the historic literature that documents the hazards of underfactored models and offer suggestions for future classification efforts.

articles_hidden.title: Neural Representations of Personally Familiar and Experimentally Familiar Faces Across Adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Stefani Morgan; Emma Tripp; Sophie D. Allen; Chris B. Martin
articles_hidden.abstract: Face recognition is thought to reflect complementary functions of two brain networks. A core system is thought to support perceptual processing of faces, whereas an extended system represents affective and biographical knowledge that supports familiarity-based discrimination. However, the representational format of face-evoked responses within structures comprising each system is not well understood. Here, we applied RSA to fMRI data to characterize the representational structure of personally familiar, experimentally familiar, and novel faces in younger and older adults. This approach revealed that perirhinal cortex (PRC), a node in the extended face processing system, represented personally familiar and experimentally familiar faces in distinct patterns of activity in young adults; personally familiar faces were repelled from one another, whereas experimentally familiar faces were drawn near one another. Corresponding results from PRC in older adults demonstrated that the representational distinctiveness of experimentally familiar faces, but not personally familiar faces, was preserved across the lifespan. In contrast to young adults, a representationally distinct code for personally familiar faces was revealed only in the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) of older adults, which is a key node in the core face processing system. Comparing across regions of interest also revealed that pSTS was representationally distinct from both the extended system and other structures comprising the core system. Lastly, we found that activity patterns in the fusiform face area and occipital face area of young adults predicted response times on a behavioral oddball task in which personally familiar and novel faces were pitted against one another.

articles_hidden.title: Double-check listening effort in adults with cochlear implants, and precise effort timing by listeners with typical hearing
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Winn; Lexi Olson; Abbey L. Thomas; Miski Mohamed; Katherine Teece
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives
Effortful listening can be a persistent source of strain for people who have hearing loss. Previous experiments have mainly described effort as varying from less to more, overlooking how listening goals might call for more effort at specific moments and less effort at other moments. This study tested listeners’ ability to aim listening effort at specific times containing key speech information, and to reduce effort when it is less needed. 
Design
Adults with typical hearing (TH) or with cochlear implants (CIs) completed a speech perception task where sentences were presented twice in immediate succession. If the sentence were initially presented clearly and in full, its repetition contained no new information. Alternatively, the initial presentation could contain a word masked by noise, demanding the listener seek out that specific word when the sentence was repeated with that word restored. Listening effort was assessed using concurrent measures of pupil dilation, microsaccade rate, and blinks. Each was analyzed using generalized additive mixed-effects modeling to determine when effort increased and decreased. 
Results
Adults with TH devoted less effort to speech repeated with no new information, showing less pupil dilation, less microsaccade inhibition, and less blink inhibition, compared to their responses to the first presentation of the sentence. They also showed stronger responses timed precisely to the moment of a restored key word when it became available in the repetition. However, listeners with CIs showed notable deviation from these patterns, including increased rather than a decreased pupil dilation when listening to a repetition of a sentence already heard fully intact. Additionally, their pupil dilations, microsaccades, and blinks were less precisely timed to key words previously missed.
Conclusions
Listeners with typical hearing can aim their effort at precise moments where information is needed, and reduce effort when listening is not necessary. Listeners with cochlear implants spread their effort across a wider range of time, and exert extra effort of “double-checking” their perceptions. The temporal control of effort is discussed as a dimension of listening that could underlie reports of fatigue and listening strain among people who use cochlear implants.

articles_hidden.title: Music as mindfulness: Focused listening reduces negative mind-wandering and strengthens attention networks
articles_hidden.authors: Carl-Richard Villanger Løberg; Stefan Koelsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative mind-wandering, a core component of rumination, is a transdiagnostic risk factor for psychiatric conditions. Here we tested a new focused music-listening method in which music served as the object of a mindfulness-like attentional practice, with sensorimotor synchronization used to stabilize attention. Healthy adults with elevated propensity for rumination (N = 77; Music n = 22, active control n = 30, passive controls n = 25) were randomized to a four-week intervention. Participants in the Music group assembled playlists of personally meaningful, positively valenced songs and practiced focused listening combined with simple sensorimotor synchronization, such as tapping or paced breathing. The active control group used a Cognitive Behavioral Therapy-informed micro-learning app, while passive controls completed experience sampling only. Daily smartphone-based experience sampling revealed reductions over time in negative mind-wandering in both active intervention groups, whereas passive controls showed no comparable change. Weekly questionnaire measures showed similar but weaker effects. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (n = 39 with complete sessions) demonstrated a pre- to post-intervention increase in task-evoked activity of the Extrinsic Mode Network in the Music group only, suggesting training-related enhancement of externally oriented attention systems. These findings identify focused music listening as a scalable form of music-based mindfulness, link its behavioral benefits to large-scale attention-network activity, and highlight its translational potential for mental health interventions and everyday well-being.

articles_hidden.title: TripTally: An Open-Access Calculator of Labor Costs Across Psychedelic Therapy Delivery Models
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Downey; Ellen Bradley; Daniel Dickison; Joshua Woolley
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy is generating substantial clinical interest, yet despite growing economic scrutiny, a practical question has received surprisingly little attention: how do specific delivery decisions drive cost? Labor costs—typically the dominant cost component of psychedelic therapy delivery—depend on a tangle of interacting design choices: the number, length, and staffing of treatment sessions (including provider qualifications, group versus individual format, and medical backup requirements), and local hourly wage rates. Together, these factors can produce order-of-magnitude differences in per-patient cost that resist easy estimation and are rarely modeled explicitly, making rational planning difficult. As psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy moves from clinical trials and state-licensed programs toward anticipated Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval, each stage bringing distinct staffing, regulatory, and reimbursement conditions, the need for flexible cost modeling is clear. To make these trade-offs visible and tractable, we developed TripTally (https://danieldickison.github.io/pat-calculator/), an open-access web calculator that, unlike existing economic analyses of fixed scenarios, allows any researcher, clinician, or policymaker to estimate labor costs using staffing configurations and wage rates specific to their own context.

articles_hidden.title: An agent’s partial knowledge of a hidden array impacts infants’ representations of object quantity
articles_hidden.authors: Melissa M. Kibbe; Jessica Beal Applin
articles_hidden.abstract: Infants can represent the quantity of a set of hidden objects, but if the number of objects hidden in a location exceeds three, infants experience “catastrophic forgetting”, failing to represent even a subset of the objects. Infants’ representations of an object also are impacted by other agents’ visual access to an object; infants represent what an agent observed about an object instead of what they themselves observed. Here, we asked whether an agent’s partial visual access to a set of objects would impact infants’ representations of the set’s quantity, and if so, whether this impact would apply when infants’ own representational limits are exceeded. Ten-14-month-olds (n=85) completed an ordinal choice task in which they watched an experimenter distribute different quantities of crackers across two containers, and were allowed to crawl to one of the containers to obtain its contents. We manipulated whether the quantities hidden were within or outside of infants’ capacity limits (1 vs. 2 or 1 vs. 4) and whether a second experimenter, who infants saw had also observed the crackers being distributed, had partial knowledge of the arrays (observing 1 vs. 1 or 1 vs. 2, respectively) or no knowledge. Infants’ container choices suggested that they used the observing agent’s perspective to represent quantity whenever she had partial knowledge of the arrays. Our results suggest that an agent’s quantity representations may mandatorily supplant infants’ own, and this may allow infants to represent a subset of objects in situations in which they would normally experience catastrophic representational failure.

articles_hidden.title: Relationship between purely verbal and numerical–verbal long-term memory in the standard conjoint recognition model
articles_hidden.authors: Michał Obidziński; Nina Bażela; Kinga Szafron; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on verbatim and gist long-term memory (LTM) within Fuzzy-Trace Theory (FTT) has largely employed verbal and pictorial materials, with limited attention to numbers. This study compares LTM for sentences without numerical content (purely verbal memory) and sentences containing Arabic digits (numerical–verbal memory) and examines the applicability of the standard Conjoint Recognition (CR) paradigm to numerical–verbal material. Participants completed six counterbalanced CR blocks: three assessing purely verbal memory and three assessing numerical–verbal memory. Results showed a strong correlation between performance across material types, with no significant difference in overall accuracy. However, significant differences emerged in underlying memory processes measured by multinomial processing tree modeling: familiarity parameters were higher for numerical–verbal memory, whereas identity and bias parameters were higher for purely verbal memory. These findings suggest that although LTM for purely verbal and numerical–verbal materials is closely related, it differs in underlying processes.

articles_hidden.title: Thought Probe Response Options, but not Probe Frequency,  Affect Thought Report Validity in a Cued Recall Episodic Memory Task
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel W. Cox; Michael J. Kane; Christopher N. Wahlheim
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to maintain focus on task-relevant information is often measured using thought probes requiring participants to report their momentary attentional states. Research using this approach demonstrates substantial heterogeneity in thought probe features, raising concerns about measurement validity. In episodic memory tasks, such variation may systematically affect the precision of estimating attention–memory relationships. Two between-subjects experiments examined effects of varying thought probe response options and frequency on thought reports, subsequent recall, and their association. Participants completed paired-associate, cued recall tasks including thought probes during study. In Experiment 1, 128 participants received probes with either two response options (on-task vs. off-task) or three (on-task vs. task-related vs. off-task). Including a task-related option reduced on-task more than off-task reports between groups. Recall was more accurate for items presented during on- than off-task states, especially when the task-related option was included. In Experiment 2, 128 participants received two or four probes during study, always with three response options. Thought report rates and memory accuracy did not differ significantly between probe frequencies. These findings suggest that, within cued recall paradigms, attention–memory associations are generally robust to thought probe variation, but three-option probes that isolate task-related thoughts may characterize attentional states more precisely.

articles_hidden.title: Reimagining Empirical Aesthetics Through Cross-Cultural Perspectives
articles_hidden.authors: Kohinoor Monish Darda; Dyutiman Mukhopadhyay; Nandini Chatterjee Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-cultural empirical aesthetics examines how aesthetic experience converges and varies across cultural contexts. In this short review, we synthesize recent work on visual art, music, and dance, with emphasis on the audience perspective within the psychology of art: how viewers, listeners, and observers perceive, feel, evaluate, and make meaning from artworks and performances. Evidence suggests that some perceptual and affective cues, such as harmony, contour, tempo, loudness, rhythm, and synchrony, can support partially shared responses, while aesthetic judgments are shaped by enculturation, expertise, familiarity, identity, context, and culturally patterned attention. These findings suggest that aesthetic experience arises from dynamic interactions between universal perceptual mechanisms and culture-specific interpretive frameworks. Using rasa theory from Indian aesthetics as a test case, we argue that cross-cultural empirical aesthetics should embrace a pluralistic, culturally grounded approach that employs theoretical constructs that best capture aesthetic experience within diverse artistic traditions.

articles_hidden.title: Attentional network processing in children and adults shows comparable behavioural effects but distinct ERP and time–frequency activity
articles_hidden.authors: Praghajieeth Raajhen Santhana Gopalan; Otto Loberg; Jarmo Hamalainen; Paavo H. T. Leppänen
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual attention comprises alerting, orienting, and executive-control networks. Although these networks are behaviourally evident in childhood, age differences in the neural processes supporting them remain unclear. Typically developing 12–13-year-old children (n = 77) and 19–33-year-old adults (n = 21) performed the Attention Network Test while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Behavioural performance was assessed using reaction time and accuracy. Neural processing was examined using event-related potentials (N1 and P3 amplitudes and latencies) and induced time–frequency analyses of theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), and beta (13–25 Hz) band activity. Significant alerting, orienting, and executive-control effects were observed in reaction time, with children responding more slowly overall than adults. Children showed longer N1 latencies than adults during the orienting comparison, indicating slower early target-related processing. Alerting cues increased target-related N1 amplitudes similarly in both groups. Children, but not adults, showed larger P3 amplitudes during incongruent than congruent trials, suggesting greater conflict-related neural processing during executive control in late childhood. Time–frequency analyses showed that alerting modulated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity similarly in both groups. Orienting-related theta activity differed between age groups, with children showing higher theta power for spatial- than centre-cue trials, whereas adults showed lower theta power for spatial- than centre-cue trials. Alpha-band activity also differed between orienting conditions similarly in both groups. These findings indicate that children and adults can show comparable behavioural attentional network effects despite differences in neural processing. The results further suggest that electrophysiological measures of attentional processing continue to mature beyond late childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health, Functional Impairment, and Self-Efficacy in Teachers: The Role of Stress-Management Strategies
articles_hidden.authors: Raquel Messi Falcoski; Fernando Eduardo Padovan-Neto
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Teachers frequently experience psychological symptoms that may impair occupational functioning. This study examined the associations between sociodemographic, professional, and psychological factors and mental health, functional impairment, and self-efficacy, with a focus on stress-management strategies within a social cognitive framework.
Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted using snowball sampling with 536 teachers and 307 adults from the general population. Participants completed validated measures of anxiety (GAD-7), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), perceived stress (PSS-10), functional impairment (WHODAS 2.0), and teacher self-efficacy (TSES-SF). Additional data included sociodemographic and professional characteristics, mental health diagnosis, treatment status, and engagement in stress-management strategies. Group differences were analyzed using chi-square and t-tests, while Spearman correlations and multiple linear regressions were used to identify predictors.
Results: Teachers reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, depressive symptoms, perceived stress, and functional impairment compared to the general population. Within the teacher sample, older age and engagement in stress-management strategies were consistently associated with lower psychological distress. Functional impairment and perceived stress negatively predicted self-efficacy.
Conclusion: These findings highlight the importance of behavioral strategies and contextual factors in supporting teachers’ mental health and professional functioning. Interventions targeting stress management may help reduce functional impairment and promote self-efficacy in educational settings.

articles_hidden.title: Validation Study of the Swedish Child Post-Traumatic Cognitions Inventory in Maltreated Children
articles_hidden.authors: Ole Hultmann; James Stålsjö; Valgeir Thorvaldsson; Anke de Haan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: 
Dysfunctional post-traumatic cognitions (PTCs) play a central role in the development and maintenance of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The Child Post-Traumatic Cognitions Inventory (CPTCI) is a self-report questionnaire assessing dysfunctional PTCs in minors, available in a 25-item original version (CPTCI-25) and a 10-item short form (CPTCI-10). 

Objective: 
This study evaluated the psychometric properties of the Swedish CPTCI (CPTCI-Swe) in its original and short form.  

Method: 
The sample consisted of 77 patients (9-17 years) at a Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) clinic, all with histories of exposure to intimate partner violence and/or child abuse. Data was collected prior to treatment. 

Results: 
Confirmatory factor analyses supported the two-factor structure - permanent and disturbing change (CPTCI-PC) and fragile person in a scary world (CPTCI-SW) - for both versions. Internal consistency was good across the four subscales, although lower for the CPTCI-10 Scary World subscale. The observed associations between dysfunctional PTCs and psychopathology were not as consistent as in previous studies, but we nevertheless consider convergent validity for both the CPTCI-25 and CPTCI-10 established. Neither the CPTCI-25 nor the CPTCI-10 predicted PTSD diagnosis. However, both subscales of the CPTCI-25 emerged as significant predictors of continuous clinician-assessed posttraumatic stress symptoms. 

Conclusions: 
Overall, the CPTCI-Swe is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing dysfunctional PTCs in maltreated children. Depending on time-constraints or when the CPTCI is used repeatedly for monitoring purposes, the CPTCI-10 might be a good alternative to the CPTCI-25. More validation studies on the CPTCI-10 across trauma types are needed to fully understand its clinical utility

articles_hidden.title: Trends in well-being of liberal women
articles_hidden.authors: Paul H. P. Hanel
articles_hidden.abstract: Conservative influencers, politicians, and writers have repeatedly claimed that feminism has made liberal women unhappier. Using an 11-wave repeated cross-sectional design spanning from 2002 to 2023 across 15 European countries (N = 279,530), we found no support for this claim. Well-being did not decline for liberal women aged 14-17, 18-29, and 30-44, nor did it for liberal men, or for moderate or conservative women and men. In fact, the well-being of liberal women aged 45 years or older rose over the study period, as did the well-being of conservatives and moderates, for women and men. These findings remain robust across different operationalisations of well-being, political orientation, and age grouping. Cross-sectionally, well-being declined with age, even as the older groups' well-being rose over the study period. Further, conservatives reported higher well-being consistently across age, gender, and survey rounds. Together, our findings contradict a central claim of prominent conservative writers and politicians.

articles_hidden.title: The risk-stigma paradox: How risk-focused HIV prevention produces and distorts vulnerability
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah E. Stutterheim
articles_hidden.abstract: We currently have a diverse toolbox of HIV prevention modalities that can be leveraged to reduce new HIV infections. Unfortunately, a focus on changing risk perceptions in HIV prevention persist despite limited evidence. In this viewpoint, I describe how an individual-level focus on risk perception fuels stigma while stigma obscures risk perception. I argue that efforts to bolster HIV prevention should focus first and foremost on ascertaining the various determinants of uptake for the various prevention modalities available, and acknowledge that people’s preferences for prevention strategies are neither universal nor static. We should therefore engage in ongoing monitoring of the many sociocognitive and structural determinants of the different prevention modalities over time, and make our sexual health services free from stigma, judgment, and risk eligibility criteria.

articles_hidden.title: Image Database for Everyday Affective Spaces (IDEAS): an open-access database of high-quality and standardized affective images of indoor environments
articles_hidden.authors: Fatih Deniz; Yvonne A. W. de Kort; Linghan Zhang; Kynthia Chamilothori
articles_hidden.abstract: We spend about 90% of our time in indoor environments. These environments strongly influence our health, behavior, and psychological well-being, yet we know surprisingly little about how indoor characteristics shape our affective and approach-avoidance responses. This gap exists partly because previous studies relied on small, self-curated image sets created based on differing criteria, limiting generalizability and reproducibility. To address this, we introduce the Image Database for Everyday Affective Spaces (IDEAS), an open-access dataset of 1,800 high-quality, real-world photographs from the six most frequented indoor environments: offices, living rooms, dining rooms, kitchens, bedrooms, and restaurants. These images were rated by 900 participants on valence, tense arousal, energetic arousal, and approach-avoidance in two online studies. We examined the relationship between valence, tense arousal, and energetic arousal in our dataset using seven theoretical models. Our analyses revealed a strong negative correlation between valence and tense arousal ratings of indoor scenes, whereas valence and energetic arousal, as well as energetic arousal and tense arousal, were largely independent, providing support for the three-dimensional core affect model. Demographic variables had minimal influence on affective ratings, while participants showed high inter-rater reliability. IDEAS offers a valuable resource for advancing environmental preference and broader environmental psychology research, enabling more nuanced investigation of how specific indoor environments and their characteristics shape emotional experience. Beyond normative affective scores, the dataset includes a comprehensive set of low-, mid-, and high-level visual features, individual ratings, demographic data, and copyright information. The IDEAS dataset is available on the OSF (https://osf.io/g9ze5) and GitHub (https://github.com/FatihcDeniz/Image-Database-for-Everyday-Affective-Spaces).

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Triangular Human-Machine Interface Icons on Takeover Performance from L3 automation: Behavioural, Ocular, and Psychophysiological Insights
articles_hidden.authors: Courtney Michael Goodridge; Gaëtan Merlhiot; Natasha Merat
articles_hidden.abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) can create interactive Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) that adapt to the road environments and/or attract driver attention to important information. Higher levels of automation may take humans out-of-the-loop, hence effective HMIs are paramount for facilitating fast and safe takeovers. This driving simulator study investigated whether low-level visual features of AR-HMI icons impacted the orientation of driver attention and consequential takeover performance. Drivers (N = 14) in a within-participants experimental design used an SAE Level 3 automated driving system, either with or without a mentally loading non-driving related task (NDRT), before being presented with a takeover request (TOR) to merge into ongoing traffic whilst travelling on a 2-lane motorway. TORs were either urgent (time to collision [TTC] = 7 s) or planned (TTC = 30 s) and consisted of an auditory tone paired with a circular icon, a triangular icon, or no icon. Eye movements, electrodermal activity, and vehicle dynamics were recorded to investigate driver takeover performance. Results indicated that triangular AR-HMI icons were associated with an earlier physiological arousal response, faster takeover times, and increased minimum TTCs for urgent TORs. Conversely, no evidence was found for beneficial takeover performance for the planned TORs. These results indicate that HMI icon shape may facilitate faster and safer takeovers during critical events. We discuss how angular shapes are linked to improved takeover behaviours and why the benefits may only be present if drivers have optimal mental workload.

articles_hidden.title: Tailoring relative phase estimation methods to movement shape. A practical approach to estimate the Arnold tongue with testing codes on human data and simulation of discrete and continuous signals.
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Le Guennec; julien lagarde
articles_hidden.abstract: The relative phase ϕis a key variable in the study of coordination dynamics across many disciplines. Several estimation methods exist and are used interchangeably in the study of sensorimotor synchronization, despite the limitations of certain methods when analyzing inharmonic (aka discrete) movements. In this study, we document differences in estimates of key variables used to describe coordination dynamics, the mean ϕand its standard deviation, calculated using a pointwise method and using the Hilbert transform with signal centering or with a correction of the non-linearity. We applied these methods to experimental data from a tapping task with an incremental increase in metronome frequency. The increase in frequency allowed us to observe differences between methods in inharmonic movements at low synchronization frequencies and in near-sinusoidal movements at higher frequencies. To complement this analysis, we conducted stochastic numerical simulations of non-linear oscillators and with ghost attractors to mimic signals from discrete movements. We compared the mean and SD ϕestimates to a gold standard based on the Arnold tongues framework. Our experimental and simulation results show that the mean and SD ϕestimates obtained from the Hilbert transform are biased for inharmonic signals, we recommend using the pointwise method in this context. With near-sinusoidal signals, both methods provide equivalent results. We propose a practical approach to estimate the quality of synchronization, sharing free testing codes, human data and simulation of discrete or continuous movements.

articles_hidden.title: Strategy Use Determines the Changing-State Effect: Evidence from a Strategy Instruction Manipulation
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Radloff; Judith Schweppe
articles_hidden.abstract: The changing-state effect (CSE), the finding that changing-state sound disrupts working memory more than steady-state sound, is a robust empirical phenomenon of auditory distraction. Attentional capture accounts and interference-by-process accounts make opposing predictions under which condition the effect occurs. Only interference-by-process accounts predict that the CSE depends on order processing in the focal task. Previous demonstrations of a CSE in non-order-based tasks have been interpreted as evidence for attentional capture, but quasi-experimental evidence indicates that participants’ use of order-based strategies in the non-order-based missing scan task may have caused the CSE (Hughes & Marsh, 2020). However, this finding was not replicated in a subsequent study (Radloff & Schweppe, 2026). Therefore, we manipulated strategy use experimentally in a missing scan task under steady-state and changing-state sound by instructing participants to apply rehearsal (order-based) or a checklist strategy (non-order-based). The findings are consistent with interference-by-process accounts with a significant interaction between sound and instructed strategy such that a significant CSE was observed only in the rehearsal group. Moreover, Bayesian effect size estimation indicated strong evidence for a null effect in the checklist condition.

articles_hidden.title: Momentary Associations of Autonomic Nervous System Activity Measured via Heart Rate Variability with Affective and Arousal States
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Hachenberger; Anna Exner; Denny Kerkhoff; Sebastian Ludyga; Axel Mayer; Christian Rominger; Andreas R. Schwerdtfeger; Angelina Sutin; Claudia Voelcker-Rehage; Sakari Lemola
articles_hidden.abstract: Affective and biophysiological states are inherently linked, which is partly due to the activity of the autonomic nervous system. Heart rate variability is a commonly used indicator of autonomic nervous system activity. The present study examines the associations between heartrate variability indicators with perceived arousal and affective states using two 14-day experience sampling studies combined with ambulatory assessment of physical activity and heart rate variability. A total of 197 individuals (72.1% female) aged 18 to 29 years provided 11,269 measurements with complete surveys and corresponding valid accelerometry and electrocardiography data. In particular, we investigated heart rate and the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) as indicators for cardiac activity. We found a positive within-person association between heart rate with positive affect and perceived energetic arousal, while the association was negative for RMSSD. The opposite pattern was found for negative affect. No associations of heart rate or RMSSD with perceived tense arousal or generally on the between-person level were found. Mediation analyses revealed that the associations between heart rate variability and affect were partly mediated by perceived energetic arousal. The results of this study suggest that intraindividual fluctuations in heart rate variability indicators are associated with fluctuations in energetic arousal and affect. This study suggests a primarily state-dependent nature of the relationship between the autonomic nervous system activity and affect and highlights perceived energetic arousal as a potential mediator between them.

articles_hidden.title: A Short Scale for Assessing the Desire for Governmental Intervention in Climate Policy Research
articles_hidden.authors: Sonja Grelle; Wilhelm Hofmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Effective climate mitigation requires governmental intervention, yet its success hinges on public support. The Integrative Public-Policy-Acceptance (IPAC) framework identifies the desire for governmental intervention (DGI) as a motivational foundation of climate policy acceptance. A brief, validated DGI measure is valuable for research designs comparing multiple policy types and domains or using repeated assessments, but is currently missing. In this preregistered study (N = 500, Germany), we developed and validated a short DGI scale combining conceptual item screening, dimensionality analyses, and model-based short-form optimization (Ant-Colony-Optimization, graded-item-response theory). Starting from 20 items, we established a unidimensional 15-item pool and derived a 3-item scale with excellent reliability, strong factor loadings, and high item information. In multilevel analyses of repeated policy evaluations nested within participants, DGI predicted climate policy acceptance over and above problem awareness, providing evidence of incremental and discriminant validity. We additionally provide the full 15-item pool for broader content coverage.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Singularity and Compassion Fade: Replication and extensions of Experiments 1a and 3 in Västfjäll et al. (2014)
articles_hidden.authors: Lewend Mayiwar; Shubin Yu; Yooeun Jeong; Richard Rekdal; Tuan Viet; Ihor Rudko; Matilda Dorotic; Gilad Feldman
articles_hidden.abstract: Västfjäll et al. (2014) found support for “compassion fade”, that affective reactions and charitable donations decrease as the number of victims increases. In a pre-registered experiment with a U.S. sample recruited through CloudResearch Connect (N = 1207), we conducted a replication and extension of Studies 1a and 3 from Västfjäll et al. (2014). In the replication of Study 1a, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims (one vs. two children) on hypothetical donation amount, positive- or negative affect, perceived impact of donations (all |d|s ≤ 0.16) or for any mediation effects. In the replication of Study 3, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims or relatedness on donation amount, perceived need, positive affect, or negative affect of donations (all ηp2 ≤ 0.012). Bayesian analyses indicated moderate to strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for most effects, and equivalence testing indicated that seven of eight effects were smaller than our conservative smallest effect size of interest. Overall, our findings fail to replicate the original compassion fade effects and suggest limitations on their generalizability across various dependent measures and contexts. Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A2TGB

articles_hidden.title: Autistic Burnout Severity Items – French Translation (ABSI-Fr)
articles_hidden.authors: Capucine Rebours; Patrick Raynal; Jeanne Kruck
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic burnout is increasingly recognized in the literature as a state of profound physical and mental exhaustion, distinct from occupational burnout and depression, experienced by autistic adults. The Autistic Burnout Severity Items (ABSI), developed by Arnold et al. (2023), is among the few tools designed to capture the severity and multidimensional nature of this experience. Here we present the ABSI-Fr, a French-language translation and cultural adaptation of the ABSI. The translation followed a structured process: an initial French translation was produced and reviewed by an independent translator, then examined for clarity and acceptability by two successive panels of autistic adults (n = 12 and n = 8), whose feedback informed revisions to wording and phrasing. The finalized version was back-translated into English and compared to the original by an independent translator to verify conceptual equivalence. The ABSI-Fr comprises 26 items distributed across six dimensions (emotional and somatic distress, social withdrawal and communication, cognitive dysfunction and slowing, general exhaustion, autistic self-awareness and self-regulation, and memory disruption), plus three additional items assessing meltdown-related behaviours, reported separately and excluded from the total score. Items are rated on a 7-point Likert scale, with a "not applicable" option for items that do not apply to the respondent's situation. This preprint provides the instrument, administration instructions, and scoring guidelines to make the ABSI-Fr available to French-speaking researchers and clinicians. A separate psychometric validation study, examining the factor structure, reliability, and validity of the ABSI-Fr, is currently underway and will be reported elsewhere.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging Rodent and Human Cognition: A Framework for Translational Cognitive Assessment in Brain Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Silvia Gimenez; Alvaro Colomina; Marina Esteve; Antonio Perrote; Paula Matas; Claudia Cos; Marta Pardo Andres
articles_hidden.abstract:
Neurocognitive dysfunction is a core feature of psychiatric, neurodegenerative, and addictive disorders, exerting a profound impact on functional outcome, quality of life, and long-term prognosis. Across conditions, impairments in learning, memory, attention, and executive function often persist beyond symptomatic remission and are poorly addressed by current treatments, which have historically prioritized affective, motor, or psychotic symptoms over cognition. Despite substantial advances in cognitive neuroscience, translation between preclinical findings and human cognitive outcomes remains limited, reflecting persistent challenges in how cognitive constructs are operationalized and assessed across species. 
This review provides a timely and integrative perspective on translational cognitive assessment by critically examining how classical and emerging rodent paradigms contribute to understanding human cognitive dysfunction within a co-clinical framework. Rather than advocating for a single optimal model, we propose a framework based on methodological pluralism, arguing that cognitive dysfunction is multidimensional and therefore requires complementary experimental approaches selected according to the cognitive construct and research question under investigation 
Classical behavioral paradigms remain indispensable because of their historical continuity and mechanistic value, whereas newer technologies (including touchscreen testing, automated home-cage systems, immersive virtual reality, and AI-assisted behavioral analysis) provide complementary strengths in construct validity, standardization, and alignment with human cognitive assessment. 
By explicitly linking experimental design choices to cognitive constructs, neural accessibility, and translational goals, this review outlines key considerations for selecting and combining paradigms in preclinical studies of cognition. We frame technological innovation as a means to refine construct validity and cross-species alignment rather than as a replacement for established methods. By integrating methodological advances with principles of construct validity and cross-species alignment, this review provides a conceptual framework for improving translational cognitive research and for guiding the selection of behavioral paradigms in studies of psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Selective attenuation of neural responses to own infant's face in early motherhood: A longitudinal MEG study
articles_hidden.authors: Elisa Vuoriainen; Piia Astikainen; Xueqiao Li; Qianru Xu; Santeri Yrttiaho; Mikko J. Peltola
articles_hidden.abstract: The transition to parenthood is associated with heightened neural responsiveness to infant cues, particularly to one’s own infant. Yet it remains unclear how this sensitivity changes with caregiving experience. Magnetoencephalography was recorded from 16 first time mothers viewing images of their own infant, an unfamiliar infant, and an unfamiliar adult at two timepoints spanning infancy and early toddlerhood. We examined early orbitofrontal activity (~140 ms), structural face encoding (M170, ~170 ms), and later motivated attention indexed by the late positive potential (LPP, ~300–600 ms). Source-level brain data were analyzed with a depth-weighted minimum-norm estimate. Results showed that early LPP responses in the fusiform cortex and late LPP responses in fusiform and occipital regions were larger for own infant faces at the first session but decreased to the level of other faces by the second session. In contrast, early orbitofrontal activity and M170 responses were not modulated by face type or session, and M170 responses showed high temporal stability. These findings indicate that neural activity associated with motivated attention to one’s own infant attenuates across early motherhood, whereas early responses reflecting perceptual and affective processes remain stable. The findings provide longitudinal evidence for changes in maternal neural reactivity to one’s own infant.

articles_hidden.title: The significance of SIGs: Reflections from the first five years of the EHPS Habit Special Interest Group
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Gardner; Robert Edgren; Daniel John Phipps; Eike Kofi Buabang; Eleonoora Hintsa Figueiredo; Barbara Mullan; Phillippa Lally
articles_hidden.abstract: Since 2011, the EHPS has supported several Special Interest Groups (SIGs). SIGs are networks designed to connect EHPS members who have shared interests, facilitate knowledge exchange, and establish collaborations outside of the annual conference. Fifteen years on, seven SIGs exist within the Society, supporting networks of members including those with interests in methodological approaches, social justice and representation, theory and application. In this paper, we draw on our experiences of five years of running the EHPS ‘Habit’ SIG to illustrate some of the benefits that SIGs confer on their members, and the broader health psychology community. We provide examples of how the Habit SIG has allowed its members to steer the course of habit research in health psychology, created a forum for generating and debating new ideas, and strengthened collaborations and community while also supporting career development among early career researchers. We present the Habit SIG as a blueprint for how specialisms within the EHPS can flourish through the establishment and maintenance of SIGs.

articles_hidden.title: The Perceived Impact of Confidence on Therapeutic Process and Effectiveness: An International Qualitative Exploration with Schema Therapists
articles_hidden.authors: Liam Spicer; Andy Allen; Robert Brockman; Clare Wilson; Joanne Brooker
articles_hidden.abstract:
Therapist confidence is increasingly recognised as an important variable that influences the
therapeutic alliance, technique delivery, and client outcomes. Within schema therapy, confidence
may be shaped by the therapists’ own early maladaptive schemas and mode activation, yet little
empirical work has explored how schema therapists understand this relationship. This qualitative
study examined schema therapists’ perceptions of the factors that influence their confidence,
how confidence shapes their therapeutic work, and how confidence develops over time. Twenty-
two schema therapists, either accredited with or in the process of accreditation with the
International Society of Schema Therapy, completed an anonymous online qualitative survey.
Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes and 10 subthemes were
generated. The first theme, lack of confidence and perceived impacts, described the influence of
personal schemas including defectiveness, failure, and self-sacrifice on therapists’ confidence,
emotional attunement, and engagement with schema therapy techniques. The second theme,
changes in confidence, outlined how self-awareness, personal therapy, supervision, accreditation,
and client outcomes contributed to the development of confidence across the professional
lifespan. The third theme, perceived benefits of confidence on client work, highlighted how
confidence supported emotional attunement, flexibility in the use of therapeutic techniques, and
creativity in session. Overall, the findings show that confidence is a dynamic and relational
process that interacts with therapists’ own schemas and professional experiences. Supporting
therapist confidence through schema focused supervision, personal schema work, experiential
learning, and training may enhance attunement and the effective delivery of schema therapy.
Implications for supervision, training, and future research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Tales of the unexpected: psychedelic trial design solutions
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Carhart-Harris; Will Alexander Lucas; Lorenzo Pasquini; Alexa Molinaro; Hannes Kettner; Patrick A. McConnell; Jennifer Mitchell
articles_hidden.abstract: This article spotlights problematic assumptions and practices in clinical psychedelic research that together hamper the field’s ability to demonstrate causal identification, contributing to confusion and misunderstanding: (1) the main problematic assumption is that pretreatment expectancy causes therapeutic response; while expectancy predicts response to most treatments, it is becoming increasingly clear that the same is not true for psychedelic therapy—and we offer a plausible hypothesis for why; (2) the main problematic practice is the double-blind procedure, which is ecologically invalid, ethically questionable, and fails to achieve its purpose (causal identification) due to functional unblinding; we propose alternative trial designs that can circumvent the need for participant blinding while improving our ability to draw strong inferences regarding the causal action of psychedelic therapy.

articles_hidden.title: Scaling Fidelity Across States: The Effects of Fidelity of Delivering of the Pathways-to- Success Identity-based Motivation Program on Student Trajectories
articles_hidden.authors: Daphna Oyserman; Alysia Burbidge; Yahan Huang; Nicholas Sorensen
articles_hidden.abstract: Students commonly wish for futures requiring educational credentials but (mis)interpret their metacognitive difficulty when thinking about or working on school tasks and goals as implying that these futures are not for them, undermining their goal striving and outcomes. Prior research documents that teachers can train other teachers to deliver Pathways-to-Success–a supporting identity-based motivational program–and that students who receive it with fidelity have more positive academic trajectories. This paper addresses the concern that promising program results often fail to replicate across contexts and at scale by examining the effects of the fidelity with which Pathways-to-Success is delivered on student trajectories across context and at scale. In six cohorts in two federally funded cluster-randomized trials, we assess the total effects of fidelity on student trajectories, controlling for their baseline scores on outcomes of interest and whether their school was randomly assigned to treatment or delayed treatment. We nest students (N=4892) in the classrooms in which they received Pathways-to-Success (n=200). Our structural equation models reveal that students who receive Pathways-to-Success with higher fidelity have better trajectories–they attain higher GPA and standardized math proficiency scores, are at lower risk of course failure, miss a smaller proportion of instructional days, and score higher in social-emotional competency. Regarding depression, almost half of students in our sample are at risk of depression (>CES-D cutoff score); fidelity directionally but not significantly reduces symptom frequency. Receiving Pathways-to-Success with fidelity provides a scalable, context-stable path to support students’ identity-based motivation and bolster their academic and well-being trajectories.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the role of coping strategies, personality traits and mindfulness with self-care in leukemia patients
articles_hidden.authors: Fatemeh Khajeh Hasani Rabari; Fatemeh Rezaei; Fatemeh Mirzai; Fatemeh Sedighi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Leukemia is one of the most common cancers, and several factors play a role in aggravating the disease process. The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between coping strategies, personality traits, and mindfulness with self-care in leukemia patients.
Materials and Methods: The research design was descriptive-correlation. The statistical population of the research included patients with leukemia in Shariati and Sina hospitals in Tehran in the second half of 2023. 250 people were selected by the convenience sampling method. The data were collected using the Coping with Stressful Situation Questionnaire (CISS), the Neo Five-Factor Personality Characteristics Questionnaire, the Freiburg Mindfulness Questionnaire Short Form (FMI-SF), and the Self-Efficacy Self-Care Questionnaire (SUPPH) and analyzed with a step-by-step regression test with SPSS software.
Findings: The results showed that the relationship between self-care and problem-oriented, emotion-oriented and avoidance strategies and the characteristics of extroversion, openness to experience, adaptability, conscientiousness and mindfulness has a significant positive relationship and a significant negative relationship with neuroticism. Also, the results showed that mindfulness, problem-oriented strategy, neuroticism, openness to experience and conscientiousness predict a total of 58% of the variance of self-care in patients with leukemia.
Conclusion: Considering the effect of problem-oriented strategy, neuroticism, openness to experience and conscientiousness in self-care, it is suggested to organize courses to improve self-care in order to improve psychological health and increase self-care in patients with leukemia.

articles_hidden.title: Does Looking Like Meat Help? Visual Similarity and Consumer Evaluations of Plant-Based Steaks
articles_hidden.authors: Bojana Većkalov; Femke van Horen
articles_hidden.abstract: Plant-based meat alternatives (PBMAs) are often developed to be as similar to animal meat as possible, yet the extent to which such similarity benefits consumer preference remains unclear. Across two online studies (total N = 809), we examined how visual similarity to meat, as a central cue guiding consumers’ decision making at point-of-purchase, shapes evaluations of plant-based steaks using a comparative judgment paradigm. In both studies, plant-based steaks that were perceived as more similar to meat steaks were generally liked more. However, this relationship was not uniform across consumers. Vegans and vegetarians, as well as frequent PBMA consumers preferred lower levels of visual similarity, with evidence for diminishing returns at very high levels of similarity. Omnivores preferred visual similarity to be as high possible, whereas flexitarians fell in between. In sum, our findings suggest that visual similarity is generally beneficial, but the strength and shape of this relationship shifts depending on consumer segment and characteristics. These findings have implications for sustainable product design and marketing.

articles_hidden.title: Musica ex machina: Towards AI-supported research into mechanisms of music-based therapies and interventions
articles_hidden.authors: Daniela Ruiz; Alejandra Perez; King-Chi Yau; Che Ling Michelle Mok; Vincent Zhong; Martina de Witte; Mario Valderrama; Mark Ettenberger; Artur Jaschke
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The expanding literature on music-based therapies and interventions makes it increasingly difficult for clinicians and researchers to identify relevant evidence on treatment mechanisms, moderators, mediators, and outcomes. 

Objective: This study explored whether artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) methods could support the organisation and retrieval of information from this literature.
Methods: An automated PubMed search using the terms “music therapy”, “music intervention”, and “sound therapy” retrieved 4,396 articles. Four approaches were evaluated: (i) expert-defined terminology, (ii) KeyBERT-based keyword extraction with k-means clustering, (iii) Word2Vec-based abstract representations with k-means clustering, and (iv) a BERT-based question-answering (QA) system for retrieving specific answers and source passages.

Results: The expert-defined approach identified a limited set of frequently occurring terms, whereas KeyBERT generated a broader vocabulary and 10 clusters of related abstracts. Word2Vec produced 50 clusters, but the mean silhouette coefficient was 0.20, indicating weak cluster separation. The QA system retrieved potentially relevant passages from source articles. However, its answers and scores changed when the amount of input text or wording of the query was modified.

Conclusions: AI-supported clustering and QA methods may help clinicians and researchers navigate the growing literature on music-based therapies and interventions. However, these findings are preliminary. Further work should focus on improving domain-specific model performance and representativeness. Such systems should support literature retrieval and professional judgment rather than replace clinical expertise.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health Profiles in Aging: A Dual-Factor Approach Using Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
articles_hidden.authors: Arielle Bonneville-Roussy; Sophie Rochette Bragg; Alexanne Landry; Laurence Perrier; Olivier Vivier; Isabelle Rouleau; Sébastien Grenier
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives. 
Mental health (MH) is increasingly conceptualized, according to the dual-factor model (DFM), as the coexistence of well-being and ill-being rather than simply the absence of illness. However, this model has seldom been applied to aging populations. This study aims to move beyond deficit-based models of aging by examining the DFM in older adulthood using indicators of well-being and ill-being. In addition, we examined the profiles’ invariance across age cohorts, their sociodemographic correlates, and validated them against clinical diagnoses of mental illnesses.
Methods. 
We used a sample of 44,528 participants aged 46 to 92 years from the baseline (Time 0) and first follow-up (Time 1) waves of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. Validated measures of well-being (life satisfaction and social support) and ill-being (depression and loneliness) served as the MH variables at T1. We conducted Latent Profile Analysis and assessed measurement invariance to identify distinct MH profiles and their stability across age cohorts. We then used multinomial logistic regression to examine sociodemographic correlates (T0) of the profiles and their relationships with clinical diagnoses of MH disorders.
Results. 
Five distinct, age-invariant profiles emerged, each characterized by different levels of well-being and ill-being. The most adaptive profiles accounted for over 80% of the sample across age groups. Among the clinical diagnoses, mood disorder showed the largest effect across profiles.
Discussion.
The results are consistent with Keyes' (2002) conceptualization of the DFM. Our findings underscore the importance of focusing on MH and highlight the protective role of well-being in the aging population.

articles_hidden.title: How the Paradoxical Timetable Cure (PTC) Fosters Post-Traumatic Growth and Self-Compassion Among Long-Term Grief Sufferers Following COVID-19 Bereavement
articles_hidden.authors: Mehrdad Etemadi; Mohammad Nabiei; Yoones Rajaei; Mohamad Reza Naeiji; Mahdieh Rahmanian; Erfan Abdollahi Chirani; Amirmahdi Amraei; Fatemeh Mirzai
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The present study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of the Paradoxical Timetable Cure (PTC) on post-traumatic growth and self-compassion among long-term grief sufferers following COVID-19 bereavement.

Methods and Materials:  Employing a pre-test, post-test design with a control group, this study included a two-month follow-up period. Thirty individuals in Kermanshah, identified in 2023 as suffering from prolonged grief disorder (PGD) as per the Prolonged Grief Disorder Scale (PGD-13-R; Prigerson et al., 2021), were purposively selected based on specific criteria. Subsequently, they were randomly assigned into two equal groups: an experimental group receiving PTC and a control group with no intervention. Data were collected using the Post-Traumatic Growth Questionnaire (PTGQ; Tedeschi & Calhoun, 1996) and the Self-Compassion Scale (SCS; Neff et al., 2003). Statistical analysis was performed using univariate and multivariate analyses, along with repeated measures ANCOVA, in SPSS version 25.

Findings: The analysis revealed that the PTC significantly improved post-traumatic growth (P < 0.001, F = 7.40) and self-compassion (P < 0.001, F = 4.75) among participants coping with long-term grief following COVID-19 bereavement.

Conclusion: The study's findings indicate that PTC is effective in fostering post-traumatic growth and self-compassion among long-term grief sufferers after COVID-19 bereavement. The efficacy of PTC in enhancing these constructs suggests its value as a therapeutic approach for individuals experiencing prolonged grief due to the pandemic.

articles_hidden.title: Screening for paternal perinatal affective symptoms: Psychometric properties of the Perinatal Assessment of Paternal Affectivity (PAPA 2.0) in the Polish context
articles_hidden.authors: Grażyna Kmita; Diana Puzio; Eliza Kiepura-Nawrocka; Alicja Niedźwiecka; Karolina Waśkiewicz; Justyna Hermaniuk; Franco Baldoni; Francesca Agostini; Michele Giannotti
articles_hidden.abstract: Paternal perinatal mental health has been gaining considerable attention in contemporary scientific literature. Correlational and longitudinal associations have been established between paternal depressive and anxiety symptoms,  maternal mental health and child development. Yet, we still lack assessment instruments tailored to fathers’ specific affective symptom profile that could prompt early detection and intervention. The present study examined the psychometric properties of the Polish adaptation of the Perinatal Assessment of Paternal Affectivity questionnaire (PAPA version 2.0), which represents a further development of PAPA tool published in 2022. The prenatal assessment included 213 fathers in the third trimester of their partners’ pregnancy, while 72 fathers participated in the postnatal phase. Reliability, concurrent validity, factorial structure and associations between prenatal and postnatal scores were evaluated. PAPA 2.0  demonstrated high internal consistency before and after childbirth. Its total scores showed moderate-to-high positive correlations with depressive symptoms, perceived stress, global psychological distress and postnatal EPDS scores, indicating satisfactory concurrent validity. Exploratory factor analysis suggested a two-factor structure with one item - describing risky behaviors - showing poor item discrimination, which may point to the need for this item’s reformulation in future studies. Prenatal and postnatal PAPA scores were significantly associated, suggesting relative stability of paternal affective symptoms across the perinatal period. The study is limited by its convenience sample, high educational and urban bias as well as pandemic-related substantial postnatal attrition. Despite these limitations, the findings support PAPA 2.0 as a promising screening tool for identifying paternal perinatal affective symptoms in Polish fathers.

articles_hidden.title: Reframing Self-Perception: Efficacy of Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) on Self-Disgust, Physical Appearance Perfectionism, and Self-Esteem in Girls with Anorexia Nervosa
articles_hidden.authors: Fatemeh Mirzai; Niloofar Nikbakht; Zahra Norouziani; Erfan Abdollahi Chirani; Farshid Fathy Karkaragh; Pardis Mazroei
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Anorexia nervosa (AN) presents unique psychological challenges, including deep-seated feelings of self-disgust, rigid physical appearance perfectionism, and diminished self-esteem. The aim of this study was to investigate the effectiveness of intensive short-term dynamic psychotherapy (ISTDP) on self-disgust, physical appearance perfectionism, and self-esteem in girls with AN.

Methods: This semi-experimental study used a pre-test, post-test, and follow-up design with a control group. The statistical population of the research included all girls with AN in Tehran, Iran, who had been referred to counselling centers and nutritionists in 2023. Forty of them aged 14 to 19 were selected using the convenience sampling method. Initially, 20 participants were selected for each group, but 3 participants from the control group were excluded due to absence of more than three sessions. The experimental group received 15 sessions of ISTDP, while the control group received no intervention. Data were collected through the use of the Overton et al. Self-Disgust Scale (SDS), Yang and Stoeber Physical Appearance Perfectionism Scale (PAPS), and Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES). Data were analyzed using univariate, multivariate, and repeated measures of covariance in SPSS software.

Results: ISTDP effectively reduced self-disgust (P = 0.001, F = 0.151) and physical appearance perfectionism (P = 0.001, F = 8.830), and enhanced self-esteem (P = 0.001, F = 52.388) in girls with AN.

Conclusion: ISTDP was able to reduce self-disgust and physical appearance perfectionism and increase self-esteem, and this change continued in the follow-up.

articles_hidden.title: There is No Good Reason to Not Follow-Up on an Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: John Protzko
articles_hidden.abstract: While experimental interventions are popular in the psychological sciences, we are not taking full advantage of them. In this paper, we show between 1/3 to ½ of interventions that could plausibly create long-term change in people simply conduct no follow-up after the intervention ended. The results attained p < .05, were written up, but no investigation of long-term effects were conducted. We highlight how long-term follow-up provides deeply valuable information not only about the intervention but about the underlying theory, regardless of the permanence of the intervention effects. We highlight how fadeout or persistence can inform feedback loops or the power of contextual effects. We provide information on how to practically conduct long-term follow-up after an intervention, and highlight unique problems to the intervention with long-term follow-up. Overall, we argue there is no good reason for not following-up on an intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Cannabis use influences the effect of episodic simulation on scene vividness and prosocial intentions
articles_hidden.authors: A. Dawn Ryan; Alyssa MacKinnon
articles_hidden.abstract:
Rationale/ Background: The ability to imagine hypothetical scenarios (i.e., episodic simulation) is a critical component of emotion regulation, problem solving, and planning behaviours. Neurocognitive research has demonstrated considerable overlap between brain regions that are active when remembering the past and imagining these hypothetical events. Because of the shared neural underpinnings, those with established memory issues have also been shown to have difficulty imagining hypothetical future scenarios. To date, little research has examined whether the established memory issues found in cannabis users extends to future thinking deficits, and indeed no work has examined whether this translates to planned future behaviours.
Methods: The present experiment compared episodic simulation in cannabis users and controls. Participants read brief scenarios depicting people facing everyday problems (e.g., being locked out of their house) and then imagined vivid scenarios in which they help the person in need or completed a control condition. Participants rated their willingness to help the person and phenomenological experiences associated with the scenario.
Results: We demonstrate a reduced effect of episodic simulation on scene vividness and willingness to help in regular cannabis users and with increased frequency of use. However, emotional concern and perspective taking increased in all groups following episodic simulation. Further, we demonstrate that cannabis use negatively impacted the mediating role of scene vividness on willingness to help, while the indirect effect of perspective taking was relatively unchanged.
Conclusions: These findings suggest that while cannabis use may impair the vividness of imagined future scenarios, other components of future thought remain intact.

articles_hidden.title: Common and distinct effects of age and depression on cognitive effort-based decision-making
articles_hidden.authors: Mengzhe Wei; Jennifer Lee Crawford; Joset A. Etzel; Tammy English; Renee J Thompson; Todd Samuel Braver
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive control is central to decision-making and goal-directed behavior, but the mental effort it requires is often perceived as costly, especially in the context of aging. Although age-related differences in cognitive effort discounting have primarily been studied in healthy adults, major depressive disorder (MDD), which is associated with altered reward valuation, may modify these patterns. In this preregistered study, we examined whether age was differentially associated with cognitive effort discounting in adults with and without MDD (N=134, ages 35-74). We first estimated subjective value (SV), indexing cognitive effort costs, then assessed choices between options that varied in SV. Replicating prior work, SV declined as cognitive load increased, suggesting less willingness to engage in more effortful tasks. Age-related differences in this discounting pattern were only evident among individuals with MDD but not among healthy controls. Specifically, among individuals with MDD, older age was associated with lower SV at low loads, but a shallower decline in SV as difficulty increased. Across diagnostic groups, the positive association between task accuracy and SV weakened with older age. Finally, the relative SV of the more cognitively demanding task (compared to the less demanding task) predicted the willingness to engage with it. This association was also weakened with age across diagnostic groups, suggesting that as individuals get older, their decisions may be less guided by the SV difference between high- and low-effort options. Together, these findings showcase the combined and distinct effects of aging and MDD in altering the mechanisms of cognitive effort evaluation and decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Framing Effects in Choices With Somewhat Risky Options
articles_hidden.authors: Prachiti Garge; Michael L DeKay
articles_hidden.abstract: When a certain option and a risky option are both described as potential gains, people typically choose the certain option; when the same two options are described as potential losses, people typically choose the risky option. This famous preference pattern is the risky-choice framing effect. Despite the seeming rarity of sure things and all-or-none risks in real life, surprisingly little research on this effect has involved options with intermediate levels of risk. In this research, we identified four types of “somewhat risky” options, combined them with each other and with certain and all-or-none options to create 15 risk comparisons in both gains and losses in each of four domains (cancer, drought, investment, and wildfire), and conducted two preregistered experiments in which we varied risk comparisons between or within participants in both student and online samples (N = 2,586 after exclusions). We found significant framing effects in almost all risk comparisons, greatly expanding the range of decisions in which framing is relevant. In addition, we assessed how well 12 versions of risky-choice theories accounted for participants’ choices. Across experiments and samples, versions of prospect theory (PT) and transfer-of-attention-exchange theory (TAX) generally outperformed versions of fuzzy-trace theory (FTT), the priority heuristic, and other accounts. PT’s and TAX’s performance was largely due to the S-shaped value function rather than the theories’ other mechanisms (e.g., PT’s loss aversion, TAX’s weight transfer). FTT’s performance was harmed by its failure to predict framing effects in choices between certain options and somewhat risky options without zero outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Feasibility and clinical outcomes of a virtual psychotherapy platform for moderate to severe depression and anxiety: a pilot randomized controlled trial
articles_hidden.authors: Mindy Hong; David Yadush; Siddharth Suri; Madelyn Frumkin; Russell DuBois
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health disorders are a leading contributor to global disability and are associated with reduced quality of life, increased morbidity and increased healthcare utilization. In recent years, technology-enabled virtual therapy platforms, which integrate multiple synchronous and asynchronous care components, have emerged as scalable approaches for expanding access to therapeutic support. However, randomized evidence supporting efficacy is limited. A pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted to examine feasibility, engagement and clinical outcomes of a virtual therapy platform (BetterHelp) versus a waitlist control group on adults with moderate-to-severe anxiety or depression. 86 participants (51.2% female, 72.1% White) were randomized to receive 12 weeks of virtual therapy or waitlist control. Patient-reported anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9), stress (PSS-10), sleep quality (JSS-4) and workplace productivity (WPAI-GH) outcomes were collected at baseline, 4 weeks and 12 weeks. Adjusted linear mixed effects models were conducted to evaluate the change in clinical outcomes over time. Engagement was measured through the number of individual and support group therapy sessions completed, number of worksheets completed, and number of messages exchanged with a therapist. At 12 weeks, 76.5% and 64.7% of the intervention group achieved MCID in anxiety and depression, respectively, compared to 48.5% and 43.8% of the control group. Among participants randomized to the virtual therapy group who engaged in individual or support group therapy (21/44, 47.7%), participants completed 3.4 therapy sessions, 2.4 worksheets, sent 41.7 messages to their therapists, and reported an Net Promoter Score (NPS) of 8.7. Virtual therapy participants had significantly lower GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores compared to the control group at both 4 (GAD-7: AMD: -1.9 [-3.7, -0.2], p = 0.03, g = -0.46; PHQ-9: AMD: -2.0 [-4.0,-0.01], p = 0.049, g = -0.43) and 12 weeks (GAD-7: AMD: -3.0 [-4.7, -1.3], p < 0.001, g = -0.72; PHQ-9: AMD: -2.4 [-4.3, -0.4], p = 0.02, g = -0.51). No significant differences in stress, sleep quality and workplace productivity outcomes were observed between groups. Although this pilot study lacks statistical power to draw definitive conclusions about treatment efficacy, findings suggest a multimodal approach combining therapist support across both synchronous and asynchronous modalities may help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression among adults with higher clinical severity.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Culture on the Processing of Spatial Frequencies during Recognition of Homogeneous Objects
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Cousineau; Francis Gingras; Émilie Désaulniers; Daniel Fiset; Caroline Blais
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological research often relies on Western participant samples, neglecting global diversity and overlooking cultural influences on visual perception.
