Studies show that cultural upbringing affects how people process visual stimuli, with East Asians displaying broader attentional patterns and different eye movements compared to Westerners, leading to variations in spatial frequency (SF) processing during face recognition. This study examined whether these cultural differences in SF processing extend beyond faces to Greebles. Participants (50 East Asians and 83 Westerners) took part in an online study that used a data-driven SF sampling method to measure their SF tunings to Greebles. Results showed that East Asians relied more on lower SF, ranging from 2 to 4 cycles per object, than Westerners. These findings suggest that cultural differences in SF processing are not restricted to faces but may extend to other visually homogeneous object categories that share face-like structural properties.

articles_hidden.title: Transnational Activism and Civic Engagement among Burmese American Refugee Youth
articles_hidden.authors: Xiang Zhou; Phoebe Tu-Phi Pham; Mengxi Zhang; Jenni Thang
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on refugee youth has predominantly centered on challenges and deficits, often overlooking their resilience, contributions, and the positive roles they play in their new communities, including activism and civic engagement (ACE). This study addresses that gap by focusing on Burmese refugee youth, one of the largest resettled groups in the U.S. in recent history. Specifically, we examined four types of activities—protesting, donating, distributing information, and signing petitions—across three domains: ethnic/local (Burmese American causes), transnational (Myanmar causes), and general (other causes). The sample comprised 99 Burmese American adolescents from refugee backgrounds. Over half engaged in at least one ACE activity in the last six months. Transnational engagement was most common, followed by ethnic and general ACE. An explorative person-centered analysis revealed three profiles: moderately engaged (60%), transnationally engaged (11%), and highly engaged (20.7%). Results were discussed in the context of the global refugee crisis and the 2021 February 1 Myanmar coup d'état. These findings have important implications to expand the current conceptual model of activism and civic engagement among refugee and migrant youth.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Seeing and Knowing: The Development of an Intuitive Theory of Attention
articles_hidden.authors: Rui Zhang; Marlene Berke; Julian Jara-Ettinger
articles_hidden.abstract:
Where someone looks, and for how long, is a remarkably rich signal about their mind. It reveals
what they find interesting, what they like, and what is new to them. These inferences are
possible because as adults, we understand that people don’t just encode whatever is visible to
them. This is instead modulated by what they choose to attend to, and for how long. Across
four experiments (N = 220), we asked whether children understand these nuances. We found
that unlike adults, children showed only partial expectations about what draws attention,
expecting longer looking for larger sets by age six, but not for more complex or more varied
objects (Exp. 1). However, children as young as five understood that an agent who looked
longer formed a more accurate representation of what they saw (Exp. 2), and that they are more
likely to look longer at things they find desirable (Exp. 3). Finally, six-year-olds, but not five-
year-olds, inferred that agents who already know about a toy are less likely to look for an
extended duration (Exp. 4). Together, these results suggest that an intuitive theory of attention
is partly in place by age five and continues to develop past age six.

articles_hidden.title: Statistical Assessment of a Synastry Algorithm for Personal Relationships and High-Performance Dyads: A Blind Replication Study
articles_hidden.authors: Phillip Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: Carl Jung and many others have attempted to validate astrology with the scientific method. This research used an algorithm based on the ancient process of synastry to examine the combined birth charts for pairs of people and to calculate a number that measures astrological compatibility, the Starscore. The average Starscore for participant-blind Prolific and CloudResearch survey respondents who provided the birthdate and location for themselves and their closest relationship was statistically higher than the average for one million random Starscores with small effect sizes. In addition, the Starscore for champion pairs in artistic swimming, figure skating, doubles tennis and for winners and runners-up of The Amazing Race were significantly different from the random group. False discovery rate and family-wise error rate analyses supported the statistical significance of the close relationship surveys. While not proof of causation, these correlations support Jung’s theory that the positions of the planets in our solar system could be related to the development of human life, and they support Jung’s belief that studying astrology may contribute to our understanding of human behavior. If independent researchers replicate these findings, the resulting evidence could provide a stronger empirical basis for evaluating astrology’s potential relevance to psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Tailoring relative phase estimation methods to movement shape. A practical approach to estimate the Arnold tongue with testing codes on human data and simulation of discrete and continuous signals.
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Le Guennec; julien lagarde
articles_hidden.abstract: The relative phase ϕis a key variable in the study of coordination dynamics across many disciplines. Several estimation methods exist and are used interchangeably in the study of sensorimotor synchronization, despite the limitations of certain methods when analyzing inharmonic (aka discrete) movements. In this study, we document differences in estimates of key variables used to describe coordination dynamics, the mean ϕand its standard deviation, calculated using a pointwise method and using the Hilbert transform with signal centering or with a correction of the non-linearity. We applied these methods to experimental data from a tapping task with an incremental increase in metronome frequency. The increase in frequency allowed us to observe differences between methods in inharmonic movements at low synchronization frequencies and in near-sinusoidal movements at higher frequencies. To complement this analysis, we conducted stochastic numerical simulations of non-linear oscillators and with ghost attractors to mimic signals from discrete movements. We compared the mean and SD ϕestimates to a gold standard based on the Arnold tongues framework. Our experimental and simulation results show that the mean and SD ϕestimates obtained from the Hilbert transform are biased for inharmonic signals, we recommend using the pointwise method in this context. With near-sinusoidal signals, both methods provide equivalent results. We propose a practical approach to estimate the quality of synchronization, sharing free testing codes, human data and simulation of discrete or continuous movements.

articles_hidden.title: Generative AI Use in Entrepreneurship: An Integrative Review and an Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Jackson G. Lu; Gerui Gloria Zhao; Anna Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to understand how GenAI can both empower and entrap entrepreneurs, highlighting GenAI’s role as a double-edged sword at each stage of the entrepreneurial process. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality but introduce hallucinations and training data biases; boost entrepreneurial self-efficacy but heighten entrepreneurial overconfidence; increase functional breadth but decrease relational embeddedness; and boost productivity but fuel “workslop” and erode critical thinking, learning, and memory. Moreover, we identify core features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. We also explore boundary conditions (e.g., entrepreneurs’ metacognition, domain expertise, and entrepreneurial experience) that shape the magnitude of these effects. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework offer practical implications for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically throughout the entrepreneurial process while managing its risks.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of diagnostic labelling on self-reported depression symptoms: A randomized controlled experimental study
articles_hidden.authors: Michael P. Hengartner; Lorenz A. Juen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Psychiatric diagnostic labels alter how people interpret common emotional distress, but it is unclear if psychiatric labelling increases reporting of depression symptoms. 
Methods: University students (n=260) recruited during the stressful exams period completed the PHQ-8, a popular depression rating scale, and were then randomized 1:1 to labelling intervention (automated feedback indicating increased depression scores plus definition of depression) or control group (no feedback; only definition of mental wellbeing). Both groups then completed the PHQ-8 a second time and convenience subsample (n=131) also a third time 24 hours later, in addition to a brief measure of individual depression concepts assessing whether people differentiate between depression episodes and acute stress reactions (stringent concept) or not (expanded concept). 
Results: PHQ-8 baseline scores indicated at least mild depression in three-fourths and moderate-to-severe depression in one-third of the sample. Depression labelling, relative to control condition, caused reductions in PHQ-8 scores. Independent of the labelling intervention, expanded depression concepts were associated with more stable PHQ-8 scores and stringent depression concepts with marked reductions.
Conclusion: Contrary to our hypothesis, imposing a depression label on people experiencing acute stress did not increase depression scores. Instead, we found that labelling was associated with reductions in depression scores, as were stringent depression concepts. This suggests that people with initially inflated depression scores who perceive depression as conceptually different to acute stress reactions tend to adjust their scores on a depression rating scale. Further research into the expansiveness of depression concepts and the reporting of symptoms is required to verify this interpretation.

articles_hidden.title: Measurement Reliability, Construct Validity, and Transparent Reporting in Original and Replication Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Cas Goos; Marjan Bakker; Jelte M. Wicherts; Michele B. Nuijten
articles_hidden.abstract: While published (replication) studies using measures to assess psychological phenomena need to transparently report information on measurement procedures, validity, and reliability to allow verification and use in future (replication) research, earlier results highlighted common poor reporting of psychological measurement. Here, we investigated the measurement reporting in a sample of 77 measures within 56 Many Labs replications and related original articles (Ebersole et al., 2016, 2020; Klein et al., 2014, 2018) and found that the information relevant for reusing measures was reported in full in around half the replication measures, and only 5.2% in the original studies. We also observed that only around a third of multiple-item measures in original studies and 11.4% in replications reported reliability coefficients, with comparable proportions for reporting any convergent, discrimant, predictive, or factorial validity evidence. We performed checks of the reliability and unidimensionality of multiple-item measures using the openly available Many Labs item response data. We observed that the reliability and unidimensionality of the measures was rarely stable across labs. These results corroborate existing findings that measurement reporting in published research lacks transparency, and that poor measurement reporting often obscure insufficient reliability and validity. We offer suggestions on how to improve measurement reporting practices and increase the use of validated measures.

articles_hidden.title: Biopsychosocial Moderators of Links between Maternal Depressive and Anxiety Symptoms during Pregnancy and Child Socioemotional Outcomes: A Multi-Cohort Study
articles_hidden.authors: Annaleena Holopainen; Jana Runze; Luisa Bergunde; Jasminka Štefulj; Gabija Jarašiūnaite-Fedosejeva; Alexia Karain; Jonathan Handelzalts; Danny Horesh; Bea Van den Bergh; Mary Carmen Hernández Martínez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Prenatal exposure to maternal depressive and anxiety symptoms may have lasting effects, such as increased internalizing and externalizing behavior during childhood. However, not all children are equally affected. The Multidimensional Conceptualization of Prenatal Influences on Psychological and Health Outcomes Across the Lifespan Framework highlights biopsychosocial factors that may moderate this association and require further investigation. 

Methods
This study combined data from four European cohorts (N = 7,597) to examine biopsychosocial factors – child sex, mode of birth, subjective birth experience, child temperament, social support, and parity – as potential moderators of the associations between maternal prepartum depressive or anxiety symptoms and child internalizing or externalizing behavior at 3-5 years of age. 

Results
Higher prepartum depressive symptoms were associated with higher child internalizing and externalizing behavior, while higher trait and state anxiety symptoms were associated with higher externalizing behavior only. Associations between state anxiety symptoms and both internalizing and externalizing behavior were stronger for first-born children, while findings regarding the moderating role of mode of birth were inconsistent. Child sex, subjective birth experience, child temperament, and social support were not significant moderators.

Conclusions
Prepartum depression and anxiety presage emotional and behavioral difficulties perceived in the child, in particular externalizing problems. Mode of birth and birth order emerged as moderators of these associations. Yet, as most candidate moderators were not empirically supported, they may operate through pathways other than modifying susceptibility to prenatal maternal distress.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Singularity and Compassion Fade: Replication and extensions of Experiments 1a and 3 in Västfjäll et al. (2014)
articles_hidden.authors: Lewend Mayiwar; Shubin Yu; Yooeun Jeong; Richard Rekdal; Tuan Viet; Ihor Rudko; Matilda Dorotic; Gilad Feldman
articles_hidden.abstract: Västfjäll et al. (2014) found support for “compassion fade”, that affective reactions and charitable donations decrease as the number of victims increases. In a pre-registered experiment with a U.S. sample recruited through CloudResearch Connect (N = 1207), we conducted a replication and extension of Studies 1a and 3 from Västfjäll et al. (2014). In the replication of Study 1a, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims (one vs. two children) on hypothetical donation amount, positive- or negative affect, perceived impact of donations (all |d|s ≤ 0.16) or for any mediation effects. In the replication of Study 3, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims or relatedness on donation amount, perceived need, positive affect, or negative affect of donations (all ηp2 ≤ 0.012). Bayesian analyses indicated moderate to strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for most effects, and equivalence testing indicated that seven of eight effects were smaller than our conservative smallest effect size of interest. Overall, our findings fail to replicate the original compassion fade effects and suggest limitations on their generalizability across various dependent measures and contexts. Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A2TGB

articles_hidden.title: Lexical and affective organizers of (novel) meaning
articles_hidden.authors: Celia Martínez Tomás; Fritz Guenther; Daniele Gatti; José Antonio Hinojosa
articles_hidden.abstract: Novel (or pseudo-) words lack stored lexical representations and thus are (often) assumed to be semantically empty. Although, challenging this idea, recent studies showed that novel words can evoke semantic and affective responses, these findings do not directly reveal the semantic content that speakers attribute to these unfamiliar forms. We tested this by asking participants to generate open-ended definitions for real and novel valenced words. Definitions were represented via sentence embeddings and examined through consensus, representational similarity and content decoding analyses. Definitions independently generated for the same pseudoword were more semantically similar than definitions generated for different pseudowords, demonstrating cross-speaker convergence in attributed meaning. Participants who produced better-fitting definitions for real words also tended to do so for pseudowords, indicating cross-domain individual differences in semantic-definition behavior. Valence was recoverable from definition embeddings for both real words and pseudowords, and it consistently organized the semantic geometry of pseudoword definitions across four different embedding models. Together, these findings show that unfamiliar word forms constrain the meanings generated by different speakers in systematic and (partly) shared ways, drawing on semantic and affective knowledge also involved in familiar-word processing. Theoretically, this work has implications for theories of language learning by demonstrating that novel meaning acquisition is a structured process driven by general semantic competence, rather than arbitrary association. It also challenges embodied views of language by showing that abstract emotional knowledge (rather than transient affective states) serves as a primary organizing geometry for processing unfamiliar linguistic stimuli.

articles_hidden.title: Interpreting FMS and SSQ Cybersickness Ratings via User Tolerance in Virtual Reality
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Kelly; Michael Dorneich; Stephen Gilbert
articles_hidden.abstract: Cybersickness remains a persistent challenge limiting the usability of virtual reality (VR), yet commonly used subjective measures such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) and the Fast Motion Sickness (FMS) scale are often difficult to interpret in terms of user outcomes. In particular, there is limited guidance on how specific values on these scales relate to user tolerance or the likelihood that users will discontinue a VR experience due to discomfort. This work addresses this gap by calibrating cybersickness severity interpretations against early termination of a VR experience. In Study 1 (N = 183), participants played an immersive VR game for up to 20 minutes and were free to terminate the experience at any time. Using a Behavioral Risk Banding (BRB) framework, logistic regression linked a modified 0-10 version of the FMS (FMS-10) and post-exposure SSQ scores to dropout probability, yielding behaviorally grounded risk severity bands (mild, moderate, severe, extreme). Survival analyses then showed how these bands mapped onto tolerance over time, revealing a transitional region marked by heightened individual variability. Study 2 (N = 304) evaluated the robustness of these categories across variation in VR content and mitigation context by applying the Study 1 thresholds without re-estimation. Although absolute dropout risk varied, the ordering and behavioral meaning of severity categories were preserved. Together, these results provide a practical, behaviorally grounded framework for interpreting cybersickness ratings in terms of user tolerance and usability across VR contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Milena Philomena Maria Musial; Sam Hall-McMaster; Kanji Shimomura; Ayaka Kato; Erik Lukas Bode; Clarissa Grundmann; Claudia Ebrahimi; Kenji Morita; Samuel J. Gershman; Tanja Endrass
articles_hidden.abstract: The successor representation (SR) is a learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (n=260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (n=260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant, particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy and instead more on model-free control in alcohol-related contexts. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.

articles_hidden.title: Working with Lived-Experience Advisory Groups to Advance Equity in Health Psychology Research in the Netherlands and Flanders
articles_hidden.authors: Nadine van der Waal; Maité Van Alboom; Maya Braun; Klaske Tiemstra; Thomas Gültzow; Meeke Hoedjes; Gera Nagelhout; maya schroevers; Laurens van Gestel; Dimitri Van Ryckeghem
articles_hidden.abstract:
Persistent health disparities, rooted in unequal distributions of power, resources and opportunities, emphasize the urgent need for more inclusive research practices in health psychology. This paper presents citizen advisory groups, composed of individuals with lived experience of health inequities, as a feasible approach to foster such practices. Citizen advisory groups provide researchers with insight into the lived experience of these individuals, facilitating research that is aligned with their context and needs. Compared to full-scale participatory research, these groups require relatively modest resources while still enabling meaningful community engagement.
In the Netherlands and Flanders, citizen advisory groups have gained traction in recent years. Drawing on experiences from existing groups, literature, and researchers’ input from conference roundtables, this paper aims to disseminate experiences with, and lessons learned from working with advisory groups. Thereby, this paper contributes to researchers’ knowledge about the use and implementation of advisory groups. This helps to support researchers in assessing whether a citizen advisory group is suitable for their work, aiming to lower the barriers to start one. 
This paper covers how citizen advisory groups may overcome researchers’ barriers to inclusive research, the value of advisory groups across different phases of the research process, and how to overcome challenges in the implementation and sustainability of citizen advisory groups. Ultimately, the paper presents citizen advisory groups as a concrete step towards more inclusive research practices in health psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroplasticity in Adolescents: The role of sleep, resilience and continuous connectivity.
articles_hidden.authors: Maanya Sharma; Ananta Ganjoo; Gaurangi Khetwal
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroplasticity refers to the brain’s inherent capacity to reorganise its structure and function in response to experience, learning, and stress across the lifespan. Psychological resilience, in turn, reflects an individual’s ability to adapt, cope, and maintain functional stability in the face of adversity. Research increasingly suggests that these processes are not independent; rather, they are deeply interwoven and sensitive to disruptions in basic biological systems such as sleep. This paper therefore explores the relationship among sleep deprivation, neuroplasticity, psychological resilience, and cognitive decision-making during adolescence. It examines how the highly susceptible and adaptable adolescent brain responds to environmental influences, particularly sleep patterns and continuous digital connectivity. The paper explores the biological mechanisms underlying neuroplasticity and how these processes support learning, emotional regulation, and adaptive functioning. It also considers how sleep contributes to synaptic reorganisation, memory consolidation, and overall brain efficiency during a critical development period. Furthermore, researchers examine how modern lifestyle factors, including increased screen exposure, may interact with sleep and neural development. The research integrates psychological and neurobiological perspectives to provide an understanding of adolescent brain function. Ultimately, it aims to highlight the importance of sleep and balanced environmental engagement in supporting healthy cognitive and developmental outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Growing up in an Age of Economic Inequality: A Social-Cognitive Developmental Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Eddie Brummelman; Katherine McAuliffe; Jamie Amemiya
articles_hidden.abstract: Economic inequality has reached extreme levels worldwide, and children will bear its burden. How do children perceive and explain economic inequality? And how do these perceptions and explanations, in turn, shape their development? We address these questions by proposing an integrative social-cognitive developmental framework. According to the framework, when children enter a new context, they consider a series of questions: (1) Is there inequality? (2) What causes inequality? (3) What does inequality say about me? (4) What does inequality say about us? (5) And do I address inequality? We suggest that children’s perceptions and explanations of economic inequality—above and beyond exposure to the inequality in itself—have profound consequences for mental health, social relationships, motivation, and egalitarianism (e.g., whether children rectify or perpetuate inequality). Children’s perceptions and explanations, then, might serve as levers for intervention to help children navigate the current age of inequality.

articles_hidden.title: When the self makes things look clearer: Self-association biases perceptual evaluation rather than sensory processing
articles_hidden.authors: Xueyan Jiang; Ruizhe Zhang; Zhiqiang Luo; Hu Chuan-Peng; Chuyao Yan
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-associated information receives privileged access during perceptual processing, but does this priority alter perception itself or how perceptual evidence is interpreted and evaluated? Across seven experiments (N = 302), we tested this question using perceived stimulus clarity as a direct measure of subjective visual experience while systematically manipulating physical stimulus clarity. Using reconstruction and two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) tasks, we first found that self-associated stimuli were consistently perceived as clearer than other-associated stimuli across different levels of physical clarity. However, this subjective clarity advantage reflected a shift in clarity criterion, as self-associated stimuli were more likely to be judged as clear despite showing no improvement in the ability to discriminate physical clarity differences. Beyond clarity judgments, we further examined subjective confidence and found that self-association increased confidence when sensory evidence was ambiguous. However, when perceptual performance was assessed using an objective visual feature, orientation, no self-associated advantage was observed in orientation estimation or discrimination. Finally, hierarchical Bayesian observer modeling provided evidence that the self-associated bias arose from later decision processes rather than changes in sensory evidence. Together, these findings demonstrate that self-association does not enhance sensory representations but instead modulates the evaluation of perceptual evidence, biasing subjective judgments such that self-associated stimuli appear clearer without greater perceptual sensitivity.

articles_hidden.title: Bounded rationality and human development
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel David Jones
articles_hidden.abstract: Although multi-scale, multi-directional feedback between genes, brain, cognition, and behaviour is the cornerstone of well-evidenced interactionist models of human development (e.g., Gottlieb, 2007), contemporary theories of neurodevelopmental variation and disorder characteristically describe only unidirectional cascades across this hierarchy. To complement this view, I present a new theory of the cognitive and behavioural origins of individual differences in human development. This account is grounded in the ideas of restricted search and satisficing that are central to the bounded rationality paradigm (Simon, 1955, 1956, 1990), and which set this account apart from claims that agents optimise utility functions or maximise their learning. I outline a simple model of adaptive restricted search and satisficing that incorporates reciprocal influences on development and learning, and integrate a broad contemporary empirical literature in support of this model. This work motivates the novel position that adaptive restricted search and satisficing not only amplify neurodevelopmental differences beyond their primary neurogenetic origins (explaining developmental multifinality) but also provide a route by which disparate primary causal processes are anchored to common phenotypes (explaining developmental equifinality). While the primary focus of this paper is on early developmental variation and conditions of clinical significance, I argue that bounded rationality offers a general paradigm through which to understand the emergence of individual differences across the lifespan, from delay, to psychopathology, to expertise. The recommendation of this report is that cognitive and behavioural feedback – specifically bounded rational choice – should be embedded more widely into causal process models of the origins of individual differences in human development.

articles_hidden.title: The Deservingness Mismatch and Political Discontent
articles_hidden.authors: Troels Siegumfeldt Bøggild; Michael Bang Petersen
articles_hidden.abstract: Political discontent is high across many Western democracies, with ramifications for regime stability and social cohesion. We argue that discontent—proxied by political distrust, dissatisfaction with democracy, populism, powerlessness, and low efficacy— reflects a deservingness mismatch: the gap between which groups citizens believe should receive help and their perceptions of who actually does. Using observational and experimental survey data from the United States and Denmark (total N = 4,892), we present three findings. First, citizens experience substantial mismatches, and these predict all five indicators of discontent. Second, citizens prefer that most groups receive more help, implying that correcting the mismatch would require expanding help across many groups simultaneously—a politically and fiscally daunting task. Third, the mismatch operates over and above political ideology and personal group identification, suggesting the existence of a broadly shared moral disenfranchisement with contemporary society. We reconceptualize political discontent as a wicked problem rooted in deep-seated psychological intuitions with strong inertia due to practical and political barriers in aligning politics with citizens’ moral expectations.

articles_hidden.title: Impaired functional double dissociation in motor-to-sensory transformation mediates aberrant predictive coding in auditory verbal hallucinations
articles_hidden.authors: Fuyin YANG; Chen Zhang; Chunbo Li; Xing Tian
articles_hidden.abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations (AVHs), the experience of hearing voices in the absence of corresponding external stimuli, are widely attributed to failures of self-monitoring. However, theoretical models and empirical investigations have primarily localized the underlying dysfunction to abnormalities within auditory cortices. Recent studies have revealed that the motor system exerts predictive regulation over auditory processing, suggesting that AVHs are not merely an abnormal auditory processing but also involve distinct, functionally dissociable impairments in motor-to-sensory transformation. How these impairments dynamically manifest in motor-to-sensory neural circuits remains unclear. This review synthesizes recent findings on the functional interactions between motor and sensory systems and proposes a hierarchical neurobiological framework for predictive coding in AVHs across two dimensions: temporal precision and spatial circuit architecture. In the temporal dimension, mismatches between motor-based predictions and sensory feedback disrupt the precision of predictive coding and Bayesian inference, giving rise to three forms of predictive dysfunction: excessively weak predictive signals, excessively strong predictive signals, and impaired predictive updating. In the spatial dimension, we characterize the spatiotemporal disintegration of the frontal-temporal-thalamic circuit underlying AVHs, focusing on both circuit-level disruption and hierarchical computational misalignment between predictive and perceptual signals. By explicitly linking the temporal precision of predictive coding to the spatial architecture of sensorimotor circuits, this study provides a unified mechanistic framework that bridges cognitive, computational, neurobiological, and clinical perspectives on AVHs.

articles_hidden.title: Learning to Speak Up: Oral Comprehensive Examinations and the Preparation of Health Students at a Hispanic-Serving Institution
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Almond
articles_hidden.abstract: At Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), equitable education requires more than access to knowledge; it requires practice articulating that knowledge in contexts shaped by power and hierarchy. This article presents an equity-oriented assessment model, scaffolded oral comprehensive examinations, in an undergraduate health psychology course at an urban HSI in which health service degree programs account for nearly one in five degrees offered. It argues that oral examinations cultivate professional competency by requiring students to explain structural inequity, translate complex health concepts in real time, and engage figures of authority. The article describes the exam design, the learning shifts observed across two administrations, and the implications, limitations, and future directions for HSI health educators.

articles_hidden.title: Changing Contributions of Emotion and Reward Information to Learning Through Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Phaneuf-Hadd; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Leah Somerville
articles_hidden.abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8-22 years completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hindered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially affected by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Linguistic Consistency and Validation of the Mental Health Quotient (MHQ) Across 21 Languages in the Global Mind Project
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Newson; Oleksii Sukhoi; Tara Thiagarajan
articles_hidden.abstract: The Mental Health Quotient (MHQ), the core instrument of the Global Mind Project (GMP), has previously been validated in English across measures of internal consistency, test–retest reliability, and criterion validity against clinical and functional outcomes. As the MHQ is now administered in 23 languages, corresponding validation of its translated versions has not previously been reported. Here we assess two properties of the MHQ across 21 languages with more than 10,000 responses each (and, for five additional lower-volume languages, more than 1,000 responses) collected in the GMP in 2025: (1) convergent and discriminant validity, evaluated as the correlation between conceptually similar and dissimilar item pairs, and (2) sampling stability, evaluated as the coefficient of variation (CV%) of the aggregate MHQ score across repeated random samples of varying size. Similar item pairs showed consistently high absolute correlation across languages (mean r ≈ 0.6), while dissimilar item pairs showed consistently low correlation (mean r ≈ 0.08–0.13), with narrow variation across languages and across country groups sharing the same language. The sampling-stability CV% was likewise low and consistent across languages, averaging 2.8% at n = 1,000 and rising to 6.6% at n = 200, with the least consistent language (Tamil) still showing acceptable stability. These results extend the MHQ's validation beyond English, supporting both the fidelity of its translations and the stability of the GMP's online data acquisition methodology across linguistic and cultural contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Trait Prediction:  What Personality Computing Can Contribute to Personality Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Eric Grunenberg; Ramona Schoedel; Jana Berkessel; Gabriela S. Blum; Kristin Jankowsky; Niclas Kuper; Le Vy Phan; Cornelia Sindermann; Larissa Sust
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality computing refers to the integration of machine learning methods with digital data to address personality-relevant research questions. To date, the approach has often been narrowly equated with the prediction of personality traits, leaving much of its potential untapped. This article broadens that view and outlines what personality computing can contribute to personality psychology beyond trait prediction. We discuss four domains in which the approach speaks to questions currently shaping the field: (1) informing personality theories, (2) sharpening the focus on within-person processes and the individual, (3) grounding research in observable behavior, and (4) developing tailored personality interventions. We then situate this within the wider interdisciplinary landscape, where computer science and computational social science have developed the approach along partly different lines, and where personality psychology has a distinct contribution to make. Realizing this potential will require large and intensive longitudinal datasets, methodological expertise within the field, shared standards for how such work is conducted and reported and sustained attention to the ethical questions raised by personality-relevant digital data. Personality computing is neither a panacea nor a replacement for established approaches, but a complementary set of tools that can extend the methodological repertoire of personality research.

articles_hidden.title: Embodied Models of Health: A Theoretical Framework of Mind-Body Unity
articles_hidden.authors: Peter J Aungle; Pierre-Marie Matta; Daniel L. Chen; Ellen Langer
articles_hidden.abstract: In this article, we review the literature on placebo effects and its overlap with the literature on health mindsets. We propose an Embodied Models of Health theoretical framework to account for the array of mind-body effects discussed in our literature review. While beliefs and expectations are widely acknowledged as fundamental drivers of placebo effects – physiological improvements that result exclusively and directly from psychological processes – the role of attention is often neglected in theoretical accounts of the placebo phenomenon and remains poorly understood. We argue that placebo effects and health mindsets are a product of continuous interaction between attention, beliefs, and expectations. We end by discussing novel predictions generated by the Embodied Models of Health framework and highlight opportunities to leverage the role of attention in mind-body dynamics to improve health and wellbeing.

articles_hidden.title: Modeling Environmental Behavior: Lessons from Social Computational Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Veronika Wendler; Anne Saulin; Tony Craig; Caroline Moraes; Yansong Li; Chunliang Feng; Lei Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Addressing climate change requires a better understanding of environmental behavior. Yet environmental-behavior research has largely focused on single observed outcomes, with limited use of computational models to identify the processes through which these behaviors emerge. Many environmental decisions are also socially interdependent, meaning individuals often must weigh personal costs against benefits for others, future generations, and collective outcomes. Social computational neuroscience provides formal models for examining precisely such value-based and social decisions, making it a useful foundation for environmental research. However, environmental decisions also have distinctive features, as their consequences are often delayed, uncertain, and difficult to observe directly. We therefore propose that repeated, computationally structured tasks can complement conventional environmental experimental designs by estimating latent decision processes rather than only measuring behavioral outcomes. We introduce computational frameworks from social computational neuroscience, focusing on subjective-value, reinforcement-learning, drift-diffusion, and agent-based models, and discuss how to adapt them to study environmental behavior. We illustrate this approach with an eco-product choice task integrating product design, learning from feedback, visual attention, and choice. Overall, we propose social computational neuroscience as a framework for linking individual decision mechanisms to socially situated and collective environmental behavior, contributing to the emerging field of environmental social neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive evidence for prospective links between self-efficacy and depression during adolescence: reanalysis and commentary on Nguyen et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on statistically significant cross-lagged parameters, Nguyen et al. argued that self-efficacy and depressive symptoms exert reciprocal longitudinal influences during adolescence. However, cross-lagged estimates in observational data may reflect statistical artifacts rather than genuine influencing processes. To evaluate the robustness of these conclusions, we applied multiple analytic approaches to data simulated to reproduce the correlations and sample characteristics reported by Nguyen et al. Across models, estimated effects varied markedly in both magnitude and direction, yielding evidence for both decreasing and increasing associations between the constructs. Meta-analytic synthesis of these alternative estimates produced effects that were not significantly different from zero. These findings suggest that the conclusions drawn by Nguyen et al. may be premature and that the reported cross-lagged associations could reflect statistical artifacts. Consistent with multiverse principles, we recommend evaluating prospective associations across several plausible models and basing substantive conclusions on the overall pattern of findings.

articles_hidden.title: No convincing evidence for prospective effects between perceived social support, school adaptation, and depression: A reanalysis and comment on Meng et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using cross-lagged panel analyses, Meng et al. concluded that perceived social support, school adaptation, and depression exert reciprocal longitudinal influences among Chinese vocational students. However, cross-lagged coefficients may reflect statistical artifacts rather than true prospective effects. To evaluate this possibility, we analyzed simulated data constructed to reproduce the sample characteristics and correlation structure reported by Meng et al. Alternative analytic approaches yielded markedly different conclusions, including positive, negative, and near-zero prospective effects among the study variables. When these estimates were synthesized meta-analytically, the resulting overall effects were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that the reported longitudinal influences may not provide reliable evidence of prospective relationships. Consistent with multiverse principles, we recommend evaluating hypotheses across multiple plausible models and basing conclusions on the combined evidence rather than on a single analytic specification.

articles_hidden.title: Authoritarianism in Action
articles_hidden.authors: Ana P. Gantman; Jordan Wylie; Wil Cunningham; Nicolette Dakin; Connie Pui Yee Chiu; Brendan Michael Fee
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, we take a behavioral approach to the psychological study of authoritarianism. We specify authoritarian behavior as the products of interactions between people and official systems of power, which forward the personal and political interests of some over others, at the expense of the rule of law. In doing so, we focus on hybrid authoritarianism, or the leveraging of legitimate systems of adjudication for quashing pluralism and consolidating power.  We seek to explain current and historical authoritarian tactics—punishing dissidents, persecuting minorities, and codifying ingroup norms into law–as satisfying immediate motives like retribution or obedience, and made more or less likely by existing predispositions (e.g., for conformity) and particular environments (e.g., anomie). Our view highlights the unique affordances for social control that official systems of power make available, and in doing so, we also identify new tactics that meet our criteria of authoritarian behavior (e.g., selective rule enforcement, inequitable administrative burden). In sum, we provide a framework for understanding authoritarianism from a behavioral perspective, provide a bridge between individual ideology and current and historical authoritarian tactics, and highlight novel avenues for the psychological study of both authoritarianism and punishment more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: Misidentification Delusion Contents and Aberrant Prediction Errors in the General Population
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Meyer; Deanna Greco; Constance Lubinski; Philip R. Corlett
articles_hidden.abstract: Misidentification delusions – e.g., "My partner is an impostor” – occur most strikingly in rare neuropsychological cases, which are relatively immune to empirical study. Theorizing from these cases augurs commitments to a modular mental ontology. But what if misidentification beliefs were common? This would open the field to empirical study as never before. Moreover, if these beliefs could pre-date the index brain damage (albeit in attenuated form), it would challenge explanatory accounts which posit modular mechanisms for aberrant belief formation. We find that misidentification belief contents are prevalent in the general population; about a quarter of our online sample endorsed at least one (111 of 395 were endorsers). Furthermore, endorsing misidentification predicted relatively weaker Kamin blocking – an index of aberrant prediction error processing. Intriguingly, domain-general computational motifs related to particular phenomenological contents. Overall, these results invite an experimental exploration of misidentification delusions and further development of explanatory theories, beyond the status quo.

articles_hidden.title: A pilot study assessing the clinical significance of neurorehabilitation: A retrospective study using FIM+FAM, NPDS, and RCS-E.
articles_hidden.authors: Bipana Thapa; Adenekan Oyefeso
articles_hidden.abstract: This pilot study assessed the impact of neurorehabilitation by analysing changes in patient outcomes from admission to discharge using three key measures: the Functional Independence Measure, the Functional Assessment Measure (FIMFAM), the Northwick Park Dependency Scale (NPDS), and the Rehabilitation Complexity Scale-Extended (RCS-E). A retrospective analysis was conducted on the records of 31 patients admitted to a neurorehabilitation centre between April 2021 and March 2023. Paired t-tests were performed to assess statistically significant changes in these outcome measures, and the Reliable Change Index (RCI) was calculated to determine the clinical significance of observed changes. Significant improvements were found across all the measures. The FIM+FAM scores indicated enhanced motor and cognitive function (p<.0001), with the average score increasing by 28.19. NPDS scores reflected reduced care needs (avg. scores reduced by 8.42, p<.0001), similar to the reduced average scores (2.45) from the RCS-E (p<.0001), signifying decreased rehabilitation needs. The results exceeded RCI thresholds across measures, indicating clinically meaningful improvement; future work will include MDC thresholds for service-level benchmarking.

articles_hidden.title: School Distress and Attendance Difficulties for Neurodivergent Pupils: A Complex Interplay of Drivers, Feelings, and (A Lack of) Support
articles_hidden.authors: Chloe Fielding; Deborah M Riby; Sinead Mullally; Rachel Jewers; Mary Hanley
articles_hidden.abstract: School distress is a key driver of increasing attendance difficulties among neurodivergent children and young people (CYP) in the UK. Despite this, public and policy discourse often frames attendance difficulties as CYP ‘won’t’ rather than ‘can’t’ attend school, prioritising attendance over wellbeing. Research centring the lived experiences of neurodivergent CYP is needed to understand key contributors to attendance difficulties, their emotional experiences, and ways to improve support. 139 CYP and their parents/carers completed online questionnaires, including standardised measures of anxiety and sensory differences. CYP rated statements about school life and answered qualitative questions about school challenges, feelings about attendance difficulties, support, and suggested changes. Qualitative and quantitative findings identified anxiety and sensory experiences as key drivers of attendance difficulties. CYP described complex, mixed emotions about attendance, often feeling relieved yet simultaneously worried when absent from school. Although around 30% reported feeling supported by a trusted adult, many felt they received no helpful support. Participants highlighted the need for more inclusive sensory environments and greater staff understanding and support. School distress and attendance difficulties are complex and multifaceted. Effective interventions and policies must prioritise CYP’s wellbeing in parallel with attendance, rather than focusing solely on numerical attendance targets.

articles_hidden.title: Explaining Emotion Co-Occurrence: Comparison of Parsimonious, Formal Theories Using Multimodal, Within-Person Data
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastian Kueppers; Janis Zickfeld; Shukoofeh Ghadertootoonchi; Jens Lange
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion theories should explain when and how emotions co-occur. Investigating emotion co-occurrence, Lange and Zickfeld (2023) found support for the network theory of emotions. This theory suggests that emotions co-occur because the networks of interacting components that represent emotions partly overlap. However, Lange and Zickfeld’s evidence is limited to self-reports and between-person analyses. We substantially extended their work by applying between- and within-person network analytic tools to self-report, physiological (i.e., heart rate, respiration rate, skin conductance, goosebumps), and facial expression data of awe and fear. We compared five parsimonious, formalized theories of emotion co-occurrence derived from distinct emotion, network, and dimensional approaches to emotions. Consistent with Lange and Zickfeld’s (2023) findings, between-person analyses showed that the network theory best explains the co-occurrence of awe and fear. In contrast, the within-person analyses did not allow definitive conclusions regarding the competing theories. We discuss the utility of theory formalization, and highlight the need for the collection of within-person, multimodal emotion data for advancing research on emotion co-occurrence.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Normative Trajectory: Understanding Individual Differences in Adolescent Reward- Related Motivation and Risk for Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Ashley C Parr; Valerie J. Sydnor; Beatriz Luna
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is characterized by pronounced changes in incentive motivation that support exploration, learning, and the transition to independence in adulthood. Population-average developmental models have been instrumental in defining these normative changes and have shaped contemporary theories of adolescent neurodevelopment. However, growing evidence indicates that individuals differ substantially in how reward-related motivational systems mature. Despite this, the developmental sources and long-term consequences of this variability remain poorly understood. In this Review, we suggest that individual differences in developmental trajectories – including their timing, tempo, duration, and overall shape – represent an important framework for understanding vulnerability and resilience across psychopathology. We propose that reward-related motivational trajectories emerge through continual interactions between neuroplasticity and environmental experience. Early life experiences scaffold the developmental conditions from which incentive motivational systems mature, whereas ongoing experiences during adolescence calibrate these trajectories through experience-dependent plasticity. Using dopamine (DA)-sensitive mesocorticolimbic circuitry as the primary developmental system supporting reward and incentive motivation, we review evidence from longitudinal neuroimaging, animal models, and behavioral studies demonstrating how neurobiological maturation and environmental experience interact to shape developmental trajectories. We highlight growing evidence that person-centered developmental trajectories better characterize heterogeneity in substance use and other neuropsychiatric outcomes in comparison to population-average developmental trends. Finally, we discuss emerging methodological approaches – including dense longitudinal designs, flexible nonlinear modeling, normative developmental modeling, and person-centered trajectory analyses – that provide new opportunities to identify when developmental trajectories diverge, which biological and environmental mechanisms drive these individual differences, and how they relate to long-term outcomes. By shifting the focus from describing normative developmental change to understanding why individuals diverge from expected developmental trajectories, this framework provides a foundation for identifying mechanistically informed developmental phenotypes, individualized windows of vulnerability and resilience, and developmentally timed prevention and intervention strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Being who you are: phenotype-genotype congruency and wellbeing
articles_hidden.authors: A.J.M.R. Geijsen; René Pool; Meike Bartels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Differences in wellbeing are shaped by genetic predispositions and environmental influences, yet recommendations for improving wellbeing are often framed as universally beneficial. We examined whether wellbeing is higher when individuals’ observed phenotypes correspond more closely to their genetic predispositions. 
Methods: We used data from 18,748 participants of the  Netherlands Twin Register. Phenotype-genotype congruency was examined across social, health, and lifestyle-related phenotypes using a triangulation approach with three complementary methods. First, cross-sectional generalized estimating equation models tested whether difference scores between phenotypes and corresponding polygenic scores were associated with wellbeing. Second, response surface analyses (RSA) modelling linear, non-linear, and interaction effects of phenotype and genotype. And third, longitudinal multi-level models using repeated measures of phenotype-genotype difference scores and wellbeing over time.
Results: Greater phenotype–genotype congruency was associated with higher wellbeing for BMI, neuroticism, sleep duration, and social interaction in cross-sectional analyses,. Longitudinal analyses showed similar associations for BMI, neuroticism, self-rated health, sleep duration, social interaction, and TV time. Effect sizes were small but generally consistent across models. In contrast, RSA did not support phenotype–genotype congruency effects. BMI, neuroticism, and social interaction showed partial congruency patterns, but neither satisfied the congruency criteria (Humberg et al., 2019). 
Conclusions: Across phenotypes, higher congruency between phenotypes and genetic predispositions was associated with higher wellbeing in difference score models, but were not confirmed by RSA. The findings suggest that phenotype–genotype congruency may be relevant for wellbeing in some domains, and that replication is needed to better understand the complexity of wellbeing.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Labels: Data-Derived Profiles Better Describe Children and Young People’s Needs in Education
articles_hidden.authors: Jo Hutchinson; Emre Deniz; Megan Frith; Kathryn Asbury; Dianne Newbury; Umar Toseeb
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Children and young people (CYP) with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) have poorer outcomes compared with those without SEND. It remains unclear how to best identify CYP with SEND. We examined whether profiles of CYP needs align with SEND identification and whether they discriminate young adult outcomes better than current SEND identification. Methods. We analysed data from three population-based cohorts in England: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (N = 15,645); Millennium Cohort Study (N = 18,827); Twins Early Development Study (N = 7,859). We fitted latent mixture models to data on social and behavioural, emotional, and cognitive functioning. We did this separately for each cohort at three developmental stages: early childhood (age 3-5 years); middle childhood (age 7-9 years); adolescence (age 13-18 years). We ran logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses to determine whether data-derived sub-groups discriminate young adult outcomes better than SEND identification. Results. There were CYP with similar profiles of strengths and challenges: typically developing; global difficulties; cognitive difficulties; and social, emotional, behavioural difficulties. Up to a third of CYP experienced difficulties at two or more developmental stages, indicating high levels of persistent educational need in England. SEND identification only partially overlapped with the data-derived sub-groups. Agreement was highest for global and cognitive difficulty sub-groups and lowest for emotional difficulties sub-groups. Difficulty sub-groups showed consistent associations across a range of young adult outcomes. Data-derived sub-groups discriminated university degree attainment, receipt of state benefits, anti-social behaviour, and mental health outcomes better than SEND identification, whereas SEND identification performed better only for GCSE attainment. Conclusions. Current SEND identification only partially captures underlying persistent educational need in England. Descriptive profiles of CYP’s strengths and challenges are likely to be a better alternative to the current SEND system for identifying CYP at risk of poor outcomes post compulsory education.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental variation from rational choice
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel David Jones; Dara Tan; Paul Rauwolf
articles_hidden.abstract: Rational choice theory offers a normative account of the allocation of bounded cognitive resources under constraints. This work has focused largely on static solutions, leaving the developmental implications of rational choice relatively under-researched. Conversely, developmental science has in general overlooked the role of an individual's choices, actions, and habits in shaping rather than merely reflecting developmental variation, from delay to psychopathology to expertise. The aim of this paper is to characterise the developmental implications of rational inattention, a leading framework within rational choice theory, and in doing so develop a normative account of how adaptive behaviour reciprocally shapes the emergence of diversity in intelligent behaviour. The thesis we develop is that rational choice – behaviour that is adaptive not only to the structure of the environment but to the constraints of the agent – shapes neurodevelopmental variation beyond the neurogenetic factors that promote that behaviour. We begin by presenting static solutions to rationally inattentive choice problems, before turning to adaptivity and learning over time. We demonstrate that adaptive behaviour contributes unique variance to developmental outcomes and predicts inertia in changing environments. Finally, we distil the key features of rationally inattentive behaviour and corresponding empirical support from the developmental science literature. The strength of this approach is to demonstrate that some of the signatures of diversity in intelligent behaviour across the lifespan can in principle fall out of a minimal set of rational assumptions. This has implications for how we think about and respond to individual differences in human development.

articles_hidden.title: Risks of Using Large Language Models in Grading: LLMs and Humans Prefer LLM-Generated Writing Over Human’s but LLMs Show a Stronger Systematic Bias
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew HC Mak
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent studies suggest that large language models (LLMs) can approximate human grading performance, raising the prospect of their use in educational assessment. However, an important question remains: can LLMs evaluate student work fairly? In Study 1, we examined whether LLM evaluators exhibit systematic preference when grading psychology dissertations from three sources: (a) dissertations authored by 1,426 undergraduate students, (b) the same dissertations rewritten by GPT-4 or GPT-5 (i.e., paraphrased), and (c) dissertations fully generated by GPT models using student-written abstracts as prompts. Across three families of evaluators (GPT, Gemma, Qwen), LLMs consistently assigned the lowest scores to student-authored dissertations, intermediate scores to GPT-rewritten dissertations, and the highest scores to fully GPT-generated dissertations (student-authored < GPT-rewritten < fully GPT-generated). In Study 2, we tested the generalisability of this pattern using abstracts rather than the entire dissertations and observed the same graded preference across three of the four LLM evaluators. To assess whether humans also demonstrate the same graded preference, we conducted a preregistered experiment with 300 human raters who scored student-authored, GPT-rewritten, or fully GPT-generated abstracts. Human raters scored student-authored and GPT-rewritten abstracts similarly, although both were rated significantly lower than the fully GPT-generated abstracts (student-authored ≈ GPT-rewritten < fully GPT-generated). Importantly, though, the effect size for the contrast between student vs. fully GPT-generated abstracts was considerably smaller in humans (Cohen’s d = 0.58) than in LLM evaluators, where Cohen’s ds > 0.85. These findings provide evidence that LLMs generally have a strong bias to favour LLM-generated content, more so than humans’, raising important concerns about the fairness of deploying LLMs as evaluators in educational settings.

articles_hidden.title: A Review of How Linguistic Context Shapes Incidental Word Learning During Reading and the Adaptive Binding of Context (ABC) Theoretical Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew HC Mak; Kate Nation
articles_hidden.abstract: From mid-childhood onwards, much vocabulary growth occurs through independent reading. In this review, we examine how the linguistic contexts surrounding unfamiliar words influence incidental word learning, aligning with emerging perspectives that view word meanings as context-sensitive representations that are updated and refined across encounters. Specifically, we review evidence concerning six contextual characteristics: contextual presence, contextual informativeness, contextual valence, topic familiarity, topic interest, and contextual diversity. Two characteristics emerge as relatively consistent facilitators of learning: Words are learned more successfully when they occur in familiar topics and in texts that readers find interesting. In contrast, the effects of the remaining contextual characteristics are more conditional, and/or less evidenced. For example, contextual informativeness appears more beneficial for L2 than L1 readers, and more semantically diverse contexts tend to hamper initial meaning learning of abstract but no necessarily concrete words. We propose the Adaptive Binding of Context (ABC) Framework to unify these heterogenous and disparate findings. It assumes that unfamiliar words are initially encoded as part of the situation model constructed during reading and that linguistic context influences word learning through three interrelated pathways: constraining meaning inference, regulating attention, and linking new words to existing knowledge. Critically, the relative contribution of these pathways varies adaptively as a function of word characteristics, readers’ cognitive and linguistic resources, and the current state of word-specific knowledge. This perspective helps explain why the same contextual characteristic may facilitate learning under some conditions but not others. More broadly, we argue that contextual influences on word learning are best understood as adaptive rather than fixed, highlighting the need for research that moves beyond asking whether a particular contextual characteristic facilitates learning and instead asks when, for whom, and at what stage of learning it is most beneficial. We conclude by outlining priorities for future research.

articles_hidden.title: De la communication médiatisée par l’IA à l’usurpation d’authenticité : quels risques pour la confiance épistémique dans les relations intimes et thérapeutiques ?
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Schmidt; Royce Anders; Benjamin PUTOIS
articles_hidden.abstract:
Contexte. L’essor rapide des systèmes d’intelligence artificielle générative a conduit à l’émergence de la communication médiatisée par l’IA (AI-mediated communication, AIMC), dans laquelle un système algorithmique intervient directement dans la production du langage et de l’expression affective. Si l’AIMC est de plus en plus utilisée dans les relations intimes et les contextes thérapeutiques, ses implications cliniques et éthiques demeurent largement sous-théorisées.
Méthode. Une recherche systématique de la littérature a été réalisée dans MEDLINE afin d’identifier les travaux empiriques et théoriques portant sur l’AIMC et ses effets interpersonnels, psychologiques et cliniques.
Résultats. La littérature existante met en évidence des résultats ambivalents. D’une part, l’assistance par l’IA peut améliorer l’efficacité communicationnelle dans des interactions instrumentales ou transactionnelles. D’autre part, lorsque la communication est censée véhiculer une présence subjective, un engagement personnel ou une responsabilité morale, l’AIMC peut fragiliser les perceptions d’authenticité et de confiance, en particulier lorsque son usage est implicite. Afin de conceptualiser ce risque spécifique, nous proposons la notion d’usurpation d’authenticité, distincte de l’usurpation d’identité, qui désigne le déplacement silencieux du travail subjectif, intentionnel et affectif par lequel une personne se rend présente à l’autre.
Implications cliniques. L’usurpation d’authenticité est susceptible d’affecter particulièrement les relations fondées sur la confiance épistémique, telles que les relations intimes et la psychothérapie, ainsi que les populations vulnérables (traumatismes complexes, trouble de l’attachement). En psychothérapie, l’AIMC non divulguée pourrait compromettre l’alliance thérapeutique.
Conclusion. Ces éléments plaident pour une posture de précaution, fondée sur la transparence, la prévention de la cyberviolence relationnelle et la clarification des usages de l’IA, ainsi que pour le développement de recherches empiriques visant à tester les hypothèses cliniques formulées.

articles_hidden.title: A two-timescale framework for gut–brain influences on arousal, motivation, and affect
articles_hidden.authors: Nikolina Birimac; Irene Perez-Montalvo; Soyoung Q Park; Ignacio Rebollo
articles_hidden.abstract: The same brain can think, feel, and perform differently from one hour to the next. Cognitive neuroscience has traditionally explained this variability through fluctuations in neural activity and network dynamics within the brain itself. Yet the brain continuously receives bodily signals that convey physiological state and energy availability. Here, we propose a two-timescale framework for gut–brain communication. We argue that the gut influences cognition, mood, and arousal through two partially distinct but interacting pathways operating at different temporal scales. On a fast timescale, rhythmic gastric activity, cycling approximately every 20 seconds, may bias neural excitability and large-scale brain dynamics. We propose that stomach–brain coupling functions as an “arousal dial,” biasing the brain towards internally oriented and metabolically efficient states. On a slower timescale, metabolic hormones such as ghrelin, GLP-1, insulin, and leptin fluctuate across minutes to hours, providing information about metabolic state. We hypothesise that these hormonal signals act as an “energy gauge,” tuning motivation, reward sensitivity, and affective state according to energy availability. We review evidence linking gastric rhythms and metabolic hormones to arousal, cognition, reward, and mood, and outline predictions for dense within-person neuroimaging, physiological, and endocrine studies of mental fluctuations.

articles_hidden.title: Retained Activity and Psychological Capital in Ukrainian Academic Populations, 2024
articles_hidden.authors: Volodymyr Evheniiovych Momot; Viktoriia Sokolova
articles_hidden.abstract:
Research on Ukrainian higher education under war has documented institutional adaptation in detail, but individual psychological resources remain largely unmeasured, and where activity appears as a coping factor, its content is rarely distinguished from its presence.

This study reports psychological capital (PCQ-24) across three independent Ukrainian academic collections in 2024 (N = 240): faculty at a private university in Dnipro (N = 76), students at the same university (N = 61), and students at two state universities in front-line Zaporizhzhia (N = 103).

Retained activity predicted psychological capital in every sample; geography and demography did not. The employment contrast replicated in two independent student collections under different assignment procedures (g = +0.62, 95% CI [+0.05,+1.23]; g = +1.43). Among faculty, self-rated research activity predicted psychological capital (b = +0.40, p < .0001, R² = 0.31). Location, displacement, gender and age showed no large effects, with Bayes factors weakly supporting the null (BF₀₁ = 2.4–2.9); displacement, available here at individual level, replicated a null reported in earlier work on this population.

Four structural analyses characterise the construct. Profile analysis shows samples differing in elevation rather than shape (variance ratio 58:1). Clustering, blind to all covariates, yields a stable partition (88%) falling along research activity (p = .0006) rather than demography. Network modelling identifies Hope as most central — robustly among students (96–99% of resamples), contested with self-efficacy among faculty (52%). Mokken scaling reveals a reproducible difficulty gradient (ρ = .67–.82) in which Resilience is retained longest and Optimism relinquished first, a possible early depletion marker.

A further claim, more tentative, concerns which activity qualifies. Conservation of Resources holds that investment implies return, predicting that only activity reproducing what was invested generates resource. Two contrasts support this: volunteering dropped out when controlled against research activity (p = .20), and among equally employed students those working in their field scored higher (g = 0.64, p = .023), though this did not survive multivariate control at n = 58. Students holding employment and a merit stipend scored lower than employed non-stipend holders (g = −0.48; BF₀₁ = 0.96), an effect absent among non-working students. These contrasts were formulated after inspecting the data and rest on the weakest links in the chain.

At the institutional level, a single case documents a university resuming teaching eighteen days after suspension in February 2022, enabled by organisational competence built for a different crisis. We propose a refinement to Hobfoll's resource caravan passageways: a passageway defines what is possible but does not itself produce passage through it.

Magnitudes varied across replications (g = 0.62–1.43); the pooled value should not be interpreted.

articles_hidden.title: Digital implementation: Developing digital mental health skills in the psychological workforce using e-learning.
articles_hidden.authors: Helen Pote; Alesia Moulton-Perkins; Gemma Rides
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Digital mental health (DMH) delivery is expanding across psychological services, yet many practitioners lack the digital skills and confidence required for safe and effective online practice. In order to support digital implementation within mental health governmental and professional bodies emphasise the urgent need to develop digital competencies in the workforce and the need for scalable training solutions.

Aims: To develop and evaluate a national e-learning package designed to improve digital mental health competencies, confidence and attitudes among novice psychological practitioners in the UK.

Methods: A four-module e-learning package was produced using Sheth et al.’s five-phase e-learning development framework. Content aligned with the British Psychological Society’s Digital Competence Framework. First-year students from three clinical psychology doctoral training programmes participated in the e-learning and completed pre- and post-training measures of digital competence (Digital Competencies for Applied Psychological Practitioners, DCAPP), attitudes towards digital interventions and confidence. Quantitative data were analysed using paired t-tests. Qualitative user feedback was gathered and synthesised using deductive thematic analysis. 

Results: Eighty-three students completed the e-learning and 52 provided matched pre-post data. Overall digital competencies significantly improved, including students’ digital mental health knowledge and abilities. Attitudes towards digital interventions became more favourable and confidence in practising digitally increased. Qualitative findings indicated the modules were comprehensive, relevant and engaging, with valued interactive elements such as reflective exercises, quizzes and video content. Some students found modules lengthy and suggested shorter videos, improved time estimates, and downloadable summaries. Minor technical issues and diversity considerations were also identified.

Conclusions: The e-learning package effectively enhanced DMH competencies, attitudes and confidence among novice psychological practitioners. Embedding competence-based digital training into preregistration curricula supports workforce readiness and contributes to scaling digitally enabled care pathways.

articles_hidden.title: Risk-Free Study Designs Miss the Weak Trust–Behavior Link in Human–Automation Interaction: Evidence From Two Virtual Reality Experiments
articles_hidden.authors: Tobias Rieger; Steffen Hoesterey; Linda Onnasch
articles_hidden.abstract: Theories and practitioners alike assume that trust—a latent construct—causally predicts behavior. In human–automation and human–AI interaction, a system's characteristics (e.g., its reliability) are often thought to shape trust, which in turn supposedly predicts how much a human depends on the system. However, little evidence thus far supports this claim, particularly under risk, which theory treats as a precondition for a trust–dependence link. We addressed this gap in two laboratory experiments that used virtual reality to manipulate risk immersively, as part of the environment.
