In Experiment 1, we varied system reliability (low vs. high) and risk (absent vs. present) between subjects and tested whether several trust measures mediated the effect of reliability on dependence behavior. Trust mediated this effect only under risk, and only for a single-item measure. Thus, a standard no-risk design would have missed the link entirely. However, even the single-item trust measure explained little of the variance in behavior. In Experiment 2, conducted entirely under risk, we replicated the single-item trust mediation but found two further mediators: external regulation (the felt pressure to monitor the system) and one's perceived competence relative to the system. None of them, however, explained more than a small portion of variance within dependence behavior. Thus, even where trust predicted behavior, it did so weakly and non-uniquely. Subjective measures therefore cannot substitute for measuring behavior—whether or not trust theory is correct.

articles_hidden.title: The Phenomenology of Advanced Meditation Experiences and Interpretation of the Nature of Human Consciousness
articles_hidden.authors: Patrizio Tressoldi; Fabio Mattiussi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Forty-five long-term meditators with a minimum of five years of continuous daily practice were requested to describe their highest meditative experiences using the micro-phenomenological self-inquiry (MPSI) method and to provide their interpretation of the nature of human consciousness.
The first-person accounts of meditators consistently reported profound and stable experiences of body and identity transcendence, often describing non-dual states and a pervasive sense of unity. Most participants understood consciousness to be universal in nature and not reducible to a byproduct of the brain.
These first-person accounts offer novel insights into the characteristics of long-term meditation experiences and the fundamental nature of consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: A Pattern of Relatively Conserved Fluency Indicates Preclinical Minor Cognitive Decline
articles_hidden.authors: Rain Simons; Andrew R. A. Conway
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: When neuropsychological testing is used for medical assessment of cognition, individual differences in premorbid ability may not be accounted for, leaving some individuals at risk for under-detection of impairment. We investigated whether patterns of relative performance in different cognitive domains could be used to detect early-stage cognitive decline in the absence of baseline performance data and irrespective of individual differences in overall performance.
Method: In an exploratory secondary analysis of data from 200 older adults followed longitudinally, we used profile analysis to compare the domain-specific performance of those who experienced minor cognitive decline over a 12-to-18-month interval with those who did not experience decline.
Results: We found that having experienced minor cognitive decline in the preceding 12 to 18 months was associated with a pattern of higher performance in fluency relative to performance in six other cognitive domains. In our study, this pattern of relative performance could be used to identify recent decline with 79.5% accuracy, 95% CI [73.2%, 84.9%], even without knowledge of overall performance. However, individuals who performed in the top third at baseline could not be shown to exhibit the same pattern of cross-domain cognitive performance following decline.
Conclusions: A pattern of higher performance in fluency relative to other cognitive domains may indicate recent minor cognitive decline. Results suggest that knowledge of a patient’s baseline cognitive ability or intelligence can inform the interpretation of neuropsychological test results. This study should be replicated using a dataset for which early adulthood cognitive scores are available.

articles_hidden.title: A Systematic Review of Effects of Long-Term and Advanced Meditation on Mental Health: Psychiatric Symptoms, Stress, and Challenging Events
articles_hidden.authors: Terje Sparby; Jerron Chan; Oliver Andersson Hugemark; Vanessa Naughton; Matthew Sacchet
articles_hidden.abstract: Meditation research has grown considerably, yet its clinical implications for advanced and long-term practitioners remain poorly understood. Meditation’s mental health implications extend beyond benefit, encompassing psychiatric risk, adverse experiences, and differentiating between meditative progress and psychopathology. This review synthesizes evidence on how advanced and long-term meditation affects psychiatric symptomatology, stress, and challenging practice-related experiences. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search across PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Embase on April 5, 2026 identified 1,229 articles, of which 52 met inclusion criteria following rigorous screening. Although findings suggest advanced practice confers deeper mental health benefits than non-advanced practices, significant literature gaps remain. Terminology is inconsistent across studies, adverse event monitoring is largely absent, and no established frameworks exist for distinguishing between potentially transformative challenges and the onset of psychopathology. Addressing these gaps demands safety-centered research protocols, clear risk stratification criteria, and evidence-based clinical guidelines governing contraindications and appropriate practitioner support.

articles_hidden.title: Two separable axes of intervention in a dependency-ordered recovery geometry
articles_hidden.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles_hidden.abstract: Catatonia recovers through capacities returning in a fixed dependency order, and benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy work without a known target. On an evidence-coupled bistable cascade over that order we take three quantities to be externally accessible: the root capacity, the coupling between capacities, and accumulated evidence. Here we show that evidence has no external port and the other two act on disjoint regions. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so acute conversion needs an excursion, whereas an additive excitatory drive converts on its own. Above one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, propagation separates into immediate, metastable and confined. On the modelled branch coupling alone shifts the resting first stage, so a treatment effective in both states is predicted to have separable excursion and coupling components, identifiable in model coordinates.

articles.title: Statistischer Quartalsbericht 3/2019
articles.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles.title: the em—dash fails to em–erge: a registered null result for U+2014 in Polish and an exploratory function-word shift in 60,275 Sejm interpellations, 2015–2025
articles.authors: PRZEMYSŁAW CZUMA
articles.abstract:
Since the release of ChatGPT (30 November 2022) a belief has spread that the em-dash "—" reveals text written with the help of a language model. This preregistered study tested that claim on 60,275 single-author written parliamentary questions (interpelacje) submitted to the Polish Sejm between 2015 and 2025. The decision rule was registered on OSF before the data were seen.

The cue does not work in Polish. The registered hypothesis was not confirmed: in the decisive cell the share of documents containing an em-dash rose by 1.73 percentage points, but the confidence interval of that difference includes zero (−4.44 to +8.07 pp), so the second condition of the two-part decision rule was not satisfied, and three registered disconfirmation conditions fired. Follow-up tests point to the cause: models writing in Polish, and machine-translation flows, put a shorter dash there – the en-dash "–". The marker is anglocentric and is not suitable for Polish.

An exploratory analysis measured something else: the frequency of Polish closed-class words (conjunctions, prepositions, particles) that a writer does not choose consciously. The reference point was an independently published corpus of Polish human-written and model-written texts, frozen together with its reading rule before measurement. From 2024 the distribution of these words moves toward the profile of the models (rank correlation rho = +0.368; 95% CI +0.228 to +0.461), while at a placebo date – the 2019 change of parliamentary term, where no such effect is expected – it does not move at all (−0.070; difference +0.438, +0.221 to +0.611). The shift survives four term-change controls.

The change is small but widespread, and that is the correct description of its strength. Inside a single parliamentary office it is barely visible (median rho +0.125), yet it points the same way in 61 of 84 offices that could be measured separately (72.6%, one-sided p = 2·10⁻⁵), against 53.8% at the control date, which is what chance produces.

There is no sudden jump at the date of the ChatGPT release. The change becomes visible in 2024 and unambiguous in 2025, and the shape of the transition (ramp versus late step) is not identified. The result describes a shift across a whole population of documents and allows no statement about the authorship of any single document or about any individual member of parliament. It does not establish a cause: changes in office staff, in subject matter and in editing practice remain possible explanations alongside tools. An independent reimplementation, with no access to the author's code, reproduced the corpus, the deduplication, the author panel and the headline analyses from raw HTML down.

articles.title: CLAIM: Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging - A Theory of How Conversational AI Shapes Minority and Majority Voices in Group Deliberation
articles.authors: Hoang Phuong Nhi Do; Suzanne van Gils; Christoph Lutz
articles.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes communicative spaces preceding social interaction, yet its effects are often studied in isolation from subsequent group dynamics. Recognizing this gap, we propose the Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging (CLAIM) theory, which argues that pre-deliberative AI interaction calibrates perceived opinion legitimacy and shapes voice in group deliberation. Drawing on AI sycophancy, the Spiral of Silence, and multi-level legitimacy literature, CLAIM proposes that high AI sycophancy increases validity and propriety beliefs, whereas opposition from AI deflates them. Moreover, structural opinion status moderates these effects: AI sycophancy can generate a compensatory voice effect for opinion-minority participants, while AI challenge can produce compounded silencing. Additionally, a legitimacy shock may emerge when minority-opinion holders encounter group compositions that contradict AI-calibrated legitimacy beliefs. Together, CLAIM extends AI sycophancy research by theorizing conversational AI as a legitimacy-calibrating force that can reshape voice in group deliberation, particularly under structural communicative inequality.

articles.title: Detecting Coordinated Posting Behavior on Social Media. Introducing and Evaluating the Embedding-Based Tool ‘coorsim’
articles.authors: Daniel Thiele; Miriam Milzner
articles.abstract: The detection of coordinated behavior on social media is an effective heuristic for uncovering organized manipulation of online publics. Existing detection tools rely on identifying identical or lexically similar content disseminated rapidly by networks of accounts. However, these tools are ill-suited to detect the coordinated posting of semantically similar content. This is a shortcoming in the age of LLMs that enable the large-scale generation of diverse yet semantically equivalent content. In this paper, we introduce and systematically evaluate coorsim, an open source R package for for detecting semantically similar coordinated posting. The package provides a platform-agnostic end-to-end workflow encompassing embedding retrieval, coordinated community detection, automated community labeling, and visualization. We systematically evaluate its performance against the most comprehensive benchmark dataset of known influence operations to date, covering 15 international campaigns. Across 3,780 evaluated parameter combinations, the best stable configuration achieved an overall F1 of 0.69. Using multilevel Bayesian regression models, we isolated the influence of parameter choices. We also provide a qualitative assessment of automatically generated community labels. Our results demonstrate that coorsim provides a valid, albeit not flawless, contribution to closing a gap in the landscape of computational tools for detecting coordinated online behavior.

articles.title: What Drives Legislative Anger? Multimodal Evidence from South Korea's National Assembly
articles.authors: Haejo Kang; Songpo Yang
articles.abstract: Legislative anger is often understood as expressive representation, a signal that legislators passionately defend constituent interests. We argue that partisan blame underpins these displays, especially when parties attack one another over alleged misconduct. Using deep-learning models, we measure vocal and facial anger across 355 hours of plenary debate in South Korea's 20th National Assembly (2016-2020), covering 11,060 speech segments by 247 legislators. We find that anger peaks when legislators discuss scandal, at twice the level of policy debate. Moreover, a quasi-experiment around the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye shows that the same legislators become angrier in opposition and calmer in government. These findings challenge accounts that treat legislative anger primarily as constituency signaling and highlight how partisan blame and institutional position shape emotional expression in legislatures.

articles.title: LINGUISTIC STRATEGIES IN MISINFORMATION: A SEMANTIC-PRAGMATIC FRAMEWORK FOR DETECTING MANIPULATION IN MEDIA DISCOURSE
articles.authors: ANGELICA JEANICE MARTINS ANDERSEN
articles.abstract: This article identifies recurrent patterns of linguistic behaviour characteristic of misinformation and proposes a semantic-pragmatic approach to analysing manipulation in media texts. Through the application of five mechanisms – implicature (GRICE, 1975; HORN, 2011; SPERBER; WILSON, 1995), presupposition (SCHLENKER, 2011; SIMONS, 2005; STALNAKER, 1973), modality (VON FINTEL, 2006), genericity (CARLSON, 2011; MÜLLER, 2003), and deverbal nominalisation (GRIMSHAW, 1990, 2011) – it demonstrates how these resources are exploited to constrain inferential paths and generate interpretive distortions. Although other mechanisms are available, the study focuses on these five because they are most frequently exploited in misinformation discourse. The analysis identifies five main manipulative strategies: (1) the suggestion of misleading meanings through implicatures, which allow the speaker to maintain plausible deniability by keeping manipulative content outside the truth-conditional level of the utterance; (2) the naturalisation of controversial content as established fact; (3) the exploitation of modal asymmetry to obscure the boundary between speculative possibility and normative necessity; (4) the promotion of essentialist universalisations through generic and vague reference; and (5) the suppression of information about agents and responsibilities. These strategies are exemplified by a 2023 news story on inclusive terminology in healthcare, which serves as a paradigmatic case for revealing the linguistic architecture of misinformation. The results contribute to the semantics-pragmatics interface by operationalising the distinction between what is said and what is implicated, and by revealing the recurrent patterns through which ordinary pragmatic mechanisms are strategically exploited to produce manipulative effects in media discourse.

articles.title: Housing and the False Promise of Abundance
articles.authors: Sophie Bandarkar; Tahir de Noronha; Maximilian Buchholz
articles.abstract: Following the publication of Klein and Thompson’s (2025) remarkably popular book, Abundance has emerged as the key diagnosis and remedy for America’s housing affordability challenges. The book’s central argument, along with allied academic work, is that deregulation will substantially increase housing supply and in turn meaningfully improve housing affordability. We argue this framework rests on inconclusive and contested empirical ground. First, a thorough literature review of relevant research demonstrates the links between deregulation, supply, and prices are much weaker and more complex than abundance advocates suggest. Second, returning to descriptive evidence shows that the basic facts which motivate the abundance argument are also contested. There is no incontrovertible evidence of a major supply shortage in the U.S. The abundance movement’s hyper fixation on housing supply and deregulation risks foreclosing possibilities for other targeted interventions that have a greater potential for remedying the affordability crisis.

articles.title: From Division to Action? Mobilizing Women Through Gender Inequality Framing
articles.authors: Colette Marcellin
articles.abstract: Though American women face significant economic, political, and social inequality, it has been far more challenging to mobilize women around this inequality than some other groups. In this paper, I use a multi-method approach to causally examine how women respond to mobilization efforts from women's movements and organizations. First, in a survey experiment, I find that frames that raise awareness of gender inequality and emphasize the need to build on women's progress significantly influence women's participatory intentions and political attitudes. To examine effects among those who are already engaged around issues of inequality, I then conduct a field experiment with a women's political organization. Results from this study suggest more mixed effects of outreach about gender inequality and progress, with null effects on email engagement yet increases in donation behavior. This paper has important implications for academic research on political behavior and applied strategies to engage women in the context of recent social movements and elections.

articles.title: Branding at the Water’s Edge: Perceived Elite Polarization of Ukraine Aid, 2022–2024
articles.authors: Haoran Shi; Wanting Wang; Dario Krpan
articles.abstract: United States assistance to Ukraine began with broad bipartisan support and acquired a durable partisan structure within eighteen months. We treat that transformation as a naturally occurring case for observing party brand formation, which requires parties both to occupy distinct positions and to speak about those positions consistently. Drawing on 37,312 sentences from 11,819 news articles published between March 2022 and December 2024, we annotated each sentence on one general aid dimension and three explanatory dimensions using a large language model, masking party and politician references so that positions were recovered from what a sentence conveys rather than from prior association with a party. Aggregating to articles and then to months produced continuous series of between-party polarization and within-party message coherence as represented in news coverage, which we combined into a Party Brand Index. Polarization on General Ukraine Aid Stance increased, with the fitted gap between the final and initial months widening by 11.71 points, and it did so through three persistent level shifts rather than gradual drift. Both parties moved toward opposition and Republicans moved further. Among the explanatory dimensions, the framing that set foreign commitments against domestic priorities aligned most closely with the aid stance gap, although that ordering did not survive dependence-preserving resampling. Neither party's message coherence tracked polarization from month to month, yet Republican coverage converged substantially across the period while Democratic coverage did not. Brand formation was therefore neither smooth, nor symmetric, nor synchronized, and the two conditions a brand requires advanced within the same party on different schedules.

articles.title: AGIR: a theory-based framework to evaluate impacts of game-based interventions for sustainability transitions
articles.authors: Sylvain Dernat; Clara Fiorio; Myriam Grillot; Gilles Martel; Médulline Terrier-Gesbert
articles.abstract:
Background: Game-based interventions (GBI) increasingly embed simulation games within broader transformation processes targeting sustainability challenges. However, evaluation frameworks remain predominantly session-centred and learning-oriented, offering limited insight into how in-game dynamics translate into real-world practice change. This gap is particularly critical for GBI seeking to influence behaviours, coordination mechanisms, and institutional trajectories over extended time horizons.
Method: This article proposes a framework for Assessing Game-based Interventions in Real-world contexts (AGIR), a theory-based tool designed to assess multi-level change processes in GBI. Drawing on program evaluation theory, behavioural sciences, and simulation and gaming research, AGIR structures evaluation across six levels (L0–L5): from game design and in-session dynamics (L0–L1), through learning (L2) and behavioural change (L3), to practice change (L4) and transformative systemic impacts (L5). The framework explicitly models mechanisms, contextual factors, and temporal pathways linking intervention design to sustainability outcomes.
Contribution: AGIR’s contribution is threefold: it reinforces theoretical foundations by explicitly connecting design choices with evaluation concepts; it provides a comprehensive reference point enabling comparison across contexts through standardised levels and hypothesised mechanisms; and it functions as a formative accompaniment tool supporting ex ante hypothesis formulation, in itinere adjustments, and ex post impact analysis. By shifting evaluation from end-point outcome measurement toward process-oriented understanding of contribution, AGIR addresses longstanding calls for rigorous yet practical frameworks adapted to complex, action-oriented interventions.
Conclusion: The framework is designed for adaptability across intervention contexts while preserving theoretical coherence. Though resource-intensive, AGIR offers practitioners and researchers a structured approach to assess whether and how GBI contribute to sustainable change, fostering an evaluation culture essential for demonstrating the impact potential of simulation games.

articles.title: The Competitiveness and WellFair: An approach of Angola Competitiveness Fail
articles.authors: Nerhum Sandambi
articles.abstract: Competitiveness can, in particular, be a powerful means of improving efficiency and the high quality of products on offer, which significantly drive the market and naturally ensure the greatest possible diversity of products available. On the other hand, some countries, such as Angola, and other developing countries, naturally exhibit a significant lack of a competitive environment; this is further evidenced, for example, by the weak business environment that exists. The weakness of the private sector further helps to explain this situation; for example, in Angola, the two most significant companies are state-owned enterprises, which naturally ensure high and significant sustainability for the Angolan economy as a whole. On the other hand, the strong presence of the informal economy contributes to the creation of a poor competitive environment. Certain fundamental conditions are naturally identified as other key factors contributing to this economic inefficiency, chiefly the lack of adequate economic infrastructure. In many key industries, there is naturally a high degree of concentration; for example, in the telecommunications sector, where Unitel holds the majority share of the market. This concentration, in particular, typically leads to a high level of inefficiency in the services provided. Other services, such as water supply and electricity distribution, naturally exhibit high levels of concentration within the economy; these concentrations are, in particular, reinforced by the nature of the companies involved, the majority of which are public enterprises. Thus, in general, the analysis shows that high levels of industry concentration reduce the diversity of key products on offer and contribute significantly to negative impacts on overall welfare. In Angola in particular, this evidence is strongly consistent with the lack of local production, as the majority of basic needs are met through imported goods. According to the evidence, the absence of a strong competitive environment leads the market towards the emergence of negative externalities.

articles.title: Classification testing: A new framework for drawing qualitative conclusions from quantitative estimates
articles.authors: Andrew C. Eggers; Zikai Li
articles.abstract: Social scientists rely on hypothesis testing to support their research conclusions, but the standard tests are designed for testing one hypothesis rather than adjudicating between rival possibilities.  We develop a new framework, "classification testing", as an alternative. Instead of selecting one hypothesis to test, a researcher conducting a classification test decides what qualitative distinctions ("classes") are most substantively relevant; the test either assigns the estimand to a class  with error control similar to that of a conventional hypothesis test,  or declares the result inconclusive. We argue that classification testing is superior to current practice not just when the objective is to adjudicate between rival possibilities but also when there is one research hypothesis to be tested, because classification testing exposes that hypothesis to refutation.  We illustrate the framework by applying it to a well-known media experiment and offer an R package to aid in implementation.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Co-Writing the Self: Conversational AI as a Reflective Partner in Narrative Identity Reconstruction
articles.authors: Reginah Pearl Malebogo Lerubisi
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in writing and reflective practice, yet limited empirical research has examined how sustained interaction with conversational AI may mediate narrative identity. This study explores how ongoing engagement with ChatGPT shaped self-reflection, authorship, authenticity, and the interpretation of lived experience. Guided by an interpretivist paradigm, the study employed analytic autoethnography based on sustained interaction with ChatGPT across a purposively bounded longitudinal conversational corpus on academic, professional, and personal contexts. Conversational transcripts and reflective journal records were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Narrative Analysis, integrating Narrative Identity Theory and Post-Phenomenology. Analysis identified interconnected processes through which ChatGPT shifted from an information tool towards a reflective conversational partner, supported narrative integration, mediated reflection and decision-making, and prompted ongoing negotiation of authenticity and human authorship. ChatGPT contributed linguistic formulation, conceptual organisation, and alternative interpretive possibilities; however, experiential ownership, evaluative authority, and ethical responsibility remained with the researcher. The study develops the Human–AI Narrative Co-Construction Framework (HANCF) to conceptualise narrative reconstruction as a recursive process of AI-mediated reflection governed by human evaluative and narrative authority. The findings suggest that conversational AI may participate in narrative identity reconstruction without possessing narrative identity or displacing human authorship. The study contributes an autoethnographic account of sustained human–AI interaction and offers a framework for understanding how reflective partnership with conversational AI may extend human meaning-making while preserving experiential and ethical authority.

articles.title: Algorithmic Patriarchy: Artificial Intelligence, the Feminisation of Poverty, and the Limits of Governance
articles.authors: Azucena Carrasco-Toronjo
articles.abstract: Nearly fifty years after Diana Pearce named the feminisation of poverty, the systems now deciding who gets hired, credited, or cared for were trained on the same discourse that has kept it in place. Patriarchal capitalist structures have long depended on women's unpaid labour while excluding women from the rewards of the economy they sustain. Neoliberal governance extended that arrangement, swapping a structural vocabulary of poverty for one of resilience, self-improvement, and personal responsibility. The neoliberal discourse brought the shrinking of the welfare state, and with it, a new vocabulary that spread from policy papers to self-help writing, human resources content, and coaching material. It has been produced at internet scale for four decades through the same text now training large language models (LLMs). Currently, this new vocabulary is embedded in the systems that screen résumés, and intertwined with the caseworkers who draft eligibility determinations. To understand algorithmic patriarchy and its relationship with the feminisation of poverty, this paper connects two bodies of scholarship: work on how neoliberal governance produces individualising discourse, and work on how AI systems inherit bias from training data. My contribution is to name and trace the mechanism by which patriarchy, neoliberalism, and unconscious bias combine to produce a vocabulary, reproduced by artificial intelligence systems, that may sustain the feminisation of poverty. Current governance frameworks audit outcomes but not the discourse producing them. This paper argues that language matters, and that identifying the unconscious bias it carries is a precondition for its measurement and correction – the basis on which governance bodies can design policies bypassing their own invisible limitations.

articles.title: Agent-based Modeling and Simulations
articles.authors: Aytalina Kulichkina; Annie Waldherr
articles.abstract: Computational modeling and simulations have become increasingly relevant in the social sciences, offering powerful approaches for studying complex social phenomena. This chapter focuses on agent-based modeling (ABM) and its advantages for computational communication researchers, particularly for those who are just starting out. We introduce ABM, explain its core principles, and explore different types of models and their purposes. Through illustrative examples, we show how ABM has been and can be applied to address important research questions in communication science and related disciplines. The chapter then provides a practical step-by-step guide for conducting simulation research, outlining each step of the modeling cycle according to established methodological standards. We also highlight the importance of transparency and reproducibility through open science practices. Finally, we discuss emerging trends, such as the integration of large language models, which may shape the future of computational modeling and simulations in our field. This chapter aims to equip researchers, especially beginners in computational communication science, with a solid conceptual foundation and practical tools for incorporating ABM into their work.

articles.title: Canvassing Mobilizes and Increases Vote Share: Evidence from a Local Election in Seattle
articles.authors: Nicholas Ottone
articles.abstract: A long line of research has shown that door-to-door canvassing is a potent campaign tactic for increasing turnout and, in some cases, vote share. More recent work has theorized, however, that canvassing effects are largest in low-salience elections without party cues and concentrated among occasional voters canvassed closer to Election Day. In this research note, I test these theoretical expectations by examining the effect of canvassing in a February local election in Seattle for a housing-related ballot measure. Using a novel geo-coded dataset of seventy doorknocking campaigns over three months, I find that voters more proximate to canvassing operations were more likely to vote and that proximate precincts had a slightly higher vote share for the targeted ballot measure. Moreover, consistent with recent theorizing, I find that turnout effects were concentrated among targeted Democrats canvassed soon before the election.

articles.title: The sociolinguistic labor of incarcerated people
articles.authors: Gabriella Licata; Robert Tyler; Mesro Coles; Anthony Habib Watkins; Brian Asey Gonsoulin
articles.abstract: Through participatory action research, we draw on interviews with 40 incarcerated students to examine how linguistic practices are shaped by institutional power in carceral environments. We argue that the magnitude of surveillance under incarceration produces sociolinguistic labor: the effortful management of one’s communicative repertoire. Our analysis identifies a distinctive form of dual-direction sociolinguistic labor, whereby incarcerated individuals are required to extend their repertoires both toward stigmatized vernaculars to gain social capital and toward hyperstandardized registers for institutional capital. We examine this dynamic across educational, social, and procedural domains, with particular attention to boardspeak—an emotionally-constrained, bureaucratic register through which rehabilitation is performed and assessed at a Board of Parole hearing. By situating these practices within broader critical linguistic theories and perspectives, we show incarcerated people self-surveil and create, prompting varying levels of sociolinguistic labor and innovation that are mediated by race, ethnicity, ability, socioeconomic class, and in-group membership. These findings demonstrate how high-stakes, surveilled environments intensify the stakes of language use and reshape the boundaries of communicative agency.

articles.title: Sufism, Politics and Violence: Reading Notes
articles.authors: Abbas Aroua
articles.abstract: This paper attempts to shed some light on the nexus “Sufism-Politics-Violence” and to show how Sufism, like other religious currents, spans a wide spectrum and how it would be misleading to consider Sufis’ approach to politics and violence in an indiscriminate way. The aim is to draw the attention of academics and policy makers to the fact that opposing Sufis to other Islamic currents such as the Muslim Brotherhood, the Salafis or the Tablighis is not the right way to prevent or counter extremism. On the contrary, such an approach is not only ineffective but may be counterproductive and prompt sectarian violence.

articles.title: Addressing Violence and Extremism: The Importance of Terminology
articles.authors: Abbas Aroua
articles.abstract: The aim of this paper is to provide some elements that will hopefully contribute to a more accurate definition of the terms used in the context of extremism and violence, to attempt a descriptive model of the extremization process that encompasses the various paths leading to violence, and to discuss the various approaches to de-extremization. Contrary to the claim of some proponents of hard security approaches, explaining extremism and terrorism is not equivalent to justifying such phenomena. Understanding the process of extremization is a necessity for all those responsible for peace and security because it enables them to deal with it more effectively. Since “violent extremism” is often used to refer to Islamic contexts, which is in itself problematic, there will be some focus on the Islamic perspective in this paper.

articles.title: Uncovering the Hidden Magnitude of Within-Race/Ethnicity Skin Tone Inequality
articles.authors: Luyin Zhang; Varsha Menon; Sam Trejo
articles.abstract: Decades of research have linked skin tone to meaningful inequalities in health and social outcomes among individuals in the same self-identified racial/ethnic group. Yet efforts to document and understand within-race/ethnicity skin tone stratification have been hampered by a fundamental data problem: in most social surveys and biomedical databases, skin tone is either not collected or measured imprecisely using coarse categories based on a single observer’s judgment. In this study, we begin by conducting an online survey to quantify the reliability of existing interviewer-rated skin tone measures. Then, using elastic net regression, we build a genomic prediction model for skin tone among Black and Hispanic participants in the Add Health study, with the goal of improving the accuracy and availability of skin tone measurement in admixed populations. Finally, we use these DNA-based skin tone measures in two longitudinal studies to explore within-race/ethnicity skin tone inequality in contemporary America. Predicted skin tone yields substantially steeper gradients in socioeconomic status and racial classification, indicating that interviewer-rated measures meaningfully understate the degree of social stratification operating within racialized groups. Our results suggest that genetically derived skin tone predictions represent a promising new tool for advancing research on colorism – and, via the ancestry disequilibrium regression framework we introduce, a path toward identifying the causal effects of skin tone.

articles.title: Dépolarisation idéologique en Afrique du Nord
articles.authors: Abbas Aroua
articles.abstract: Cette contribution tente d'abord de montrer l'impact négatif des polarisations idéologiques aiguës sur la transition démocratique en prenant comme exemples les expériences de l’Algérie, de l’Egypte, de la Libye, du Maroc et de la Tunisie. Elle examine ensuite la scène politique en Afrique du Nord et les tensions idéologiques en son sein et souligne l’importance d’éviter le piège de considérer les courants idéologiques nord-africains comme des blocs monolithiques mais plutôt comme des spectres larges comprenant des acteurs aux attitudes et comportements politiques variés. Elle expose aussi des modèles qui aident à penser la gestion de la différence et le renforcement de la cohésion dans une société pluraliste tirés des traditions occidentale et islamique, et propose « l’espace de médiation protégé » comme mécanisme de dépolarisation idéologique.

articles.title: Waiting Spaces as Mental Health 'Gyms': A Research through Design Framework for the Situated Activation of Wellbeing Micropractices Where People, Time, and Infrastructure Converge
articles.authors: Carolina Andrea Cárdenas Fernández
articles.abstract:
Cities have expanded access to physical wellbeing by placing exercise equipment in parks and public squares: infrastructure can offer opportunities for practice without requiring a gym, a fee, or deliberate search. This study asks whether a similar logic can extend to everyday mental wellbeing: can urban infrastructure facilitate voluntary activation of wellbeing micropractices where people, time, and urban infrastructure already converge, without additional time, financial cost, or specialized access?
Using a Research through Design (RtD) approach, this study develops the Wellbeing Practices in Waiting Spaces (WPWS) framework through four phases: (1) qualitative clinical exploration using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (N = 8); (2) iterative design and urban prototyping in Amsterdam, Milan, and Barcelona; (3) exploration of everyday appropriation across seven countries (N = 41); and (4) comparative analysis of public-space wellbeing interventions. Low rates of voluntary flow interruption in high-flow contexts were treated as a generative finding, suggesting that instrumental movement may constrain attentional availability, leading the inquiry toward stationary contexts: waiting spaces.
Three interdependent components of situated activation emerged: (1) spatio-temporal conditions shaping attentional availability (when); (2) inner human capacities, including mindfulness, appreciation, and compassion (what); and (3) visual mediating devices providing legible, brief, voluntary invitations to wellbeing micropractices (how). Across the urban prototypes, voluntary flow interruption, defined as stopping for ≥5 seconds, ranged from 1% to 5%. In Phase 3, 85.4% of participants reported mentally repeating the phrase, and 60.9% reported sharing it.
WPWS is proposed as a transferable design architecture rather than a fixed intervention. It reconceptualizes waiting spaces as an underused spatio-temporal condition for situated activation, while recognizing that this proposition has not yet been empirically tested against other urban contexts. The findings do not establish causal or clinical effects, but provide a foundation for investigating how existing urban infrastructure can expand everyday access to wellbeing practices.
Keywords: Urban wellbeing; Waiting spaces; Latent wellbeing infrastructure; Situated activation; Mental health equity; Trauma-informed design; Wellbeing micropractices.

articles.title: The Social Stratification in Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy, Use Frequency, and Workplace Acceptance in 11 European countries
articles.authors: zhuofei lu; Yao Ma; Wei Zhuang; Yucheng He
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) has diffused rapidly across Europe, yet who feels able to
use it—and who is willing to work with it—remains poorly understood. Using the
latest CRONOS-3 panel of the probability-based European Social Survey (N =
7,556; 11 European countries, fielded in 2025), we model six separate measures
of GenAI literacy and use frequency, together with acceptance of GenAI as an
assistant and as a peer in the workplace, using country-clustered estimators with
wild-bootstrap inference. Acceptance is strongly role-differentiated: a majority
accept GenAI as an assistant, but only one in ten as a peer. Both competence and
acceptance are sharply stratified by education, age, and gender—and the gender
divide is the most consistent pattern of all: women trail men on every one of the
six literacy and use measures and on both acceptance outcomes, and the deficit
appears in behavioural use as well as in self-assessed skill, so it cannot be reduced
to gendered self-assessment alone. GenAI literacy and use frequency in turn
strongly predict acceptance in both roles. Cross-national variation is substantial,
but with only 11 countries no association between national media, scholarly, or
AI-talent environments and individual outcomes survives strict small-cluster and
multiple-testing corrections, so national context is treated descriptively. GenAI
competence and workplace acceptance thus emerge as socially stratified from the
outset—with women consistently furthest behind—an early-forming divide that
risks hardening as GenAI becomes workplace infrastructure.

articles.title: The Selective Politicization of Diversity Advertising
articles.authors: A.I. Loureiro Lopes; Alberto Lopez Ortega; Mariken Anna Catharina Geertruida van der Velden
articles.abstract: Corporations increasingly feature minority families in mainstream advertising, positioning themselves as inclusive civic actors. Yet whether audiences read such representation as ordinary marketing or as a political statement—and whether all minorities are read alike—remains unclear. We field a pre-registered survey experiment in the Netherlands (N≈1,500), randomly exposing respondents to a supermarket advertisement depicting a control (white, heterosexual), Muslim, or same-sex family. Minority-family advertisements are perceived as substantially more political than the control and shift perceptions of the brand to the ideological left, both in abstract placement and in concrete party association. These effects are markedly selective: the Muslim-family advertisement is read as roughly twice as political as the same-sex advertisement, and is the only condition to lower purchase intention, and does so precisely through the perception that it is political. Issue attributions are domain-specific: the same-sex advertisement moves perceived brand support for LGBTQ+ rights, the Muslim advertisement perceived support for immigration—and, contrary to expectations, these reactions are broad rather than confined to right-wing consumers. The findings reveal a selective politicization of corporate inclusion, in which ethno-religious diversity is politicized and commercially penalized while sexual-orientation diversity is comparatively normalized.

articles.title: The Paperwork of Grief: Administrative Burden as a Defence Against Death Exposure in Clinical Care
articles.authors: Chukwudi Egbuonu
articles.abstract: Administrative work (documentation, the electronic record, the proliferation of meetings, the referral of distress onward to specialists) is treated almost universally in the clinician-wellbeing literature as a cause of burnout to be measured and reduced. This paper argues that in the most death-saturated settings of medicine (the cancer ward, the intensive care unit, the palliative service) that same burden may also do something the literature has not noticed: function as a social defence against sustained exposure to dying, offering clinicians a bounded, completable, finite task to retreat into when the bedside offers only problems that often end in death. The argument revives Isabel Menzies Lyth’s 1959 account of hospital routine as a collective defence against anxiety and brings it forward to the era of the electronic record, joining four literatures (on documentation burden, on death exposure and numbing, on terror management, and on the social defences of institutions) that have not previously been read together. If the conjecture holds, the prevailing prescription to strip administration away on efficiency grounds alone risks removing an unrecognised container without supplying a deliberate one, and the proper task is not to reduce paperwork but to distinguish what merely numbs from what genuinely contains, and to design containment for those who work among the dead. The claim is interpretive and bounded to high-mortality settings; the paper sets out how it could be tested and the competing explanations it complements rather than displaces.

articles.title: Climate policy is domestic politics: Mechanisms shaping the political feasibility of mitigation
articles.authors: E. Keith Smith; Christina Eder; Sarah Gomm; Gabriele Spilker; Isabelle Stadelmann-Steffen
articles.abstract: The Paris Agreement shifted the central challenge of climate mitigation from international burden-sharing to domestic politics. In high-emitting countries, the binding constraint on near-term emissions cuts is no longer the absence of effective policy instruments, but their political feasibility, that is, governments' capacity and willingness to adopt, implement, and sustain mitigation policy over time. We review the political feasibility of climate mitigation along four dimensions: stakeholder interests and influence, public opinion and social norms, political-economic context and institutional constraints, and distributional effects and inequality. Using the policymaking process as our analytical lens, we trace how these dimensions hinder or enable mitigation at successive stages of agenda-setting, formulation, and implementation. We synthesise this literature into a practical framework for making mitigation politically feasible, identify a set of persistent misconceptions that obstruct progress, and outline near-term actions that the evidence supports. The central challenge of mitigation is no longer identifying effective instruments, but making them politically feasible under real-world conditions.

articles.title: Statistischer Quartalsbericht 2/2021
articles.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles.title: Leveraging LLMs to assist tourists at destinations – The opportunities and risks of deploying open-source humanoid robots
articles.authors: Yash Pandey; Spencer Kayser; Marius Portmann; Siamak Layeghy; Sara Dolnicar
articles.abstract: LLMs are transforming tourist search behaviour. Tourists currently access LLMs on phones, tablets, and laptops. Open-source humanoid robots change this: the LLM becomes embodied and physically situated at the destination. This conceptual paper develops a framework for understanding the consequences of deploying open-source humanoid robots in tourism. The framework rests on two constructs. Embodied authority transfer describes how tourists reattribute LLM output from a private planning tool to the destination's official service infrastructure when delivered by a robot hosted in a tourism setting. Capability asymmetry describes the gap between what an embodied LLM can fluently discuss and what it can accurately know or actually do. The article discusses deployment scenarios and risk, and offers a detailed research agenda.

articles.title: You Have My Attention: Offline Events and the Temporal Dynamics of Online Harassment in Politics
articles.authors: Sabrina Kreyzerman; Inessa De Angelis
articles.abstract: The online harassment of politicians has become a defining feature of contemporary digital politics. While existing research has documented the forms and consequences of online harassment, less attention has been paid to how salient offline events shape its temporal dynamics. This study examines the relationship between salient offline events, such as wildfires and political resignations, and online harassment directed at Canadian federal Members of Parliament (MPs) on YouTube throughout 2024. We find that while a baseline level of harassment is consistently present, salient offline events are associated with short-term fluctuations in harassment, with comments increasing in the few days following an event. However, enduring structural factors, particularly MPs' gender and political party affiliation, are stronger predictors of harassment than offline events. By foregrounding time as an analytical dimension, this research advances our understanding of how offline events shape the temporal dynamics of online harassment while highlighting the structural factors that sustain it.

articles.title: Ambiguity-Robust Dictionaries using Contextualized Embeddings
articles.authors: Jamil Civitarese; Sylvan Zheng
articles.abstract: Keyword dictionaries remain widely used in text analysis for their simplicity, transparency, and replicability. However, sensitivity to keyword selection and inability to account for context introduce measurement error that attenuates estimates and obscures real relationships. We introduce ambiguity-robust dictionaries, a text-as-data method that leverages contextual word embeddings to produce more precise measures while preserving the key advantages of dictionary approaches. Our method generates contextualized embeddings for all keyword instances, then applies constrained fuzzy clustering to determine the degree of each instance's membership in a target cluster defined by a small set of researcher-identified anchor words. This approach allows the construction of ambiguity-robust document level word counts, increasing precision and reducing sensitivity to keyword selection. We demonstrate the method using three applications:  UN environmental discourse, ethnic bias in Kenyan judicial politics, and moral language in US Congressional speech. In each application, our method yields substantively more robust and precise estimates than conventional approaches.

articles.title: The Rise and (Partial) Retreat of DEI Claims in Recruiting
articles.authors: Janet Xu; Reuben Hurst; Shanshan Liu
articles.abstract: In recent years, and especially after the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, U.S. employers increasingly affirmed commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Donald Trump's second administration has sought to reverse this shift. Yet how far pro-diversity language actually rose in employers' recruiting, and how much of that rise has since been undone, has not been established. Drawing on the near-universe of U.S. online job postings between January 2016 and February 2026—371.1 million postings from 2.7 million employers—we find that pro-diversity claims appeared in 7–12% of job postings until mid-2020, then rose 152% to a peak of 25.4% postings on the eve of the 2024 election. They fell 21% thereafter, to 19.9% by February 2026. Declines were sharper among federal contractors but proportionally similar for Democratic- and Republican-leaning employers. The reversal is unprecedented, yet partial: it has undone roughly a third of the post-2020 rise, but pro-diversity claims remain twice as common as in June 2020.

articles.title: Ageism by Default: Representational Ageism as an Upstream Risk in Medical AI
articles.authors: Alexander Seifert
articles.abstract: Age bias in medical AI is often treated as a performance problem, a perspective that fails to recognize an already existing risk: Generative systems may produce narrow, default representations of later life that enter health communication, patient personas, training materials, and care documentation. Because these representations potentially determine the needs, risks, and forms of support that take priority before clinical decisions are made, representational ageism should be addressed in bias audits, design documentation, procurement, and participatory review.

articles.title: Generational Warfare Online? Social Media Use and Intergroup Attitudes in a National Survey
articles.authors: Andrew Micah Lindner
articles.abstract: Content analyses document vitriolic generational discourse across social media platforms, yet surveys reveal moderate attitudes among the public. Does social media exposure create extreme generational attitudes? Using nationally representative survey data (n=1,221), this study examines whether total social media use and platform-specific usage patterns correlate with generational self-identification and intergroup attitudes among American adults. Results reveal limited associations with even frequent users not exhibiting greater generational antagonism. Platform-specific analyses reveal few significant effects, though YouTube use is associated with more favorable attitudes toward other generations. These largely null findings suggest extreme online discourse does not reflect typical users’ attitudes, implying that reasons for extreme discourse are connected to visibility mechanisms, such as algorithmic amplification and creators’ strategic performance. The study also demonstrates the risks of inferring population attitudes from content analysis.

articles.title: Humility in Journalism: The epistemic virtue that allows journalists to learn from experiences of others
articles.authors: Gregory P Perreault; Claudia Mellado
articles.abstract: Journalists have long been associated with a strong ego and the hubris necessary to share the news as “the way it is.” But overlooked, and perhaps more important, is the humility required by journalists to gather new knowledge in the first place. Through the lens of joy and journalistic epistemology, the present study explores interviews with 27 journalists in Chile and the United States in regards to their experiences with humility. Journalists broadly believed that their work could be done without humility, but that good journalism necessitated humility. The best journalists, across these national contexts, were considered to be those who were humble: which journalists defined as being willing to listen, to learn, to be corrected and to apologize for mistakes.

articles.title: Do Large Language Models Reproduce Question-Wording Effects? A Type-Level Map from Published Split-Ballot Experiments
articles.authors: Howard Kim
articles.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can stand in for human survey respondents is contested: some studies report striking correspondence with human data, others report systematic failure. We argue the question is mis-posed as a binary and answer it instead with a type-level map. We assembled 56 experiment pairs from published split-ballot experiments in the Time-sharing Experiments for the Social Sciences (TESS) archive - verbatim condition wordings with condition-level response distributions computed from public raw data - spanning ten classic questionnaire-design manipulations in the Schuman-Presser tradition. LLM respondents were conditioned on demographic profiles sampled from each original study's own probability-sample respondents and answered one condition each (n = 300 per condition, three seeds), in a preregistered design with a fully disclosed pilot, same-item internal replication on new seeds, and a hash-locked corpus. Reproduction divided by effect type. Semantics-based effects - lexical wording, question form, and equivalency framing - moved in the human direction on 7 of 8 significant pairs; because those pairs cluster in four studies, cluster-robust tests leave this as a consistent pattern rather than a confirmed one (study-level permutation p = .13). On a common, range-standardized effect scale the semantic-family correlation is r = .32 (cluster-bootstrap CI [.05, .79]; Spearman rho = .58), with magnitudes attenuated to roughly one-fifth to one-third of the human effects. Cognitive-burden-based effects failed as mechanism predicts: forced-choice response-order effects were at chance (1 of 4), and a recall-instruction effect was flat. Two model-specific signatures emerged, each anchored in a single item pair: acquiescence to a socially undesirable assertion vanished (human effect +.39; LLM -.00; z = -7.8), a pattern consistent with alignment training, and the models over-acquiesced to contradictory generic assertions (agreement sum 1.82 vs. .81 in humans). On six pilot-unexposed extension pairs, significant-pair signs matched in 5 of 6 model-pair evaluations across two models, which weakens simple literature-memorization accounts but cannot exclude pretraining exposure. We also document a mid-study behavioral discontinuity of a commercially served model under a stable model name, consistent with serving-version drift. Overall, the evidence supports an exploratory, direction-oriented use of LLM panels for pretesting semantic wording manipulations, and cautions against any use as a general-purpose effect estimator.

articles.title: Hype as a Critique of Communication: What Exaggeration Costs, Seen Through Five Lenses
articles.authors: Maximilian Roßmann
articles.abstract: Calling something hype is a charge against communication. Yet it rarely specifies the fault. Was the claim inaccurate, oversold, over-promised, or crowding out something more deserving? Different lenses of communication theory show different faults, and different remedies. Exaggeration buys reach, assent, uptake, frame dominance, and resonance, often several at once. What differs is the cost. Read as information transfer, exaggeration spends the discriminating power of language; as rhetoric, the credibility of the speaker and their peers; as a speech act, the coordinating force of commitment and assertion; as discourse, the space in which opposing views can be uttered and acknowledged; as a pattern of reception, the contestability of a social representation held in common. These are over-generalization, over-selling, over-commitment, over-shadowing, and over-resonance. None requires intention. A field can overshoot through contributions that are individually calibrated and sincere, and where speakers relinquish control over reception, hype becomes a matter of platform design and power. Each lens is blind to what the others register, and a remedy reaches only those positioned to apply it.

articles.title: Backlash and the Limits of Immigrant Solidarity
articles.authors: Priyanka Sethy; Marco M. Aviña
articles.abstract: Does anti-immigrant backlash unite the people it targets? Using Cooperative Election Study data from 2010--2025, we track the pro-immigration attitudinal gradient, from third-generation US-born respondents to noncitizens, through Donald Trump's rise. The gradient contracted and remained smaller afterward; the fully adjusted 2010--2024 estimate is a 0.133-SD reduction from third-generation US-born respondents to noncitizens. Recurring items show why: third-generation respondents liberalized more, while naturalized citizens moved modestly toward restriction on conditional legalization. The contraction appears both on policies governing new immigration and on policies affecting immigrants already present, survives timing, measurement, composition, local-context, and unrelated-outcome checks, and is smaller among immigrants with longer residential tenure, homeownership, and higher income. Republican and conservative immigrants also shift less---not more---than simple cue-taking predicts. Backlash can make a category politically salient without making the people associated with it more politically aligned.

articles.title: Do Large Language Models Reproduce Question-Wording Effects? A Type-Level Map from Published Split-Ballot Experiments
articles.authors: Howard Kim
articles.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can stand in for human survey respondents is contested: some studies report striking correspondence with human data, others systematic failure. We argue the question is mis-posed as a binary and answer it with a type-level map. We assembled 56 experiment pairs from published split-ballot experiments in the TESS archive (verbatim condition wordings; condition-level distributions computed from public raw data), spanning ten classic questionnaire-design manipulations in the Schuman-Presser tradition. LLM respondents were conditioned on demographic profiles sampled from each original study's own probability-sample respondents (n = 300 per condition, three seeds), in a preregistered confirmatory design with a fully disclosed pilot, new-seed confirmation, and a hash-locked corpus. Reproduction divided sharply by effect type. Semantics-based effects (lexical wording, question form, equivalency framing) were reproduced in direction (7 of 8 significant pairs; r = .72), with magnitudes systematically shrunk (slope = .52). Cognitive-burden-based effects failed as mechanism predicts: forced-choice response-order effects were at chance and a recall-instruction effect was flat. Alignment training suppressed acquiescence to a socially undesirable assertion (human effect +.39; LLM -.00; z = -7.8), and models over-acquiesced to contradictory assertions (agreement sum 1.82 vs. .81 in humans). Results held on six pilot-unexposed extension pairs (5/6 significant-pair sign matches across two models), disfavoring contamination explanations. We also document mid-study behavioral drift of a commercially served model under a stable model name. LLM pretesting of survey questions is defensible as a conditional, direction-oriented screen within the semantic domain, not as a general-purpose effect estimator.

articles.title: Cognitive Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Labor Process and Knowledge Authority in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
articles.authors: 王本杰
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering knowledge-intensive work, including programming, writing, design, analysis, and management. Unlike earlier forms of automation that were often concentrated on physical operations or clearly defined executional tasks, generative AI can produce text, code, classifications, and proposals within the workflow itself. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the displacement of particular tasks, but in the possibility that activities once associated with professional judgment become increasingly mediated by corporate technological systems. This paper examines that possibility through the concept of “cognitive degradation.” Drawing on Marx’s analysis of machinery and fixed capital, Braverman’s account of labor-process control and deskilling (Braverman, 1974), and Burawoy’s emphasis on worker agency and consent (Burawoy, 1978; 1979), the paper defines cognitive degradation narrowly. It occurs when AI takes over cognitive tasks previously performed by workers, workers’ effective authority over the criteria and application of judgment declines, and that shift is stabilized through organizational rules, technological systems, or labor institutions. The concept therefore should not be treated as synonymous with deskilling, declining productivity, or algorithmic management. To explore the mechanism, the paper examines three ideal types rather than three directly comparable causal cases: boundary-setting in the Writers Guild of America (WGA), internalization in AI-assisted software development, and institutional mediation through German co-determination. The cases show that AI can increase productivity without necessarily reducing workers’ skills, while still altering how knowledge and judgment are organized. The paper argues that the central issue in AI-mediated labor is therefore not whether machines replace workers, but whether workers retain meaningful authority over the definition, evaluation, and application of knowledge. The paper further proposes that sustained changes in such authority may affect occupational autonomy, skill formation, and bargaining power. Claims about macro-level class restructuring, however, remain propositions for future empirical research rather than conclusions established by the cases examined here.

articles.title: Creative offloading and creative agency in AI-assisted educational game design: A thematic analysis of student reflection essays
articles.authors: Eemeli Eiste; Antti Koskinen; Muhterem Dindar; Kristian Kiili
articles.abstract: Generative AI has raised growing educational concerns regarding cognitive offloading and the preservation of students’ creative agency in creative learning tasks. This study examined how higher education students reflected on their creative agency when using generative AI as a design partner during the ideation and initiation phase of an educational game design assignment. Using a qualitative case study approach, we thematically analysed reflection essays written by 26 students following an AI-supported game design activity in a university course. The analysis identified a spectrum of reflected creative agency patterns related to how students described delegating, evaluating, and directing creative work with generative AI. Students’ reflections described strategic forms of offloading in which AI was positioned as a complementary support tool while evaluative judgment and authorial direction were retained. At the same time, reflections also revealed more unregulated forms of offloading characterised by overreliance on AI, unclear interaction strategies, and diminished ownership of creative decisions. These patterns sometimes coexisted within individual reflections, suggesting that creative agency may vary across offloading decisions rather than represent fixed student characteristics. The study introduces the concept of creative offloading as a lens for understanding student-AI interaction in creative educational tasks.

articles.title: Beyond the Deepfake: Synthetic Persuasion and the Infrastructural Transformation of Political Communication
articles.authors: Daniele Battista
articles.abstract: Political communication research has approached deepfakes primarily as deceptive audiovisual artifacts whose democratic relevance depends on realism, detection, and the possibility of misleading citizens. This perspective remains necessary but is increasingly insufficient. Generative artificial intelligence now enables political actors and intermediaries to produce, adapt, personalize, and recirculate persuasive text, image, audio, video, and conversational content at a scale that exceeds the conventional deepfake problem. This article develops the concept of synthetic persuasion to describe political influence processes in which AI-generated, AI-transformed, or AI-assisted symbolic content is deliberately embedded in communicative strategies designed to shape attention, interpretation, evaluation, identity, trust, or behavior. Building on a focused theory-building synthesis of research on deepfakes, political persuasion, platformization, algorithmic visibility, fact-checking, and AI governance, the article proposes the Synthetic Persuasion Infrastructure (SPI) model. The model distinguishes four analytically connected stages: production, platform embedding, amplification, and reception-recirculation. It argues that the political power of synthetic content cannot be reduced to successful deception: persuasion may also operate through narrative congruence, repetition, identity reinforcement, uncertainty, strategic disclosure, and hybrid-media amplification. Six propositions translate the model into falsifiable expectations for future comparative and experimental research. The article concludes that the democratic challenge posed by generative AI lies less in the existence of isolated synthetic objects than in the emergence of infrastructures capable of producing and circulating persuasive variants continuously across platforms and publics.

articles.title: Advancing open research information: exploring the persistence of proprietary bibliographic databases
articles.authors: Tanya Lee; Kathleen Gregory; Alexander Rushforth
articles.abstract:
Purpose – “Research information”, which informs how research is searched,
conducted, monitored, and evaluated, is usually made available in proprietary
databases in ways which often restrict its use. Recently, there has been a movement
towards opening research information through the creation of systems such as
OpenAlex, but their adoption remains inconsistent. In this study, we explore challenges
which university stakeholders face in switching from proprietary to open databases for
research information.

Design/methodology/approach – We conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with
university stakeholders in the Netherlands, a particularly proactive environment in the
Open Research Information movement. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic
analysis and informed by literature in platform capitalism and infrastructure studies.

Findings – The analysis shows that even in seemingly progressive environments,
systemic change remains challenging. Longstanding routines, technical dependencies,
and embedded practices present challenges for universities to disengage from
proprietary databases and their complementary services. Concerns about the viability
and further development of open databases became apparent through the context of
collective action dilemmas perceived by interviewees. Importantly, we find that platform
capitalism, a framework often employed in analyzing proprietary companies, is not
sufficient to explain these hesitancies. 

Originality/Value – Our findings highlight the challenges faced in an under-researched
area of open science: the adoption of open research information. Our study is relevant
to open science advocates and for institutions struggling with similar challenges. Our
analysis makes a conceptual contribution through treating claims about the platform
dominance of proprietary databases as empirical questions and highlighting the
importance of stakeholder agency, contingency and variation.

articles.title: Building a Sustainable Educational System in an Era of Declining Birthrate ―A Theory of School Education Reform―
articles.authors: Shigenori Tanaka
articles.abstract: This paper proposes a reconstruction of Japan’s school education system in the context of a declining-birthrate society, using the QDT (Quatro Dynamic Thinking) model as its analytical foundation. The QDT model is a four-dimensional thinking framework comprising Diving (deep thinking), Expanding (expansive thinking), Networking (network thinking), and Flowing (fluid thinking), and offers a method for multilayered, dynamic, and holistic analysis of educational reform. The educational crisis precipitated by demographic decline is understood here not merely as a problem of quantitative contraction, but as a phenomenon that exposes the structural obsolescence of an education system originally built to align with an industrialized society. The paper first clarifies the nature of the problem through a three-layer Diving Thinking analysis (surface, intermediate, and deep levels), then develops multidirectional solutions through Expanding Thinking. It further constructs a pentagonal collaboration model through Networking Thinking, and outlines a hypothetical phased implementation roadmap spanning 2026 to 2036 through Flowing Thinking. Building on this foundation, the paper introduces the paradigm of a “learning ecosystem,” and through concepts designed to innovate conventional education — fractal transformation, the living curriculum, and the QDT model itself — sketches a blueprint for a next-generation education system that Japan or other countries could pioneer on the global stage. Finally, the paper draws on an actual regional case to illustrate the proposed direction for educational reform. What this paper ultimately presents is not merely a logic of institutional change, but a reform vision grounded in the evolving consciousness of all stakeholders involved in education.

articles.title: Measuring and Repairing Document Conversion Errors in the Michigan Child Welfare Policy Manual
articles.authors: Nanyi Deng
articles.abstract:
Author Note (August 18, 2026): This preprint is currently undergoing systematic review and revision. An updated version will be posted upon completion. Readers are encouraged to consult the latest version of the manuscript.
Child welfare practice is governed by documents written for people to read. A state policy manual specifies how quickly a caseworker must see a child after the child returns home, and it does so in a PDF laid out for the eye. Any system that answers questions from such a manual must first convert it into text, and that conversion step is rarely measured. This study measures it. Five test documents were constructed to replicate the layout of the Michigan Children’s Protective Services Manual, with identifiers replacing its words. The identifiers run consecutively, so that a loss reads as a gap in a counted run and a person can see it without tooling, and each one ends in a check code, so that a converter driven by a language model cannot supply a convincing replacement for whatever it dropped. The same artifact is therefore verifiable by a person reading it and by a script counting it, and the tool under test cannot repair the evidence before either of them looks at it.
Four converters were evaluated on the test documents, and the two generations of the commercial service were evaluated on the manual itself, for a total of 31 documents and 328 pages. No converter was adequate for every property required by a retrieval corpus. The older generation invented 43 section headings that appear nowhere in the source, and the corpus assembled from it labels a column in a contact-standards table with the wrong requirement, so it lists three contacts with each child at intensive risk, where the manual states one. The current generation’s cheapest tier deletes the opening line of every paragraph beginning Exception:, which is how this manual marks the cases a rule does not cover. None of these failures garbles the text. Each produces fluent prose that reads as policy and states a rule the manual does not contain. The study then reports a repair procedure that derives document structure from the PDF’s geometry, and fifteen checks that halt conversion if any fail. Every check passes across all 31 documents, measured against the same documents from which the repair rules were derived. A fourth failure property emerged only after presence, level, and order had all reached their best values: 380 paragraph boundaries across 200 of the 328 pages were marked in the source by vertical spacing that the converter does not read.

articles.title: El poseedor que no existe: la reivindicación contra el ocupante material y la regla de cierre del artículo 915 del Código Civil (comentario a la sentencia de la Corte Suprema de 29 de julio de 2026, rol N° 34.734-2026)
articles.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles.abstract:
La Primera Sala de la Corte Suprema, en sentencia de 29 de julio de 2026 (rol N°

34.734-2026), declaró inadmisible por falta de preparación el recurso de casación en la forma y

rechazó por manifiesta falta de fundamento el de fondo, deducidos contra la sentencia de la Corte

de Apelaciones de Chillán que, confirmando el fallo de primer grado, acogió la acción

reivindicatoria dirigida por la dueña y poseedora inscrita de un inmueble contra sus ocupantes

materiales. El recurso planteaba la objeción clásica del sistema registral: si conforme a los artículos

724 y 728 del Código Civil nadie adquiere la posesión de un inmueble inscrito sin inscripción, el

ocupante material no es poseedor, y la reivindicatoria del artículo 889 —acción del dueño no

poseedor contra el poseedor no dueño— se queda, en rigor, sin demandado. La Corte responde con

dos movimientos: constata que el dueño inscrito privado de la tenencia material carece de la

posesión «cabal e íntegra» que exige el artículo 700, y convoca el artículo 915 como regla de cierre

—siguiendo a Alcalde— que integra los supuestos de legitimación pasiva de la acción, de modo

que los artículos 889 y 915 cumplen una misma función y se tratan unitariamente. El fallo

consolida una línea de cinco pronunciamientos en trece meses y la blinda procesalmente con el

artículo 782 del Código de Procedimiento Civil. Este comentario reconstruye el caso, sitúa la

decisión en la disputa centenaria entre inscripción-ficción e inscripción-garantía, examina la

legitimación pasiva resultante y sus consecuencias prácticas frente al precario, extrae la lección
