procesal del recurso de forma no preparado y cierra con un decálogo de litigación. La tesis: el

sistema registral define al poseedor, pero la tutela restitutoria persigue al que ocupa; entre el papel

y el suelo, el artículo 915 tiende el puente.

articles.title: Great Expectations? Researchers in Germany are Optimistic about the Potential of Grant Lotteries.
articles.authors: Christophe Heger
articles.abstract: In this study I investigate researchers’ expectations towards the potential advantages of grant lotteries in a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions provided by the Scientists Survey of the German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies (DZHW). I describe the saliency of the two debates on bias in grant peer review and on grant lotteries, as well as researchers’ levels of experience with grant peer review. I use both descriptive statistics and analytical models to investigate which characteristics shape scientists’ relative grant lottery optimism. I find that experienced and more senior scientists are significantly less optimistic about grant lotteries. Saliency and reviewer workload are positively associated with optimism. I conclude that, even though saliency of the issue remains sparse, researchers are generally optimistic about grant lotteries, yet also aware of some of their potential disadvantages.

articles.title: Individual perception of bias in grant peer review strongly associated with openness towards the introduction of lotteries.
articles.authors: Christophe Heger
articles.abstract: This study of a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions investigates researchers’ individual perception of bias in grant peer review and their openness towards the potential introduction of grant lotteries, as well as the potential link between the two concepts. Indeed, bias in peer review is often cited in the theoretical debate on grant lotteries. But even though researchers are both very involved in and strongly affected by grant decision-making, there is not enough empirical evidence on their perspective. I find that bias perception is very prevalent, openness is generally rare and researchers who perceive more bias in grant peer review are more open towards grant lotteries in a substantial and statistically significant way.

articles.title: ¿Cuáles son los balances del Mayo Feminista de 2018?
articles.authors: Valentina Lastra; Camila Stipo Lara; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Tamara Vidaurrazaga; Rocío Gallardo
articles.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo presenta resultados intermedios del proyecto Anillo ATE220009 "Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista" (2022-2025), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID) de Chile. A partir de 21 entrevistas realizadas entre abril y diciembre de 2024 a (ex)estudiantes universitarias de La Serena, Antofagasta, Santiago, Valparaíso, Concepción y Valdivia que participaron activamente en las movilizaciones feministas de mayo de 2018, el texto examina las expectativas que motivaron dichos procesos, las percepciones sobre los avances logrados a nivel institucional, social y personal, y las limitantes que enfrentaron las estudiantes, incluyendo obstáculos normativos, represalias institucionales y la instalación de sentidos comunes punitivistas. El cuaderno cierra con reflexiones emergentes sobre el rol de las funas, la tensión entre lo sancionatorio y lo transformador, y los desafíos pendientes para los feminismos universitarios.

articles.title: Domestic Peace Deficit: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Gender-Based Violence through Institutional, Relational, and Structural Peace Failures
articles.authors: Ijeoma Ezeukwu
articles.abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) continues to persist at high levels despite decades of legal reform, policy intervention, and scholarly attention. Existing approaches, drawn from criminology, public health, sociology, psychology, and law, have generated important insights into individual acts, risk factors, and immediate responses. Yet they remain less equipped to explain the cumulative institutional conditions that allow harm within domestic and intimate life to endure across the life course. This paper introduces the Domestic Peace Deficit (DPD) as a conceptual framework that addresses this gap. DPD explains how cumulative institutional failures undermine peace within domestic life by shaping exposure to violence, access to protection, and recognition of harm. Its central contribution is to treat the household as a peace system rather than merely a private social space or a site of interpersonal violence. Drawing on and extending insights from structural violence, positive peace, feminist peace research, human security, the ecological model of GBV, and intersectionality, the framework organises analysis around three pillars: the Violence and Coercion Deficit, the Agency and Relational Peace Deficit, and the Institutional and Structural Support Deficit. The paper defines domestic peace, formalises the deficit concept, outlines core principles, describes how the framework was developed, sketches pathways of accumulation, a future measurement agenda, and states the framework's principal limitations. DPD does not replace existing theories; it integrates and extends them into a coherent architecture centred on the domestic sphere. In doing so, it offers researchers, policymakers, and practitioners a tool for understanding why formal protections so often fail to produce lived safety, and for designing responses that address institutional recognition, accountability, and the intergenerational transmission of harm.

articles.title: Identity Claims in Political Speech
articles.authors: Asli Ceren Cinar; Mirya Holman; Tyler Simko
articles.abstract: Social identities shape political behavior, but when, how, and why do people talk about these identities? We introduce the concept of identity claiming: publicly identifying oneself as a member of a social group to establish standing and strengthen political appeals. Drawing on five corpora of political communication, including congressional newsletters, campaign biographies, social media, and public comments at school board and city council meetings, we show that elites and members of the public regularly make identity claims. The identities they invoke are not random: claims match the setting, deserving reference groups are used more frequently, and identity claims associated with increased vocal pitch. Experimental and social media evidence shows that speech with identity claims prompts engagement from the audience. Our work shows how ordinary people and political elites strategically and frequently engage in identity politics in their public communication.

articles.title: Das gelesene Buch. Lesen und Geschmackspräferenzen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz
articles.authors: Carolin Amlinger; Luca Keiser; Oliver Nachtwey; Jörg Rössel
articles.abstract:
This preprint presents descriptive findings from a standardised online survey on book reading conducted in Germany, Austria and Switzerland in May and June 2026 (N = 6,427; quota-sampled by gender, age, region and education). It asks how reading practices and literary preferences are socially distributed across the German-speaking countries.
The findings suggest that what divides the reading public is not how much is read but whether people read at all: the share of avid readers varies only between 5 and 13 per cent across social groups, whereas the share of non-readers ranges from 7 to 30 per cent. Education marks the sharpest boundary, with the decisive break falling between the highly educated and everyone else rather than along a continuous gradient. Gender and having been read to in childhood operate as independent axes, while age structures taste more than volume. Evaluative criteria follow the same logic: immersion and involvement dominate across all groups, but formal criteria such as stylistic quality and complexity gain weight with education. At the same time, the cultural legitimacy of the book remains broadly acknowledged, including among those who barely read.
The analysis is deliberately descriptive and serves as a first step towards subsequent multivariate analyses of the social and literary space.

articles.title: Standardising Access to Digital Platform Data: A Taxonomy for Social Research
articles.authors: Futoon Abushaqra; Damiano Spina; Amanda Lawrence; Daniel Angus; Robert Glasgow
articles.abstract:
[This manuscript has been submitted for peer review]
Abstract: Recent regulations granting individuals the right to access their personal data stored on digital platforms have reshaped the landscape of data collection. Under frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union and the 2019 New York SHIELD Act, platforms are now required to provide users with mechanisms to retrieve and inspect their own data; commonly referred to as Data Download Packages (DDPs). These developments have enabled new forms of data collection through data donation, where users voluntarily share their DDPs for research purposes. However, the structure, format, and granularity of DDPs vary significantly across platforms and over time, posing challenges for researchers, especially those without technical expertise. Responding to these challenges, this paper contributes to the Australian Internet Observatory's broader agenda of building national research infrastructure for independent, public-interest platform research. We propose a taxonomy for categorising DDPs across different platforms, alongside a schema repository that systematically describes the content of each DDP, including its structure, data types, and formats. These contributions support a more consistent and comprehensive understanding of DDPs across diverse platforms, with a particular focus on social media and digital services, and enable their effective use in both academic and applied research contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Cost of Safe Abortion Care in Kigali, Rwanda: A Retrospective Analysis of Hospital Billing Data
articles_hidden.authors: Melina Gaju Uwamwezi; Stephanie Küng; Ritah Mukashyaka; Allan Higiro; Lawrence Rugema; Alain Favina; Aflodis Kagaba; Margaret Giorgio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Rwanda has progressively liberalized its abortion law over the past decade, most recently through a 2024 order decentralizing safe abortion care (SAC) to health centres and clinics. However, the financial accessibility of legally provided SAC remains poorly understood; existing cost evidence in Rwanda focuses on post-abortion care, which has a different clinical and cost profile. This study assessed the direct facility-based costs of legally provided SAC in Kigali, Rwanda.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of itemized hospital billing data from the Health Development Initiative (HDI) Rwanda for 236 SAC patients treated at 4 public and 1 private facility in Kigali from June 2022 to December 2024, including total costs and costs across 9 categories. Total and category-specific costs were compared by visit type using the Mann-Whitney U test; associations between characteristics and visit type were assessed using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests.
Results: The median total cost of a SAC visit was 62,353 RWF (range: 282-256,100 RWF). Consultation fees (94.9%) and commodities (92.8%) were incurred by nearly all patients, while medical acts (76.3%), imaging (75.4%), and laboratory tests (70.8%) were also common. Two-thirds of patients (66.1%) were treated as inpatients, with a mean length of stay of 3.1 days. Inpatients incurred more than twice the mean total cost of outpatients (96,572 RWF vs. 47,167 RWF; p<0.001), driven by significantly higher costs across most categories except examinations. Visit type varied by age group (p=0.014); adolescents (15-18 years) were least likely to be inpatients.
Conclusions: Legally provided SAC in Kigali carries a non-trivial financial burden relative to household income, and heavy reliance on inpatient care, inconsistent with WHO guidance, inflates costs. These findings point to the need for a standardized SAC tariff, alignment of admission practices with evidence-based guidelines, and further research into drivers of cost variation in abortion care access.

articles_hidden.title: Locating the evidence: a Minimal Geography scale for the geographic locatability of research, demonstrated on LGBTQ+ fertility studies
articles_hidden.authors: Boyana Buyuklieva; Hanxi Wang; Martin Gozzi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Reporting checklists require a setting to be stated, but are satisfied at any granularity: "conducted in the United States" complies while remaining placeless. Access to fertility care and assisted reproduction depends heavily on where people live, and evidence-appraisal frameworks (GRADE indirectness, CERQual relevance) presuppose that a study's setting can be ascertained. Yet how practically locatable a study's evidence is (i.e., whether a reader can tell where it was produced) has rarely been treated as a measurable property. 

Methods: We introduce Minimal Geography (MG), a five-point ordinal scale rating how precisely a study's evidence can be resolved to a real place, from placeless (MG 1) to a named local site whose own population was sampled (MG 5), with a self-contained codebook. We applied it to 116 primary studies of LGBTQ+ fertility intentions identified through a scoping review, recording the verbatim source excerpt behind every rating. A second coder blind-rated a 10% sample.

Results: Geographic locatability is strongly bimodal: 91 of 116 studies (78.4%) are vague (MG 1-2), two sit at the anonymised midpoint, and 23 (19.8%) are clearly locatable (MG 4-5). We observe the locatable minority to be concentrated in named specialist clinics, predominantly in the US. Quantitative studies were far more often locatable than qualitative ones, reflecting how each design recruits. Blind double-coding showed 75% band agreement and a linearly weighted kappa of 0.68. The instrument, codebook, and dataset are openly deposited (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21496412) to invite comparator corpora test of whether our observed bimodal distribution is distinctive or typical.

Conclusions: Reporting compliance is not locatability and we discuss the coarsest-safe-level reporting (CSLR). We conclude that CSLR must state the most specific geography compatible with participant safety, and importantly, flag deliberate masking.

articles_hidden.title: Five Percent Re-runnable: An Audit of Disclosure in LLM-Based Social Science
articles_hidden.authors: Huazhang Shen
articles_hidden.abstract: We audited 133 arXiv papers from 2023–2026 (full text obtainable for 129), plus 38 DOAJ-listed open-access journal articles as a comparison group, checking seven disclosure fields in each. We define a study as re-runnable when three conditions hold together: it names a specific model snapshot, its prompt text is obtainable, and it provides code or data. Seven of 129 papers (5%) are re-runnable. Two figures stand out: 29% name a specific model snapshot, and 1 paper in 129 reports a random seed. The structural finding is that of the 21 papers whose prompt text is obtainable at all, about half (11) have it only in a code repository rather than in the paper. The journal group discloses less on six of seven fields, but n=38 is too small to separate that difference from sampling variation — we therefore read this as no evidence that peer review supplies the missing material, not as evidence that it makes disclosure worse.

articles_hidden.title: Local Governance and Maternal Health Outcomes: A Case Study of Nepal’s Decentralized Health Reforms
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: Nepal has made impressive gains in reducing maternal deaths in the last 25 years. The maternal mortality ratio dropped from 539 to 151 deaths per 100,000 live births between 1996 and 2022. During the same period, skilled birth attendance rose from 9% to 77% and institutional delivery from 8% to 79%. Alongside these improvements have been major reforms in the health system, especially decentralization. The Local Self-Governance Act of 1999 assigned local bodies responsibility of health facilities. In 2015, the Constitution of Nepal established a federal system with 753 local governments responsible for basic health services. This case study explores the role of decentralization in improving maternal health outcomes in Nepal. It draws on data from national demographic and health surveys, policy documents and global health estimates. The study finds that decentralization was helpful as it increased local resources, improved community participation, strengthened accountability and supported national programs such as the Aama Program. However, the challenges remain and include inadequate local capacity, lack of clarity of roles, quality gaps and disparities between rich and poor, urban and rural and between provinces. Nepal’s experience provides important lessons for other countries looking to reduce maternal mortality rates through devolved health systems.

articles_hidden.title: A New Approach of Applying the 360-Degree Method for Performance Assessment of Managerial Levels in Mega-Companies
articles_hidden.authors: Saber Mirzaei Ahandani
articles_hidden.abstract: Questionnaires play the most important role in scientific papers and workplaces. Considering various applications, questionnaires may be designed in different shapes and types. In any case, it is critical to have a questionnaire with appropriate content and a pleasing design. There has been a lot of study done on the validity and reliability of questionnaires used in performance assessments of managerial levels, but users are not sure whether their data is valid or not, yet (Before, it was observed that respondents used steady responses due to boring shapes of the options in questionnaire). This matter has a direct effect on projects or processes you are going to do. This paper considers a questionnaire using in performance assessment of managerial levels in a large company, and presents a new form of questionnaire which combines 5-point Likert scale with competencies definitions. New questionnaire is able to solve some problems in assessment of performance such as invalid data and low return rate. Cronbach's alpha (reliability of this questionnaire) using SPSS software is 0.891.

articles_hidden.title: A Replication Framework for Observational Research: From Specification Restriction to Specification Expansion
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Ben-Menachem; Ari Galper; Nic Fishman
articles_hidden.abstract: Sociology has remained relatively insulated from debates about the "replication crisis." Heeding calls to consider replication more deeply, we introduce a distinction between two types of research reforms that have emerged in the wake of the crisis: specification-restricting and specification-expanding reforms. Specification restriction is often promoted as a way to increase the repeatability of research findings by controlling false positives. We argue that this statistical justification is less compelling in observational contexts---where the assumptions licensing false-positive control are harder to sustain and rigid ex ante analytical commitments can instead enshrine fragile specifications---than in experimental contexts. We further argue that apparently low replication rates do not necessarily imply a high prevalence of false positive findings. Instead, we propose a replication framework centered on specification-expanding reforms, stronger incentives for confirmatory research, and meta-analysis. This approach equips sociologists to assess the repeatability of findings and build a more cumulative discipline.

articles_hidden.title: No drain, no gain? The problems with unequal exchange
articles_hidden.authors: Niall Reddy; Virgilio Urbina Lazardi
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent empirical work (Hickel et al. 2021, 2022) appears to show that the Global South is being ``drained" of resources and value on a vast scale through unequal exchange (UE) and/or ecologically unequal exchange (EUE). Headline estimates of the aggregate value of this extraction have been widely taken to substantiate two politico-normative issues: that the South is systematically exploited through international price formation, and that this drain constitutes a binding constraint on Southern development and a precondition for Northern prosperity. This paper argues that neither claim is supported by the new measurement agenda. It shows that new drain estimates rely on untenable premises -- in particular, claims of North-South parity in productivity and export composition. Stipped of these assumptions, Hickel et al's method can't yield a counterfactual ``fair price" vector, meaning that their estimates are ungrounded and indeterminate. Moreover, even granting the estimates, they do not sustain an underdevelopment thesis. In standard growth regressions and long-run club-convergence tests, higher measured drain is non-negative and often positively associated with Southern growth once conventional fundamentals are controlled for. The paper suggests ways that research in ecological economics can be placed on a firmer conceptual footing.

articles_hidden.title: Examining reasoning in process recording: An exploration of instructions in guiding students towards social work competencies
articles_hidden.authors: Jemel P. Aguilar; Debra Crist; Huangshu Xu; Maria Mangiameli; Shirin Sultana
articles_hidden.abstract: This article describes an exploratory study of a sample of process recording instructions from field manuals used by social work programs. Process recording in this study is conceptualized as a mechanism for assessing competency-based education, in which students, supervisors, and faculty members gain insight into students’ professional reasoning procedures, strengths, and weaknesses. Ideally, instructions should lead students to demonstrate reasoning aligned with social work competencies; supervisors would examine students’ reasoning, and field faculty members can assess field-seminar-level professional reasoning. Using logic models to analyze how the instructions work, we found considerable gaps in the logic of process recording instructions that do not align with the goals of competency-based education or social work’s emphasis on evidence-based practice. We found that undefined learning mechanisms, assumed integration, unstructured evaluation, and vague learning goals hampered the connection between process recording and competency-based education. We discuss the implications of these findings for social work’s emphasis on competency-based education, evidence-based practice, and professional reasoning, and we call for further research on process recording in social work education.

articles_hidden.title: Using Theories of Social Exchange and Status Construction in Mixed-Group Cooperative Learning Practices
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph M Quinn; Valerie K. Barron
articles_hidden.abstract: Classroom group work can reproduce broader social inequalities when status-based expectations shape whose contributions are valued or ignored. Intergroup Contact Theory (IGCT) proposes conditions of contact that can reduce prejudice but provides limited explanation of the interactional processes through which these conditions generate cooperation or alter status expectations. We integrate IGCT with the Theory of Social Commitments and Status Construction Theory to identify micro-level structural mechanisms that instructors can leverage to create more equitable intergroup interactions that can also enable social learning and bias reduction toward underrepresented groups. Drawing on these theories, we propose a three-part strategy: forming strategically mixed-status groups, designing highly joint tasks that create mutual dependence and shared responsibility, and providing process-centered feedback that rewards cooperation while making diverse forms of competence visible. Together, these practices can foster positive relational experiences, disrupt status-based performance expectations, and reduce inequities in participation and evaluation. We argue that incorporating these interactional mechanisms into the IGCT framework strengthens contact-based approaches to cooperative learning and offers instructors a theoretically grounded strategy for making diverse classrooms sites of prosocial intergroup contact and positive meaning-making about categorically dissimilar peers.

articles_hidden.title: Deleting the call does not delete the evidence: a within-recording validity test for passive-acoustic whale-call detection benchmarks
articles_hidden.authors: Dharit Shah
articles_hidden.abstract:
Problem. Detection benchmarks in passive acoustic monitoring are built from temporally
clustered events, so a period that contained an annotated call may differ from a period that
never did in more than the call itself.

Diagnostic. We delete the annotated call from a positive window, replace that interval
with background from the same window, leave every other sample intact, and measure ablation
AUC — P(call-removed positive scores above true negative). Null 0.5; higher means more
shortcut. A splice control applies the identical operator to windows that never held a call.

Findings. On the DCLDE 2013 right whale upcall benchmark the trained detector scores a
same-recording ablation AUC of 0.635 [0.552, 0.710] — both arms from the same 15-minute
source recording, 887-window negative pool — against the 0.5 no-shortcut null. The splice
control sits at the null (0.483 [0.455, 0.510], 889-window frozen stimulus), so the cut is not
the effect. Pooled values are larger and partly a between-recording contrast; they are
reported beside the headline and never instead of it. Two spectrogram representations never
trained on the task reproduce the within-recording separability under a fitted logistic
readout (raw tile 0.688 [0.606, 0.772]; random projection 0.687 [0.598, 0.770]), so
detectors inherit it rather than create it. It replicates across 30 SanctSound day-sites
(same-day-site 0.566 [0.528, 0.604]). Five preregistered mechanisms — hard negatives,
receptive field, context access, capacity, temporally matched negatives — were tested and all
five failed: we report a measurement, not a mechanism. A preregistered second benchmark in
a killer whale regime, its clustering precondition verified in advance, did not detect the
effect: zero of four evaluable provider × species cells survive multiplicity correction on the
same-recording-day estimand.

Recommendation. Report ablation AUC beside average precision, and name its estimand.

---

articles_hidden.title: Population Development In The Roman Empire
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrik Vachet Rasmussen
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper addresses the problem of reconstructing the population development of 
the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire despite the scarcity, inconsistency, and indirect 
nature of the available evidence. Its primary objective is to produce a continuous population 
curve spanning from 508 BC to AD 395, which is internally consistent in the assumptions of 
underlying growth and other factors over time. To achieve this, the study critically integrates 
multiple methodological approaches, including Beloch’s area-and-density estimates, Lo 
Cascio’s revisions, and Scheidel’s demographic critiques, alongside archaeological, 
economic, and comparative demographic evidence.  
By combining these methods and cross-validating their results, a coherent framework 
is established for estimating both population levels and growth rates. It adopts moderate 
empire-wide growth assumptions, 2-3‰ annually, while allowing for significant variation 
between core and newly incorporated territories. This enables the interpolation between key 
chronological benchmarks and the extension of estimates across periods lacking direct 
evidence.  
The resulting reconstruction yields a continuous demographic trajectory showing the 
full consequences of the growth assumptions.

articles_hidden.title: Exposure to Homeless Shelters and Support for Policy Remedies
articles_hidden.authors: Jacob Brown; Adrian C. Pietrzak; Alexander Sahn
articles_hidden.abstract: American cities have rapidly built new homeless service facilities - shelters and supportive housing - over the last decade in response to rising homelessness. We study how voters react to these facilities once they are built and operational, leveraging a pair of statewide ballot propositions to fund new homeless services in California. We find that voters living closest to newly opened facilities became more supportive of spending on homelessness services compared to those living further away. We argue and show using survey data that new shelters increase the salience of homelessness in the minds of voters, driving positive policy feedback. We rule out the effects of positive changes in street conditions, improvements over existing land-uses, and financial self-interest as alternative mechanisms. Our findings suggest that voters can reward policy action and that NIMBY opposition may be more prospective than retrospective.

articles_hidden.title: How Segregation Fuels the Far Right: Higher-Educated Social Relationships Buffer the Politically Radicalizing Effect of Economic Insecurity
articles_hidden.authors: Jona de Jong; Tarek Jaziri-Arjona
articles_hidden.abstract:
In recent decades, economic insecurity has driven some lower-educated voters
to the far right, while others have not moved. We argue that segregation explains
this variation: Higher-educated friends and relatives hold relatively progressive
views and norms against the far right, preventing lower-educated citizens from
politically translating economic insecurity into far-right support. Using existing
panel data from the Netherlands and original data from the U.S. and Germany,
we find that lower-educated individuals in higher-educated networks are much less
likely to respond to economic insecurity by moving to the far right. Differential
access to economic resources does not explain this effect. Rather, novel network
modules and an experimental manipulation of network salience show that network
education levels condition how individuals politicize insecurity. These findings show
that others affect how we make political sense of change, and suggest that societal
resilience against growing far-right appeal depends on the mutual integration of its
citizens.

articles_hidden.title: Stakeholders’ perceptions of AI-assisted obstetric ultrasound in rural and urban Kenya: a qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Emmah Ng'ang'a
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools gain popularity in maternal healthcare, understanding community and health system perspectives is essential for inclusive and ethical implementation. This study explores stakeholder views on AI-supported ultrasound for pregnancy care in Kenya, that emphasized trust, equity, system readiness, and the importance of community engagement.
Methods: A qualitative study was conducted in two Kenyan settings: Nairobi (urban) and Kilifi County (rural). Fifty-five semi-structured interviews and three focus group discussions were conducted with pregnant women, partners, healthcare providers, Sub-County Health Management Teams (SCHMTs), Community Health Promoters (CHPs), and community and religious leaders. Data were analyzed inductively using grounded theory principles.
Results: The participants viewed AI with cautious optimism. While many welcomed its potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and access, concerns emerged around data privacy, informed consent, quality of care, and over-automation. Reliability or trust was linked to transparency, human oversight, and the use of local data. Participants highlighted structural challenges, including weak referral systems and staffing gaps, raising questions about the health system’s readiness to integrate AI. Fears of equity and “pilotitis”, short-lived projects without sustainability, were also expressed.
Conclusion: Findings from this study suggest that AI implementation in maternal health may need to go beyond technology development and deployment.  Developers and relevant stakeholders may need to consider co-designing with communities, alignment with health system realities, and the integration of ethical principles such as equity, accountability, and transparency.

articles_hidden.title: Sovereign ESG and the Hydrological Constraint: Rethinking the Determinants of Water Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Aneta Kargol-Wasiluk; Katarzyna Lewkowicz-Grzegorczyk; Carlo Drago; Alberto Costantiello; Angelo Leogrande
articles_hidden.abstract: Water stress is read in the sustainability literature as either a physical or an institutional outcome, but the two readings have never been tested jointly within the sovereign ESG framework. This paper estimates the environmental, social and governance determinants of the freshwater withdrawal-to-availability ratio across up to 170 economies observed between 2002 and 2022, drawing on the World Bank Sovereign ESG Data Portal. Three equations share the same dependent variable and differ only in the pillar supplying the regressors. Each is developed along three tracks: panel econometrics, comprising pooled OLS, fixed and random effects, between and weighted least squares estimators and two-step difference and system GMM; a competition among six clustering algorithms assessed on eleven internal validity indices; and a competition among six supervised learners used to validate the specification rather than to forecast. Water stress proves overwhelmingly structural, with 99.1 per cent of its log variance lying between countries. The governance block explains 38 per cent of cross-sectional and 4 per cent of within-country variation. The level of institutional quality, measured as the first principal component of four Worldwide Governance Indicators and absorbing 91.9 per cent of their variance, is unrelated to water stress in every estimator; its composition is not, with accountability relative to state capacity carrying a coefficient of −1.10 between countries. The dominant predictor across all three tracks is the female-to-male labour force participation ratio, whose partial dependence reveals a discontinuity concentrated in a five-point interval. Under cross-validation with countries held out, no flexible learner outperforms ordinary least squares.

articles_hidden.title: Designing Biodiversity Credit Schemes: Combining Implementation Scale and Certification Metrics for Farmers' Participation
articles_hidden.authors: Kota Mameno; Masayuki Sato; Yasushi Shoji; Takahiro KUBO
articles_hidden.abstract: Biodiversity credit schemes have gained attention as a mechanism for mobilizing private finance for biodiversity conservation. As primary suppliers of biodiversity outcomes in agricultural landscapes, farmers’ willingness to participate is critical to the success of these schemes. However, little is known about farmers' preferences for biodiversity credit designs, particularly regarding metrics used to certify biodiversity outcomes and the spatial scales at which biodiversity credits are implemented. To our knowledge, this is the first study to provide empirical evidence on how certification metrics and implementation scales influence farmers' preferences for voluntary biodiversity credit schemes. A discrete choice experiment with a latent class model were applied to examine Japanese farmers' preferences for alternative biodiversity credit schemes. The results showed substantial heterogeneity in farmers' willingness to participate in biodiversity credit schemes, with approximately half of the farmers belonging to a participation-averse group. In both groups, implementation scale was the primary determinant of participation decisions. Farmers preferred individual farmland scale implementation over coordinated participation. Certification metric exerted limited influence on participation decisions, suggesting that ecosystem-based credits can be implemented without substantially reducing farmers' willingness to participate. Additional bonuses increased participation among farmers already willing to participate, but had little effect on initially reluctant farmers . Membership analysis indicated that willingness to participate was positively associated with biodiversity policy awareness, biodiversity-friendly farming practices, pro-biodiversity attitudes, and expectations of branding-related benefits. Expanding voluntary biodiversity credit markets, therefore, requires not only financial compensation but also information provision, demonstration projects, and communication of potential market benefits.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the relationship between Productivity and Healthcare Systems
articles_hidden.authors: Nerhum Sandambi
articles_hidden.abstract: The approach explored the relationship between the Productivity and healthcare systems, particularly applied to developing Countries. Main results show that, majority Countries in developing worlds, do not have particularly the strongest affirmation and capacity to create and generate a strong healthcare systems. The majority societies are stunk in developing. These Countries in particular, have for example, a high level of Inefficiency to allocate the public expenditure to the sector in particular. However, the study shows that countries with weak healthcare systems are, naturally, the countries that have a lower labour productivity. Furthermore, this evidence is particularly enough to help understand how for example most developing Countries do not intend the respective expenditure to guarantee high quality healthcare systems and to improve health to society in particular, on the other hand, the existence of a high level of budget in these countries increases the healthcare systems in general. Thus, many of these Countries, the lowest level of healthcare expenditure, show that these Countries are naturally incapable to drive social protection in particular. On the other hand, when this evidence is particularly characterized, the Country does not improve for example the economic performance. Furthermore, high quality institutions, mainly the political institutions for example, help naturally to increase the quality of healthcare systems in general.

articles_hidden.title: Statistischer Quartalsbericht 3/2022
articles_hidden.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles_hidden.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles_hidden.title: HORMUZ STRAIT GEOPOLITICAL DISRUPTIONS AND PERSONAL FINANCIAL VULNERABILITY: A Case Study of Mid-Career Professionals in India's Private Higher Education Sector (2019-2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Jainish Bhagat
articles_hidden.abstract: Geopolitical disruptions in critical maritime infrastructure create ripple effects throughout economies, affecting not just international trade but also individual household financial security. This study examines how the Hormuz Strait tensions (2019-2024) impacted personal financial management decisions among mid-career professionals (35-50 years old) employed in India's private university sector. Using mixed-methods research combining survey data (N=847 respondents across 23 private universities in India) and longitudinal financial records, we document that geopolitical uncertainty increased personal financial stress markers by 34-42%, with impacts concentrated among professionals with high exposure to import-dependent sectors, international travel, or savings in foreign currency. We identify three financial vulnerability channels: (1) increased cost-of-living pressures (rising inflation, higher education costs), (2) income volatility (uncertain salary increments, job insecurity), and (3) behavioral shifts (increased precautionary savings, risk-averse investment decisions, delayed major financial commitments). Heterogeneous effects are substantial: professionals in oil-sector-dependent cities experienced 56% higher financial stress; those with daughters in higher education abroad reported 27% greater concern about rupee depreciation. We propose targeted policy interventions including employer-provided geopolitical risk hedging, financial literacy programs emphasizing crisis management, and institutional mechanisms for salary stability during global shocks. This research bridges macroeconomic disruption literature with personal finance vulnerability, contributing to understanding of how global events transmit into household-level financial decision-making in emerging markets.

articles_hidden.title: The empirically inscrutable climate-economy relationship
articles_hidden.authors: Finbar Curtin; Matthew G. Burgess
articles_hidden.abstract: Empirical models of the macro-level climate-economy relationship project climate change impacts ranging from trivial to catastrophic. This wide range suggests identification challenges. Here, we show that such models indeed face identification challenges that are axiomatic and irreducible. The climate-economy relationship has qualitatively important variation across space and time, due to complex regional heterogeneity and affluence-driven adaptation, among other factors. Empirical models must assume away some of this variation to preserve degrees of freedom. Influential observations caused by economic disasters and miracles, along with low signal-to-noise ratios, create additional challenges. We illustrate these challenges theoretically and then empirically by replicating and sensitivity testing prominent climate-econometric studies. The estimation challenges create economically meaningful sensitivities and fragilities. We recommend a cautious and uncertainty-emphasizing approach to applying climate econometrics to public and private decision-making. Importantly, however, our analysis does not dismiss the existence of a negative carbon externality nor economically beneficial efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

articles_hidden.title: Application of Justice in Nepal: A Case Study of  Rape Criminal Cases
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: Legally Nepal has come a long way in addressing sexual violence, but there is a huge gap between the law in the books and the justice in reality. Rape cases in Nepal are showing disturbing trend. There are strict laws in place, but victims often face apathy, delay and systemic roadblocks that deny them the justice they deserve. Studies show that 70 to 90 percent of sexual violence incidents go unreported, due to fear of stigma, retaliation and lack of faith in the justice system. This case study examines the application of justice in rape criminal cases in Nepal by analysing the legal framework, statistical trends, landmark cases, systemic challenges and voices of survivors who continue to fight for justice.

articles_hidden.title: Recycling fabricated narratives about an early-career researcher is not a valid defence: a reply to Caruso et al.
articles_hidden.authors: Saul Newman
articles_hidden.abstract: Here, I respond to Caruso et al. regarding their recent paper defending the Sardinian blue zone. Despite the brevity of the work, the paper relies on an extensive set of straw-man arguments, falsehoods, and libels. These appear deployed as little more than a coping mechanism in the absence of arguments, and the errors and misrepresentations are tallied below. However, rather than restrict the reply to raising these issues, it seems appropriate to use this venue to highlight some of the far deeper problems with the blue zones concept as a scientific, social, and financial enterprise. That is, it seems worthwhile to address this paper on a few scientific failings first, and its many logical and ethical failures second.

articles_hidden.title: Antidemocratic Policing in America: The Institutionalization of Historical Trauma
articles_hidden.authors: Angelina Inesia-Forde
articles_hidden.abstract: Countries have begun reforms to align their police forces with a democratic policing culture. Despite significant progress, the United States has failed to fulfill a key aspect of democratic governance: democratic policing. Consequently, the gap between law and departmental policy, and policing culture continues to widen. This study aims to contribute to Forde’s theory by applying the antidemocratic framework at the institutional level to describe policing practices that have received widespread attention by exploring police misconduct through a power lens of regressive strategies. The sample includes extant literature and data from exonerees. This study uses an innovative methodology grounded in the GQI and integrated with grounded theory analysis to answer the research question: How does Forde’s antidemocratic framework, rooted in historical trauma and political demoralization, manifest in contemporary police-civilian interactions? Forde’s antidemocratic concepts—nativism, social distinctions, misinformation, fear, dehumanization, and subjugation—frame this study. The framework underpins the understanding of antidemocratic policing and how micro-level disempowerment and macro-historical trauma (colonialism) converge in modern institutions. The primary finding is that antidemocratic practices are institutionalized. Future studies on democratic policing could inform the field and policymakers on whether misconduct, particularly excessive use of force, is a symptom of police demoralization.

articles_hidden.title: Energy Transitions and Political Transformation: Evidence from the Shale Oil Revolution
articles_hidden.authors: Christian J. Baehr
articles_hidden.abstract: An outstanding question in climate politics is how oil-exporting governments will respond to a global clean energy transition. I argue that persistent oil revenue shortfalls strain social contracts in oil-exporting states, compelling governments to enact targeted governance reforms under tightening fiscal constraints. I exploit the sudden emergence of the U.S. shale oil industry as an exogenous supply shock to examine how oil exporters adjust to sustained revenue declines. Using a difference-in-differences design, I find governments exposed to the shale revolution did not respond through broad political liberalization or public goods retrenchment and instead adopted targeted reforms. Systematic evidence on specific reform uptake and a case study indicate these reforms protected public goods provision and curtailed private capture, consistent with a political survival motive driven by rising mass public threats. The findings point to an asymmetric resource curse, in which oil shortfalls generate political responses distinct from those produced by windfalls.

articles_hidden.title: Infrastructural Mothering under Ukrainian Displacement
articles_hidden.authors: Tamara Fedotiuk; Lisa Marzano; Emma Victoria Ward; Valentyna Voloshyna; Antonia Bifulco
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines how displaced Ukrainian mothers with children organise adaptation under ongoing war, institutional fragmentation and temporal uncertainty. Drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with internally displaced mothers in Ukraine and Ukrainian mothers displaced to the United Kingdom, alongside four focus groups with service providers, the study compares how two displacement regimes shape care work, service access and future planning. The findings show that mothers’ care-centred aspirations motivate infrastructural mothering: unpaid emotional, administrative, educational and relational labour through which they create conditions for children’s stabilisation. As mothers direct time, skills and resources towards children, their employment, language learning, psychosocial recovery, belonging and future-planning capabilities may become suspended. By conceptualising adaptation as relational  and care-mediated, the study advances refugee integration scholarship, feminist care theory, and comparative forced migration research by demonstrating how distinct displacement regimes reorganise maternal labour and unevenly distribute adaptation opportunities within displaced families.

articles_hidden.title: Authoritarian Lenses and the Dynamics of Exclusion: The Radical Right in Chile
articles_hidden.authors: Lisa Zanotti; Fabian Villalobos-Machuca; Francisco Roldán Duque; Joaquín Valenzuela-Pastén; Sofía Cuadra
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter examines the Chilean radical right through conceptual lenses developed primarily in the European context, using the case to assess the limits of those categories beyond their region of origin. It advances two conceptual claims. First, drawing on Stenner (2005), it argues that authoritarianism is better understood not as an ideology on a par with nativism, but as an individual predisposition activated by perceived normative threat — a lens through which social change is interpreted rather than a fixed doctrine. Second, it argues that nativism, understood as the fusion of nationalism and xenophobia in defence of ethnic homogeneity, is too narrow for a region where migration flows involve culturally proximate populations, and that civic-cultural nationalism captures the Chilean case more accurately. The chapter traces the rise of José Antonio Kast and the Republican Party and the subsequent emergence of the Libertarian Party and Team Patriota, and shows how authoritarian predispositions combine with nationalist, anti-feminist and anti-communist frames to construct migrants, feminists, sexual minorities and leftist actors as outgroups.

articles_hidden.title: Black Feminist Social Work: Centering Black Women's Knowledge in Social Work Theory, Education, Research, Policy, and Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Vanessa M. Talley
articles_hidden.abstract: Social work acknowledges Black Feminist Thought as a framework and praxis, yet the profession has not established a social work framework that explicitly centers Black women’s epistemologies as foundational to education, theory, research, policy, and practice. Although social work maintains a historical commitment to social justice, person-in-environment, and human rights perspectives, dominant theories and knowledge systems continue to reflect Eurocentric assumptions regarding knowledge production and professional expertise. This article introduces Black Feminist Social Work (BFSW) as a conceptual framework that centers Black women’s individual and collective lived experiences, intellectual traditions, historical resistance, and knowledge to inform social work theory, education, research, policy, and practice. Drawing upon Black feminism, Black Feminist Thought, Womanism, Intersectionality, and the profession’s ethical commitments, the BFSW framework proposes a necessary shift from positioning Black women primarily as a population to be studied to recognizing them as producers of transformative knowledge. This article introduces four organizing principles, the Four C’s: Centering, Contextualizing, Co-Creating, and Changing, as foundational processes for Black Feminist Social Work and discusses the implications for curriculum development, clinical practice, research methodologies, policy advocacy, and future scholarship. Rather than positioning Black Feminist Social Work as an alternative specialization, this framework argues that centering Black women’s knowledge expands the social work profession’s capacity to pursue equity, liberation, and social transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Social Stressors and Gender Inequalities in Post-COVID-19 Syndrome: Evidence from a Population-Based Cohort in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolai Gröpler; Meike Dirks; Andrea Hildebrandt; Thomas Keil; Ann-Kathrin Knak; Sina M. Pütz; Mandy Roheger; Antje Wulff; Gundula Zoch
articles_hidden.abstract: Women report post-COVID-19 symptoms more often and more severely than men, but the contribu-tion of socially structured stress exposure to this difference is largely unexamined. Social stressors are particularly relevant in the context of infectious diseases such as COVID-19, as they may influ-ence health outcomes through hormonal processes and their impact on immune function. This study examines whether stressors and coping resources in work and family life are associated with post-COVID-19 symptoms and whether they account for sex/gender differences in it. Integrating psycho-logical and sociological perspectives with contemporary medical knowledge, we hypothesized that social stressors influence the development of post-COVID-19 symptoms and, in part, explain sex and other socio-economic disparities. We utilized data from population-based COVIDOM study within the German National Pandemic Cohort Network (NAPKON-POP, 2020-23, N=2,941), recruited by local health authorities on the basis of a positive PCR test irrespective of symptom burden. 86 per-cent of women vs 76 of men reported at least one persistent symptom complex, with women report-ing a 4point higher Post-COVID Syndrome Score on the 0-59 scale. Results from stepwise linear regression models confirm statistically significant sex differences in symptom burden that mostly withstood adjustment for medical composition and social stressors. Accounting for perceived stress and resilience attenuated them by roughly one third, leaving a substantial and statistically significant residual gap between women and men. Overall, these findings suggest that sex differences in post-COVID-19 symptoms are bound up with differences in stress exposure and coping resources, and, thus, complement biological explanations.

articles_hidden.title: Guarantee Fulfillment, Asymmetry, and Desire Shutdown: Exploratory Multi-Level Evidence and Measurement Development for an Existential Guarantee System Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Yong Yue
articles_hidden.abstract:
Terror Management Theory (TMT) holds that cultural worldviews buffer death anxiety by offering symbolic immortality and literal safety. But what happens when the worldview's promises fail to deliver? This paper introduces the Existential Guarantee System (EGS) theory, which proposes that societies function as guarantee systems: they promise rewards (stable income, status, family, housing) in exchange for participation, and threaten punishments (poverty, shame, exclusion) for exit. The Guarantee Fulfillment Rate (GFR) is the perceived rate at which these promises actually deliver. EGS predicts that when GFR declines, positive promise expectations decay first while negative sanction expectations persist — producing a Guarantee Asymmetry Index (GAI) that tracks the divergence, and downstream consequences including desire shutdown and post-goal disappointment.

We present multi-level exploratory evidence for EGS across three measurement levels: (1) a preregistered pilot study (N = 68 after exclusion) developing a GFR/GAI scale with good internal consistency (GFR α = .94; desire-shutdown α = .84; sanction α = .88) and exploratory signals consistent with all five preregistered hypotheses, including a mechanical-overlap decomposition showing the asymmetry signal is direct (|r(GFR–S)| = .37 < |r(GFR–P)| = .78; composite GFR–GAI r = −.69); (2) an individual-level proxy test in a national probability sample (CGSS 2023, N = 11,326): opportunity-fairness beliefs predict ideal children count (β = .209, p < .0001) with the steepest slope in the youngest cohort (18–35: β = .306) — an age-gradient double confirmation (youngest cohorts hold the lowest fulfillment expectations and respond most strongly); (3) macro-level panel evidence (38 countries, 35 years): youth unemployment (an absolute-fulfillment proxy) predicts fertility decline (β = −.0099, p = .0012, two-way fixed effects), with relative-inequality proxies (Gini) showing the opposite direction — fulfillment failure is about absolute attainability, not relative distribution.

All results are honestly graded: directional predictions matched expectations across all tests, but construct-level inference is limited to exploratory signals pending a fully powered preregistered study (N ≥ 300). The paper is positioned as the first empirical proof-of-concept and measurement-development wave for EGS — not as confirmatory validation. We discuss the Korea paradox (world-lowest fertility with low youth unemployment) as explained by housing costs (price-to-income ratio 24.4, top 12% globally), and the theoretical and practical implications for AI companionship as a novel guarantee system.

articles_hidden.title: The AI Governance Execution Gap: Organizational Readiness as a Condition for Ethical AI Governance
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Jo Montgomery
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence governance frameworks increasingly specify accountability, human oversight, risk management, transparency, and lifecycle monitoring, but formal adoption does not establish that an organization can carry those commitments into consequential operational decisions. This conceptual paper argues that organizational readiness is a necessary condition for ethical AI governance. It defines the Governance Execution Gap as the distance between governance expectations and the institutional capacity to exercise decision authority, route risk, produce evidence, monitor deployed systems, and intervene when conditions change. Drawing on organizational readiness theory, the Technology-Organization-Environment framework, established AI governance standards and policy, and scholarship on translating AI ethics principles into practice, the paper develops an AI Governance Readiness Framework with five interdependent domains and corresponding Governance Execution Gates. It also introduces an Accountability Gap that distinguishes visibility, assigned responsibility, decision authority, and practical capacity to act. The central normative claim is that accountability and human oversight are ethically meaningful only when organizations can make those responsibilities executable under real operating conditions. A practitioner-oriented scorecard and illustrative cybersecurity triage scenario demonstrate how the model may support decisions without claims of empirical validation. The framework is proposed as a testable conceptual model for future empirical evaluation across high-consequence environments.

articles_hidden.title: Sociotechnical Transition and Uncertainty in the Lithium Mining Industry: Technologies, Politics and Transparency
articles_hidden.authors: Iván Ojeda-Pereira; Sebastián Herrera-León; Marcelo Lufin; Fernando Campos-Medina
articles_hidden.abstract: Technological transitions in extractive industries are commonly assessed through technical and environmental performance, whilst their social and ethical dimensions receive little systematic attention. This article addresses that gap through the adoption of direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies in Chile, the world’s second largest lithium producer and the leading producer from salt flats. The National Lithium Strategy promotes these technologies as a response to social tensions over the use of water and brine in fragile ecosystems, and the conditions of their implementation remain open. Drawing on interdisciplinary work between the engineering sciences and the social sciences, we ask which technological and social uncertainties experts identify in this transition. Two expert workshops were held with 20 participants from industry, the State and academia, and their contributions were examined through inductive qualitative content analysis. The findings show five uncertainties: (i) there is no consensus on which technologies will be implemented or on the criteria for choosing them; (ii) the effects of brine reinjection lack conclusive evidence; (iii) the role and agency of the State remain undetermined; (iv) no mapping exists of the actors regarded as valid participants in the debate; and (v) there is no agreement on how the social sustainability of this change should be measured. We propose five public information infrastructures as a design response to these uncertainties, whilst acknowledging that transparency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ethical sociotechnical governance in the extractive industries of the Global South.

articles_hidden.title: Inside the meat locker: anticipatory self-censorship and pressure on the vocabulary of American science
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander C Tsai
articles_hidden.abstract: The U.S. federal grant terminations of 2025 have had a chilling effect on American science. Grantees whose awards have been renegotiated under threat of termination must now determine how the revised terms constrain the language they use when reporting their findings in peer-reviewed publications. Standing in the meat locker of anticipatory compliance, scientists face strong incentives to adopt conservative interpretations of what the revised terms require. In this commentary, I describe a case that surfaced during editorial review, in which an author excised disfavored terminology from a manuscript. Manuscript-level effects of this kind will ordinarily be invisible because pre-submission sanitization leaves no observable counterfactual in the published record. My concerns about the implications for the field are grounded in three recent episodes in U.S. history—the freeze on federal funding for gun violence research; the near-elimination and ongoing dismantling of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality; and the Toomey “hit list” of grants on HIV prevention and sexual behavior—each of which had durable adverse consequences for American science even without the backing of Stalinist repression. The post-Lysenko experience suggests that even if formal restrictions can be imposed and rescinded rapidly, the damage to human capital, training pipelines, and institutional trust may outlive the political conditions that produced them. Author-side strategies for lexical compliance (awkward periphrases, coded substitutions, and portfolio segregation) offer little defense against a determined state adversary. Their principal virtue is to make private accommodations visible as coordinated acts performed under duress—which is not nothing, because scientists deserve to have their compliance recorded accurately as compliance rather than as consent.

articles_hidden.title: From Knowledge to Behaviour Change: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of the Tide Turners Plastic Challenge in India
articles_hidden.authors: Tarun Kumar Verma; Diogo Veríssimo
articles_hidden.abstract: Plastic pollution is a global environmental crisis which demands not only technological and policy responses but also changes in societal practices. The UN Environment Programme's Tide Turners Plastic Challenge (TTPC) addressed it by driving behaviour change through youth engagement. This mixed-methods evaluation study was conducted in India, comprised a pre–post randomised controlled trial in Delhi (n = 272) and Gujarat (n = 392), and 56 semi-structured interviews across six states, focused on the most engaged participants. TTPC participants outperformed the non-participants in personal responsibility (22%), problem recognition (23%), recycling knowledge (21%), peer environmental discussions (35%), and household recycling (55%). Qualitative results show that TTPC increased knowledge, fostered responsibility, and enabled youth-led adaptations to single-use plastics. However, structural barriers persisted, including inadequate waste infrastructure, limited digital access, economic constraints, and social exclusion. Voluntary behaviour change initiatives require a combination of motivational engagement and investment in enabling infrastructure to sustain impact.

articles_hidden.title: The Fruits of Finitude: Reflexive Minimalism in Epistemology and Ethics
articles_hidden.authors: Max Sedlmair
articles_hidden.abstract:
Reflexive Minimalism is a foundational paper proposing a minimal criterion for epistemic and normative stability: reflexive stability. A claim or norm is admissible only if it can survive its own application and does not undermine the conditions of reasoning, justification, or disagreement.

The paper begins from epistemic finitude: finite agents cannot certify possession of final, unquestionable truth about ultimate reality. This does not imply relativism. Rather, it motivates reflexive humility: truth may be sought seriously, but no finite agent may treat their grasp of it as absolute possession.

Applied to ethics, the framework rejects coercion grounded in uncertifiable ultimate claims and protects the shared space in which reasons can be given, challenged, and revised.

This text serves as the programmatic foundation for a broader research project. A shorter core statement and further focused spin-offs will develop selected implications of the framework in epistemology, ethics, and related fields.

articles_hidden.title: Two Cycles, Not One: A Continuous-Time Point-Process Analysis of Reciprocal Violence in the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Carlin Percha
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether violence in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict is reciprocal — each side's lethal action provoking the other's — has been studied largely through vector-autoregression on time-binned counts, an approach that obscures the timing, branching structure, and directionality of response. We model lethal violence in the two directions as a bivariate Hawkes process, a continuous-time self- and mutually-exciting point process, using individual-incident fatality records from the Second Intifada through October 2023. Reciprocal excitation is genuine but profoundly asymmetric: a single Palestinian-to-Israeli event triggers on the order of one subsequent Israeli lethal event, nearly thirty times the reverse coupling. The asymmetry survives placebo, regime-detection, and flexible-baseline checks designed to rule out a common-driver confound, and goodness-of-fit testing confirms the models describe the data adequately. Allowing the couplings to take either sign, we find no evidence of deterrence in either direction. The strength of the Israeli response is statistically indistinguishable across the conflict's two main eras, but its speed is not: the characteristic response lag roughly halves between the Intifada and the later Gaza-war period, a temporal change binned methods cannot represent. Resolving the Israeli-to-Palestinian direction into its Gaza and West Bank theaters reveals that they operate as nearly independent systems: violence within each is strongly self-exciting while cross-theater coupling is negligible, and the reciprocal dynamic that dominates the pooled analysis is localized almost entirely to the West Bank, whereas Gaza's violence is driven by internal escalation. What appears in aggregate as a single cycle is, spatially, two barely-interacting logics — a separation we argue reflects the differential governance of the two territories rather than any natural division of the conflict. A three-stream extension shows settler violence to be a distinct channel: reactive to Palestinian action, increasingly self-exciting, and temporally preceding rather than following state violence. All findings replicate on an independently constructed event dataset. We document these regularities for 2000–2023 and set out why we do not extend them through the subsequent war: individual-incident records for that period exist, but not on a footing commensurable with the present analysis.

articles_hidden.title: Double Robust, Flexible Adjustment Methods for Causal Inference: An Overview and an Evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Nathan Isaac Hoffmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Double robust methods for flexible covariate adjustment in causal inference have proliferated in recent years. Despite their apparent advantages in overcoming model misspecification, these methods are rarely used by social scientists. It is also unclear whether these methods actually outperform more traditional methods in finite samples. This paper has two aims: It is a guide to some of the latest methods in double robust, flexible covariate adjustment using machine learning, and it tests them against more traditional statistical methods and flexible, non-double robust methods using simulated, cross-sectional data where the treatment effect is known. Double robust methods covered include Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW), Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE), and Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML). Results suggest that these methods do outperform traditional methods in a wide range of simulations, but only when paired with flexible machine learning estimators. Notably, G-computation with the same flexible estimators obtains almost identical results, and standard regression methods have only slightly higher bias. In the scenarios considered in this paper, flexibility and robustness to heterogeneous treatment effects appear to be more important properties than double robustness.

articles_hidden.title: The Quest for Peace in the Islamic Tradition
articles_hidden.authors: Abbas Aroua
articles_hidden.abstract: The Muslim world is one of the regions with the highest densities of conflict in the world (intra- and interstate). Yet it is one of the poorest ones in terms of conflict transformation resources both theoretical and practical. The foundational texts of the Islamic religion and the practices of the Prophet of Islam and the early Muslim community provide enough teachings to elaborate a comprehensive theory of conflict and peace. But the historical events the Muslim community went through and particularly the major political conflicts (the Big Fitna*) in the first decades of Islamic history prevented the emergence of a healthy approach to conflict. Today there is an increasing awareness for the need in the Muslim world to master the techniques of conflict analysis and transformation. This can be measured by the increasing number of young Muslims being trained in mediation or pursuing academic curricula in conflict transformation. The aim of this contribution from a Muslim author is to provide peace workers with a few resources from the Islamic tradition that can be used when addressing a conflict rooted in an Islamic context. Using the internal resources and a language understood by the conflicting parties has proven to be effective in conflict transformation. The concepts developed in the modern theory of conflict and peace may be expressed in words the parties are familiar with, and this is what this book aims to show. In chapter 1, ten basic Islamic concepts are briefly presented: dīn, islām, īmān, ihsān, rahma, haqq, karāma, ‘adl, jihād and sharī'a. These concepts are useful keys to understanding Islām; some of them are often misunderstood and misused. They will guide the discussions of the meaning of peace in the Islamic tradition. In chapters 2-4, the issues of peace and war, conflict and conflict transformation are addressed. In chapter 5, the value of work in the Islamic tradition and the requirements for decent work are then discussed, work conditions and environment being crucial for social justice and social peace. In chapter 6, the focus is put on the work of goodness, a concept that in the Islamic tradition goes beyond predication and humanitarian work and represents a holistic approach to human security. Chapter 7 addresses some issues related to Islam-West relations and the tensions that may arise between Muslims and Westerners, as well as the appropriate way to deal with them.

articles_hidden.title: The Salafiscape in the wake of the ‘Arab spring’
articles_hidden.authors: Abbas Aroua
articles_hidden.abstract: This contribution aims to show that Salafi typologies are not static but change in time with the evolution of social and political contexts, and that no typology can fully grasp the complexity of the Salafi field. It proposes an alternative typology, based on how Salafis view and approach cultural, economic, political and military power, and gives a number of policy recommendations on how to deal constructively with Salafism.

articles_hidden.title: Four Criteria for Differentiating Religious Entities
articles_hidden.authors: Abbas Aroua
articles_hidden.abstract: The attitude towards religion and an undifferentiated approach of religious currents result in many contexts in disastrous policies that cause undesired tensions in both Muslim and non-Muslim societies. This paper presents four criteria that help approaching religious currents in a differentiated way, considering their non-homogeneity and the wide diversity within them.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Advisers in Mediating Worldview Conflicts
articles_hidden.authors: Abbas Aroua
articles_hidden.abstract: Mediation as an assisted negotiation is a complex process involving the parties in conflict and a third party (the mediator/facilitator), as well as several “fourth parties” who can either be “constructive contributors” with a beneficial role, who help support and steer the process in a positive direction, promote understanding, and encourage open communication to help the parties reach a resolution, or “spoilers” with a harmful role, who obstruct, disrupt, or undermine the process, often creating conflict or preventing resolution. A good mediation process design is one that identifies from the outset all constructive contributors and harnesses their beneficial role, as well as all spoilers and neutralizes their potential harm. This contribution addresses the role of advisers in mediation processes and presents examples of the involvement of advisers in processes conducted by Cordoba Peace Institute – Geneva (CPI) over the last two decades in relation to worldview conflicts.

articles_hidden.title: SOBRE LA PERSONALIDAD AUTORITARIA DE LOS MEXICANOS (2021-2024)
articles_hidden.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles_hidden.abstract: Este artículo analiza la evolución de la personalidad autoritaria en México entre 2021 y 2024 utilizando una versión adaptada de la Escala F de Adorno et al. (1950). A través de un diseño de tendencia con muestras probabilísticas independientes, se evalúan variables sociodemográficas, ideológicas e institucionales. Los hallazgos revelan un incremento significativo en el autoritarismo de la población mexicana al finalizar el periodo estudiado. Si bien se confirman determinantes clásicos como la educación, la religiosidad y la ideología, el análisis multivariado mediante regresión logística ordinal sugiere una reconfiguración: el autoritarismo ha mutado hacia una versión más cultural e identitaria, menos ligada a la estructura social tradicional. El estudio concluye que el fenómeno persiste y se adapta, impulsado por la polarización política y crisis normativas, rechazando la hipótesis de estabilidad y reafirmando la relevancia de instrumentos psicométricos refinados para auditar la cultura política en contextos democráticos contemporáneos.

articles_hidden.title: Blood-pressure reading and quality-control choices move India's raised-blood-pressure prevalence several times beyond its sampling error: an executable multiverse analysis of NFHS-4 and NFHS-5
articles_hidden.authors: Dharit Shah
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. National estimates of raised blood pressure from the same survey microdata differ substantially across published analyses of India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS). NFHS measures blood pressure on a single occasion, so every estimate here concerns raised blood pressure on one measurement occasion, not clinically diagnosed hypertension. How much of the spread across published estimates is attributable to defensible analytical choices, rather than to sampling variation, has not been established.

Methods. We encoded the analytical decisions of 20 published NFHS hypertension papers into an executable specification registry and ran 144 prospectively specified analyses (72 per round) on NFHS-4 and NFHS-5 person-recode microdata, crossing eligible population, blood-pressure reading-selection algorithm, quality-control scope, case definition and survey estimand. Estimates use a Taylor-linearized ratio estimator with sex-by-five-year-age post-stratification to household-roster targets, which corrects the differential blood-pressure coverage of the NFHS-4 male subsample. Two estimand families are reported separately rather than pooled.

Results. Holding case definition, eligible population and estimand fixed, the five reading-selection and quality-control algorithms move prevalence by 1.58 to 3.07 percentage points, which is 4.5 to 19.6 times the design-based standard error of the estimate. Only 70 of 480 sibling estimates fall inside a given specification's own 95% confidence interval, and 66 of 120 specifications have confidence intervals containing no sibling at all. Within a fixed case definition, state rankings are reproducible: every within-definition bootstrap interval lies entirely above the across-definition interval in both rounds. Disparity directions are robust, with all 432 specification-by-gap combinations positive and 428 surviving Holm correction. On the specifications matching India's national NCD monitoring indicator, the reading-rule choice alone moves the monitored quantity by 46% of the reduction the 25% relative-reduction target demands.

Conclusions. Reading-selection and quality-control choices, each individually defensible and each drawn from published practice, move an Indian national prevalence estimate several times beyond its reported precision. These are the fields least often reported: the blood-pressure validity thresholds are clearly reported by 3 to 4 of 20 papers, and no paper reports every field needed to reconstruct its own analysis. Levels should be reported as ranges over defensible specifications; rankings and disparity directions can be reported as point findings. Code, specification registry with per-field source quotes, and the full results archive are deposited.

articles_hidden.title: Five lenses for co-creation across epistemic difference in transdisciplinary research
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Charette; Laura Levin; R. Shayna Rosenbaum; Caitlin R. Mullin; J. Douglas Crawford; Giuseppina D'Agostino; Sean Hillier; Gunnar Blohm
articles_hidden.abstract:
Co-creation has become an increasingly promiment approach to collaborative research in domains including health, education, sustainability, and design. Yet existing frameworks are
designed for discipline-specific settings, offering limited guidance for research that spans heterogeneous epistemic traditions, institutional contexts, and value systems. This scoping
review examines peer-reviewed articles to map dominant co-creation practices, rationales, and evaluation strategies. It reveals that most existing approaches are applied in relatively stable epistemic contexts, where problems, values, methods, and success criteria are well established. Drawing on science and technology studies and adjacent critical traditions, we argue that the central challenge of transdisciplinary co-creation is not simply expanding participation but negotiating epistemic plurality.
