Building on this diagnosis, we propose five complementary conceptual lenses (boundary objects, co-production, situated knowledge, critical institutional reflexivity, and multi-scalar evaluation) that together provide a theoretical and practical framework for organizing co-creation in transdisciplinary research settings. This framework reconceptualizes co-creation as an ongoing practice of negotiating problems, authority, evidence, and evaluation across heterogeneous systems of knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: The Paperwork of Grief: Administrative Burden as a Defence Against Death Exposure in Clinical Care
articles_hidden.authors: Chukwudi Egbuonu
articles_hidden.abstract: Administrative work (documentation, the electronic record, the proliferation of meetings, the referral of distress onward to specialists) is treated almost universally in the clinician-wellbeing literature as a cause of burnout to be measured and reduced. This paper argues that in the most death-saturated settings of medicine (the cancer ward, the intensive care unit, the palliative service) that same burden may also do something the literature has not noticed: function as a social defence against sustained exposure to dying, offering clinicians a bounded, completable, finite task to retreat into when the bedside offers only problems that often end in death. The argument revives Isabel Menzies Lyth’s 1959 account of hospital routine as a collective defence against anxiety and brings it forward to the era of the electronic record, joining four literatures (on documentation burden, on death exposure and numbing, on terror management, and on the social defences of institutions) that have not previously been read together. If the conjecture holds, the prevailing prescription to strip administration away on efficiency grounds alone risks removing an unrecognised container without supplying a deliberate one, and the proper task is not to reduce paperwork but to distinguish what merely numbs from what genuinely contains, and to design containment for those who work among the dead. The claim is interpretive and bounded to high-mortality settings; the paper sets out how it could be tested and the competing explanations it complements rather than displaces.

articles_hidden.title: The Best-Partner Paradox: Encounter Paths Strongly Determine Partner Identity but Only Moderately Affect Population-Level Relationship Welfare in an Agent-Based Model
articles_hidden.authors: Zi-Ru JIANG
articles_hidden.abstract: Partner choice is commonly framed as a search for the uniquely ‘best’ person, yet romantic relationships emerge from sequential encounters, mutual acceptance, accumulated interaction, and exposure to unpredictable life events. We developed a theoretical agent-based model to distinguish two questions that are often conflated: how strongly encounter history determines who becomes partnered with whom, and how strongly it determines the resulting distribution of long-term relationship outcomes. Each simulated world contained 750 agents who searched over 20 rounds, evaluated five candidates per round, and formed relationships through mutual acceptance. Agents differed in excellence, relationship ability, and value position. Five choice strategies were compared: maximizing partner excellence, maximizing compatibility, balancing excellence and compatibility, satisficing, and random choice. Formed relationships accumulated dimensionless relationship capital over 30 simulated years through compatibility-dependent growth, relationship ability, stochastic favorable and adverse events, opportunity conversion, repair, and diminishing returns. Across 2,000 paired Monte Carlo worlds, maximizing compatibility produced the highest population welfare when singlehood was assigned a baseline value of 1.0. Its welfare exceeded excellence maximization by 0.0521 (95% bootstrap CI 0.0511–0.0530; paired Cohen’s d_z = 2.31), primarily because compatibility maximization generated a substantially higher pairing rate, although balanced choice produced the highest conditional mean relationship capital. Complete replacement of encounter schedules changed partner identity for 99.25% of agents paired in both simulations, close to the 99.73% independent-random-matching benchmark, yet changed mean relationship capital by only 11.45% on average and changed population welfare by less than 0.001. Mechanism ablation showed that repair after adverse events and compatibility-dependent growth were essential to welfare. A 15 × 15 robustness atlas found compatibility maximization optimal in 70.67% of 225 stochastic regimes, excellence maximization in 15.56%, and balanced choice in 13.78%, demonstrating that no strategy was universally optimal. Rankings stabilized well before 2,000 worlds. The model therefore identifies a best-partner paradox: the identity of one’s eventual partner can be highly contingent even when the attainable distribution of relationship outcomes is much less contingent. These results are theoretical consequences of the specified mechanisms and do not estimate real-world marriage probabilities or causal effects.

articles_hidden.title: Digital Transformation Capabilities and Supply Chain Finance Resilience: An Integrated AI–Blockchain–Analytics Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Jainish Bhagat
articles_hidden.abstract:
Supply chain finance (SCF) plays a pivotal role in maintaining liquidity and operational continuity across global value networks. However, systemic supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic volatility, and information asymmetry frequently expose SCF programs to severe friction and default risks. While digital transformation is widely touted as a catalyst for supply chain resilience, empirical evidence regarding the explicit mechanisms through which distinct digital transformation capabilities enhance Supply Chain Finance Resilience (SCFR) remains fragmented. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), and Information Processing Theory (IPT), this study develops and tests an integrated framework evaluating the direct and indirect impacts of Artificial Intelligence Capability (AIC), Blockchain Capability (BC), and Data Analytics Capability (DAC) on SCFR, mediated by Digital Trust in SCF Platforms (DT).
Using a computational research simulation methodology, a respondent-level dataset (N=500) representing supply chain, finance, operations, and IT decision-makers across international enterprises was algorithmically generated under a defensible latent-variable covariance structure. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was executed to evaluate the measurement and structural models. The structural analysis reveals that AIC (β=0.241,p<.001), BC (β=0.312,p<.001), and DAC (β=0.284,p<.001) significantly and positively drive Digital Trust in SCF Platforms, explaining 54.2% of its variance (R^2=0.542). Digital Trust, in turn, exerts a substantial direct effect on SCFR (β=0.385,p<.001). Furthermore, direct effects on SCFR were confirmed for DAC (β=0.218,p<.001) and AIC (β=0.152,p=.002), whereas the direct link from BC to SCFR was non-significant (β=0.071,p=.158). Formal mediation testing using percentile bootstrapping confirmed that Digital Trust fully mediates the relationship between Blockchain Capability and SCFR, while partially mediating the relationships for AIC and DAC. The overall structural model accounts for 58.6% of the variance in Supply Chain Finance Resilience (R^2=0.586,Q_"predict" ^2=0.412).
This methodological prototype advances theoretical understanding by unpacking the granular capability configurations necessary to foster digital trust and financial resilience in supply networks. For practitioners and policymakers, the findings highlight that investing in blockchain technology yields minimal resilience benefits unless coupled with platform-wide digital trust mechanisms, whereas AI and analytics offer dual-pathway benefits across operational and relational domains.

articles_hidden.title: La reserva de plazas de PDI permanente para personas con discapacidad
articles_hidden.authors: Francisco J Plaza Martín
articles_hidden.abstract: Este trabajo analiza la aplicación de la reserva legal de plazas para personas con discapacidad en el acceso al PDI permanente de las universidades públicas españolas entre 2016 y 2025. El artículo 59 del Estatuto Básico del Empleado Público protege y desarrolla, entre otros derechos,  el acceso en condiciones de igualdad a las funciones públicas (artículo 23.2 de la Constitución Española). A partir de solicitudes de información pública dirigidas a las universidades, se observa el incumplimiento generalizado de este deber de reserva, así como déficits de trazabilidad, información homogénea y control institucional. El problema detectado no debe describirse únicamente como una suma de omisiones administrativas universitarias, sino como un déficit de implementación de una política pública legalmente obligatoria.

articles_hidden.title: Estimating Regional Industry Employment from Economic Location Mechanisms: A Constrained Spatial Disaggregation for European Geographies
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Boero
articles_hidden.abstract: Fine-scale employment by industry is largely unavailable across European municipalities, yet it underpins regional economic analysis, environmental-economic extensions, and the regionalization of input--output accounts. This paper presents a mechanism-driven, constrained spatial disaggregation framework that estimates industry employment down to the Local Administrative Unit level while preserving official totals exactly at every geographical level. The economic mechanisms that shape where activity locates --- settlement, infrastructure and accessibility, natural-resource endowments, and inter-industry co-location --- are represented as a reproducible input dataset assembled from official and remote-sensing sources; a family of constrained allocation models, combined by a cross-validated convex ensemble, is trained on data-rich United States geographies and transferred to Europe under official Eurostat totals as constraints. Validated against independent national statistics in Italy, France, Germany, and Spain, the estimates reproduce the observed spatial distribution of employment within the held-out uncertainty of the models themselves, and the error does not inflate down the four-step disaggregation. The framework is open, inspectable, and reproducible, providing internally consistent fine-scale employment estimates wherever sub-national industry data are sparse.

articles_hidden.title: When Does Generative AI Become a Developmental Resource? A Multilevel Taxonomy of Enactment Conditions
articles_hidden.authors: Andreea Nicolau; Sonja Rispens; Pascale Marie Le Blanc; Kees Maton; Piet J. R. van Gool; Ad Kleingeld
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) creates a developmental ambiguity for organizations: it can support learning, reflection, and judgment, but it can also accelerate task completion while reducing engagement with the cognitive and social processes through which capabilities develop. This study asks which multilevel conditions shape whether GenAI is enacted as a resource for learning and continuous development or as a shortcut for task completion. Drawing on an inductive, multi-stakeholder qualitative study with 41 organizational actors, we use thematic analysis to identify empirical categories and morphological principles to organize them into a multidimensional taxonomy of GenAI enactment. The taxonomy identifies four interrelated dimensions: Organizational Conditions, Capability Conditions, Decision Drivers, and GenAI Enactment. Interpreting these findings through the automation–augmentation paradox, we show that automation- and augmentation-oriented uses are not fixed properties of technologies or tasks but contextually produced orientations shaped by an iterative system of societal/institutional, organizational, and individual-related conditions. The study contributes to AI and management research by specifying the condition architecture through which GenAI becomes more or less developmental in practice. We argue that learning-oriented GenAI integration requires attention to the multilevel conditions that preserve verification, reflection, feedback, and accountable judgment when task completion no longer necessarily develops capability.

articles_hidden.title: Caring connections: A systematic review of health and wellbeing benefits of intergenerational farming activities
articles_hidden.authors: Rosamund Harrington; Marissa Lindquist; Susan Darzins; Mark Trotter; Robin Drogemuller; Heidi Olsen; Gert-Jan Pepping; Suzanne Kuys
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background and Objectives: Intergenerational farming activities, including care of plants, animals, and surrounding environments, enable connection with nature and participating generations.  This systematic review aimed to determine health and wellbeing impacts of intergenerational farming activities for older adults, children/youth and community; key factors contributing to establishment, engagement in, and sustainability of intergenerational farming programs: and whether they support ‘ageing-in-place'.
Research Design and Methods: A systematic search was undertaken of five databases. Studies could be qualitative and/or quantitative, involve an intergenerational activity/program inclusive of older adults and children/youth, report health and wellbeing outcomes and be written in English. Adopting a social ecological lens, qualitative data were synthesised and reported thematically. Quantitative data were descriptively presented.  
Results: Twenty-two studies were included. Seven themes relating to health and wellbeing impacts were identified: physical health benefits, psychological benefits, positive relationships and interpersonal skills, community and belonging, purposeful work or learning, environmental engagement, and connection to culture. Factors impacting establishment, engagement in, and sustainability of activities included planning and implementation considerations, partnerships, agency and anticipated future opportunities/benefits. No studies reported if, or how, intergenerational farming activities support ‘ageing-in-place’. 
Discussion and Implications: Intergenerational farming activities appear to offer holistic health and wellbeing benefits, reflecting Indigenous approaches to healing through connections to land, culture, and community. Establishing sustainable programs requires planning, training and partnerships. More robust research utilising objective measures is required to support findings. Further investigation is needed. Furthermore, studies investigating how intergenerational farming supports ‘ageing-in-place’ is recommended.

articles_hidden.title: Corruption in Nepal's Local Governments: A Case Study of Institutional Weaknesses and Citizen Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: This case study deals with corruption in public procurement at the local government level in Nepal. Nepal established 753 local governments with substantial responsibility for public spending, including procurement of goods, works and services, following the adoption of the Constitution in 2015. Mostly today, public spending is the responsibility of local governments, especially on capital investment in infrastructure, such as roads, schools, health facilities and water supply systems. But the speed of devolution of responsibilities has not been matched by adequate systems of transparency, accountability and integrity. This paper explores the nature and extent of corruption in local government procurement in Nepal, drawing on publicly available data from the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority, Transparency International, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and government audit reports. The analysis shows that procurement is a high-risk area for corruption at the local level. Corrupt practices are many and include bid-rigging, inflated costs, shoddy work, kickbacks, collusion among bidders, political interference with contract awards, etc. The data show that many local governments do not follow procurement rules well, publish limited information and have weak oversight. Audit reports frequently find irregularities in procurement by local government. The paper investigates factors leading to procurement corruption including weak institutional capacity, political interference, lack of transparency, limited oversight by citizens and poor enforcement. The report ends with recommendations for improving procurement integrity, including better procurement rules, more transparency, capacity building, stronger oversight, more citizen participation, and accountability enforcement.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Blame: School Violence, Youth Despair, and the Failure of Containment in Recent Philippine Shootings
articles_hidden.authors: Rhine Lesther Tague
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent school-related shootings in the Philippines, especially the June 2026 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban and the August 2026 shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, generated public pressure to locate a single cause: a teacher, a game, a security failure, a disturbed child, a family failure. This paper argues that such explanations are emotionally understandable but causally insufficient. Drawing on incident reporting, official and reported-official statements, verified WHO Global School-based Student Health Survey data, DepEd Region VIII memoranda, public-health and threat-assessment literature, and C. G. Jung's Modern Man in Search of a Soul, the paper proposes a different representation: recent Philippine school violence should be understood as a failed ecology of containment. In this frame, adolescent grievance, despair, humiliation, or rupture become dangerous when they converge with firearm access, missed warning signs, weak disclosure pathways, digital scripts or grooming environments, livestream/notoriety affordances, and institutions that are not yet able to metabolize distress before it turns into public violence. The argument does not claim that Jungian "spiritual crisis" is a forensic motive. Rather, Jung helps name the meaning-layer of youth collapse: psychic pain, futurelessness, shame, and disconnection are real in their effects even when they cannot be reduced to one external cause. The paper concludes that prevention must move beyond blame toward containment: firearm accountability, threat assessment, confidential reporting, anti-bullying systems, psychosocial support, digital-platform safeguards, and living forms of youth meaning and belonging.

articles_hidden.title: Staying Long Enough to Stop Seeing: Autoethnography, Long-Term Immersion, and Tourism Research
articles_hidden.authors: Rob Burton
articles_hidden.abstract: Autoethnographic tourism research has typically been based on discrete journeys or bounded periods of fieldwork, leaving the epistemological implications of long-term residential immersion comparatively underexamined. This article argues that sustained residence produces a distinctive form of knowledge grounded not simply in prolonged observation but in the transformation of perception over time. Drawing on more than a decade of living and working across Nanjing, Hangzhou, and Wenzhou, China, it proposes a three-stage framework of estrangement, normalisation, and critical re-estrangement. Initial unfamiliarity heightens attention; repeated exposure subsequently renders once-remarkable features ordinary and increasingly invisible; disciplined analytical attention can then return the researcher to these normalised environments with a capacity to recognise recurrence, pattern, and institutional continuity. Through examples of everyday urban landscapes and the seasonal infrastructure underlying Hangzhou's elevated-highway flower displays, the article demonstrates how long-term immersion makes visible processes that shorter encounters may register only as isolated events or spectacles. Critical re-estrangement therefore offers a methodological means of converting habituation from an apparent limitation of long-term residence into an analytical resource.

articles_hidden.title: Detention as a disabling institution: Age-related health disparities in the US immigration detention system
articles_hidden.authors: Caitlin Patler
articles_hidden.abstract: From 2008 to 2018, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement apprehended over two million noncitizens in the US interior. However, data on detained immigrants' health is limited, with a particular lack of research on older detained immigrants, despite the distinct vulnerabilities aging individuals confront within and outside carceral settings. Immigrants face diverse structural challenges as they age, and incarcerated individuals experience accelerated aging and have worse health relative to non-incarcerated individuals, due to exposure to structural disadvantage, coupled with the health harms of incarceration itself. Using data from the Immigrant Detention Survey (n=495) and the National Health Interview Survey (n=8,383), and drawing on theories of aging in carceral settings, immigrant health and aging, and immigration policies as structural determinants of health, I address two critical and unresolved questions: What is the health profile of older detained adults, relative to younger adults? How do age-related health disparities among detained immigrants compare to those of non-detained immigrants? My findings reveal age-related health disparities in detained and non-detained populations. I also find much higher rates of poor health among detained immigrants than in the non-detained population, regardless of age. Results suggest immigration detention may be considered a mass disabling institution linked to poor health across the life course and may exacerbate age-related disparities, highlighting the need for more humane and equitable immigration and health policies.

articles_hidden.title: The Credibility Revolution in Political Science
articles_hidden.authors: Carolina Torreblanca; William Dinneen; Guy Grossman; Yiqing Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: How far has the credibility revolution spread through political science? We address this question by classifying 91,632 articles published between 2003 and 2023 across 156 political science journals using large language models, focusing on research design, credibility-enhancing practices, and citation patterns. We find that design-based studies, those leveraging plausibly exogenous variation to justify causal claims, have become increasingly common. In contrast, model-based approaches that rely more heavily on modeling assumptions have declined. Yet the rise of design-based work is uneven: it is concentrated in top journals and among authors at highly ranked institutions, and it is driven primarily by the growth of survey experiments. Other credibility-enhancing practices that help reduce false positives and false negatives, such as placebo tests and power calculations, remain rare. Taken together, our findings point to substantial but selective change, more consistent with a partial reform than a revolution.

articles_hidden.title: Sense of place based on shared imaginaries for caring for the chinampa socio‑ecosystem
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Paula Margain Leon; Lakshmi Charli Joseph; Jesús Mario Siqueiros-Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: Sense of place refers to the meaningful connection that people establish with a space, which can either motivate or inhibit environmental care. Understanding the mechanisms that strengthen this connection is central to promoting sustainable ways of cohabiting a place. This study proposes imagining desired futures as a mechanism to mobilise a sense of place among young people from Xochimilco in Mexico City and to catalyse new forms of care. Drawing on a qualitative methodology, the study shows that this connection became a conscious, deliberate act that enabled reflection and collective visibility of bonds with place. The findings suggest that imagining futures expands the possibilities for collective care.

articles_hidden.title: Differences in Gender Pension Gaps in public and private pensions in West Germany: An Analysis Sensitive to Interdependencies across the Life-Course
articles_hidden.authors: Carla Rowold
articles_hidden.abstract:
Gender Pension Gaps (GPG) surpass Gender Wage Gaps in most European countries. Research has largely relied on single-factor, employment-centred explanations, and we know less about how GPGs emerge from an interdependent life-course perspective. 
This study contributes by applying a life-course-sensitive decomposition to linked survey-register data for Germany (SHARE-RV), comparing gender gaps in public and private pensions based on common work-family life courses, including relative earnings positions, relevant due to pension privatization in Europe. It considers the interdependencies of employment, family life, and earnings over the life course.
GPGs occur because privileged life courses yielding high pensions are almost exclusively accessible to fathers, while female-typical life-course patterns characterised by care work and part-time employment yield low pensions. Gendered access to high-income careers drives the GPG in private pensions more strongly than in public pensions, underscoring the future risk of high GPGs given persistent gender wage inequalities and pension privatization in Germany.

articles_hidden.title: A Foot in the Door: Ethnic Employment Quotas and Democratic Attitudes in Uruguay
articles_hidden.authors: Jorge Soler-Lopez
articles_hidden.abstract: Does bringing a marginalized group into the state raise its members' trust in democratic institutions? Uruguay's 2013 Ley 19.122, reserving eight percent of public-sector hires for Afro-descendant citizens, offers a rare test on the dimension representation theory names. Using the Uruguayan household survey and eight waves of the Latinobarómetro, we document a genuine but small first stage, Afro-Uruguayan public employment rose about 1.3 percentage points, a composition shift rather than a net gain, against a target the state met only fractionally. In addition, as second stage delivered a precise attitudinal null, with equivalence tests rejecting effects larger than roughly 0.15–0.20 standard deviations. The result establishes a scope condition rather than a refutation: at this level of exposure, bureaucratic inclusion produces no measurable attitudinal return. How much inclusion is required before the representation mechanism fires remains an open and newly quantifiable question.

articles_hidden.title: The development of patriotism among youth in the EU
articles_hidden.authors: Vladislav Medintsev
articles_hidden.abstract: The article separates patriotism from nationalism and blind allegiance while examining the developmental trajectory of patriotism among young people in the European Union. Integrating identity status theory, social identity theory, and political socialization models, it constructs a developmental account of how patriotism matures from childhood through emerging adulthood. The review defines mature patriotism through four properties: differentiation, integration, criticality, and self-authorship. It identifies a shift from uncritical, affective attachment in childhood to a potential for “constructive patriotism”—characterized by critical loyalty and dual national-European identification—in later stages. Key mechanisms facilitating this maturation include open classroom climates, cross-border mobility programs like Erasmus, and digital engagement, though the article notes these opportunities are often stratified by class and education. Conversely, significant obstacles are analyzed, including populist mobilization, economic precarity, and East-West asymmetries in historical memory. The article concludes by proposing an integrative developmental-contextual model comprising three levels (substrate, elaboration, consolidation) and four moderating conditions. It argues that while a historically novel, reflexive form of patriotism is emerging among European youth, its full realization remains contingent on specific ecological conditions and faces ongoing threats from social stratification and political polarization.

articles_hidden.title: El hombre que resiseñó la racionalidad
articles_hidden.authors: Jorge Zazueta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Herbert Simon (1916–2001) es uno de los científicos sociales más influyentes del siglo XX. Premio Nobel
de Economía en 1978 y Premio Turing en 1975, sus aportaciones van desde la psicología hasta la
inteligencia artificial pasando por la teoría de la administración con una visión centrada en el concepto de
racionalidad limitada: la idea de que los seres humanos hacemos decisiones con información incompleta,
capacidad cognitiva finita y aspiraciones flexibles. Buscando soluciones suficientemente buenas en lugar
de óptimas. Este capítulo examina los tres dominios principales del legado simoniano — la teoría de
decisiones, la inteligencia artificial y las ciencias sociales computacionales — y comenta sobre su recepción
en América Latina, donde sus ideas llegaron fragmentadas y con retraso, adoptadas selectivamente por la
administración pública y la teoría organizacional, pero escasamente exploradas en su dimensión
computacional.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic Savings with Adaptive Adjustment in the Solow–Swan Model: Bistability and Escape from a Poverty Trap
articles_hidden.authors: Jorge Zazueta; Leobardo Plata
articles_hidden.abstract:
We extend the Solow–Swan growth model by replacing the constant savings rate with a
savings rate that adjusts gradually toward a capital-dependent target of Hill form. The savings
rate becomes a state variable, turning the model into a two-dimensional dynamical system. For
a sufficiently savings steep target, the system admits a poverty-trap regime with three equilibria:
the origin, a saddle, and a stable high-capital equilibrium. We characterize the stability of every
positive equilibrium by the elasticity of the savings target; in the bistable phase portrait, the
saddle’s stable manifold provides the natural separatrix between the two observed attraction
regions. We then study escape by a temporary public-investment flow. A direct geometric
argument identifies an upper forward-invariant region from which the uncontrolled system
converges to the high-capital equilibrium. If the investment flow satisfies a sufficient condition,
the policy drives capital above a buffer level in finite time; savings then catches up through
adaptive adjustment, after which the stimulus can be removed permanently. The model therefore
converts the one-dimensional threshold of a static savings specification into a two-dimensional
basin problem, where both the level of capital and the speed of savings adjustment are necessary
for escape.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring socioeconomic inequalities in healthy and sustainable diets using big data: An observational analysis of loyalty card data from a UK Retailer, 2022.
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Alan Green; Emma Wilkins; Mark S Gilthorpe; Thomas Sawczuk; Charlotte Hardman; Hannah Greatwood; Rebecca Ann Stone; Alexandra Johnstone; Michelle Morris
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Promoting healthier and more sustainable diets is needed to improve population and planetary health. However, limited evidence has described how these intersecting issues vary together by socioeconomic position. Our study uses novel large-scale retailer consumer purchase data, adjusted for known biases, to explore socioeconomic inequalities in health and environmental impacts of food and beverage purchases.

Methods: Data were household-level loyalty card records from a major UK supermarket retailer between 24th July and 31st December 2022 (n = 117 710). The health-related outcome was proportion of purchases that were ‘High in Fat, Salt or Sugar’ (HFSS), determined using the UK nutrient profile model. We estimated three environmental outcomes: total greenhouse gas emissions, total land use footprint, and total water use from food purchases. Multilevel regression with post-stratification was used to estimate each outcome measure by level of neighbourhood socioeconomic deprivation, adjusted for age, household size, distance to nearest supermarket, and urbanicity. We also described environmental outcomes by food category across level of deprivation. 

Results: Households residing in the most deprived 10% of areas purchased a larger proportion of HFSS items than households in the least deprived 10% of areas. Households in the least deprived 10% of areas had a greater absolute environmental impact. However, when considered per weight of items, households in the most deprived 10% of areas purchased items that contributed to higher greenhouse emissions per kg but had lower impacts for land use. Soft drinks, ready meals, pasta, and pastry products were identified as key food categories for targeted ‘food swaps’ to reduce environmental inequalities. 

Conclusions: Our novel application of retailer loyalty card data shows how these data can offer valuable insights for informing strategies to promote healthy, sustainable, and equitable diets. Tackling environmental inequalities in food purchases requires tailoring approaches to different population groups.

articles_hidden.title: Additional evidence on Madagascar's tourism-led growth hypothesis
articles_hidden.authors: Franck Maminirina Ramaharo
articles_hidden.abstract: We evaluate the validity of the tourism-led growth (TLG) hypothesis for Madagascar through an examination of the asymmetric relationships among economic growth, tourism activity, and financial development over the period 2007Q1-2024Q4. Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag (NARDL) modeling reveals a statistically significant long-run asymmetric effect, wherein negative shocks to tourist arrivals exert a stronger adverse impact on economic growth than the expansionary effect of equivalent increases. With respect to causal dynamics, bivariate symmetric Granger causality testing first uncovers empirical support for the TLG hypothesis. Subsequent short-run asymmetric causality then supports the conservation hypothesis, wherein negative economic growth shocks trigger positive tourist inflows. This dynamic suggests that tourism functions as a counter-cyclical shock absorber during domestic downturns. Consequently, our analysis highlights the need to pivot strategy away from mere tourist volume toward high-yield retention and investment in a resilient tourism sector.

articles_hidden.title: Are environmental and climate worries connected to individual feelings of anomie? Evidence from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study
articles_hidden.authors: Talea Bruns; Stefanie Kley
articles_hidden.abstract: Feelings of anomie manifest themselves in perceptions of meaninglessness and disorientation that are expected to arise in response to rapid social change and threatening social conditions. We analyze whether and how concerns about environmental protection and the impacts of climate change (“environmental worries”) contribute to individual feelings of anomie, based on theoretically informed hypotheses about distinct relationships across social class. Fixed-effects panel regression and random intercept cross-lagged models are used, based on data from the German Socioeconomic Panel study (GSOEP; years 2008–2023). We find that environmental worries contribute to feelings of anomie but are trumped by adverse events in individual’s life course. The contribution of environmental worries to feelings of anomie is weak compared to worries about one’s own economic situation and health. Levels of both, feelings of anomie and environmental worries, are relatively stable within individuals across the years, whereas spill-over effects between the two are seldom observed. Exclusively in the social class of lower-grade professionals a positive spill-over effect of anomie on environmental worries is observed, whereas among blue-collar workers a negative connection is found. The findings are discussed regarding their contribution to a theory-driven explanation of how climate change and environmental degradation might promote social disintegration.

articles_hidden.title: NursingWave: entry, exit, and market concentration of home-visit nursing providers across Japan's secondary medical zones, 2020–2026
articles_hidden.authors: Kunihisa Ohno
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Japan's home-visit nursing workforce faces the most acute shortage of any nursing field, and national policy deliberations moved in July 2026 from prefecture-level to secondary-medical-zone-level data. Existing evidence, however, consists of static cross-sections; the dynamics of the provider market have never been measured at zone level.
Methods: We constructed a semiannual panel of all home-visit nursing providers listed in the national long-term care information disclosure registry across 12 waves (December 2020 to June 2026), linked providers by insurance provider number, and assigned them to 330 secondary medical zones using a bitemporal municipality-to-zone crosswalk. We computed supply density per population aged 75+, cumulative entry/exit rates, turnover, corporate-group market concentration (HHI), and physician-issued home-visit nursing instructions (NDB item C007) per zone, with Theil decomposition of inequality. All sources are open data; the dataset, code, and an interactive viewer are released under CC BY 4.0.
Results: Providers grew 41.5% nationally (13,032 to 18,436), with designated stations up 48.4% and deemed medical institutions down 16.7%. Yet 43 of 330 zones (13.0%) experienced net decline, concentrated in small zones (24.3% of zones with <25,000 residents aged 75+ vs. 1.7% of large zones), which also showed 12-fold higher market concentration (median HHI 0.125 vs. 0.010). Within-prefecture disparities accounted for 38.4% of total inequality. Same-name re-registrations explained only 2.1% of 5,729 observed exits.
Conclusions: Behind aggregate growth, small zones face a triple disadvantage — lower density, net provider retreat, and single-provider dependence — invisible in prefecture statistics. Zone-level dynamic monitoring is feasible with open data alone.

articles_hidden.title: Closing The Domestic Peace Gap Applying the Domestic Peace Deficit Framework to SDG 5, SDG 16, and the Women, Peace and Security Agenda
articles_hidden.authors: Ijeoma Ezeukwu
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past three decades, the international community has adopted an unprecedented set of legal, policy, and institutional commitments to advance gender equality, protect women and girls from violence, and promote peaceful and inclusive societies, most notably through Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 5 and 16 and the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda. Yet global monitoring confirms that progress on the relevant targets remains off track, and everyday realities inside households continue to diverge sharply from these commitments. This paper argues that the principal barrier is not the absence of formal commitments but the limited capacity of institutions to translate those commitments into lived domestic security, a pattern it terms the domestic peace gap. It applies the Domestic Peace Deficit (DPD) framework, developed in a companion conceptual paper (Ezeukwu, 2026), as an implementation lens for SDG 5, SDG 16, and the four WPS pillars of Prevention, Protection, Participation, and Relief and Recovery. The paper maps DPD's three pillars against relevant SDG targets and WPS commitments, and closes with practical recommendations for governments, United Nations agencies and development partners, and civil society organisations. Its central contribution is diagnostic and practical rather than theoretical: it shows how an institutional-performance lens, rather than an institutional-presence lens, can be used to evaluate whether global commitments are producing safer households.

articles_hidden.title: Fugitive Statistics: A Verification-Chain Protocol for Preserving Policy Numbers That Exist Only Inside Documents
articles_hidden.authors: Kunihisa Ohno
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing share of policy-critical statistics is published only as tables embedded in advisory-committee documents — ad hoc tabulations produced for a single meeting, carried exclusively by PDF, with no versioned machine-readable release, no persistent identifier, and no documented reproduction path. We term these fugitive statistics, by analogy with the fugitive documents of library science — government publications that fall within the scope of a depository system yet escape its collection net. Fugitive statistics are load-bearing: they inform national workforce projections, capacity planning, and crisis-response policy, yet they are exposed to link rot, silent revision, format death, and provenance loss. Crucially, ex-post policy evaluation is possible only if the numbers used ex-ante survive: Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) could score its 7th nursing workforce projection against realized outcomes (deviations of 2.98% and 2.36% for demand and supply) only because the original projection documents remained retrievable. We present a lightweight verification-chain protocol — capture, SHA-256 hashing, independent witnessing via the Internet Archive, semantic extraction with cell-level provenance, bitemporal cataloguing, DOI deposit, and revision monitoring — and demonstrate it end-to-end on the document set of the 4th meeting of MHLW’s 2040 nursing workforce committee, in which prefecture-supplied municipal microdata were re-tabulated into secondary-medical-area statistics that exist nowhere else. All nine artifacts were captured, hashed, and independently witnessed (8/8 PDFs byte-identical to Internet Archive copies), and the embedded tables extracted under two-tier quality control (row-sum checks passed 60/60; double-entry cross-verification matched 916/916 cells), yielding a DOI-bearing dataset within one operator-day on commodity hardware. We position preservation as the precondition of accountability, and fugitive statistics as a measurable site of institutional debt: the divergence between the statistics a policy decision consumed and the statistics later available to evaluate it.

articles_hidden.title: Two Ways of Being Misled: Composition Bias, Weak Within-Municipality Progress, and a Fixed Size Gradient in Japan's Individual Evacuation Plan Statistics, 2022–2026
articles_hidden.authors: Kunihisa Ohno
articles_hidden.abstract:
Japan requires every municipality to maintain a registry of residents who cannot evacuate unaided (2013 amendment to the Disaster Countermeasures Basic Act) and, since 2021, to make best efforts to prepare an individual evacuation plan for each person listed. Progress is monitored through annual national surveys published as municipality-level tables in PDF format. We reconstruct these tables into a machine-readable panel of 1,741 municipalities across five survey waves (2022–2026; 10 source documents, plan and registry series), with documented recovery of 74 rows lost to table-rendering defects, external reconciliation of ambiguous column semantics against published national aggregates, and a complete provenance registry of corrections and known gaps.
Three findings follow, and they cut in different directions. First, the pooled statistics are misleading about direction: the median creation rate across all responding municipalities falls from 19.0% to 17.8%, whereas every continuously observed subset improves, because late-entering municipalities start low and are added faster than incumbents advance. Second, and against our own initial reading, composition control does not reveal robust progress. Within the 423 municipalities observed in all five waves, the median change is only +0.77 points over four years, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval reaching down to zero (+0.00 to +1.80; mean +3.79, CI +0.81 to +6.82; Wilcoxon p = 0.0006), and only 54.6% improved at all. The +8.3-point rise in the panel median is a shift in the position of the distribution driven by strong gains in its upper part, not the experience of a typical municipality. Third, plan creation is steeply graded by registry size in levels—the smallest quartile reaches a median of 43.3% against 9.9% for the largest—but not in growth: within-municipality change does not differ across size quartiles (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.47; municipality-fixed-effects interactions all p > 0.55). Small municipalities are ahead, not faster, and the gap shows no tendency to close.
The published series is thus misleading twice over: it reports a decline where continuously observed municipalities do not decline, and it invites the inference that composition control would reveal healthy progress, which the panel does not support. We interpret this within an institutional-debt framework: the statistical encoding of an institution (survey composition, question definitions, item discontinuation) drifts away from the institutional reality it is meant to measure, and the divergence is itself measurable—but correcting the encoding does not, here, rescue the institution's performance. The panel, extraction code, and provenance registry are archived for reuse.

articles_hidden.title: The Geography of Green Deficits: Creating a 3-30-300 Measure for all UPRNs in Great Britain
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Singleton; Mark Alan Green; Meilin Shi
articles_hidden.abstract:
The 3-30-300 rule has emerged as an influential benchmark for equitable urban green space provision, specifying that every
home should have visibility of 3 trees, 30% neighbourhood tree canopy cover, and access to public green space within 300
metres. Despite growing international application, there is no GB-wide assessment of how households meet the rule. This
paper presents the first nationally consistent operationalisation of the framework at the highest possible spatial resolution,
calculating indicators for approximately 40 million Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs) using high-resolution
tree mapping, open green space data, and network-based pedestrian routing. We generate the 3-30-300 indicators as contin-
uous measures, enabling assessment under canonical and alternative threshold specifications. Results reveal a substantial
national green deficit: only 0.7% of urban UPRNs satisfy all three thresholds, with the 30% canopy criterion the binding
constraint. The three components decouple both spatially and socio-economically. Tree visibility and canopy cover concen-
trate in affluent southern suburbs and exhibit steep positive deprivation gradients, whereas proximity to formal green space
marginally favours the most deprived urban neighbourhoods, reflecting inherited civic park provision in dense industrial-
era cities. Composite compliance is nine times higher in the least deprived decile than the most deprived, a pattern robust to
threshold relaxation. We argue the framework is best understood as three distinct policy levers rather than a single standard,
and that place-sensitive, component-specific targeting is required to avoid widening the inequalities the rule seeks to ad-
dress.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Whitechapel: A Transnational Forensic Reassessment of the Jack the Ripper Murders
articles_hidden.authors: Tina Jacobs; Alicia V. Donaldson
articles_hidden.abstract: This study presents the transnational Whitechapel linkage hypothesis, an integrated retrospective hypothesis examining whether evidence traditionally treated as unrelated may be better understood within a mobile, cross-jurisdictional offender framework. The analysis brings together the canonical Whitechapel murders of 1888, reported Rotterdam dockside killings and contemporary “Whitechapel-like” comparisons, the 1890 Mary Eleanor Wheeler Pearcey case, the testimony and subsequent archival disappearance of John Charles Pearcey, Mary Pearcey’s unusual final communications preserved in Spanish-language Fabra/Havas dispatches, the later confession attributed to a sailor using the name John Anderson, the South American voyage of the Annie Speer, and the incompletely identified 1895 Iquique death registration of Evaristo Vergara. Rather than treating any single item as dispositive, the theory uses modern forensic-psychological reasoning, behavioral case-linkage principles, temporal and geographic reconstruction, victimology, maritime mobility analysis, forensic linguistics, identity reconstruction, and alternative-hypothesis testing to ask whether the combined pattern is consistent with a mobile offender or offender network operating across port environments. The evidence presently supports a historically plausible and investigatively testable linkage model, but it does not establish a definitive identity for the Whitechapel offender. The contribution of the theory is therefore not a declaration that the case has been solved; it is a structured model explaining why the Rotterdam-London maritime corridor, the Pearcey evidence, the Anderson confession, and the Iquique records warrant examination together rather than in isolation.

articles_hidden.title: Unifying Interpretations of Probability Through Popper’s Propensity View
articles_hidden.authors: Gang Xie
articles_hidden.abstract: Confusion surrounding the foundations of probability often arises from conflating its definition with its methods of estimation or use. Statistical practice tends to mix axiomatic, frequentist, classical, and subjective perspectives without clarifying their philosophical status. This note argues that Karl Popper’s propensity interpretation offers a coherent foundational concept that underlies and unifies these approaches. Interpreting probability as an inherent dispositional property of systems aligns naturally with Kolmogorov’s probability‐space formalism and reframes frequentist long-run frequencies as practical approximations of propensities. Bayesian statistics, understood simply as a mathematical framework for updating probabilities via Bayes’ theorem, can incorporate either frequentist or subjective estimates; subjective probability is therefore not intrinsic to the Bayesian approach, despite common misconceptions. Examples from engineering reliability, scientific experimentation, and classical statistical tests illustrate the intuitive strength of the propensity view. Recognizing propensities as fundamental helps clarify the nature of uncertainty and reduces long-standing interpretive confusion.

articles_hidden.title: Why Workers Use AI Less Often: Reasons for Declining Workplace AI Use in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Marco Lünich
articles_hidden.abstract: This short report summarizes recent findings on the extent and the change in the professional use of artificial intelligence (AI) among workers in Germany. It is based on a quota-based online survey of 2,585 workers, conducted from 29 April 2026 to 11 May 2026. The focus is on how professional AI use has changed over the past three months, what reasons are cited for reduced use, and how an increase or decrease is related to individual and organizational characteristics. The majority report that their use has remained unchanged. Overall, increases predominate, while a decrease affects only a small proportion of the workforce. A decline in usage is associated with a more critical attitude toward AI, lower perceived competence and organizational support, as well as a perceived lack of added value, unreliable results, and data privacy concerns. At the same time, social differences are evident: higher-skilled workers are more likely to increase their usage, while lower-skilled workers are comparatively more likely to reduce it. This raises the question of whether AI reduces or exacerbates existing inequalities in the workplace.

articles_hidden.title: Unionization in Higher Education: An Industry-Level View
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph van der Naald
articles_hidden.abstract: This research note presents estimates of union membership and collective bargaining coverage in the higher education industry using data from the Current Population Survey. The paper analyzes the extent of union membership and collective bargaining coverage from 1983-2025, both in the industry and among faculty specifically, and estimates of the variation in union membership by employment sector, race and gender for 2024. Using a 10-year span of data, the paper also estimates union wage premiums in the industry and among faculty. This note finds union membership and bargaining coverage has remained stable over the past four decades, but documents notable gendered and ethnoracial disparities in both measures in 2024. Faculty and industry collective bargaining results in earnings premiums ranging between 4% and 5%. The findings present quantitative estimates of unionism and its material effects for higher education workers that complement recent research published by the National Center for the Study of Collective Bargaining in Higher Education and the Professions.

articles_hidden.title: HIERARCHICAL METHODOLOGY OF DMYTRO KRIVENKO: THE LIMITS OF DIALECTICS AND LEVELS OF PHYSICAL KNOWLEDGE
articles_hidden.authors: Yaroslav Dmytrovych Kivenko-Emetov
articles_hidden.abstract:
This article reconstructs the philosophical and methodological programme of Dmytro T. Krivenko (1941–1994) as a level-sensitive approach to scientific and philosophical thought. Its historical basis comprises his publications of 1973–1988 on quantitative concepts, informational levels, rational inheritance, and the coarse-graining of complex systems; his 1991 formulation of a “hierarchical model of human cognition”; and manuscripts completed during his lifetime and published posthumously as Prynat i prynatyka (1996).

The article argues that Krivenko did not merely add the notion of levels to a universal dialectical scheme. He distinguished the functions of general-philosophical, logical-methodological, and discipline-specific scientific levels. General philosophy could orient inquiry, but it could not replace measurement, mathematical constructions, models, limiting transitions, or empirical testing. Dialectics thereby ceased to operate as a self-sufficient algorithm of cognition and became one possible heuristic instrument within a broader hierarchical methodology.

Five central elements of this programme are examined: the formation of physical quantities, informational levels, the growth of informativeness, rational inheritance, and coarse-graining. Scientific development is understood neither as the simple accumulation of facts nor as a universal movement through thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. A successor theory selectively preserves confirmed observations, relations, procedures, and limiting results while changing the ontology and structure of explanation. Coarse-graining shows how knowledge may advance through a controlled loss of detail.

The anthropological and political dimension is reconstructed through the concepts of the Prynat and Prynatics. The Prynat is a holistic configuration of three levels of human Nature—the biological, the social or “sociumal,” and the spiritual—together with the individual forms through which they are expressed. All three levels are necessary, but the spiritual has the highest normative status because it integrates biological and social existence with freedom, dignity, and responsibility. Krivenko associates the absolutization of the biological with extreme nationalism and Nazism, the absolutization of the sociumal with communism, and the integrative spiritual level with democracy.

Finally, Krivenko’s programme is compared with contemporary discussions of emergence, effective theories, multilevel ontology, and later applications to quark and exploratory preon models. These comparisons are not retrospective attributions, but tests of his central principle: a deeper description is scientifically meaningful only when it preserves validated knowledge, defines its domain of applicability, constructs explicit transitions between levels, yields independent consequences, and remains open to empirical falsification.

articles_hidden.title: ¿Cómo se trabaja la intervención en masculinidades en las Universidades?
articles_hidden.authors: Camila Stipo Lara; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Rocío Gallardo; Daniela Lillo; Andrea Vera Gajardo; Antonieta Vera; Tamara Vidaurrazaga
articles_hidden.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo presenta resultados intermedios del proyecto Anillo ATE220009 "Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista" (2022-2025), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID) de Chile. A partir de un grupo de discusión realizado en Santiago en 2024 con profesionales —mayoritariamente psicólogos y trabajadores sociales— que coordinan dispositivos de intervención en masculinidades en universidades chilenas, el texto examina quiénes realizan este trabajo y cómo lo hacen, y cómo la demanda institucional tiende a reducir la intervención en masculinidades al problema de la violencia de género, privilegiando un enfoque terapéutico e individual por sobre uno comunitario. Se analiza también cómo esta labor se concentra predominantemente en la atención a estudiantes "funados" y sancionados, respondiendo a una lógica reactiva antes que preventiva, y se documentan las frustraciones de quienes ejercen este rol por la falta de enfoque comunitario, la escasez de espacios de conversación entre varones, y la posición ambigua que ocupan al ser percibidos como "defensores" de los acusados. El cuaderno concluye señalando el lugar de los varones y las masculinidades como uno de los nudos críticos en la institucionalización de la política de género en las universidades chilenas tras la revuelta feminista de 2018.

articles_hidden.title: ¿Cómo se entiende la Educación No Sexista en las universidades?
articles_hidden.authors: Carolina Muñoz; Lelya Troncoso Pérez; Rocío Gallardo; Cecilia Loaiza; Daniela Lillo; Karina Pinto; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Camila Stipo Lara; Tamara Vidaurrazaga
articles_hidden.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo presenta resultados intermedios del proyecto Anillo ATE220009 "Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista" (2022-2025), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID) de Chile, en colaboración con el Núcleo de I+D+i "Diversidad y género: abordajes feministas interseccionales" del Departamento de Trabajo Social de la Universidad de Chile. A partir de entrevistas cualitativas realizadas en 2023 y 2024 a profesionales que trabajan en direcciones o unidades de género en universidades de seis ciudades de las zonas norte, centro y sur del país, el texto examina cómo se reconoce el sexismo en las instituciones de educación superior y qué significados se atribuyen a la educación no sexista (ENS). Se analiza además cómo se operacionaliza la ENS mediante acciones heterogéneas —modelos educativos, manuales, talleres y promoción del lenguaje no sexista— y se identifican las tensiones y resistencias que limitan su avance, incluyendo la falta de obligatoriedad curricular, las resistencias del profesorado y la percepción de la ENS como una demanda radical o inviable. El cuaderno concluye que sexismo y educación no sexista son categorías mutuamente constitutivas, cuya definición se co-produce institucionalmente en un contexto de importantes limitaciones estructurales.

articles_hidden.title: ¿Cómo son las denuncias por acoso sexual, violencia y discriminación de género en las Universidades?
articles_hidden.authors: Sandra Vera Gajardo; Rocío Gallardo; Daniela Lillo; Cecilia Loaiza; Karina Pinto; Camila Stipo Lara; Tamara Vidaurrazaga; Oriana Miranda
articles_hidden.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo describe el recorrido que sigue una denuncia por acoso sexual, violencia o discriminación de género al interior de las instituciones universitarias chilenas, a partir del relato de profesionales que trabajan en unidades de género. El documento aborda las actorías y herramientas institucionales involucradas en las denuncias formales (unidades de género, comisiones técnicas, protocolos, comisiones investigadoras), los desenlaces y efectos de estos procesos en las partes implicadas, la caracterización de los casos recibidos, y las tensiones que surgen entre la jurisdicción interna de las universidades y los organismos judiciales externos. Se cierra con un resumen de los principales problemas identificados en los procesos de denuncia y sanción, entre ellos la duplicidad de procesos, la falta de recursos institucionales y los vacíos en la legislación vigente. Las entrevistas que sustentan este cuaderno fueron realizadas en 2023 y 2024 en universidades de seis ciudades de las zonas norte, centro y sur de Chile. El documento forma parte de la serie Cuadernos de Trabajo Disonantes, resultado del proyecto Anillo Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista (ATE220009), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID).

articles_hidden.title: ¿Cómo son las funas en las Universidades? Descripciones desde las Unidades de Género universitarias
articles_hidden.authors: Rocío Gallardo; Cecilia Loaiza; Karina Pinto; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Oriana Miranda; Camila Stipo Lara; Tamara Vidaurrazaga
articles_hidden.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo describe cómo ocurren las funas en las universidades chilenas, entendidas como acusaciones públicas sobre violencia de género que se producen por canales no formalizados (redes sociales, afiches, páginas web, entre otros). A partir de entrevistas realizadas en 2023 y 2024 a personas que trabajan o coordinan unidades de género en universidades de seis ciudades de las zonas norte, centro y sur del país, el documento organiza los relatos en torno a cuatro ejes: quiénes se implican en las funas y para quiénes tienen efecto, cuándo ocurren, qué posiciones existen frente a ellas, y qué tensiones enfrentan las universidades al abordarlas. Se presentan también los efectos individuales y colectivos identificados por las entrevistadas. El cuaderno forma parte de la serie Cuadernos de Trabajo Disonantes, resultado del proyecto Anillo Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista (ATE220009), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID).

articles_hidden.title: Support and contestation under the radar:  How states promote and undermine the international fight against corruption
articles_hidden.authors: Hortense Jongen; Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller
articles_hidden.abstract: This article investigates hidden forms of support for and contestation of international norms. Existing research largely focuses on publicly visible behavioural forms of contestation, such as member states’ exit from international organizations (IOs). However, less visible practices can also effectively undermine and sabotage international norms, or, conversely, strengthen them. We explore this phenomenon by researching a prominent IO in the global fight against corruption, the Group of States against Corruption (GRECO), by means of interviews with delegates to GRECO and members of the Council of Europe secretariat, complemented with an analysis of policy documents. The empirical evidence reveals five distinct types of hidden contestation and two types of hidden support. Contestation typically originates from the political macro-level rather than from the involved expert community. Member states contest GRECO’s authority through ineffective implementation, delays, obstructive voting, and by negotiating review outcomes. Conversely, peer pressure and peer support emerge as meaningful micro-level practices of norm support that counteract contestation. This study’s insights advance research on contestation and support of international norms and inform research, theory, and practice on how to strengthen the global fight against corruption.

articles_hidden.title: Coding choices and short-sequence artefacts undermine claims of a conventional Palaeolithic sign system – a comment on Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Koplenig
articles_hidden.abstract: In this comment, I show that methodological and statistical flaws undermine the central conclusions of Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026).

articles_hidden.title: Educating Physicians in Clinical Healthy Longevity Medicine: A Comprehensive Training Framework from an Academic Hospital
articles_hidden.authors: Evelyne Bischof; Sara Bonnes; Dominika Wilczok; Abigail Goshen; Chaim Haber; Tzipi Strauss
articles_hidden.abstract: Healthy longevity medicine is expanding rapidly, yet no standardized, hospital-based pathways exist for training physicians. This paper presents the first validated training framework within a dedicated hospital department. The model uniquely spans all stages of medical formation and integrates key elements of healthy longevity medicine into routine clinical workflows. It demonstrates how longevity training can be formally incorporated into approved specialty pathways while remaining fully embedded within curative medicine.

articles_hidden.title: A Healthier Start Abroad? The health at birth of the children of migrants and of those born at origin
articles_hidden.authors: Alessandro Ferrara; Marco Cozzani
articles_hidden.abstract: The health of migrants is mostly studied in relation to destination-country natives, Origin-country comparisons are rarely pursued, even though they provide a more convincing counterfactual, allowing us to (a) measure “health gains” from migration, (b) disentangle mechanisms including selectivity, cultural factors and contextual change, (c) elucidate the relationship between migration and global health inequality. We address this gap by comparing the health at birth of children born in Spain to migrant parents from 15 origin countries with that of children born in those same origin countries, using Spanish vital statistics linked to Demographic and Health Surveys and other origin-country sources. We find that, for most groups, the children of migrants are healthier at birth (measured via low birth weight) than children in their parents' origin countries. This is also true among groups disadvantaged relative to Spanish natives, and is more pronounced for non-Western and, especially, Asian-origin groups. We find limited support for cultural explanations and stronger support for both migrant selectivity and improved contextual conditions at destination. Though the latter two are not fully separable, our evidence favors the effect of the change in contextual conditions. These results suggest migration can function as an equalizing force, narrowing birthplace-based health inequalities.

articles_hidden.title: When Resources Are Scarce: Formal Mentoring as a Compensatory Resource for Sustainable Performance Expectations
articles_hidden.authors: Andreea Nicolau; Ad Kleingeld
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory, this study conceptualizes formal mentoring as a resource system and examines how mentoring functions, job resources and demands, self-empowerment, and organizational support relate to mentoring program effectiveness and sustainable performance expectations. Using cross-sectional self-report data from 71 participants in a formal peer mentoring program, we found that perceived program effectiveness was positively associated with sustainable performance expectations, defined as participants’ beliefs about their ability to sustain performance and well-being over time. Mentoring functions were positively related to program effectiveness and, indirectly, to sustainable performance expectations via perceived mentoring effectiveness. In addition, job cognitive resources, self-empowerment, and organizational support moderated the relationship between mentoring functions and program effectiveness, such that mentoring functions were most strongly associated with perceived effectiveness when these resources were lower. These findings suggest that mentoring functions may operate as compensatory resources in resource-constrained contexts. Employment status was also relevant, with full-time employed participants reporting higher program effectiveness than solopreneurs. Overall, the findings extend JD-R theory by positioning mentoring not only as a developmental intervention but also as a resource that supports sustainable human performance.
